======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Poverty in the United States
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use American English|date=April 2019}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2017}}
[[File:Poverty in the U.S. by county.png|thumb|upright=2|<div style="text-align: center">
Proportion of Americans living below the poverty line in each county of the fifty states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico according to the 2016–2020 American Community Survey</div>]]
[[File:1960- Poverty rates (US).svg |thumb |upright=1.8 |After a decline in the 1960s, poverty rates remained in a relatively stable range in subsequent decades.<ref>Table 3 from {{cite web |last1=Bijou |first1=Christina |last2=Shrider |first2=Emily A. |title=Poverty in the United States: 2025 |url=https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2026/demo/p60-290.html |website=census.gov |publisher=United States Census Burean |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260916183418/https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/p60/290/table_3_opm_hist.xlsx |archive-date=16 September 2026 |date=September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
In the United States, [[poverty]] has both social and political implications. Based on [[Measuring poverty|poverty measures]] used by the Census Bureau (which exclude non-cash factors such as food stamps or medical care or public housing), 35.9 million people, or 10.6 percent of the population, were in poverty in 2024. The rate fell 0.4 percentage points from 2023.<ref>{{cite report |title=Poverty in the United States: 2024 |url=https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2025/demo/p60-287.html |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau|U.S. Census Bureau]] |date=September 9, 2025 |page=1 |access-date=August 27, 2026}}</ref> Some of the many causes include income, inequality,{{update inline|date=September 2023}}<ref>Adams, R. H., (2004). Economic growth, inequality, and poverty: Estimating the growth elasticity of poverty, World Development 32(12), p. 1989-2014.</ref> inflation, unemployment, debt traps and poor education.{{update inline|date=September 2023}}<ref name="Western, B. 2010">Western, B. & Pettit, B., (2010). [https://www.jstor.org/stable/20749838#metadata_info_tab_contents Incarceration and social inequality.] Daedalus, 139(3), 8-19</ref> The majority of adults living in poverty are employed and have at least a high school education.<ref name="Brady"/>  Although the US is a relatively wealthy country by international standards,<ref>{{cite book |last=Zweig |first=Michael |year=2004 |title=What's Class Got to do With It? : Society in the U.S.A. in the Twenty-first Century |publisher=ILR Press |isbn=978-0-8014-8899-3 }}</ref> it has a persistently high poverty rate compared to other developed countries due in part to a less generous welfare system.<ref name="Brady">{{cite journal |last1=Brady |first1=David |title=Poverty, not the poor |journal=Science Advances |date=25 August 2023 |volume=9 |issue=34 |article-number=eadg1469 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adg1469 |language=en |issn=2375-2548|doi-access=free |pmid=37611106 |pmc=10446494 |bibcode=2023SciA....9G1469B }}</ref>

Efforts to alleviate poverty include [[New Deal]]-era legislation during the [[Great Depression]], to the national [[War on Poverty]] in the 1960s and poverty alleviation efforts during the 2008 [[Great Recession]]. The federal government has two departments which measure poverty.  Under the [[Department of Commerce]], the [[Census Bureau]] has been reporting the Official Poverty Measure (OPM) since the 1960s, while the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] defines income levels for which people are eligible for governmental anti-poverty assistance.  The OPM includes cash assistance from programs like [[Supplemental Security Income]] and [[Temporary Assistance to Needy Families]] (welfare) as part of someone's income when reporting on how many people are in poverty.  Since 2011 the Census Bureau has also been reporting a newer Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM), which includes non-cash anti-poverty government assistance like [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program]] (food stamps) and [[Medicaid]] (health care for the poor), and also accounts for regional differences in the [[cost of living]].<ref name="census.gov">{{cite web| url=https://www.census.gov/topics/income-poverty/supplemental-poverty-measure/about.html | title=About the Supplemental Poverty Measure | access-date=2023-08-29 }}</ref>{{ r | CRS_SPM }}  The SPM is considered a more comprehensive estimate of poverty.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Matthews |first=Dylan |date=2023-03-10 |title=Why even brilliant scholars misunderstand poverty in America |url=https://www.vox.com/future-perfect/2023/3/10/23632910/poverty-official-supplemental-relative-absolute-measure-desmond |access-date=2023-07-22 |website=Vox |language=en}}</ref>

For 2021, the percentage of Americans in poverty per the SPM was 7.8%, and per the OPM was 11.6%.<ref name=2021_OPM_&_SPM >{{ cite web | url=https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2022/demo/p60-277.html | title=Poverty in the United States: 2021 | last= | first= | work=Census Bureau | date=2022-09-13 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Rank|first=Mark Robert |author-link=Mark Robert Rank|date=2023 |title=The Poverty Paradox: Understanding Economic Hardship Amid American Prosperity|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hGewEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA15|location= |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|page=15 |isbn= 978-0190212636}}</ref> By the OPM, the [[poverty threshold]] for 2021 for a single person was $13,800, and for a family of four was $27,700.{{ r | 2021_OPM_&_SPM }} In 2020, the [[World Bank]] reported that 0.25% of Americans lived below the international definition of [[extreme poverty]], which is living on less than $2.15 per day in 2017 [[Purchasing Power Parity]] dollars.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fact Sheet: An Adjustment to Global Poverty Lines |url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/factsheet/2022/05/02/fact-sheet-an-adjustment-to-global-poverty-lines#:~:text=The%20new%20international%20poverty%20line,be%20living%20in%20extreme%20poverty. |access-date=April 27, 2023 |website=[[World Bank]] }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Country Profile: United States |url=https://pip.worldbank.org/country-profiles/USA |access-date=April 27, 2023 |website=[[World Bank]] }}</ref> The SPM increased by 4.6% in 2022 to 12.4%, due to the ending of pandemic stimulus payments and tax credits,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2023/income-poverty-health-insurance-coverage.html|title=Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2022|author=<!--Not stated--> |date=September 12, 2023 |website=census.gov |publisher= |access-date=September 15, 2023 |quote=The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) rate in 2022 was 12.4%, an increase of 4.6 percentage points from 2021. This increase can be attributed to key changes in federal tax policy, including the expiration of temporary expansions to the Child Tax Credit (CTC) and the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) as well as the end of pandemic-era stimulus payments. This is the first increase in the overall SPM poverty rate since 2010. }}</ref><ref name="CBSpoverty">{{cite news |last=Picchi |first=Aimee |date=September 12, 2023 |title=America's poverty rate soared last year. Children were among the worst hit.|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/poverty-rate-census-income/|work=CBS News |location= |access-date=September 15, 2023}}</ref> with around 15.3 million Americans falling into poverty over this time period according to the [[Center on Budget and Policy Priorities]].<ref name="CBSpoverty"/>

The 2020 assessment by the U.S. Census Bureau showed the percentage of Americans living in poverty for 2019 (before the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]) had fallen to some of the lowest levels ever recorded due to the record-long period of economic growth.<ref name="NPR_2020-09-15" /> However, between May and October 2020, some eight million people were put into poverty due to the [[Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic]] and the ending of funds from the [[CARES Act]].<ref name=":5" />

==History ==
{{Main|History of poverty in the United  States}}

=== Progressive era 1890s-1920s===
[[File:WAGEMAP1.pdf|alt=|thumb|Neighborhoods in Chicago color-coded by income, published in ''Hull House Maps and Papers.'']]
Catalyzed by [[Henry George]]'s 1873 book ''[[Progress and Poverty]],'' public interest in how poverty could arise even in a time of economic progress arose in the 19th century with the rise of the Progressive movement. The Progressive American social survey began with the publication of ''Hull House Maps and Papers'' in 1895. This study included essays and maps collected by [[Florence Kelley]] and her colleagues working at [[Hull House]] and staff of the [[United States Bureau of Labor]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://florencekelley.northwestern.edu/historical/hullhouse/|title=Hull House Maps and Papers|website=florencekelley.northwestern.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref> It focused on studying the conditions of the slums in Chicago, including four maps color-coded by nationality and income level, which were based on [[Charles Booth (social reformer)|Charles Booth]]'s earlier pioneering work, ''[[Life and Labour of the People in London]].''<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TgAln9ENyKAC|title=Poverty Knowledge: Social Science, Social Policy, and the Poor in Twentieth-Century U.S. History|last=O'Connor|first=Alice|date=2001|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-10255-9|language=en}}</ref>

Another social reformer, [[Jacob Riis]], documented the living conditions of New York tenements and slums in his 1890 work ''[[How the Other Half Lives]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://socialwelfare.library.vcu.edu/people/riis-jacob/|title=Riis, Jacob|date=2011-01-10|website=Social Welfare History Project|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref>

=== Great Depression ===
A group especially vulnerable to poverty consisted of poor [[sharecroppers]] and tenant farmers in the South. These farmers consisted of around a fourth of the South's population, and over a third of these people were African Americans.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://socialwelfare.library.vcu.edu/eras/great-depression/american-social-policy-in-the-great-depression-and-wwii/|title=Great Depression: American Social Policy|date=2011-01-20|website=Social Welfare History Project|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref> Historian James T. Patterson refers to these people as the "old poverty," as opposed to the "new poverty" that emerged after the onset of the [[Great Depression]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2b3ZesIFQ0oC|title=America's Struggle against Poverty in the Twentieth Century|last=PATTERSON|first=James T.|date=2009-06-30|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-04194-3|language=en}}</ref>

During the Depression, the government did not provide any [[unemployment Insurance|unemployment insurance]], so people who lost jobs easily became impoverished.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://depts.washington.edu/depress/economics_poverty.shtml|title=Economics & Poverty|website=depts.washington.edu|access-date=2019-12-10}}</ref> People who lost their jobs or homes lived in [[Shanty town|shantytowns]] or [[Hooverville]]s. Many [[New Deal]] programs were designed to increase employment and reduce poverty. The [[Federal Emergency Relief Administration]] specifically focused on creating jobs for alleviating poverty. Jobs were more expensive than direct cash payments (called "the dole"), but were psychologically more beneficial to the unemployed, who wanted any sort of job for morale.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://content.lib.washington.edu/feraweb/index.html|title=::: Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA) Photographs of King County, 1933-1935 :::|website=content.lib.washington.edu|access-date=2019-12-10}}</ref> Other New Deal initiatives that aimed at job creation and wellbeing included the [[Civilian Conservation Corps]] and [[Public Works Administration]]. Additionally, the institution of [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] was one of the largest factors that helped to reduce poverty.<ref name="Washington post">[https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/govbeat/wp/2013/11/08/poverty-in-13-states-is-worse-than-we-thought/?tid=article_nextstory Poverty in 13 states is worse than we thought] Washington Post November 8, 2013</ref>

=== War on Poverty ===
{{Main|War on Poverty}}
A number of factors helped start the national [[War on Poverty]] in the 1960s. In 1962, [[Michael Harrington]]'s book ''[[The Other America]]'' helped increase public debate and awareness of the poverty issue. The War on Poverty embraced expanding the federal government's roles in education and health care as poverty reduction strategies, and many of its programs were administered by the newly established [[Office of Economic Opportunity]]. The War on Poverty coincided with more methodological and precise statistical versions of studying poverty; the "official" U.S. statistical measure of poverty was only adopted in 1969.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fas.org/sgp/crs/misc/RL33069.pdf|title=Poverty in the United States: 2013|last=Gabe|first=Thomas|date=January 29, 2015|website=Congressional Research Service}}</ref>

=== 21st century ===
[[File:Poor People's Campaign Moral Monday (08.02.21- DC) 0504fIMG 3526 (51354888176).jpg|thumb|Rally Poor Peoples Campaign Washington DC]]
In the 21st century, the [[Great Recession in the United States|Great Recession]] helped to raise the poverty levels again. {{As of |2009}}, the number of people who were in poverty was approaching 1960s levels that led to the national war on poverty.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2010/sep/11/us-poverty-track-post-record-gain-2009/ |title=US poverty on track to post record gain in 2009 |publisher=Associated Press |date=April 13, 2009 |access-date=May 20, 2013}}</ref> The 2010 census data shows that half the population qualifies as poor or low income,<ref>[https://www.cbsnews.com/news/census-data-half-of-us-poor-or-low-income/ Census data: Half of U.S. poor or low income]. ''[[CBS News]],'' December 15, 2011. Retrieved February 10, 2014.</ref> with one in five [[millennials]] living in poverty.<ref>Jana Kasperkevic (December 26, 2014). [https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-money-blog/2014/dec/26/us-census-bureau-report-one-in-five-millennials-poverty One in five millennials lives in poverty, report finds]. ''[[The Guardian]].'' Retrieved December 26, 2014.</ref> Academic contributors to ''The Routledge Handbook of Poverty in the United States'' postulate that new and extreme forms of poverty have emerged in the U.S. as a result of [[neoliberal]] structural adjustment policies and [[globalization]], which have rendered economically marginalized communities as destitute "surplus populations" in need of control and punishment.<ref name="RoutHandB">{{Cite book|title=The Routledge Handbook of Poverty in the United States|publisher=[[Routledge]]|year=2015|isbn=978-0-41-567344-0|editor-last=Haymes|editor-first=Stephen N.|location=London and New York|pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=qnHfBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA2 2-4], [https://books.google.com/books?id=qnHfBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA346 346]|editor-last2=de Haymes|editor-first2=María V.|editor-last3=Miller|editor-first3=Reuben J.|url=https://www.routledge.com/The-Routledge-Handbook-of-Poverty-in-the-United-States/Haymes-Vidal-de-Haymes-Miller/p/book/9780415673440}}</ref>

Many international bodies have emphasized the issues of poverty that the United States faces. A 2013 [[UNICEF]] report ranked the U.S. as having the second-highest relative child poverty rates in the developed world.<ref>Fisher, Max (April 15, 2013). [https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/worldviews/wp/2013/04/15/map-how-35-countries-compare-on-child-poverty-the-u-s-is-ranked-34th/ Map: How 35 countries compare on child poverty (the U.S. is ranked 34th)]. ''[[The Washington Post]].'' Retrieved February 16, 2014. See also: [http://www.unicef-irc.org/publications/pdf/rc11_eng.pdf Child well-being in rich countries: A comparative overview]. ''[[UNICEF]] office of Research.'' p. 7.</ref> {{As of |2016 |6}}, the [[International Monetary Fund|IMF]] warned the United States that its high poverty rate needs to be tackled urgently by raising the minimum wage and offering paid maternity leave to women to encourage them to enter the labor force.<ref>[https://www.bbc.com/news/business-36599316 IMF warns the US over high poverty]. BBC, June 22, 2016.</ref> In December 2017, the United Nations special rapporteur on [[extreme poverty]] and human rights, [[Philip Alston]], undertook a two-week investigation on the effects of systemic poverty in the United States, and sharply condemned "private wealth and public squalor," declaring the state of [[Alabama]] to have the "worst poverty in the developed world."<ref name="Alston">{{cite web|url=http://www.ohchr.org/EN/NewsEvents/Pages/DisplayNews.aspx?NewsID=22533&LangID=E|title=Statement on Visit to the USA, by Professor Philip Alston, United Nations Special Rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights|last=Alston|first=Philp|author-link=Philip Alston|date=December 15, 2017|publisher=[[Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights|OHCHR]]|access-date=December 24, 2017}}</ref> Alston's report was issued in May 2018 and highlights that 40 million people live in poverty and over five million live "in '[[developing country|Third World]]' conditions."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2018/06/contempt-poor-us-drives-cruel-policies-says-un-expert|title="Contempt for the poor in US drives cruel policies," says UN expert|date=June 4, 2018|work=OHCHR|access-date=June 5, 2018}}</ref>

According to a 2020 assessment by the U.S. Census Bureau, the percentage of Americans living in poverty for 2019 (before the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]) had fallen to some of lowest levels ever recorded due to the record-long economic growth period and stood at 11.1% (adjusted for smaller response during the pandemic).<ref name=NPR_2020-09-15 >{{ cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/09/15/913131697/american-incomes-were-rising-until-the-pandemic-hit | title=American Incomes Were Rising, Until The Pandemic Hit | last=Horsley | first=Scott | newspaper=[[NPR]] | date=2020-09-16 | access-date=2020-09-16 | quote=Were it not for those survey problems, the Census Bureau estimates, median household income would have risen just 3.8% and the poverty rate would have registered as 11.1%. }}</ref> However, between May and October 2020, the [[Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic|economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic]], and the exhaustion of the funding provided by the [[CARES Act]], dragged some eight million people into poverty.<ref name=":5">{{citation |title=8 Million Have Slipped Into Poverty Since May as Federal Aid Has Dried Up |author=Jason DeParle |date= October 15, 2020 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/15/us/politics/federal-aid-poverty-levels.html |work=[[The New York Times]] }}</ref>
According to OECD, nearly 23 percent of American workers work in low-wage jobs, compared with 17 percent in Britain, 11 percent in Japan and 5 percent in Italy.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Desmond |first1=Matthew |title=Why Poverty Persists in America |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/03/09/magazine/poverty-by-america-matthew-desmond.html |agency=New York Times |date=2023}}</ref> In January 2021, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, 11.6 percent of the US population, or 37.9 million people, were living in poverty(using as an example a family of three earning less than $21,559).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=David |title=The Poverty Paradox: why is there still so much economic hardship in the US? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2023/may/10/poverty-paradox-new-book-mark-rank-us-economic-hardship |agency=The Guardian |date=2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Lee|first=Juhohn |date=March 7, 2023 |title=37.9 million Americans are living in poverty, according to the U.S. Census. But the problem could be far worse.|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/07/why-poverty-might-be-far-worse-in-the-us-than-its-reported.html|work=[[CNBC]] |location= |access-date=May 10, 2023}}</ref> In his 2023 book ''[[Poverty, by America]]'', sociologist [[Matthew Desmond]] writes that the poverty rate in the United States has not improved in half a century, with 11% of the population living in poverty in 2019, compared to 12% in 1970.<ref>{{cite news |last=Nova |first=Annie |date=March 28, 2023 |title=5 alarming stats on U.S. economic inequality in Pulitzer Prize-winning author's new book|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/28/5-alarming-stats-on-us-economic-inequality.html|work=[[CNBC]] |location= |access-date=May 10, 2023}}</ref>

Social scientist [[Mark Robert Rank]] writes in 2023 that the last four decades has seen a retrenchment of the social safety net, with a reduction in eligibility and amount of benefits transferred. This, along with the failure of the US to provide universal child care, [[Health insurance in the United States|medical insurance]] and other social benefits as done in peer countries, has resulted in the US having much higher poverty rates by comparison.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rank|first=Mark Robert |author-link=Mark Robert Rank|date=2023|title=The Poverty Paradox: Understanding Economic Hardship Amid American Prosperity|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hGewEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA116|location= |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|pages=116–117 |isbn= 978-0190212636}}</ref>

The U.S. poverty rate fell to a record low of 10.2% in 2025, affecting 34.5 million people. This marked the second straight year of decline, alongside a rise in median household income to $87,460. A family with two adults and two kids was considered in poverty if earning less than $32,649. The child poverty rate dropped to 13.4%. However, 26.7 million people lacked health insurance during the year.<ref>{{cite web |title=US poverty rate dips to lowest on record, Census Bureau says |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us-poverty-rate-102-2025-census-bureau-says-2026-09-15/ |website=reuters |access-date=15 September 2026}}</ref>

==Measuring poverty== <!-- This section is linked to from [[Diamondhead, Mississippi]] -->
There are several measures used by the U.S. federal government to measure poverty. The [[United States Census Bureau|Census Bureau]] issues the [[Poverty thresholds (United States Census Bureau)|poverty thresholds]], which are generally used for statistical purposes<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/hhes/www/poverty/about/overview/measure.html|title=How the Census Bureau Measures Poverty|website=census.gov|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100711082047/http://www.census.gov/hhes/www/poverty/about/overview/measure.html|archive-date=July 11, 2010|access-date=September 16, 2015|df=mdy-all}}</ref>—for example, to estimate the number of people in poverty nationwide each year and classify them by type of residence, race, and other social, economic, and demographic characteristics. The [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|Department of Health and Human Services]] issues the poverty guidelines for administrative purposes—for instance, to determine whether a person or family is eligible for assistance through various federal programs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aspe.hhs.gov/2015-poverty-guidelines|title=2015 POVERTY GUIDELINES|website=hhs.gov|publisher=[[United States Department of Health and Human Services]]|access-date=September 3, 2015}}</ref> Both the poverty thresholds and poverty guidelines are updated yearly.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|title=Poverty thresholds and poverty guidelines|url=https://www.irp.wisc.edu/publications/focus/pdfs/foc192.pdf|journal=Focus|publisher=University of Wisconsin–Madison Institute for Research on Poverty|volume=19|issue=2|pages=6}}</ref> More recently, the Census Bureau has begun using the Supplemental Poverty Measure as an additional statistic to measure poverty and supplement the existing measures.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) and Children: How and Why the SPM and Official Poverty Estimates Differ |url=https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v75n3/v75n3p55.html#:~:text=In%202011,%20the%20Census%20Bureau,improved%20statistical%20picture%20of%20poverty. |access-date=2023-09-13 |website=Social Security Administration Research, Statistics, and Policy Analysis |language=en}}</ref>

===Poverty income thresholds===
The poverty income thresholds originate from work done by [[Mollie Orshansky]], an American economist working for the [[Social Security Administration]]. Orshansky introduced the poverty thresholds in a 1963 ''Social Security Bulletin'' article, "Children of the Poor."<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last=Orshansky|first=Mollie|title=Children of the Poor|url=https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v26n7/v26n7p3.pdf|journal=Social Security Bulletin|volume=July 1963}}</ref>
[[File:20111110-OC-AMW-0012 - Flickr - USDAgov.jpg|thumb|The "Basic Seven", a food plan developed by the [[United States Department of Agriculture]].]]
Orshansky based her thresholds on work she had done with the [[economy food plan]] while at the [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]]. According to the USDA's 1955 Household Food Consumption Survey, families of three or more people spent one-third of their after-tax income on food. For these families, poverty thresholds were set at three times the cost of the economy food plan. Different procedures were used for calculating poverty thresholds for two-person households and persons living alone.<ref name=":7" />

Her work appeared at an opportune moment, as [[Lyndon B. Johnson|President Johnson]] declared the War on Poverty just six months later—and Orshansky's work offered a numerical way to measure progress in this effort.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v68n3/v68n3p79.html|title=Remembering Mollie Orshansky—The Developer of the Poverty Thresholds|website=Social Security Administration Research, Statistics, and Policy Analysis|language=en|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref> The newly formed [[United States Office of Economic Opportunity|Office of Economic Opportunity]] (OEO) adopted the Orshansky poverty thresholds for statistical, planning, and budgetary purposes in May 1965.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://aspe.hhs.gov/topics/poverty-economic-mobility/poverty-guidelines/further-resources-poverty-measurement-poverty-lines-their-history/history-poverty-thresholds|title=History of Poverty Thresholds|date=2015-11-23|website=ASPE|language=en|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref> Officials at the OEO were enthusiastic; as research director Joseph Kershaw remarked, "Mollie Orshansky says that when you have more people in the family, you need more money. Isn't that sensible?"<ref name=":3" />

Officials at the Social Security Administration began to plan on how to adjust poverty thresholds for changes in the standard of living. The [[Bureau of the Budget]] resisted these changes, but formed an interagency committee that, in 1969, decided that poverty thresholds would be adjusted for inflation by being tied to the [[Consumer Price Index]], rather than changes in the standard of living. In August 1969, the Bureau of the Budget designated these revised thresholds as the federal government's official definition of poverty.<ref name=":4" />

Apart from minor changes in 1981 that changed the number of thresholds from 124 to 48,<ref name=":4" /> poverty thresholds have remained static for the past fifty years despite criticism that the thresholds may not be completely accurate. Although the poverty thresholds assumes that the average household of three spends one-third of its budget on food, more recent surveys have shown that that number has decreased to one-fifth in the 1980s and one-sixth by the 1990s.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hLtK0Tlcit4C|title=Keeping Women and Children Last Revised|last=Sidel|first=Ruth|date=1998-11-01|publisher=Penguin|isbn=978-1-101-52281-3|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VM-ONqqwvFUC|title=The Forgotten Americans|last1=Schwarz|first1=John E.|last2=Volgy|first2=Thomas J.|date=1993|publisher=W. W. Norton & Company|isbn=978-0-393-31074-0|language=en}}</ref> If the poverty thresholds were recalculated based on the share of household budgets taken by food costs as of 2008, the economy food budget multiplier would have been 7.8 rather than 3, greatly increasing the thresholds by a factor of 2.6.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.brookings.edu/testimonies/why-the-united-states-needs-an-improved-measure-of-poverty/|title=Why the United States Needs an Improved Measure of Poverty|last=Blank|first=Rebecca M.|date=July 17, 2008|work=Brookings|access-date=2018-08-31|language=en-US}}</ref>

====Poverty income guidelines====

The poverty guidelines are a version of the poverty thresholds used by federal agencies for administrative purposes, such as determining eligibility for federal assistance programs. They are useful because poverty thresholds for one calendar year are not published until the summer of the next calendar year; poverty guidelines, on the other hand, allow agencies to work with more timely data.<ref name=":2" />

Poverty guidelines were issued by the OEO starting in December 1965. After the [[Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981]], responsibility for issuing the guidelines was transferred to the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|Department of Health and Human Services]].<ref name=":3" /> Poverty guidelines are also referred to as the "federal poverty level" (FPL), but the HHS discourages that term as ambiguous.<ref name=":1" />

=== Supplemental Poverty Measure ===
In 1990, a Congressional committee requested the [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] (NRC) to conduct a study on revising the poverty measure.<ref name=":4" /> The NRC convened a panel, which published a 1995 report ''Measuring Poverty: A New Approach'' that concluded that the official poverty measure in the United States is flawed; while being used to assess eligibility for anti-poverty programs, it fails to account for certain aid programs that may already be in place. It falls short by taking monetary income before taxes or tax credits, and it ignores any non-cash benefits received.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shrider 1, Creamer 2 |first=Emily 1, John 2 |date=September 2023 |title=Poverty in the United States: 2022 |url=https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2023/demo/p60-280.pdf |access-date=February 5, 2026 |website=Census.gov}}</ref>

Furthermore, the aforementioned panel noted that the thresholds are the same irrespective of geography and stated that due to "rising living standards in the United States, most approaches for developing poverty thresholds (including the original one) would produce higher thresholds today than the current ones."<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.census.gov/library/publications/1995/demo/citro-01.html|title=Measuring Poverty: A New Approach C. Citro and R. Michaels (Eds.)|last1=Citro|first1=Constance|last2=Michaels|first2=Robert|publisher=United States Census Bureau|year=1995|pages=3|chapter=Summary and Recommendations|chapter-url=https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/1995/demo/sum.pdf}}</ref>

Additionally, the report suggested an alternative measure of poverty, which uses actual expenditure data to develop a threshold value for a family of four—and then update this threshold every year and according to geographic location. This alternative measure of poverty would also change the income calculation for a family, including certain non-cash benefits that satisfied "basic needs" such as food stamps and public housing while excluding "non-basic needs" such as medical costs and child care.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/950511/poverty.shtml|title=Poverty definition flawed, more accurate measure needed|website=chronicle.uchicago.edu|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref>

The work of the panel led to the development of the Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM), which was intended to address some of the weaknesses of the existing poverty guidelines. In October 2014, the Census Bureau released a report describing the SPM and stated its intention to publish SPM measures every year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2014/demo/p60-251.pdf|title=The Supplemental Poverty Measure: 2013|last=Short|first=Kathleen|date=2015-03-10|website=census.gov|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150310022700/https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2014/demo/p60-251.pdf|archive-date=2015-03-10|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref> However, SPM is intended to "supplement" the existing poverty thresholds, not "replace" them, as poverty thresholds will remain the "official" Census Bureau measure and poverty guidelines will be derived only from the "official" poverty measures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fas.org/sgp/crs/misc/RL33069.pdf|title=Poverty in the United States: 2013|last=Gabe|first=Thomas|date=2015-01-29|website=Congressional Research Service}}</ref>

Unlike the poverty thresholds, and in line with the NRC recommendations, the SPM both includes certain non-cash benefits in a family's income and adjusts thresholds for differences in housing costs by geographic area. Additionally, the SPM thresholds are based on how much a "reference" family with two children spends on food, clothing, shelter, and utilities (FCSU).

===Criticism===

There is controversy over how accurate American poverty estimates are, with two sides debating over whether the official measures understate or overstate poverty.

====Understating poverty====
Many sociologists and government officials have argued that poverty in the United States is understated, meaning that there are more households living in actual poverty than there are households below the poverty threshold.<ref name="Dealing with Diversity">{{cite book|title=Dealing with Diversity|last=Adams|first=J.Q.|author2=Pearlie Strother-Adams|publisher=Kendall/Hunt Publishing Company|year=2001|isbn=978-0-7872-8145-8|location=Chicago, IL}}</ref>  A study taken in 2012 estimated that roughly 38% of Americans live "paycheck to paycheck."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://consumerfed.org/press_release/many-families-struggle-to-make-ends-meet-but-those-with-a-financial-plan-feel-and-do-better/|title=Many Families Struggle to Make Ends Meet, But Those With a Financial Plan Feel and Do Better · Consumer Federation of America|website=Consumer Federation of America|date=July 23, 2012 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-11}}</ref>

In 1969, the Bureau of Labor Statistics put forward suggested budgets for adequate family living. 60% of working-class Americans lived below the "intermediate" budget, which allowed for the following:<blockquote>It assumes, for example, that the family will own:

:A toaster that will last for 33 years.
:A vacuum cleaner that will last 14 years.
:The budget assumes that a family will buy a two-year-old car and keep it for four years...
Finally, the budget allows nothing whatever for savings.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TXdWbwEPIO0C|title=America in Our Time: From World War II to Nixon--what Happened and why|last=Hodgson|first=Godfrey|date=2005|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-12288-5|pages=482|language=en}}</ref></blockquote>Given that the "intermediate" budget was fairly modest, observers questioned whether poverty levels were really capturing the full extent of prosperity, challenging the long-established view that most Americans had attained an affluent standard of living in the two decades following the end of the Second World War.<ref>{{cite journal|date=2010-10-20|title=That Seventies Show|url=https://www.thenation.com/article/155492/seventies-show?page=full|journal=The Nation}}</ref>

[[File:TWO YOUTHS IN UPTOWN, CHICAGO, ILLINOIS, A NEIGHBORHOOD OF POOR WHITE SOUTHERNERS. THE INNER CITY TODAY IS AN... - NARA - 555950.jpg|thumb|A neighborhood of [[Poor White|poor white people]], [[Chicago]], 1974]]
There have also been criticism of the methodology used to develop the U.S. poverty thresholds in the first place. The poverty thresholds used by the US government were originally developed during the [[Lyndon B. Johnson#Presidency (1963–1969)|Johnson administration's]] [[War on Poverty]] initiative in the early 1960s.<ref name="GFisher">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/hhes/povmeas/publications/orshansky.html#N_20_|title=The Development of the Orshansky Poverty Thresholds and Their Subsequent History as the Official U.S. Poverty Measure|last=Fisher|first=Gordon M.|work=Poverty – Experimental Measures|publisher=U.S. Census Bureau|access-date=January 11, 2012}}</ref><ref name="GFisher 2">{{cite journal|url=http://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v68n3/v68n3p79.html|title=Remembering Mollie Orshansky – The Developer of the Poverty Thresholds|last=Fisher|first=Gordon M.|journal=Social Security Bulletin|year=2008|volume=68|issue=3|pages=79–83|publisher=U.S. Social Security Administration Office of Retirement and Disability Policy|pmid=19260619|access-date=January 11, 2012}}</ref> The thresholds were based on the cost of a food basket at the time, multiplied by three, under the assumption that the average family spent one-third of its income on food.

However, the poverty line only takes into account food purchases that were common more than 50 years ago. It assumes that Americans spend one third of their income on food; in fact, Americans typically spent less than one tenth of their after-tax income on food in 2000.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Clauson|first=Annette|date=September 2000|title=Despite Higher Food Prices, Percent of U.S. Income Spent on Food Remains Constant|url=http://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2008-september/despite-higher-food-prices,-percent-of-us-income-spent-on-food-remains-constant.aspx|journal=Amber Waves (U.S. Department of Agriculture Economic Research Service)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160711050434/https://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2008-september/despite-higher-food-prices,-percent-of-us-income-spent-on-food-remains-constant.aspx|archive-date=2016-07-11}}</ref> For many families, the costs of housing, [[health insurance in the United States|health insurance]] and [[Healthcare in the United States|medical care]], transportation, and access to basic telecommunications take a much larger bite out of the family's income than a half century ago, yet none of these costs are considered in determining the official poverty thresholds.
According to John Schwarz, a political scientist at the University of Arizona:<blockquote>The official poverty line today is essentially what it takes in today's dollars, adjusted for inflation, to purchase the same poverty-line level of living that was appropriate to a half century ago, in 1955 .... Updated thereafter only for inflation, the poverty line lost all connection over time with current consumption patterns of the average family. Quite a few families then didn't have their own private telephone, or a car, or even a mixer in their kitchen... The official poverty line has thus been allowed to fall substantially below a socially decent minimum, even though its intention was to measure such a minimum.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=leoHWY-cfOIC|title=Freedom Reclaimed: Rediscovering the American Vision|last=Schwarz|first=John E.|date=2005-01-02|publisher=JHU Press|isbn=978-0-8018-7981-4|pages=50|language=en}}</ref></blockquote>
[[File:Seeking human kindness.JPG|thumb|upright|Homeless man in [[Boston]]]]
The issue of understating poverty is especially pressing in states with both a [[Real estate pricing|high cost of living]] and a high poverty rate such as California where the [[Real estate pricing|median home price]] in 2006 was $564,430.<ref name="California median home price">{{cite web|url=https://biz.yahoo.com/bw/060627/20060627005927.html?.v=1|title=California median home price|access-date=July 6, 2006}}{{dead link|date=June 2016|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> In the [[Monterey County, California#Home prices|Monterey area]], where the low-pay industry of agriculture is the largest sector in the economy and the majority of the population lacks a college education, the median home price was $723,790, requiring an [[Household income in the United States|upper middle class income]] only earned by roughly 20% of all households in the county.<ref name="California median home price" /><ref name="Monterey County income distribution">{{cite web|url=http://factfinder.census.gov/servlet/QTTable?_bm=y&-geo_id=05000US06053&-qr_name=DEC_2000_SF3_U_QTP32&-ds_name=D&-_lang=en|title=Monterey County income distribution|access-date=July 6, 2006|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200212041813/http://factfinder.census.gov/servlet/QTTable?_bm=y&-geo_id=05000US06053&-qr_name=DEC_2000_SF3_U_QTP32&-ds_name=D&-_lang=en|archive-date=February 12, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref> Such fluctuations in local markets are, however, not considered in the federal poverty threshold and may leave many who live in poverty-like conditions out of the total number of households classified as poor.

The [[Supplemental Poverty Measure]], introduced in 2011, aims at providing a more accurate picture of the true extent of poverty in the United States by taking account of non-cash benefits and geographic variations.<ref name="SPM2016">{{cite web|url=https://census.gov/library/publications/2016/demo/p60-258.html|title=The Supplemental Poverty Measure: 2015|author1=Renwick, Trudi|author2=Fox, Liana|date=September 13, 2016|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|quote=Number and Percentage of People in Poverty by State Using 3-Year Average Over 2013, 2014, and 2015}}</ref> According to this new measure, 16% of Americans lived in poverty in 2011, compared with the official figure of 15.2%. With the new measure, one study estimated that nearly half of all Americans lived within 200% of the federal poverty line.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.epi.org/publication/poverty-measure-highlights-dire-circumstances/|title=New poverty measure highlights positive effect of government assistance|last1=Cooper|first1=David|last2=Elise|first2=Gould|date=2011-11-17|website=Epi.org|access-date=14 October 2017}}</ref>

According to American economist [[Sandy Darity, Jr.]], "There is no exact way of measuring poverty. The measures are contingent on how we conceive of and define poverty. Efforts to develop more refined measures have been dominated by researchers who intentionally want to provide estimates that reduce the magnitude of poverty."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://today.duke.edu/2011/11/povertytip|title=News Tip: Census Bureau's New Measure of Poverty Misses the Mark, Say Duke Experts|website=Today.duke.edu|date=November 7, 2011 |access-date=14 October 2017}}</ref>

[[Matthew Desmond]] writes that the "overwhelming majority" of prisoners and former prisoners of the US prison system are extremely poor, and this group is largely omitted from poverty statistics and national surveys, "which means there are millions more poor Americans than official statistics let on."<ref>{{cite book |last=Desmond|first=Matthew |author-link=Matthew Desmond|date=2023 |title=[[Poverty, by America]]|url= |location= |publisher=Crown Publishing Group|pages=22–23 |isbn=9780593239919}}</ref>

====Overstating poverty====
[[File:BLACK YOUTHS PLAY BASKETBALL AT STATEWAY GARDENS' HIGHRISE HOUSING PROJECT ON CHICAGO'S SOUTH SIDE. THE COMPLEX HAS... - NARA - 556162.jpg|thumb|Youth play in Chicago's [[Stateway Gardens]] high-rise housing project in 1973.]]

According to ''[[Vox (website)|Vox]]'', there is a "near-unanimous consensus among poverty researchers that the official poverty measure (OPM) in the United States is a disaster" primarily because of its failure to include all anti-poverty government benefits as income when calculating whether or not an individual is poor.<ref name=":6" />{{better source needed|date=September 2023}}  The OPM includes governmental anti-poverty cash aid like [[Supplemental Security Income]] and [[Temporary Assistance to Needy Families|Welfare]] but does not include non-cash aid like [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|Food stamps]], [[Section 8 (housing)|housing assistance]], and [[Medicaid]] (health care for the poor).<ref name=":6" />{{ r | CRS_SPM }}  Since 2011, the [[Census Bureau]] has started publishing the [[Supplemental Poverty Measure]] (SPM),<ref name="census.gov"/><ref name=CRS_SPM>{{cite web | url=https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R45031 | title=The Supplemental Poverty Measure: Its Core Concepts, Development, and Use | date=2022-07-19 | work=[[Congressional Research Service]] | quote=Under the official poverty measure, an individual is counted as poor if his or her family’s pre-tax money income falls below the poverty threshold. Pre-tax money income excludes the value of government noncash benefits provided either privately or publicly, such as health insurance, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, or housing assistance. It also does not consider taxes paid to federal, state, or local governments, or tax benefits (such as the Earned Income Tax Credit, EITC) that might be received by families. }}</ref> which factors some non-cash benefits into the calculation, along with regional differences in cost of living.<ref name=":6" />

Burkhauser et al. find that accounting for cash income, taxes, and major in-kind transfers and updating poverty thresholds for inflation show that a Full-income Poverty Rate based on President Johnson's standards fell from 19.5 percent to 2.3 percent over the 1963–2017 period.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nber.org/papers/w26532#fromrss|title=Evaluating the Success of President Johnson's war on poverty: Revisiting the Historical Record Using a Full-Income Poverty Measure|author1=Richard V. Burkhauser|author2=Kevin Corinth|date=December 2019|publisher=The National Bureau of Economic Research|access-date=December 9, 2019|author3=James Elwell|author4=Jeff Larrimore|series=Working Paper Series |doi=10.3386/w26532|s2cid=226931919|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Geography ==

The highest poverty rates in the United States are in the [[Territories of the United States|U.S. territories]] ([[American Samoa]], [[Guam]], the [[Northern Mariana Islands]], [[Puerto Rico]] and the [[U.S. Virgin Islands]]).<ref name="Territories_poverty">http://www.gao.gov/new.items/d10240r.pdf ''Poverty Determination In U.S. Insular Areas.'' Making a Visible Difference In American Samoa (Final Report). Retrieved August 30, 2019.</ref> In 2010, American Samoa had a per capita income of $6,311.<ref>American FactFinder - American Samoa. QuickFacts - Puerto Rico. Retrieved July 4, 2020.</ref>{{refn|group=note|The [[Northern Mariana Islands]] had a median household income of $19,958 in the 2010 U.S. Census,<ref>American FactFinder. ==Poverty and demographics using Census OPM ==
===Poverty and family status===

Among married couple families: 5.8% lived in poverty.<ref name="pov02">U.S. Census Bureau. Current Population Survey. ''Persons in Families by Family Structure, Age, and Sex, Iterated by Income-to-Poverty Ratio and Race: 2007: [http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new02_100_01.htm Below 100% of Poverty – All Races] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080930073740/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new02_100_01.htm|date=September 30, 2008}}.''</ref> This number varied by race and ethnicity as follows:

* 5.4% of all white persons (which includes white [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanics]]),<ref name="white2007">U.S. Census Bureau. Current Population Survey. ''People in Families by Family Structure, Age, and Sex, Iterated by Income-to-Poverty Ratio and Race: 2007: [http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new02_100_03.htm Below 100% of Poverty – White Alone] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090413154644/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new02_100_03.htm |date=April 13, 2009 }}.''</ref>
* 10.7% of all [[African Americans|black]] persons (which includes black Hispanics),<ref name="pubdb3.census.gov">{{cite web |url=http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new03_100_06.htm |title=Poverty 3-Part 100_06 |publisher=Pubdb3.census.gov |date=August 26, 2008 |access-date=September 16, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612124530/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new03_100_06.htm |archive-date=June 12, 2011 |df=mdy-all }}</ref>
* 14.9% of all Hispanic persons (of any race)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new02_100_09.htm |title=Poverty 2-Part 100_09 |publisher=Pubdb3.census.gov |date=August 26, 2008 |access-date=September 16, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100108025218/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new02_100_09.htm |archive-date=January 8, 2010 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> living in poverty.

Among single-parent (male or female) families: 26.6% lived in poverty.<ref name="pov02" /> This number varied by race and ethnicity as follows:

* 22.5% of all white persons (which includes white Hispanics),<ref name="white2007" />
* 44.0% of all black persons (which includes black Hispanics),<ref name="pubdb3.census.gov" />
* 33.4% of all Hispanic persons (of any race)<ref name="pubdb3.census" /> living in poverty.

Among individuals living alone: 19.1% lived in poverty.<ref name="pov02" /> This number varied by race and ethnicity as follows:

* 18% of white persons (which includes white Hispanics),<ref name="pubdb3.census_a">{{cite web |url=http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new01_100_03.htm |title=Poverty 1-Part 100_03 |publisher=Pubdb3.census.gov |date=August 26, 2008 |access-date=September 16, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100108025213/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new01_100_03.htm |archive-date=January 8, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* 28.9% of black persons (which includes black Hispanics)<ref name="pubdb3.census">{{cite web |url=http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new01_100_06.htm |title=Poverty 1-Part 100_06 |publisher=Pubdb3.census.gov |date=August 26, 2008 |access-date=September 16, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612134907/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new01_100_06.htm |archive-date=June 12, 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* 27% of Hispanic persons (of any race)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new01_100_09.htm |title=Poverty 1-Part 100_09 |publisher=Pubdb3.census.gov |date=August 26, 2008 |access-date=September 16, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612124554/http://pubdb3.census.gov/macro/032008/pov/new01_100_09.htm |archive-date=June 12, 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> are living in poverty.

===Poverty and race/ethnicity===
[[File:Poverty Rates by Sex and Work Status for Americans 65+ in 2006.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Poverty rates by sex and work status for Americans aged 65 and over]]The US Census declared that in 2014, 14.8% of the general population lived in poverty:<ref name="pov10">"[https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2015/demo/p60-252.pdf Income and Poverty in the United States: 2014]". U.S. Census Bureau</ref>

As of 2010 about half of those living in poverty are non-Hispanic white (19.6 million).<ref name="pov10" /> Non-Hispanic white children comprised 57% of all poor rural children.<ref>"[http://www.prb.org/Articles/2009/ruralchildpoverty.aspx Poverty Is a Persistent Reality for Many Rural Children in U.S.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100326135510/http://www.prb.org/Articles/2009/ruralchildpoverty.aspx |date=March 26, 2010 }}", William O'Hare (September 2009), Population Reference Bureau.</ref>

In FY 2009, African American families comprised 33.3% of [[Temporary Assistance for Needy Families|TANF]] families, non-Hispanic white families comprised 31.2%, and 28.8% were Hispanic.<ref>"[http://www.acf.hhs.gov/programs/ofa/character/fy2009/indexfy09.htm Characteristics and Financial Circumstances of TANF Recipients – Fiscal Year 2009] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120720124435/http://www.acf.hhs.gov/programs/ofa/character/fy2009/indexfy09.htm |date=July 20, 2012 }}". United States Department of Health and Human Services.</ref>

In 2023, 11.1% of the population lived in poverty, a total of 36.8 million people.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poverty in the United States: 2023 |url=https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2024/demo/p60-283.html |access-date=2025-10-21 |website=Census.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In 2009, the Census Bureau created the [[Supplemental Poverty Measure]] to measure for things left out by traditional poverty measures; according to the Official Congress website, it measures "having insufficient financial resources to achieve a specified standard of living.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Supplemental Poverty Measure: Its Core Concepts, Development, and Use |url=https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45031 |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> The SPM expands "this definition [of poverty] by including income and payroll taxes, tax credits and other noncash benefits like the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (SNAP) and housing subsidies. Necessary expenses such as child support paid, work and child care and medical expenses are deducted from SPM resources,"<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poverty Measure That Includes Noncash Government Assistance Increased to 12.9% in 2023, Up From 12.4% in 2022 |url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/09/supplemental-poverty-measure.html |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=Census.gov |language=en}}</ref>

The SPM in 2022 sat at 12.9% which has risen from 12.4% in 2022 and continues to be above pre-pandemic rates of 11.8%<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poverty Measure That Includes Noncash Government Assistance Increased to 12.9% in 2023, Up From 12.4% in 2022 |url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/09/supplemental-poverty-measure.html |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=Census.gov |language=en}}</ref>

===Poverty among Native Americans===
{{Main|Reservation poverty}}
Poverty remains high on Native American reservations. 7 of the 11 poorest counties, including the 2 poorest in the 50 states, encompass [[Lakota people|Lakota Sioux]] reservations in South Dakota.<ref>Statistics derived from U.S. Census Bureau data; U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Economic Analysis, Survey of Current Business; and DataQuick Information Systems, a public records database company located in La Jolla, San Diego, CA.</ref> This fact has been cited by some critics as a mechanism that enables the "kidnapping" of Lakota children by the state of South Dakota's Department of Social Services. The Lakota People's Law Project,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lakotalaw.org/|title=Lakota People's Law Project|website=Lakotalaw.org|access-date=14 October 2017}}</ref> among other critics, allege that South Dakota "inappropriately equates economic poverty with neglect&nbsp;... South Dakota's rate of identifying "neglect" is 18% higher than the national average... In 2010, the national average of state discernment of neglect, as a percent of total maltreatment of foster children prior to their being taken into custody by the state, was 78.3%. In South Dakota the rate was 95.8%."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.docs.lakotalaw.org/ICWA-Coalition_Report-to-Congress.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2014-01-17 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201105251/http://www.docs.lakotalaw.org/ICWA-Coalition_Report-to-Congress.pdf |archive-date=February 1, 2014 |df=mdy-all }}</ref>

Poverty in the [[Pine Ridge Indian Reservation|Pine Ridge Reservation]] in particular has had unprecedented effects on its residents' longevity. "Recent reports state the average life expectancy is 45 years old while others state that it is 48 years old for men and 52 years old for women. With either set of figures, that's the shortest life expectancy for any community in the Western Hemisphere outside Haiti."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.4aihf.org/id40.html|title=Pine Ridge Statistics|website=4aihf.org|access-date=October 14, 2017}}</ref>

In the 2013—2017 [[American Community Survey]], [[Wounded Knee, South Dakota]] (located in the [[Pine Ridge Indian Reservation]]) had the [[List of lowest-income places in the United States|7th-lowest median household income]] out of all places in the 50 states/D.C./Puerto Rico.<ref name="census2017">https://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=ACS_17_5YR_S1901&prodType=table {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20200214060615/https://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=ACS_17_5YR_S1901&prodType=table |date=February 14, 2020 }} U.S. Census Bureau. American FactFinder. Income in the past 12 months (in 2017 inflation-adjusted dollars). 2013-2017 American Community Survey 5-year estimates. ["Geography" set to "All Places within United States and Puerto Rico".] Retrieved August 30, 2019.</ref>

===Poverty among African Americans===
In 2019, the government's official poverty rate overall was 10.5% and for Blacks it was 18.8%, the historic low.  African Americans are over-represented in the poverty population: they represented 13.2% of the total population in the country, but 23.8% of the poverty population.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2020/09/poverty-rates-for-blacks-and-hispanics-reached-historic-lows-in-2019.html|title=Poverty Rates for Blacks and Hispanics Reached Historic Lows in 2019 | last=Creamer | first=John | work=[[United States Census Bureau]] | date=2020-09-15 }}</ref>

After COVID-19, the official poverty rates of African Americans has fluctuated from 17.1% in 2022, a record low, to 18.4% in 2024.<ref name="Editor">{{Cite web |date=2025-10-06 |title=The Racial Gap in Poverty Rates in the United States Is Expanding |url=https://jbhe.com/2025/10/the-racial-gap-in-poverty-rates-in-the-united-states-is-expanding/ |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education |language=en-US}}</ref> This translates to over 8 million recorded African Americans with incomes below the poverty line. The SPM has also seen a modest increase from 2022 to 2024, likely due to certain protections from COVID-19 being lifted.<ref name="Editor"/>

Burkhauser and Corinth (2026) used a wider range of data to make new estimates of poverty trends since 1939.  Their data shows that their poverty rate among Black families fell from 84% in 1939 to 51% in 1963 and 6% in 2023.<ref>Richard V. Burkhauser, and Kevin Corinth, "Poverty and Dependency in the United States, 1939–2023"  ''NBER Working Paper 34759'' (Jan. 2026) DOI 10.3386/w34759 p. 14;  summarized in  "Free Exchange: Bureaucrats v bootstraps," ''The Economist'' (Feb 2, 2026) p. 74.</ref>

=== Poverty and LGBTQ+ status ===
With data collected from 35 states from 2014-2017, the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) survey shows that 21.6% of the LGBTQ+ population is living in poverty. The number varies depending on identity:

* 12.1% of gay men
* 17.9% of lesbian women
* 19.5% of bisexual men
* 29.4% of bisexual women
* 33.7% of transgender men
* 29.6% of transgender women, and
* 23.8% of gender nonconforming people.

For comparison, 13.4% of straight men and 17.8% of straight women are living in poverty.<ref>{{Cite web |last=thisisloyal.com |first=Loyal {{!}} |title=LGBT Poverty in the United States |url=https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/lgbt-poverty-us/ |access-date=2022-10-10 |website=Williams Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

Updated data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System reported that the rate rose to 23% in 2020.<ref name="thisisloyal.com">{{Cite web |last=thisisloyal.com |first=Loyal {{!}} |title=LGBT Poverty in the United States |url=https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/lgbt-poverty-us/ |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=Williams Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> This updated data shows that poverty rates dropped for all genders and sexualities in 2021 except for lesbian women.<ref name="thisisloyal.com"/> The updates numbers, as of 2021 are as follows:

* 19.9% of bisexual women
* 17.5% of lesbian women
* 12.9% of bisexual men
* 10.3% of gay men
* The updated report includes 'transgender people' instead of a breakdown within there which sits at 21.2%

The rates for straight men living in poverty is 9.4% and straight women is 13.6%[https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/LGBT-Poverty-COVID-Feb-2023.pdf]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Bianca |last2=Bouton |first2=Lauren |last3=Badgett |first3=M.V. Lee |last4=Macklin |first4=Moriah |date=February 2023 |title=LGBT POVERTY IN THE UNITED STATES Trends at the Onset of COVID-19 |url=https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/LGBT-Poverty-COVID-Feb-2023.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=December 10, 2025}}</ref>

==== Transgender poverty ====
The rate of poverty for the transgender community is larger than any other LGBTQ+ population. The 2015 U.S. Transgender Survey shows that this percentage varies depending on racial and ethnic identity:

* 43% Hispanic or Latino
* 41% Native American or American Indian
* 38% Black or African American
* 34% Middle Eastern
* 32% Asian
* 24% White
* 40% Multiracial

The percentage of those living in poverty also increases for transgender people with HIV (51%) and disabilities (45%).<ref>{{Cite web |title=2015 U.S. Transgender Survey Report |url=https://www.ustranssurvey.org/reports |access-date=2022-10-23 |website=2022 U.S. Trans Survey |language=en-US}}</ref>

The percentage of transgender respondents to the USTS in 2022 living in poverty was 34% but did not provide a racial breakdown of these rates.<ref>{{Cite web |last=James |first=Sandy |last2=Herman Rankin Mara Keisling Lisa Mottet Ma’ayan Anaf |first2=Jody |last3=Rankin |first3=Susan |last4=Keisling |first4=Mara |last5=Mottet |first5=Lisa |last6=Anaf |first6=Ma’ayan |date=December 2016 |title=2015 U.S. Transgender Survey |url=https://transequality.org/sites/default/files/docs/usts/USTS-Full-Report-Dec17.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=US Trans Survey |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Poverty and age ===
[[File:Poverty Rates by Age 1959 to 2011. United States..PNG|thumb|upright=1.8|Poverty Rates by Age 1959 to 2015. United States.]]

As of 2010, the US Census declared that 15.1% of the general population of the United States lived in poverty:

* 22% of all people under the age of 18
* 13.7% of those between the ages of 19-21
* 9% of all people either 65 or older<ref name="pov10" />

The [[Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]] (OECD) uses a different measure for poverty and declared in 2008 that child poverty in the US is 20% and poverty among the elderly is 23%.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oecd.org/dataoecd/47/2/41528678.pdf|title=OECD (2008), Growing Unequal? : Income Distribution and Poverty in OECD Countries : COUNTRY NOTE: UNITED STATES|website=Oecd.org|access-date=14 October 2017}}</ref> [[File:Homeless children in US 2006-10.png|thumb|[[Homeless children in the United States]].<ref>Bassuk, E.L., ''et al.'' (2011) [http://www.homelesschildrenamerica.org/media/NCFH_AmericaOutcast2010_web.pdf ''America's Youngest Outcasts: 2010''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160322192547/http://www.homelesschildrenamerica.org/media/NCFH_AmericaOutcast2010_web.pdf |date=March 22, 2016 }} (Needham, MA: The National Center on Family Homelessness) page 20</ref> The number of homeless children reached record highs in 2011,<ref>[https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Society/2011/1213/Homeless-children-at-record-high-in-US.-Can-the-trend-be-reversed "Homeless children at record high in US. Can the trend be reversed?"] ''Christian Science Monitor'', December 13, 2011</ref> 2012,<ref name="coalition4homeless">[https://www.coalitionforthehomeless.org/pages/state-of-the-homeless-2012 "State of the Homeless 2012"] ''Coalition for the Homeless'', June 8, 2012</ref> and 2013<ref>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/600-homeless-children-in-dc-and-no-one-seems-to-care/2013/02/08/a728a0ea-722b-11e2-8b8d-e0b59a1b8e2a_story.html "600 homeless children in D.C., and no one seems to care"]  ''Washington Post'', February 8, 2013</ref> at about three times their number in 1983.<ref name="coalition4homeless" />]]

====Child poverty====
{{Main|Child poverty in the United States}}

In May 2009, the [[non-profit]] advocacy group [[Feeding America]] released a study based on 2005–2007 data from the [[United States Census Bureau|U.S. Census Bureau]] and the [[United States Department of Agriculture|Agriculture Department]], which claims that 3.5 million children under the age of 5 are at risk of hunger in the United States. The study claims that in 11 states, Louisiana, which has the highest rate, followed by North Carolina, Ohio, Kentucky, Texas, New Mexico, Kansas, South Carolina, Tennessee, Idaho and Arkansas, more than 20 percent of children under 5 are allegedly at risk of going hungry. (receiving fewer than 1,800 calories per day).<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2009/05/07/health/main4998190.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090510090215/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2009/05/07/health/main4998190.shtml|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 10, 2009|title=3.5M Kids Under 5 On Verge Of Going Hungry <br />Study: 11 Percent Of U.S. Households Lack Food For Healthy Lifestyle|date=May 7, 2009|work=Health|access-date=May 8, 2009|publisher=CBS NEWS|format="SHTML}}</ref>

In 2012, 16.1 million American children were living in poverty. Outside of the 49 million Americans living in food-insecure homes, 15.9 million of them were children.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://feedingamerica.org/hunger-in-america/hunger-facts/hunger-and-poverty-statistics.aspx|title=Hunger and Poverty Facts and Statistics|website=Feeding America}}</ref> In 2013, [[child poverty]] reached record high levels in the U.S., with 16.7 million [[Hunger in the United States#Children|children living in food insecure households]].<ref name="WalkerBBC" /> Many of the neighborhoods these children live in lack basic produce and nutritious food. 47 million Americans depend on [[food bank]]s, more than 30% above 2007 levels. Households headed by [[single mother]]s are most likely to be affected. 30 percent of low-income single mothers cannot afford diapers.<ref name="thenation.com">{{cite journal|url=https://www.thenation.com/article/176121/poverty-2013-when-even-diapers-are-luxury#|title=Poverty in 2013: When Even Diapers Are a Luxury|journal=The Nation|date=2013-09-11}}</ref> Inability to afford this necessity can cause a chain reaction, including mental, health, and behavioral problems. Some women are forced to make use of one or two diapers, using them more than once. This causes rashes and sanitation problems as well as health problems. Without diapers, children are unable to enter into daycare. The lack of childcare can be detrimental to single mothers, hindering their ability to obtain employment.<ref name="thenation.com" />  Worst affected are Oregon, Arizona, New Mexico, Florida, and the District of Columbia, while North Dakota, New Hampshire, Virginia, Minnesota and Massachusetts are the least affected.<ref name="WalkerBBC">{{cite news|last=Walker|first=Duncan|title=The children going hungry in America|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/magazine-21636723|access-date=March 13, 2013|newspaper=BBC News|date=March 6, 2013}}</ref> 31 million low-income children received free or reduced-price meals daily through the National School lunch program during the 2012 federal fiscal year. Nearly 14 million children are estimated to be served by Feeding America with over 3 million being of the ages of 5 and under.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://feedingamerica.org/hunger-in-america/hunger-facts/child-hunger-facts.aspx|title=Child Hunger Facts|website=Feeding America}}</ref>

A 2014 report by the National Center on Family Homelessness states the number of [[Homeless children in the United States|homeless children in the U.S.]] has reached record levels, calculating that 2.5 million children, or one child in every 30, experienced homelessness in 2013. High levels of poverty, lack of affordable housing and domestic violence were cited as the primary causes.<ref>David Crary and Lisa Leff (November 17, 2014). [http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_HOMELESS_CHILDREN?SITE=AP&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT&CTIME=2014-11-17-00-37-34 New Report: Child Homelessness on the Rise in US]. ''[[The Associated Press]].'' Retrieved November 17, 2014.</ref> A 2017 peer-reviewed study published in ''[[Health Affairs]]'' found that the U.S. has the highest levels of child mortality among 20 OECD countries.<ref>{{cite news |last= Howard|first=Jacqueline|date=January 8, 2018|title=Among 20 wealthy nations, US child mortality ranks worst, study finds|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/01/08/health/child-mortality-rates-by-country-study-intl/index.html|work=CNN|access-date= January 11, 2018}}</ref>

[[Racial inequality in the United States|Racial inequality]] is also visible when it comes to discerning poverty among children in America. In 2021, [[Children's Defense Fund]] estimated that 71% of children living in poverty are children of color.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Dawson|first=Ben|title=The State of America's Children 2021 - Child Poverty|url=https://www.childrensdefense.org/state-of-americas-children/soac-2021-child-poverty/|access-date=2022-01-04|website=Children's Defense Fund|language=en-US}}</ref>

Poverty is also associated with expanded adverse childhood experiences, such as witnessing violence, feeling discrimination, and experiencing bullying.<ref>Cronholm PF, Forke CM, Wade R, Bair-Merritt MH, Davis M, Harkins-Schwarz M, Pachter LM, Fein JA. [https://txicfw.socialwork.utexas.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/Philly-ACES-revised_2015-1.pdf Adverse Childhood Experiences: Expanding the concept of adversity]. American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 2015 Sep;49(3):354-61</ref> According to a 2016 study by the [[Urban Institute]], teenagers in low income communities are often forced to join gangs, save school lunches, sell drugs or exchange sexual favors because they cannot afford food.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/sep/12/teens-america-hunger-food-poverty US teens often forced to trade sex work for food, study finds]. ''[[The Guardian]]''. September 12, 2016.</ref>

According to the [[Save the Children]] fund, food insecurity among families with children as increased by two-thirds since March 2020. The fund further states that "the U.S. continues to lag behind most peer countries in meeting the needs of children and families during the pandemic".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.savethechildren.org/us/charity-stories/child-hunger-in-america |title=Child Hunger in America |last= |first= |date= February 23, 2021|website=[[Save the Children]] |publisher= |access-date=May 31, 2022 |quote=}}</ref>

Children living in poverty may also experience many health and developmental problems due to food insecurity and malnutrition. Children in low socioeconomic statuses are shown to have more gray matter which affects educational and life outcomes.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.acap.2016.02.010 |title=Child Poverty in the United States Today: Introduction and Executive Summary |year=2016 |last1=Dreyer |first1=Benard |last2=Chung |first2=Paul J. |last3=Szilagyi |first3=Peter |last4=Wong |first4=Shale |journal=Academic Pediatrics |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=S1–S5 |pmid=27044686 |doi-access=free }}</ref> They may have a lower immune systems due to malnutrition, and they are more likely to have chronic disease like asthma.<ref>{{cite book |isbn=0-8261-7330-6|title=Malnourished Children in the United States: Caught in the Cycle of Poverty |last1=Karp |first1=Robert J. |year=1993 |publisher=Springer }}</ref>

Child poverty more than doubled from 5.2% in 2021 to 12.4% in 2022 largely as the result of pandemic aid running out, in particular the expansion of the [[Child tax credit (United States)#American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|child tax credit]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Schneider |first=Mike |date=September 12, 2023 |title=Child poverty in the US jumped and income declined in 2022 as coronavirus pandemic benefits ended|url=https://apnews.com/article/poverty-income-health-insurance-census-623f928ddcceca2bc5e69948929d266c|work= [[Associated Press]]|location= |access-date=September 13, 2023}}</ref>

== Poverty and disability ==
[[Disability in the United States|Disabled people in the United States]] are twice as likely to live in poverty due to persistent discrimination, structural and institutional barriers to economic security, and employment disparities.<ref name="American Psychological Association">{{cite web |title=Disability and Socioeconomic Status |url=https://www.apa.org/pi/ses/resources/publications/disability |website=APA.org |publisher=American Psychological Association |access-date=23 February 2024}}</ref> In 2019, 21.6 percent of disabled people were considered poor under the Census’s Supplemental Poverty Measure.<ref name="American Psychological Association"/> People with disabilities experience income disparities in the form of a wage gap that heavily contributes to the increased risk of poverty. In 2020, workers with disabilities (ages 18–64) were paid, on average, 74 cents for every dollar paid to their non-disabled peers.<ref name="American Psychological Association"/> People with disabilities face additional challenges including an added cost of living, a lack of affordable and accessible transportation and housing, and a lack of access to affordable support and services that contribute to their increased risk of experiencing poverty. Income disparities, employment challenges, and additional barriers can cause difficulties in affording rent, as 4 in 10 disabled people in the United States are struggling to afford their rent.<ref name="American Psychological Association"/> Additionally, people with disabilities are three times more likely to not have enough to eat and are almost twice as likely to be unable to pay monthly bills.<ref name="American Psychological Association"/>
