}}Several surveys of West Virginians' religious affiliation have been made in recent years, including in 2008 by the American Religion Identity Survey,<ref>{{cite web |title=ARIS 2008 Summary Report—ARIS |url=http://commons.trincoll.edu/aris/publications/aris-2008-summary-report/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120613231230/http://commons.trincoll.edu/aris/publications/aris-2008-summary-report/ |archive-date=June 13, 2012 |website=trincoll.edu}}</ref> and in 2010 by the Pew Forum on Religion and Public Life.<ref>{{cite web |date=May 11, 2015 |title=Religious Landscape Study |url=http://religions.pewforum.org/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150214011626/http://religions.pewforum.org/ |archive-date=February 14, 2015 |website=pewforum.org}}</ref> The Pew survey results admit to a 6.5% margin of error, while the ARIS survey says "estimates are subject to larger sampling errors in states with small populations." A characteristic of religion in Appalachian communities is the abundance of independent, non-affiliated churches, which "remain unnoted and uncounted in any census of church life in the United States". This sometimes leads to the belief that these communities are "unchurched".<ref>[http://utpress.org/Appalachia/EntryDisplay.php?EntryID=013 ''Old-Time Religion''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130117094726/http://utpress.org/Appalachia/EntryDisplay.php?EntryID=013|date=January 17, 2013}}, Encyclopedia of Appalachia</ref>

The largest denomination as of 2010, according to [[Association of Religion Data Archives]], was the [[United Methodist Church]] with 136,000 members in 1,200 congregations. The second-largest Protestant church was the [[American Baptist Churches USA]], with 88,000 members and 381 congregations. The [[Southern Baptist Convention|Southern Baptist]] church had 44,000 members and 232 congregations. The [[Churches of Christ]] had 22,000 members and 287 congregations. The [[Presbyterian Church (USA)]] had 200 congregations and 20,000 members.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Association of Religion Data Archives—Maps & Reports |url=http://www.thearda.com/rcms2010/r/s/54/rcms2010_54_state_adh_2010.asp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217051349/http://www.thearda.com/rcms2010/r/s/54/rcms2010_54_state_adh_2010.asp |archive-date=December 17, 2013 |website=thearda.com}}</ref> By the 2020 ARDA study, non-denominational Protestantism became the largest Christian group, with 152,518 adherents.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 Congregational Membership |url=https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/census/congregational-membership?y=2020&y2=0&t=1&c=54 |access-date=April 15, 2023 |website=www.thearda.com}}</ref>

A 2015 survey by the [[Pew Research Center]] found that West Virginia was the seventh-most "highly religious" state in the nation.<ref>{{cite web |date=February 29, 2016 |title=How religious is your state? |url=http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2016/02/29/how-religious-is-your-state/?state=alabama |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160308115627/http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2016/02/29/how-religious-is-your-state/?state=alabama |archive-date=March 8, 2016 |website=pewresearch.org}}</ref> A 2020 survey by the [[Public Religion Research Institute]] found that 69% of the adult population was Christian, reflecting a slight decrease since the Pew Research Center's 2015 survey.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 PRRI Religious Study |url=https://ava.prri.org/#religious/2020/States/religion/m/US-WV |access-date=September 17, 2022 |website=ava.prri.org}}</ref> In 2020, a survey of nearly 1,900 West Virginians reported that 78.6% were Christian and 16.2% were unaffiliated.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sheitle |first1=Christopher P. |last2=Corcoran |first2=Katie E. |last3=Remsburg |first3=Taylor |date=February 25, 2021 |title=Religion in West Virginia, West Virginia Social Survey Report |url=https://survey.wvu.edu/files/d/8e050570-2a9b-4d24-a8dc-a800e1afe362/religion-report-accessible-version.pdf |access-date=September 21, 2022 |website=wvu.edu |publisher=West Virginia University}}</ref> In 2022, the Public Religion Research Institute estimated 67% of the state was Christian (53% Protestant, 11% Catholic, 2% Jehovah's Witness, and 1% Mormon), 28% unaffiliated, 3% [[New Age]], and 2% [[Buddhism in the United States|Buddhist]].

==Economy==
{{Main|Economy of West Virginia}}

{{See also|List of West Virginia counties by socioeconomic factors|West Virginia locations by per capita income}}

According to the U.S. [[Bureau of Economic Analysis]], in 2025, West Virginia's gross domestic product was $109.276 billion and its per capita personal income was $57,932.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SASUMMARY State annual summary statistics: personal income, GDP, consumer spending, price indexes, and employment |url=https://apps.bea.gov/itable/?ReqID=70&step=1&_gl=1*15mngjn*_ga*MTMwNTU5NTYxMC4xNzc2ODY1NjY1*_ga_J4698JNNFT*czE3NzY5ODgzNTAkbzUkZzEkdDE3NzY5ODg1NTckajQ4JGwwJGgw# |access-date=April 25, 2026 |website=U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis}}</ref> As of May 2025, the state's unemployment rate was 3.8%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=staff |first=CNBC com |date=2025-07-10 |title=40. West Virginia |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/10/west-virginia-top-states-for-business-ranking.html |access-date=2026-01-16 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref>

While per capita income fell 2.6% nationally in 2009, West Virginia's grew at 1.8%.<ref name=WVC>[http://www.wvcommerce.org/news/story/West_Virginia_improves_per_capita_ranking/1150/default.aspx "West Virginia improves per capita ranking"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101117211338/http://www.wvcommerce.org/news/story/West_Virginia_improves_per_capita_ranking/1150/default.aspx |date=November 17, 2010}}, Catherine Zacchi. West Virginia Department of Commerce. 2010. Accessed December 11, 2010</ref> Through the first half of 2010, exports from West Virginia topped $3&nbsp;billion, growing 39.5% over the same period from the previous year and ahead of the national average by 15.7%.<ref name=WVC />

''[[Forbes]]'' ranked [[Morgantown, West Virginia|Morgantown]] as the 10th-best small city in the nation to conduct business in 2010. The city is also home to [[West Virginia University]], the 95th-best public university, according to ''U.S. News & World Report'' in 2011.<ref>[http://colleges.usnews.rankingsandreviews.com/best-colleges/national-top-public "Best Colleges 2011"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090826121616/http://colleges.usnews.rankingsandreviews.com/best-colleges/national-top-public |date=August 26, 2009}}, ''U.S. News & World Report''. 2010. Accessed December 11, 2001</ref> The proportion of West Virginia's adult population with a [[bachelor's degree]] is the lowest in the U.S., at 17.3%.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.census.gov/statab/ranks/rank19.html | title=State Rankings-Statistical Abstract of the United States-Persons 25 Years Old and Over With a Bachelor's Degree or More, 2004 | publisher=Census.gov | date=January 7, 2009 | access-date=July 31, 2010 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101018014743/http://www.census.gov/statab/ranks/rank19.html | archive-date=October 18, 2010}}</ref>

The net corporate income tax rate is 6.5% while business costs are 13% below the national average.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021 |title=West Virginia Net Corporate Income Tax |url=https://tax.wv.gov/Documents/TaxForms/2021/cit120.instructions.pdf |url-status=live |website=Tax.wv.gov |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230215175747/https://tax.wv.gov/Documents/TaxForms/2021/cit120.instructions.pdf |archive-date=February 15, 2023}}</ref><ref>[http://wvcommerce.org/business/industries/default.aspx "West Virginia Industries"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101220013929/http://www.wvcommerce.org/business/industries/default.aspx |date=December 20, 2010}}, West Virginia Department of Commerce. Accessed December 11, 2010</ref>

The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that in 2014 West Virginia's economy grew twice as fast as the next fastest-growing state east of the Mississippi River, ranking third alongside Wyoming and just behind North Dakota and Texas among the fastest-growing states.<ref>{{cite web |title=Broad Growth Across States in 2014 |url=https://www.bea.gov/newsreleases/regional/gdp_state/2015/gsp0615.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150611182028/https://www.bea.gov/newsreleases/regional/gdp_state/2015/gsp0615.htm |archive-date=June 11, 2015 |website=U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis}}</ref> In 2025, 98.8% of businesses in West Virginia were [[small business]]es, employing 47.4% of the state's workforce.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2025 Small Business Profile |url=https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/West_Virginia_2025-State-Profile.pdf |access-date=February 26, 2026 |website=U.S. Small Business Administration Office of Advocacy}}</ref>

===Tourism===
[[File:Seneca Rocks by Asilverstein Oct 2013 High Dynamic Range Merge from 7 Exposures.jpg|thumb|[[Seneca Rocks]], Pendleton County]]

Tourism contributed $4.27&nbsp;billion to the state's economy and employed 44,400 people in 2010, making it one of the state's largest industries.<ref>{{cite report| publisher=AECOM| title=West Virginia Ten Year Tourism Plan| date=September 2012 |url=https://wvtourism.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/AECOM-West-Virginia-Final-Report.pdf}}</ref> Many tourists, especially in the eastern mountains, are drawn to the region's notable opportunities for outdoor recreation. [[Canaan Valley]] is popular for winter sports, [[Seneca Rocks]] is one of the premier rock climbing destinations in the eastern U.S., the [[New River Gorge]]/[[Fayetteville, WV|Fayetteville]] area draws rock climbers as well as [[whitewater]] rafting enthusiasts, and the [[Monongahela National Forest]] is popular with hikers, backpackers, hunters, and anglers.

Also drawing tourism to the state is the [[List of West Virginia state parks|West Virginia State Park]] & [[List of West Virginia state forests|State Forest]] system, which comprises 45 units covering 164,000 acres. In 2021, over 9 million people visited a West Virginia State Park, the highest number on record. This is partly due to a recent $151 million improvement project that has seen improvements at every park and forest.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Staff Reports |title=West Virginia officials mark completion $8 million in upgrades at Pipestem Resort State Park |url=https://www.wvnews.com/news/wvnews/west-virginia-officials-mark-completion-8-million-in-upgrades-at-pipestem-resort-state-park/article_a1a8cdc6-cbda-11ec-8e1b-f7a8485d0dab.html |website=wvnews |date=May 4, 2022 |access-date=December 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221219140322/https://www.wvnews.com/news/wvnews/west-virginia-officials-mark-completion-8-million-in-upgrades-at-pipestem-resort-state-park/article_a1a8cdc6-cbda-11ec-8e1b-f7a8485d0dab.html |archive-date=December 19, 2022 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In addition to such outdoor recreation opportunities, the state offers a number of historic and cultural attractions. [[Harpers Ferry National Historical Park]] is a historic town situated at the confluence of the Shenandoah and Potomac rivers. [[Harpers Ferry]] was the site of [[John Brown (abolitionist)|John Brown]]'s 1859 [[John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry|raid]] on the U.S. Armory and Arsenal. Located at the approximate midpoint of the [[Appalachian Trail]], Harpers Ferry is the base of the [[Appalachian Trail Conservancy]].

[[The Greenbrier]] hotel and [[resort]], originally built in 1778, has long been considered a premier hotel, frequented by numerous world leaders and U.S. presidents over the years.

West Virginia is the site of the [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory]], which features the [[Green Bank Telescope]]. For the 1963 Centennial of the State, it hosted two high school graduate delegates from each of the 50 States at the [[National Youth Science Camp]] near Bartow, and has continued this tradition ever since. The main building of [[Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum|Weston State Hospital]] is the largest hand-cut sandstone building in the western hemisphere, second worldwide only to the Kremlin in Moscow. Tours of the building, which is a [[National Historic Landmark]] and part of the [[Civil War Discovery Trail|National Civil War Trail]], are offered seasonally and by appointment year-round. West Virginia has numerous popular festivals throughout the year.

===Energy===
[[File:Coalseam 8618.JPG|right|thumb|[[Bituminous]] coal seam in southwestern West Virginia]]

One of the major resources in West Virginia's economy is [[coal]]. According to the [[Energy Information Administration]], West Virginia is a top coal producer in the United States, second only to Wyoming. West Virginia is located in the heart of the Marcellus Shale Natural Gas Bed, which stretches from Tennessee north to New York in the middle of Appalachia.

As of 2017, the coal industry accounted for 2% of state employment.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2017/04/25/climate/todays-energy-jobs-are-in-solar-not-coal.html|title=Today's Energy Jobs Are in Solar, Not Coal|first=Nadja|last=Popovich|newspaper=The New York Times|date=April 25, 2017|access-date=June 20, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180620052645/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2017/04/25/climate/todays-energy-jobs-are-in-solar-not-coal.html|archive-date=June 20, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Nearly all the electricity generated in West Virginia is from coal-fired power plants. West Virginia produces a surplus of electricity and leads the nation in net interstate electricity exports.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://tonto.eia.doe.gov/state/state_energy_profiles.cfm?sid=WV |title=EIA State Energy Profiles: West Virginia |date=June 12, 2008 |access-date=June 24, 2008 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516020549/http://tonto.eia.doe.gov/state/state_energy_profiles.cfm?sid=WV |archive-date=May 16, 2008}}</ref> Farming is also practiced in West Virginia, but on a limited basis because of the mountainous terrain over much of the state.

An assessment from 2012 estimated that West Virginia had the potential to generate 8,627 GWh/year from 2,772 MW of 100-meter [[wind turbines]], and 60,000 GWh from 40,000 MW of photovoltaics, including 3,810 MW of rooftop [[photovoltaics]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nrel.gov/gis/re_potential.html|title=NREL: Dynamic Maps, GIS Data, and Analysis Tools—Renewable Energy Technical Potential |website=nrel.gov|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120915115931/http://www.nrel.gov/gis/re_potential.html|archive-date=September 15, 2012}}</ref> This was based on then-existing technologies and apparently was based on some assumed requirements for the economic performance of the respective resources.

===Taxes===

West Virginia personal [[income tax]] is based on federal adjusted gross income (not taxable income), as modified by specific items in West Virginia law. Citizens are taxed within five income brackets, which range from 3.0% to 6.5%. The state's consumer [[sales tax]] is levied at 6% on most products except for non-prepared foods.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wva.state.wv.us/wvtax/foodtax.aspx |title=Food Tax |publisher=State of West Virginia |access-date=April 22, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020231023/http://www.wva.state.wv.us/wvtax/FoodTax.aspx |archive-date=October 20, 2014}}</ref>

West Virginia counties administer and collect [[property tax]]es, although property tax rates reflect levies for state government, county governments, county boards of education and municipalities. Counties may also impose a hotel occupancy tax on lodging places not located within the city limits of any municipality that levies such a tax. Municipalities may levy license and [[gross receipts tax]]es on businesses located within the city limits and a hotel occupancy tax on lodging places in the city. Although the Department of Tax and Revenue plays a major role in the administration of this tax, less than half of one percent of the property tax collected goes to state government.

The primary beneficiaries of the property tax are county boards of education. Property taxes are paid to the [[Sheriffs in the United States|sheriff]] of each of the state's 55 counties. Each county and municipality can impose its own rates of property taxation within the limits set by the West Virginia Constitution. The West Virginia legislature sets the rate of tax of county boards of education. This rate is used by all county boards of education statewide. However, the total tax rate for county boards of education may differ from county to county because of excess levies. The Department of Tax and Revenue supervises and otherwise assists counties and municipalities in their work of assessment and tax rate determination. The total tax rate is a combination of the tax levies from four state taxing authorities: state, county, schools and municipal. This total tax rate varies for each of the four classes of property, which consists of personal, real and intangible properties. Property is assessed according to its use, location and value as of July 1. WV Assessments has a free searchable database of West Virginia real estate tax assessments, covering current and past years. All property is reappraised every three years; annual adjustments are made to assessments for property with a change of value. West Virginia does not impose an [[inheritance tax]]. Because of the phase-out of the federal [[estate tax]] credit, West Virginia's estate tax is not imposed on estates of persons who died on or after January 1, 2005.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.state.wv.us/taxrev/taxdoc/tsd393.pdf |access-date=July 14, 2017 |url-status=dead |title=West Virginia Estate Tax (for decedents dying after June 30,1985) And Intestate Succession Law (for decedents dying after July 9, 1993) |publisher=West Virginia State Tax Department |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927183746/http://www.state.wv.us/taxrev/taxdoc/tsd393.pdf |archive-date=September 27, 2011}}</ref>

==Quality of life==

[[File:Poverty rates by state. US map.svg|thumb|upright=1.0|Percent of Americans living below the [[Poverty threshold#United States|poverty line]] in each U.S. state, and the [[District of Columbia]]. West Virginia has one of the highest poverty rates.]]

===Economy===
West Virginia coal exports declined 40% in 2013—a loss of $2.9&nbsp;billion and overall total exports declined 26%.<ref>[https://census.gov/foreign-trade/statistics/state/data/wv.html "State Exports via West Virginia"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413155534/http://www.census.gov/foreign-trade/statistics/state/data/wv.html |date=April 13, 2014}}, U.S. Census Bureau. March 26, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> West Virginia ranked last in the [[Gallup, Inc.|Gallup Economic Index]] for the fourth year running. West Virginia's score was −44, or a full 17 points lower than the average of −27 for the other states in the bottom ten.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/167123/economic-confidence-highest-2013.aspx |title=Economic Confidence Still Highest in D.C. in 2013. Confidence improved in most states; West Virginia still least confident |publisher=Gallup |date=February 10, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140309072739/http://www.gallup.com/poll/167123/economic-confidence-highest-2013.aspx |archive-date=March 9, 2014 |access-date=April 14, 2014}}</ref> West Virginia ranked 48th in the CNBC "Top States for Business 2013" based on measures of competitiveness such as economy, workforce and cost of living—ranking among the bottom five states for the last six years running.<ref>[https://www.cnbc.com/id/100824779 "America's Top States for Business 2013"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170822070528/https://www.cnbc.com/id/100824779 |date=August 22, 2017}}, CNBC. July 9, 2013. Accessed April 14, 2014.</ref> West Virginia ranked 49th in the 2014 State New Economy Index and has ranked in the bottom three states since 1999. West Virginia ranked last or next-to-last in critical indicators such as Workforce Education, Entrepreneurial Activity, High-Tech Jobs, and Scientists and Engineers.<ref>[http://www.itif.org/publications/2014-state-new-economy-index "2014 State New Economy Index"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819085757/http://www.itif.org/publications/2014-state-new-economy-index |date=August 19, 2014}}, Information Technology and Innovation Foundation. June 11, 2014. Accessed August 16, 2014.</ref>

===Employment===

In 2012, West Virginia's [[gross domestic product]] (GDP) grew by 3.3%.<ref>[http://bea.gov/newsreleases/regional/gdp_state/2013/pdf/gsp0613.pdf "Widespread Economic Growth in 2012"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140611064129/https://www.bea.gov/newsreleases/regional/gdp_state/2013/pdf/gsp0613.pdf |date=June 11, 2014}}, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. June 6, 2013. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> The state issued a report highlighting the state's GDP as indicating a fast-growing economy, but did not address employment indicators.<ref>[http://newsletters.wvcommerce.org/newsletters/344/issue/Governor-Releases-July-Edge-Business-Report/285/ "Governor Releases July Edge Business Report"]{{Dead link|date=November 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}, West Virginia Department of Commerce. July 9, 2013. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> In 2009–2013, the U.S. real GDP increased 9.6% and total employment increased 3.9%. In West Virginia during the same time period, its real GDP increased about 11%, while total employment decreased by 1,000 jobs from 746,000 to 745,000.

In 2013, West Virginia ranked last in the nation with an [[employment-to-population ratio]] of only 50%, compared to the national average of 59%.<ref>[http://bls.gov/news.release/pdf/srgune.pdf "Regional and State Unemployment—2013 Annual Averages"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140308014549/http://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/srgune.pdf |date=March 8, 2014}}, U.S. Bureau of Labor. February 28, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> The state lost 5,600 jobs in its labor force in four critical economic sectors: construction (1,900), manufacturing (1,100), retail (1,800), and education (800), while gaining just 400 in mining and logging.<ref>[http://workforcewv.org/lmi/datarel/DRNEWS.pdf "West Virginia's February Unemployment Rate at 6.0 Percent"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413143832/http://workforcewv.org/lmi/datarel/DRNEWS.pdf |date=April 13, 2014}}, WorkForce West Virginia. March 18, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> The state's Civilian Labor Force dropped by 15,100.<ref>[http://workforcewv.org/lmi/datarel/cnty_PR.pdf "Labor Market Information by West Virginia County February 2014"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413145550/http://workforcewv.org/lmi/datarel/cnty_PR.pdf |date=April 13, 2014}}, WorkForce West Virginia. March 25, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref>

===Wages and poverty===
[[Personal income]] growth in West Virginia during 2013 was only 1.5%—the lowest in the nation—and about half the national average (2.6%).<ref name=":3">[https://www.bea.gov/newsreleases/regional/spi/2014/pdf/spi0314.pdf "State Personal Income 2013"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413155632/https://www.bea.gov/newsreleases/regional/spi/2014/pdf/spi0314.pdf |date=April 13, 2014}}, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. March 25, 2014. Accessed April 11, 2014.</ref> Overall income growth in West Virginia in the last thirty years has been only 13%—about a third of the national average (37%). Wages of the impoverished bottom 1% income earners decreased by 3%, compared to the national average, which increased 19%.<ref>[http://s2.epi.org/files/2014/Income-Inequality-by-State-Final.pdf "Income Equality by State"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906185353/http://s2.epi.org/files/2014/Income-Inequality-by-State-Final.pdf |date=September 6, 2015}}, Economic Policy Institute. February 2014. Accessed April 11, 2014.</ref>

West Virginia's [[Poverty in the United States|poverty rate]] is one of the highest in the nation. 2017 estimates indicate that 19% of the state's population lives in poverty, exceeding the national average of 13%.<ref>{{cite web |title=Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates |url=https://www.census.gov/data-tools/demo/saipe/#/?map_geoSelector=aa_c |publisher=US Census Bureau |access-date=June 16, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620141334/https://www.census.gov/data-tools/demo/saipe/#/?map_geoSelector=aa_c |archive-date=June 20, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Population===

United Van Lines 37th Annual Migration Study showed in 2013 that 60% more people moved out of West Virginia than moved in.<ref>[http://unitedvanlines.com/mover/united-newsroom/press-releases/2014/2013-united-van-lines-migration-study.htm "United Van Lines annual migration study reveals Oregon as top moving destination of 2013"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413130511/http://www.unitedvanlines.com/mover/united-newsroom/press-releases/2014/2013-united-van-lines-migration-study.htm |date=April 13, 2014}}, United Van Lines. January 2, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> West Virginia's population is expected to decline by more than 19,000 residents by 2030, and West Virginia lost one of its three seats in the United States House of Representatives in the 2020 census.<ref>[http://www.be.wvu.edu/bber/outlook_pdfs/WV-Economic-Outlook-2014.pdf "West Virginia Economic Outlook 2014"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140402124643/http://be.wvu.edu/bber/outlook_pdfs/WV-Economic-Outlook-2014.pdf |date=April 2, 2014}}, West Virginia University College of Business and Economics. March 31, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> West Virginia is the only state where death rates exceed birth rates. During 2010–2013, about 21,000 babies per year were born in West Virginia, but over these three years West Virginia had 3,000 more deaths than births.<ref name="census1">[http://census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/news_conferences/20130314_popest_countymetro.html "2012 County/Metro Population Estimates"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140729172304/http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/news_conferences/20130314_popest_countymetro.html |date=July 29, 2014}}, U.S. Census Bureau. March 14, 2013. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref>

===Family===

Gallup-Healthways annual "State of American Well-Being" rankings reports that 1,261 concerned West Virginians rated themselves as "suffering" in categories such as Quality of Life, Physical Health, and Access to Basic Needs. Overall, West Virginia citizens rated themselves as being more miserable than people in all other states—for five years running.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://info.healthways.com/wbi2013 |title=Gallup-Healthways Well-Being Index 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413105808/http://info.healthways.com/wbi2013 |archive-date=April 13, 2014 |publisher=Gallup-Healthways |access-date=April 12, 2014}}</ref> In addition, the Gallup Well-Being Index for 2013 ranked Charleston, the state capital, and Huntington last and next-to-last out of 189 U.S. Metropolitan Statistical Areas.<ref>{{cite web |title=Provo-Orem, Utah, Leads U.S. Communities in Well-Being |last=Witters |first=Dan |url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/167984/provo-orem-utah-leads-communities.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413202835/http://www.gallup.com/poll/167984/provo-orem-utah-leads-communities.aspx |archive-date=April 13, 2014 |publisher=Gallup |date=March 25, 2014 |access-date=April 14, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The Annie E. Casey Foundation's National Index of Children's Progress ranked West Virginia 43rd in the nation for all kids, and last for white kids.<ref>[http://datacenter.kidscount.org/data "KIDS COUNT Data Center"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140419144423/http://datacenter.kidscount.org/data |date=April 19, 2014}}, KIDS COUNT Data Center. April 1, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> The Annie E. Casey Foundation's 2013 KIDS COUNT Data Book also ranked West Virginia's education system 47th in the nation for the second straight year.<ref>[http://datacenter.kidscount.org/data "2013 KIDS COUNT Data Book"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140419144423/http://datacenter.kidscount.org/data |date=April 19, 2014}}, KIDS COUNT Data Center. June 24, 2014. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref>

===Health===
[[File:Overdose death rates in the United States.png|thumb|[[United States drug overdose death rates and totals over time|Overdose death rates in the United States]]]]
United Health Foundation's "America's Health Rankings" for 2013 found that Americans are making considerable progress in key health measures. West Virginia, however, ranked either last or second-to-last in twenty categories, including cancer, child immunization, diabetes, disabilities, drug deaths, teeth loss, low birth weight, missed work days due to health, prescription drug overdose, preventable hospitalizations, and senior clinical care.<ref name=":4">[http://americashealthrankings.org/rankings "America's Health Rankings: 2013"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413145446/http://americashealthrankings.org/rankings |date=April 13, 2014}}, United Health Foundation. December 11, 2013. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> Wisconsin Population Health Institute annual "Health Rankings" for 2012 showed West Virginia spends $9,671 per capita on health care annually. El Salvador spends just $467, yet both have the same life expectancy.<ref>[http://rwjf.org/en/about-rwjf/newsroom/newsroom-content/2013/03/2013CountyHealthRankings.html "County Health Rankings Show Healthiest and Least Healthy Counties in Every State"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413155202/http://www.rwjf.org/en/about-rwjf/newsroom/newsroom-content/2013/03/2013CountyHealthRankings.html |date=April 13, 2014}}, Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. March 20, 2013. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> In 2012, according to the Census Bureau, West Virginia was the only state where death rates exceed birth rates. During 2010–2013, about 21,000 babies per year were born in West Virginia, but there were 24,000 deaths.<ref name="census1" /> In demographics, this is called a "net mortality society".<ref>[http://www.wilsonquarterly.com/sites/default/files/articles/Feat_Eberstadt.FNL.pdf "Japan Shrinks"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413144427/http://www.wilsonquarterly.com/sites/default/files/articles/Feat_Eberstadt.FNL.pdf |date=April 13, 2014}}, Wilson Quarterly. Spring 2012. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref>

The National Center for Health Statistics says national birth rates for teenagers are at historic lows—during 2007–2010, teen birth rates fell 17% nationally. West Virginia, however, ranked last with a 3% increase in birth rates for teenagers.<ref>[http://cdc.gov/nchs/data/databriefs/db89.htm "2012 County/Metro Population Estimates"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413154720/http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/databriefs/db89.htm |date=April 13, 2014}}, U.S. Centers for Disease Control. April 10, 2012. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> A study by West Virginia's Marshall University showed that 19% of babies born in the state have evidence of drug or alcohol exposure.<ref>[http://hca.wv.gov/policyandplanning/Documents/Health%20Plan%20Analysis/ApxB.pdf "Prevalence of Drug Use in Pregnant West Virginia Patients"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413150318/http://www.hca.wv.gov/policyandplanning/Documents/Health%20Plan%20Analysis/ApxB.pdf |date=April 13, 2014}}, West Virginia Health Care Authority. July 1, 2010. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> This is several times the national rate, where studies show that about 5.9% of pregnant women in the U.S. use illicit drugs, and about 8.5% consume any alcohol.<ref>[http://www.samhsa.gov/data/NSDUH/2012SummNatFindDetTables/NationalFindings/NSDUHresults2012.pdf "Results from the 2012 National Survey on Drug Use and Health: Summary of National Findings"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203035035/http://www.samhsa.gov/data/NSDUH/2012SummNatFindDetTables/NationalFindings/NSDUHresults2012.pdf |date=December 3, 2013}}, U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. September 2013. Accessed April 12, 2014.</ref> An Institute for Health Policy Research study determined that mortality rates in Appalachia are correlated with coal production. In twenty West Virginia coal counties mining more than a million tons of coal per year and having a total population of 850,000, there are about 10,100 deaths per year, with 1,400 of those statistically attributed to deaths from heart, respiratory and kidney disease from living in an Appalachian coal county.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hendryx | first1 = Michael | year = 2009 | title = Mortality from heart, respiratory, and kidney disease in coal mining areas of Appalachia | journal = Int. Arch. Occup. Environ. Health | volume = 82 | issue = 2| pages = 243–249 | doi = 10.1007/s00420-008-0328-y | pmid=18461350| bibcode = 2009IAOEH..82..243H | s2cid = 20528316}}</ref>

In 2015, [[McDowell County, West Virginia|McDowell County]] had the highest rate of [[United States drug overdose death rates and totals over time|drug-induced deaths]] of any county in the United States, with a rate of 141 deaths per 100,000 people. Four of the five counties with the highest rates of drug-induced deaths are in West Virginia (McDowell, Wyoming, Cabell and Raleigh Counties).<ref>{{cite web |title=Underlying Cause of Death, 1999–2015 Results |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |url=https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/datarequest/D76;jsessionid=E63AD90E918B8FA3E71818EFDD738927?stage=results&action=sort&direction=MEASURE_DESCEND&measure=D76.M3#Citation |access-date=January 11, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170113115619/https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/datarequest/D76;jsessionid=E63AD90E918B8FA3E71818EFDD738927?stage=results&action=sort&direction=MEASURE_DESCEND&measure=D76.M3#Citation |archive-date=January 13, 2017}}</ref> In 2022, West Virginia had the highest drug overdose death rate of any US state, at 80.9 per 100,000 people.<ref>{{cite web | title = Drug Overdose Mortality by State | publisher = U.S. Department of Health & Human Services | url = https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/pressroom/sosmap/drug_poisoning_mortality/drug_poisoning.htm | accessdate = September 21, 2024}}</ref>

American environmental attorney [[Robert Bilott]] exposed how [[DuPont (1802–2017)|DuPont]] had been knowingly polluting water with [[perfluorooctanoic acid]] (PFOA) in [[Parkersburg, West Virginia]], since the 1980s.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/01/10/magazine/the-lawyer-who-became-duponts-worst-nightmare.html?_r=0 |title=The Lawyer Who Became DuPont's Worst Nightmare |date=January 6, 2016 |author-last1=Rich|author-first1= Nathaniel |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> This battle with DuPont is depicted in the film ''[[Dark Waters (2019 film)|Dark Waters]]''.

====Life expectancy====
The residents of West Virginia [[List of U.S. states and territories by life expectancy|have a lower life expectancy]] than the national average. In 2014 life expectancy for both sexes in the state was 76.0 years compared to 79.1 years for the United States as a whole. In 2014, males in West Virginia lived an average of 73.6 years compared to a national average of 76.7 years and females lived an average of 77.5 years compared to a national average of 81.5 years. Male life expectancy in West Virginia between 1980 and 2014 increased by 4.7 years, compared to a national average of a 6.7-year increase. Life expectancy for females in West Virginia between 1980 and 2014 increased by 1.7 years, compared to a national average of a 4.0-year increase. Life expectancy for both sexes is among the lowest of all states.<ref name="US Health Map">{{cite web |title=US Health Map |url=https://vizhub.healthdata.org/subnational/usa |website=Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation |publisher=University of Washington |access-date=December 27, 2020}}</ref>

Life expectancies in 2014 for both sexes in West Virginia counties ranged from a low of 70.3 years in [[McDowell County, West Virginia|McDowell County]] to a high of 79.3 years in [[Pendleton County, West Virginia|Pendleton County]]. McDowell and several other West Virginia counties are among the counties in the U.S. with the lowest life expectancies.<ref name="US Health Map"/>

==Government and politics==
{{Main|Government of West Virginia|West Virginia Constitution}}

[[File:The West Virginia Capitol in Charleston LCCN2015631770.jpg|thumb|The [[West Virginia State Capitol]] in Charleston is home to the [[West Virginia Legislature]].]]

The [[West Virginia Legislature]] is [[bicameral]]. It consists of the [[West Virginia House of Delegates|House of Delegates]] and the [[West Virginia Senate|Senate]], both housed in the [[West Virginia State Capitol]]. It is a citizen's legislature, meaning that legislative office is not a full-time occupation, but rather a part-time position. Consequently, the legislators often hold full-time jobs in their community of residence.

Typically, the legislature is in session for 60 days between January and early April. The final day of the regular session ends in a bewildering fury of last-minute legislation to meet a constitutionally imposed midnight deadline. During the remainder of the year, monthly interim sessions are held in preparation for the regular session. Legislators also gather periodically for 'special' sessions when called by the governor.

The [[List of Governors of West Virginia|governor]], elected every four years on the same day as the U.S. presidential election, is sworn in during the following January. Governors of West Virginia can serve two consecutive terms but must sit out a term before serving a third term in office. The title of [[Lieutenant governor (United States)|Lieutenant Governor]] is assigned by statute to the [[Lieutenant Governor of West Virginia|senate president]]. West Virginia's current governor is [[Patrick Morrisey]].

West Virginia's highest court is the [[Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia|Supreme Court of Appeals]]. The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia is the busiest appellate court of its type in the United States. West Virginia is one of 11 states with a single appellate court. The state constitution allows for the creation of an intermediate court of appeals, but the Legislature has never created one. The Supreme Court is made up of five justices, elected in nonpartisan elections to 12-year terms. For the purpose of courts of general jurisdiction, the state is divided into 31 judicial circuits. Each circuit is made up of one or more counties. Circuit judges are elected in non-partisan elections to serve eight-year terms.

West Virginia is an [[alcoholic beverage control state]], but unlike most such states, it does not operate retail outlets, having exited that business in 1990. It retains a monopoly on wholesaling of [[Distilled beverage|distilled spirits]] only. West Virginia is one of 27 states that do not have a [[Capital punishment in the United States|death penalty]], and it was the only state in the southeastern United States to have abolished it until 2021, when [[Capital punishment in Virginia|Virginia]] did so as well.

West Virginia is regarded as a heavily Republican, [[Red states and blue states|"deep red"]] state at the federal level.<ref name="slate.com" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/democrats-getting-destroyed-key-senate-142414525.html?soc_src=mediacontentstory|title=Democrats Are Getting Destroyed In Key Senate States|website=yahoo.com|date=March 4, 2014 |url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202084343/https://finance.yahoo.com/news/democrats-getting-destroyed-key-senate-142414525.html?soc_src=mediacontentstory|archive-date=February 2, 2017}}</ref> Since [[2000 United States presidential election|2000]], West Virginians have supported the Republican candidate in every presidential election, nearly always by increasing margins.

The [[2008 United States presidential election in West Virginia|2008 presidential election]] was the last to date in which the Democratic nominee won any of the state's counties. In every election since 2008, West Virginia has voted Republican and Virginia has voted Democratic.

In the [[2024 United States presidential election in West Virginia|2024 presidential election]], Republican [[Donald Trump]] won all of the state's counties and 69.97% of the vote, the highest percentage any party has won in the state's history. Meanwhile, Virginia voted for a Democratic nominee who lost the popular vote, with the two states differing by 48 percentage points in margin.<ref>{{cite web|title=Official 2024 Presidential General Election Results |url=https://www.fec.gov/documents/5644/2024presgeresults.pdf |publisher=[[Federal Election Commission]] |date=January 16, 2025 |access-date=January 18, 2025 }}</ref> West Virginia was Trump's best performance in 2016.<ref name="Leip, David">{{cite web|url=http://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/|title=General Election Results—West Virginia|publisher=United States Election Atlas|access-date=November 18, 2016|author-last1=Leip|author-first1= David|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180709214827/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/|archive-date=July 9, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

At the state level, West Virginia's politics were largely dominated by the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] from the [[Great Depression]] through the 2000s. This was a legacy of West Virginia's very strong tradition of union membership.<ref name="slate.com">{{cite journal|last=Woodruff |first=Betsy|date=October 29, 2014|title=Goodbye West Virginia |url=http://www.slate.com/articles/news_and_politics/politics/2014/10/republicans_are_turning_west_virginia_red_how_the_democrats_lost_control.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170721085311/http://www.slate.com/articles/news_and_politics/politics/2014/10/republicans_are_turning_west_virginia_red_how_the_democrats_lost_control.html|archive-date=July 21, 2017|journal=Slate|quote=But by 2000, tectonic changes in the state's politics were underway. West Virginians tended to be economically liberal but socially conservative, and as social issues like abortion came to the forefront in national politics, the state started looking better for Republicans. The leftward tilt of the national Democratic Party helped matters, too.}}</ref> After the 2014 midterm elections Democrats controlled the governorship, the majority of statewide offices, and one U.S. Senate seat, while Republicans held one U.S. Senate seat, all three of the state's [[U.S. House]] seats, and a majority in both houses of the [[West Virginia Legislature]]. In the 2016 elections, the Republicans held on to their seats and made gains in the State Senate and gained three statewide offices.<ref>{{cite news | title=The Latest: GOP maintains majority in West Virginia Senate | url=http://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/national-politics/article113238573.html | date=November 9, 2016 | newspaper=[[Miami Herald]] | access-date=November 9, 2016 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110111716/http://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/national-politics/article113238573.html | archive-date=November 10, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last1=McElhinny | first1=Brad | title=W.Va. Republicans celebrate Trump win and GOP gains | url=http://wvmetronews.com/2016/11/09/w-va-republicans-celebrate-trump-win-and-gop-gains/ | date=November 9, 2016 | publisher=[[West Virginia MetroNews]] | access-date=November 10, 2016 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110161351/http://wvmetronews.com/2016/11/09/w-va-republicans-celebrate-trump-win-and-gop-gains/ | archive-date=November 10, 2016}}</ref>

Evangelical Christians comprised 52% of the state's voters in 2008.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/2008/results/polls/#val=WVP00p1 |work=CNN |title=Local Exit Polls—Election Center 2008—Elections & Politics from CNN.com |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100605132422/http://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/2008/results/polls/#val=WVP00p1 |archive-date=June 5, 2010}}</ref> A poll in 2005 showed that 53% of West Virginia voters are [[anti-abortion]], the seventh highest in the country.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2005/50StateAbortion0805SortedbyProLife.htm |title=SurveyUSA - 50 State Abortion 0805 Sorted by Pro Life |publisher=SurveyUSA.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100221052419/http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2005/50StateAbortion0805SortedbyProLife.htm |archive-date=February 21, 2010}}</ref> A 2014 poll by Pew Research found that 35% of West Virginians supported legal abortion in "all or most cases" while 58% wanted it to be banned "in all or most cases".<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.pewforum.org/religious-landscape-study/compare/views-about-abortion/by/state/ |title=Views about abortion by state |publisher=Pew Research Center|work=2014 U.S. Religious Landscape Study |access-date=October 11, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181012014543/http://www.pewforum.org/religious-landscape-study/compare/views-about-abortion/by/state/ |archive-date=October 12, 2018}}</ref>

A September 2011 [[Public Policy Polling]] survey found that 19% of West Virginia voters thought [[same-sex marriage]] should be legal, while 71% thought it should be illegal and 10% were not sure. A separate question on the same survey found that 43% of West Virginia voters supported the legal recognition of same-sex couples, with 17% supporting same-sex marriage, 26% supporting civil unions but not marriage, 54% favoring no legal recognition and 3% not sure.<ref>{{cite press release |title=WV against gay marriage, for Tea Party, Steelers, Reds/Bucs |date=September 15, 2011 |publisher=Public Policy Polling |url=http://www.publicpolicypolling.com/pdf/2011/PPP_Release_WV_0915.pdf |access-date=September 20, 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120723060028/http://www.publicpolicypolling.com/pdf/2011/PPP_Release_WV_0915.pdf |archive-date=July 23, 2012}}</ref> In 2008, 58% favored troop withdrawal from Iraq while just 32% wanted troops to remain.<ref>{{cite web |title=West Virginia: McCain 45% Obama 38% |date=September 25, 2008 |website=Rasmussenreports.com |publisher=Rasmussen Reports |url=http://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/politics/elections2/election_20082/2008_presidential_election/west_virginia/west_virginia_mccain_45_obama_38 |access-date=July 31, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120301004702/http://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/politics/elections/election_2008/2008_presidential_election/west_virginia/west_virginia_mccain_45_obama_38 |archive-date=March 1, 2012 |url-status=deviated}}</ref> On fiscal policy in 2008, 52% said raising taxes on the wealthier individuals would benefit the economy, while 45% disagreed.<ref>{{cite web |title=Election 2008: West Virginia Presidential Election|website=Rasmussenreports.com|publisher=Rasmussen Reports |url=http://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/politics/elections2/election_20082/2008_presidential_election/west_virginia/election_2008_west_virginia_presidential_election |date=October 21, 2008 |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=deviated In a 2020 study, West Virginia was ranked as the 16th hardest state for citizens to vote in.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=J. Pomante II |first1=Michael |last2=Li |first2=Quan |title=Cost of Voting in the American States: 2020 |journal=Election Law Journal: Rules, Politics, and Policy |date=December 15, 2020 |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=503–509 |doi=10.1089/elj.2020.0666 |s2cid=225139517 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Transportation==
{{Main|Transportation in West Virginia}}

[[File:View of New River Gorge Bridge.jpg|thumb|The iconic [[New River Gorge Bridge]] near [[Fayetteville, West Virginia|Fayetteville]]]]
[[File:Morgantown Personal Rapid Transit.jpg|thumb|[[Morgantown Personal Rapid Transit]]]]

Highways form the backbone of transportation systems in West Virginia, with over {{convert|37300|mi|km}} of public roads in the state.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wvdot.com/3_roadways/3_roadways.htm |title=West Virginia Department of Transportation, accessed June 9, 2006 |publisher=Wvdot.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091024223558/http://www.wvdot.com/3_roadways/3_roadways.htm |archive-date=October 24, 2009}}</ref> Airports, railroads, and rivers complete the commercial transportation modes for West Virginia. Commercial air travel is facilitated by airports in Charleston, Huntington, Morgantown, Beckley, Lewisburg, Clarksburg, and Parkersburg. All but Charleston and Huntington are subsidized by the federal [[United States Department of Transportation|Department of Transportation's]] [[Essential Air Service]] program. The cities of Charleston, Huntington, Beckley, Wheeling, Morgantown, Clarksburg, Parkersburg and Fairmont have bus-based public transit systems.

[[West Virginia University]] in Morgantown boasts the [[Morgantown Personal Rapid Transit|PRT (personal rapid transit) system]], the state's only single-rail public transit system. Developed by [[Boeing]], the WVU School of Engineering and the [[United States Department of Transportation|Department of Transportation]], it was a model for low-capacity light transport designed for smaller cities. Recreational transportation opportunities abound in West Virginia, including hiking trails,<ref>de Hart, A, and Sundquist, B., Monongahela National Forest Hiking Guide, West Virginia Highlands Conservancy, Charleston, West Virginia 1993.</ref> [[rail trails]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wvrtc.org |title=West Virginia Rails-to-Trails Council, accessed June 9, 2006 |publisher=Wvrtc.org |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829215645/http://www.wvrtc.org/ |archive-date=August 29, 2010}}</ref> ATV off-road trails,<ref>{{cite web |author=Southern West Virginia |url=http://www.trailsheaven.com/ |title=Hatfield and McCoys Trail web site, accessed June 6, 2006 |publisher=Trailsheaven.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100702070729/http://www.trailsheaven.com/ |archive-date=July 2, 2010}}</ref> white water rafting rivers,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wvwhitewater.com/ |title=WV White Water web site, access June 6, 2006 |publisher=Wvwhitewater.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100727125107/http://www.wvwhitewater.com/ |archive-date=July 27, 2010}}</ref> and two tourist railroads, the [[Cass Scenic Railroad]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cassrailroad.com/ |title=Cass Scenic Railroad web site, accessed June 9, 2006 |publisher=Cassrailroad.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090225094114/http://www.cassrailroad.com/ |archive-date=February 25, 2009}}</ref> and the [[South Branch Valley Railroad|Potomac Eagle Scenic Railroad]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.potomaceagle.info/ |title=Potomac Eagle Scenic Railroad, accessed June 6, 2006 |publisher=Potomaceagle.info |date=February 20, 2010 |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100926230922/http://potomaceagle.info/ |archive-date=September 26, 2010}}</ref>

Rail lines in the state used to be more prevalent, but many lines have been discontinued because of increased automobile traffic. Many old tracks have been converted to [[rail trails]] for recreational use, although the coal-producing areas still have railroads running at near capacity. [[Amtrak]]'s ''[[Cardinal (train)|Cardinal]]'' roughly parallels I-64's path through the state. [[MARC Train|MARC]] trains serve commuters to [[Washington, D.C.]] in the eastern panhandle. In 2006 [[Norfolk Southern]] along with the West Virginia and U.S. Government approved a plan to modify many of the rail tunnels in West Virginia, especially in the southern half of the state, to allow for double-stacked cars (see [[Intermodal freight transport|inter-modal freight]]). This is expected to also help bring economic growth to the southern half of the state. An Intermodal Freight Facility is located at Prichard, just south of Huntington.

Because of the mountainous nature of the entire state, West Virginia has several notable tunnels and bridges. The most famous of these is the [[New River Gorge Bridge]], which was at a time the longest steel single-arch bridge in the world with a 3,031-foot (924 m) span. The bridge is also pictured on the West Virginia [[State quarter]]. The Fort Steuben Bridge (Weirton-Steubenville Bridge) was at the time of its construction one of only three cable-stayed steel girder trusses in the United States. "The Veterans Memorial Bridge was designed to handle traffic from the Fort Steuben Bridge as well as its own traffic load", to quote the ''Weirton Daily Times'' newspaper.<ref name="Gossett Fort Steuben Bridge permanently closed">{{Cite news |url=http://www.weirtondailytimes.com/page/content.detail/id/515883.html |title=Fort Steuben Bridge permanently closed |last=Gossett |first=Dave |date=January 15, 2009 |work=Weirton Daily Times |access-date=February 2, 2009 |archive-date=February 20, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210220154035/https://www.weirtondailytimes.com/ |url-status=dead}}</ref> The 80-year-old Fort Steuben Bridge (Weirton-Steubenville Bridge) was permanently closed on January 8, 2009. The [[Wheeling Suspension Bridge]] was the first bridge built across the [[Ohio River]] in 1849 and for a time was the longest suspension bridge in the world. It is still the oldest vehicular suspension bridge in the United States still in use.

===Roads===
[[File:The Veterans Memorial Bridge, a cable-stayed bridge across the Ohio River between Steubenville, Ohio, and Weirton, West Virginia LCCN2015632005.tiff|thumb|right|The [[Veterans Memorial Bridge (Steubenville, Ohio)|Veterans Memorial Bridge]] carries US 22 from [[Weirton, West Virginia|Weirton]] into Ohio.]]

West Virginia is crossed by seven [[Interstate Highways]]. [[Interstate 64|I-64]] enters the state near [[White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia|White Sulphur Springs]] in the mountainous east, and exits for [[Kentucky]] in the west, near [[Huntington, West Virginia|Huntington]]. [[Interstate 77|I-77]] enters from [[Virginia]] in the south, near [[Bluefield, West Virginia|Bluefield]]. It runs north past [[Parkersburg, West Virginia|Parkersburg]] before it crosses into [[Ohio]]. I-64 and I-77 between Charleston and Beckley are merged as a toll road known as the [[West Virginia Turnpike]], which continues as I-77 alone from Beckley to Princeton. It was constructed beginning in 1952 as a two-lane road, but rebuilt beginning in 1974 to Interstate standards. Today almost nothing of the original construction remains. [[Interstate 68|I-68]]'s western terminus is in [[Morgantown, West Virginia|Morgantown]]. From there it runs east into [[Maryland]]. At the I-68 terminus in Morgantown, it meets [[Interstate 79|I-79]], which enters from Pennsylvania and runs through the state to its southern terminus in [[Charleston, West Virginia|Charleston]]. [[Interstate 70|I-70]] briefly runs through West Virginia, crossing the northern panhandle through [[Wheeling, West Virginia|Wheeling]], while [[Interstate 470 (Ohio–West Virginia)|I-470]] is a bypass of Wheeling (making Wheeling among the smallest cities with an interstate bypass). [[Interstate 81|I-81]] also briefly runs in West Virginia through the [[eastern panhandle]] where it goes through [[Martinsburg, West Virginia|Martinsburg]].

The interstates are supplemented by roads constructed under the Appalachian Corridor system. Four Corridors are complete. Corridor D, carrying US 50, runs from the Ohio River, and I-77, at Parkersburg to I-79 at Clarksburg. Corridor G, carrying US 119, runs from Charleston to the Kentucky border at Williamson. Corridor L, carrying US 19, runs from the Turnpike at Beckley to I-79 near Sutton (and provides a shortcut of about {{Convert|40|mi|km|abbr=}} and bypasses Charleston's urban traffic for travelers heading to and from Florida). Corridor Q, carrying US 460, runs through Mercer County, entering the state from [[Giles County, Virginia]] and then reentering Virginia at [[Tazewell County, Virginia|Tazewell County]].

Work continues on the long-delayed Corridor H, which will carry US 48 from Weston to the Virginia line near Wardensville. As of 2018, a section from Weston to Kerens just past Elkins, and another section from Wardensville to Davis are complete. Other projects under development are a four-lane upgrade of WV 10 from Logan to Man and then of WV 80 from Man to Gilbert, which is about half completed; and four-lane upgrades to US 52 from Bluefield to Williamson, known as the "King Coal Highway" and from Williamson to Huntington, known as the "Tolsia Highway" which are many years from completion. A project known as the "Coalfields Expressway" is also ongoing, and will carry US 121 from Beckley west across Raleigh, Wyoming, and McDowell counties, entering Virginia near Bishop.

==Education==
{{Main|Education in West Virginia}}
West Virginia is one of the lowest-scoring U.S. states for [[education in the United States|education]], and has one of the lowest [[List of U.S. states and territories by educational attainment|levels of educational attainment]] of any state. As of 2022, just 10% of adults over the age of 25 had a [[Postgraduate education|postgraduate degree]] and 24% had a [[bachelor's degree]], compared to 17% and 35% nationally. In [[Virginia]] it was 18% and 42%, respectively.<ref name = "CensusData">{{cite web |title=EDUCATIONAL ATTAINMENT |url=https://data.census.gov/cedsci/table?q=S1501&g=0100000US%240400000&tid=ACSST1Y2021.S1501&moe=false&tp=false |publisher=U.S. Census Bureau |access-date=18 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220919003628/https://data.census.gov/cedsci/table?q=S1501&g=0100000US%240400000&tid=ACSST1Y2021.S1501&moe=false&tp=false |archive-date=19 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

According to [[National Assessment of Educational Progress|The National Assessment of Educational Progress]], it is significantly below the national average in mathematics, reading, writing, and science. The surrounding states of Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky, Ohio, and Pennsylvania score higher than or equal to the national average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NAEP State Profiles |url=https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/profiles/stateprofile |access-date=February 27, 2023 |website=www.nationsreportcard.gov |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Culture==

=== West "by God" Virginia ===
West Virginia is often called "West 'by God' Virginia." The term first appeared in online-accessible publications in 1926, when students at the [[University of Virginia]] wrote an article in the ''Virginia Spectator'' claiming that West "by God" Virginia women could consume corn liquor on its own, without having to mix it with other liquids. A 1939 academic article by [[Harold Wentworth (lexicographer)|Harold Wentworth]] of the [[West Virginia University|WVU]] History department had a footnote claiming that the term originated from when a native West Virginian, annoyed at being called a Virginian, claimed that he instead hailed from "West 'by God' Virginia."<ref>{{Cite web |last=McCormick |first=Liz |date=2019-08-28 |title=From Corn Liquor to State Pride - Origins of 'West by God Virginia' |url=https://wvpublic.org/from-corn-liquor-to-state-pride-origins-of-west-by-god-virginia/ |access-date=2024-12-17 |website=West Virginia Public Broadcasting |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Sports===

West Virginia is home to college sports teams from two schools—West Virginia and Marshall—that play in NCAA Division{{nbsp}}I. West Virginia is also home to several professional minor league baseball, football, hockey, and other sports teams.

===Music===
{{Main|Music of West Virginia}}

====Appalachian music====

West Virginia's folk heritage is a part of the [[Appalachian folk music]] tradition, and includes styles of [[Musical styles (violin)#Fiddle|fiddling]], ballad singing, and other styles that draws on English folk and [[Ulster Scots people|Scots-Irish]] music. Camp Washington-Carver, a Mountain Cultural Arts Center located at [[Clifftop, Fayette County, West Virginia|Clifftop]] in [[Fayette County, West Virginia|Fayette County]], hosts an annual Appalachian String Band Festival.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wvculture.org/stringband/ |title=Appalachian String Band Festival |publisher=Wvculture.org |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100729203742/http://www.wvculture.org/stringband/ |archive-date=July 29, 2010}}</ref> The Capitol Complex in Charleston hosts The Vandalia Gathering, where traditional Appalachian musicians compete in contests and play in impromptu jam sessions and evening concerts over the weekend.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wvculture.org/vandalia/ |title=Vandalia Gathering |publisher=Wvculture.org |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100828120221/http://www.wvculture.org/vandalia/ |archive-date=August 28, 2010}}</ref> The Augusta Heritage Center sponsored by Davis & Elkins College in [[Elkins, West Virginia|Elkins]] in [[Randolph County, West Virginia|Randolph County]] produces the annual [[Augusta Heritage Festival]], which includes intensive week-long workshops in the summer that help preserve Appalachian heritage and traditions.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.augustaheritage.com/about.html |title=Augustaheritage.com |publisher=Augustaheritage.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100814045504/http://www.augustaheritage.com/about.html |archive-date=August 14, 2010}}</ref>

====Classical music====

The West Virginia Symphony Orchestra was founded in 1939, as the ''Charleston Civic Orchestra'', before becoming the ''Charleston Symphony Orchestra'' in 1943. The first conductor was William R. Wiant, followed by the conductor Antonio Modarelli, who was written about in the November 7, 1949 ''Time Magazine'' for his composition of the ''River Saga'', a six-section program piece about the Kanawha River according to the ''Charleston Gazette''{{'}}s November 6, 1999, photo essay, "Snapshots of the 20th Century".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wvgazette.com/static/century/gz1106.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080410001327/http://www.wvgazette.com/static/century/gz1106.html|url-status=dead|title=WVgazette.com|archive-date=April 10, 2008}}</ref> Before coming to Charleston, Modarelli had conducted the [[Wheeling Symphony Orchestra]] and the [[Philadelphia Orchestra]], according to the orchestra's website.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wvsymphony.org/orchestra.php|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081106023605/http://www.wvsymphony.org/orchestra.php|url-status=dead|title=West Virginia Symphony Orchestra|archive-date=November 6, 2008}}</ref>

The [[Pulitzer Prize]]-winning 20th-century composer [[George Crumb]] was born in Charleston and earned his bachelor's degree there before moving outside the state. There had also been a series of operatic-style concerts performed in Wheeling during mid-century as well.

====Musical innovation====

The West Virginia Cultural Center in Charleston<ref>[http://www.wvculture.org/agency/cultcenter.html West Virginia Cultural Center] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060118022112/http://www.wvculture.org/agency/cultcenter.html |date=January 18, 2006}}. Retrieved January 19, 2006.</ref> is home to the West Virginia Department of Arts, Culture and History,<ref>[http://www.wvculture.org/ West Virginia Division of Culture and History] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080216093731/http://www.wvculture.org/ |date=February 16, 2008}}. Retrieved January 19, 2006.</ref> which helps underwrite and coordinate a large number of musical activities. The center is also home to ''[[Mountain Stage]]'', an internationally broadcast live-performance music radio program established in 1983 which is carried by many affiliates of [[National Public Radio]].<ref>In 2001, Mountain Stage debuted a television show featuring many of the radio program's guests. [http://www.mountainstage.org/ Mountain Stage] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091030234033/http://www.mountainstage.org/ |date=October 30, 2009}}. Retrieved January 20, 2006.</ref> The program also travels to other venues in the state such as the [[West Virginia University]] Creative Arts Center in Morgantown.<ref>[http://www.tourmorgantown.com/ Greater Morgantown Convention & Visitors Bureau] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060203191923/http://www.tourmorgantown.com/ |date=February 3, 2006}}. Retrieved January 20, 2006.</ref>

The center hosts concerts sponsored by the Friends of Old Time Music and Dance, which brings an assortment of acoustic roots music to West Virginians.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ballman |first=Stephen |url=http://www.footmad.org |title=Footmad |publisher=Footmad |date=October 30, 2002 |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110123063312/http://www.footmad.org/ |archive-date=January 23, 2011}}</ref> The center also hosts the West Virginia Dance Festival, which features classical and modern dance.<ref>[http://www.wvculture.org/dance/index.html West Virginia Dance Festival] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060103120203/http://www.wvculture.org/dance/index.html |date=January 3, 2006}}. Retrieved January 20, 2006.</ref>

Every year, [[Camp Washington Carver]] in Clifftop, [[Fayette County, WV]], hosts a five-day mountaintop gathering of traditional string band musicians with contests, concerts, workshops, square dances, camping and vendors. The event attracts 3,000 fans of old time Appalachian music, a precursor to [[Bluegrass music|bluegrass]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wvculture.org/explore/camp-washington-carver/string-band-music-festival/|title=Appalachian String Band Music Festival}}</ref>

Huntington's historic [[Keith-Albee Theatre]], built by brothers A.B. and S.J. Hyman, was originally opened to the public on May 7, 1928, and hosts a variety of performing arts and music attractions. The theatre was eventually gifted to [[Marshall University]] and is currently going through renovation to restore it to its original splendor.

Every summer [[Elkins, West Virginia|Elkins]] hosts the Augusta Heritage Festival, which brings folk musicians from around the world.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.augustaheritage.com |title=Augustaheritage.com |publisher=Augustaheritage.com |date=July 4, 2010 |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100722165028/http://www.augustaheritage.com/ |archive-date=July 22, 2010}}</ref> The town of [[Glenville, West Virginia|Glenville]] has long been home to the annual West Virginia State Folk Festival.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.etc4u.com/folkfest/ |title=West Virginia State Folk Festival |publisher=Etc4u.com |access-date=July 31, 2010 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110125231313/http://www.etc4u.com/folkfest/ |archive-date=January 25, 2011}}</ref>

The Mountaineer Opera House in [[Milton, West Virginia|Milton]] hosts a variety of musical acts.

[[John Denver]]'s hit song "[[Take Me Home, Country Roads]]" describes the experience of driving through West Virginia. The song mentions the [[Shenandoah River]] and the [[Blue Ridge Mountains]], both features traversing the easternmost extremity of the state's "eastern panhandle", in [[Jefferson County, West Virginia|Jefferson County]]. On March 8, 2014, West Virginia Governor Earl Ray Tomblin signed House Concurrent Resolution 40 naming "Take Me Home, Country Roads" the fourth official state song of West Virginia.

Symphony Sunday is an annual event hosted by the [[West Virginia Symphony Orchestra]] held in June. It is a day full of music by community groups, food, and family fun, culminating in a free performance by the West Virginia Symphony Orchestra with a fireworks display following. The event began in 1982 and is held on the front lawn of the [[University of Charleston]].

The [[Daily Mail Kanawha County Majorette and Band Festival]] is West Virginia's longest-running music festival. It is for the eight public high schools in Kanawha County. The festival began in 1947. It is held at the [[University of Charleston Stadium at Laidley Field]] in downtown Charleston.
