journal |author1=Nian Abdi |author2=Afroz Saz |author3=Alamet Betul |date=11 April 2018|title=های پیامد و سفید ازدواج آن در ایران کشور |trans-title=The consequences and whiteness of its marriage in Phenomenon |website=Iran Open Data |date=5 April 2022|language=en |url=https://iranopendata.org/en/pages/56e |access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Ahmady |first=Kameel Various factors such as economic crises and cultural and social changes in cities are reasons for the increase in the number of cohabitation in Iran. In other words, the emergence of [[capitalism]], the increase of job insecurity, the emergence of moral [[liberalism]], the revision of cultural traditions, the anonymity of people in cities, the elimination of the concepts and functions of neighborhoods, changes in family structures and the emergence of temporary relationships are among the major reasons for white marriage in Iran.<ref name=":1"/><ref name=yyyy/><ref name=LATimes/><ref name=a-45206118/><ref name=":2"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=برساخت اجتماعی ازدواج سفید |trans-title=The social construction of white marriage alternative to traditional marriage? - DW - 8/11/1396 |website=dw.com |language=fa February 2023}}</ref>

New research published by social anthropologist [[Kameel Ahmady]] and his team under the title '''''House with Open Door'':''' ''A Comprehensive Research Study on White Marriage (Cohabitation) in Iran'' reveals the previously concealed and multi-dimensional aspects of this phenomenon at the macro level, focusing on the [[Tehran]], [[Mashhad]] and [[Isfahan]] metropolitan areas. The research pieces argues that this phenomenon is more prevalent among educated and post-graduate young people who have migrated to metropolitan areas for work and education.<ref name=":1"/><ref name=yyyy/><ref name=a-45206118/><ref>{{Cite news |author=Niloufar Rostami |date=14 August 2019|title=IranWire Speaks to Wife of Jailed Iranian-British Anthropologist |website=IranWire |language=en |url=https://iranwire.com/en/features/66235/ |access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Kameel Ahmady |website=The Human Trafficking & Modern Slavery Expert Directory |url=https://www.humantraffickingexperts.com/main/business_details/359 |access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>

===Europe===
In the [[European Union]], cohabitation is very common. In 2014, 42% of all births in the 28 EU countries were nonmarital.<ref name=tps00018>{{cite web |title=Tables, Graphs and Maps Interface (TGM) table |date=11 August 2016|url=https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/tgm/table.do?tab=table&plugin=1&language=en&pcode=tps00018 |access-date=11 February 2019|archive-date=9 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190909025921/https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/tgm/table.do?tab=table&plugin=1&language=en&pcode=tps00018 |url-status=dead |website=Eurostat}}</ref> In the following European countries the majority of births occur outside marriage: [[Iceland]] (69.9% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>), France (59.7% in 2016<ref>{{cite web |title=Naissances hors mariage en 2018 |website=www.insee.fr |url=https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/2381394#tableau-Donnes}}</ref>), [[Bulgaria]] (58.6% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>), [[Slovenia]] (58.6% in 2016<ref>{{cite web |title=Births, Slovenia, 2016 |website=www.stat.si |url=https://www.stat.si/StatWeb/en/News/Index/6768}}</ref>), [[Norway]] (56.2% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>), [[Estonia]] (56.1% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>), Sweden (54.9% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>), [[Denmark]] (54% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>), [[Portugal]] (52.8% in 2016<ref>{{cite web |website=Pordata.pt |date=28 April 2016|url=http://www.pordata.pt/en/Portugal/Live%20births%20outside%20of%20marriage%20%20with%20parents%20co%20habiting%20or%20not%20(percentage)-620 |title=Live births outside of marriage, with parents co-habiting or not (%) in Portugal |access-date=26 March 2017}}</ref>), and the [[Netherlands]] (50.4% in 2016<ref name=tps00018/>).
 
While couples of all ages cohabit, the phenomenon is much more common among younger people. In late 2005, 21% of families in Finland consisted of cohabiting couples (all age groups).<ref>{{cite web |date=1 June 2006|title=The Finnish population structure of 2005 |url=http://www.stat.fi/til/perh/2005/perh_2005_2006-06-01_tie_001.html |website=Statistics Finland |language=fi}}</ref> Of couples with children, 18% were cohabiting.{{citation need |date=June 2023}} Of ages 18 and above in 2003, 13.4% were cohabiting.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.stat.fi/til/evaa/2003/evaa_2003_2004-05-31_kat_002_en.html |title=Elected MPs and candidates by family type in 2003 |website=Statistics Finland |language=en}}</ref> Generally, cohabitation amongst Finns is most common for people under 30. Legal obstacles for cohabitation were removed in 1926 in a reform of the [[Criminal Code of Finland|Criminal Code]], while the phenomenon was socially accepted much later on. In France, 17.5% of couples were cohabiting as of 1999.<ref name=Vanier />

====United Kingdom====
{{main|Cohabitation in the United Kingdom}}
In the United Kingdom today, more than half of babies are born to people who are not married (roughly 51% as of 2021<ref>{{Cite web |title=Over half of children in England and Wales now born to unmarried parents |url=https://www.manchester.ac.uk/about/news/over-half-of-children-in-england-and-wales-now-born-to-unmarried-parents/ |access-date=23 July 2026|website=Over half of children in England and Wales now born to unmarried parents |language=en}}</ref>).

The [[Victorian era]] of the late 19th century is famous for the Victorian standards of personal morality.  Historians generally agree that the middle classes held high personal moral standards and rejected cohabitation. They have debated whether the working classes followed suit. Moralists in the late 19th century such as [[Henry Mayhew]] decried high levels of cohabitation without marriage and illegitimate births in London slums. However new research using computerized matching of data files shows that the rates of cohabitation were quite low—under 5% – for the working class and the urban poor.<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Rebecca Probert |title=Living in Sin |magazine=BBC History Magazine |date=Sep 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=G. Frost |title=Living in Sin: Cohabiting as Husband and Wife in Nineteenth-Century England |publisher=Manchester University Press |year=2008}}</ref>

Falling marriage rates and increased births outside marriage have become a political issue, with questions of whether the government should promote marriage or focus on the status of a parent rather than a spouse; the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] support the former whilst [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] and the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] support the latter.<ref>{{cite web|title=Marriage and cohabitation: key issues for the 2010 Parliament|work=UK Parliament |url=http://www.parliament.uk/business/publications/research/key-issues-for-the-new-parliament/social-reform/marriage-and-cohabitation/|access-date=22 August 2015}}</ref> There are also differences between [[England and Wales]] and [[Scotland]], with the latter being more accepting of cohabitation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Family Matters – Cohabitation |publisher=Scottish Government |url=http://www.gov.scot/Topics/Justice/law/17867/fm-couples-root/fm-couples-cohabitation|access-date=22 August 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924040817/http://www.gov.scot/Topics/Justice/law/17867/fm-couples-root/fm-couples-cohabitation|archive-date=24 September 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website=Family Law Week|title=Lessons to be learned for cohabitation cases in England, says Lady Hale in Supreme Court Scottish case |url=http://www.familylawweek.co.uk/site.aspx?i=ed98906 |access-date=22 August 2015|archive-date=10 March 2023|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230310081023/https://www.familylawweek.co.uk/site.aspx?i=ed98906}}</ref>

====Bulgaria====

In Bulgaria, there has been a rapid increase in cohabitation after the fall of Communism. The transition from communism to market economy had a great impact on the demographic behavior of the population. After the fall of Communism, the legal and social pressure to get married has declined, and the population has started to experience new life styles.<ref name="Elena von der Lippe"/> As of 2014, 58.8% of children were born to unmarried mothers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Population and Demographic Processes in 2014 (Final Data) |publisher=Republic of Bulgaria: National Statistical Institute |url=https://nsi.bg/sites/default/files/files/pressreleases/Population2014_en_2Y19BGI.pdf|access-date=7 August 2022}}</ref>

====Czech Republic====

The marriage rates in Czech Republic have fallen dramatically during the past decades. In the 1970s to 1980s, about 96–97% of women married; in 2000 it was estimated that only 75% of women would ever marry.<ref name="paa2004.princeton.edu">{{Cite web |last=Kantorova |first=Vladimira |title=Marriage or cohabitation: First union formation in the Czech Republic |url=https://paa2004.princeton.edu/papers/41732 |access-date=7 August 2022|website=princeton.edu |archive-date=7 August 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220807132131/https://paa2004.princeton.edu/papers/41732 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The [[age at first marriage]] for women has increased from being in the range of 21.4–21.8 years in the 1970s and 1980s,<ref name="paa2004.princeton.edu"/> to being 29.6 in 2011.<ref>{{cite web |title=FirstMariages by Age, Sex, Measurement, Country and Year |website=UNECE Statistical Database |publisher=United Nations Economic Commission for Europe |url=https://w3.unece.org/PXWeb2015/pxweb/en/STAT/STAT__30-GE__02-Families_households/051_en_GEFH_FirstMariages_r.px/table/tableViewLayout1/ |access-date=26 June 2023}}{{verification failed|date=June 2023|reason=Query returned "data not available".}}</ref> In the early 1990s, predictions were made by some Czech demographers that cohabitation would increase during the next decades; and indeed, there has been a marked increase in the number of people who live in non-marital couple relations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hamplová |first=Dana |date=5 June 2002|title=Marriage and Cohabitation: Qualitative Differences in Partnership Arrangements |journal=Sociologický časopis |trans-journal=Czech Sociological Review |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=771–788 |url=http://sreview.soc.cas.cz/pdfs/csr/2002/06/05.pdf |access-date=7 August 2022}}</ref> In 2016, 48.6% of births were to unmarried women.<ref name=tps00018/>

====Germany====
Until the 1980s, it was illegal for unmarried couples to cohabitate, which made it impossible for many same-sex couples to live together. At this point the [[Bundesgerichtshof]] ruled that cohabitation could not be banned as it was protected by the [[Basic Law]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Von 1933 bis heute: Lesben und Schwule in Deutschland und der DDR |url=https://www.lsvd.de/de/ct/934-von-1933-bis-heute-lesben-und-schwule-in-deutschland-und-der-ddr |website=www.lsvd.de |access-date=1 November 2021|language=de}}</ref>
As in other western societies, patterns of family life have been changing in Germany during the past decades. This has not created a [[moral panic]], but has been seen more as an ongoing social evolution.<ref name="lawfamger">{{cite web |url=http://lawfam.oxfordjournals.org/content/15/1/88.short |title=Cohabitation in Germany – rules, reality and public discourses |work=oxfordjournals.org|access-date=13 January 2016}}</ref> Cohabitation, divorce rates, lone parents, and people's reluctance to marry or to have children have increased.<ref name="lawfamger"/> However, with regards to family formation and long term cohabitation instead of marriage, there are very strong differences between the regions of former [[West Germany]] and [[East Germany]] (which was formally Communist). Significantly more children are born out of wedlock in eastern Germany than in western Germany. In 2012, in eastern Germany 61.6% of births were to unmarried women, while in western Germany only 28.4% were.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Klärner |first=Andreas |date=22 July 2015|title=The low importance of marriage in eastern Germany – social norms and the role of peoples' perceptions of the past |url=https://www.demographic-research.org/volumes/vol33/9/33-9.pdf |access-date=7 August 2022|website=Demographic Research}}</ref> A [[Panel data|longitudinal survey]] found that union stability was significantly higher for cohabiting mothers in eastern Germany than western Germany, due to differences in German society.<ref name="germanypmc">{{cite journal |vauthors=Schnor C |title=The Effect of Union Status at First Childbirth on Union Stability: Evidence from Eastern and Western Germany |journal=Eur J Popul |volume=30 |issue= 2|pages=129–160 |year=2014 |pmid=24882913 |pmc=4037585 |doi=10.1007/s10680-013-9304-7}}</ref>

====Greece====
In [[Greece]], family dynamics remain conservative. The principal form of partnership is marriage, and extramarital childbearing and long term cohabitation are not widespread. For instance, in 2016 only 9.4% of births were outside marriage, which is the lowest percentage among the European Union member states.<ref name=tps00018/> [[Religion in Greece]] plays a very important role in society; it was only in 1983 that [[civil marriage]] was introduced in the country. The new laws modernized [[family law]], abolished [[dowry]], and provided for equal rights for "[[Legitimacy (family law)|illegitimate]]" children.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marcos |first1=Anastasios C. |last2=Bahr |first2=Stephen J. |date=2001 |title=Hellenic (Greek) Gender Attitudes |journal=[[Gender Issues (magazine)|Gender Issues]] |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=21–40|doi=10.1007/s12147-001-0009-6 |s2cid=143989412 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=AROUND THE WORLD; Greece Approves Family Law Changes |agency=Reuters |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/01/26/world/around-the-world-greece-approves-family-law-changes.html# |newspaper=The New York Times|date=26 January 1983}}</ref><ref>{{cite conference |last=Demos |first=Vasilikie |date=11 August 2007|title=The Intersection of Gender, Class and Nationality and the Agency of Kytherian Greek Women |conference=Aannual meeting of the American Sociological Association}}</ref> According to a 2008 study: "Greek society still remains conservative and birthing outside marriage, although protected by law, remains in many ways socially unacceptable."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.internationaljournalofcaringsciences.org/docs/vol1_issue3_04_sapountzi.pdf |title=Greek mothers' perceptions of their cooperation with the obstetrician and the midwife in the delivery room.}}</ref> Despite this, there have been further legal changes providing for a modern "western" outlook on family life, including Law 3719/2008 dealing with family issues, including Article 14 of the law, which reduced the separation period (necessary before a divorce in certain circumstances) from four years to two years.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www2.ohchr.org/English/bodies/cedaw/docs/54/CEDAW-C-GRC-7.pdf |title=Consideration of reports submitted by States parties under article 18 of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women |publisher=Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women}}</ref>

====Hungary====
The literature on second demographic transition argues as well that highly educated women are more prone to engage in cohabitation, although the reasons are different: they are less concerned with respecting the societal norms.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Lesthaeghe R |year=1983 |title=A Century of Demographic and Cultural Change in Western Europe: an Exploration of Underlying Dimensions |journal=Population and Development Review |volume=9 |issue=3| pages=411–435 |doi=10.2307/1973316| jstor=1973316}}</ref> Some scholars argued that cohabitation is very similar to being single in the sense of not giving up independence and personal autonomy.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Rindfuss RR, van del Heuve A |year=1990 |title=Cohabitation: A precursor to marriage or an alternative to being single? |journal=Population and Development Review |volume=16 |issue=4| pages=703–726 |doi=10.2307/1972963| jstor=1972963}}</ref>

In Hungary, cohabitation was an uncommon phenomenon until the late 1980s and it was largely confined to the divorced or widowed individuals.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Carlson E, Klinger A |year=1987 |title=Partners in life: Unmarried couples in Hungary |journal=European Journal of Population |volume=3 |issue=1| pages=85–99 |doi=10.1007/bf01797093| pmid=12280732 |s2cid=3691282}}</ref> Among the ethnic groups, Gypsy/Roma tended to have higher rates of cohabitation, mainly due to their reluctance to register their marriages officially.<ref>{{cite book |last=Barany |first=Zoltan |year=2002 |title=The East European Gypsies. Regime Change. Marginality, and Ethnopolitics |publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref> Since the 1980s, cohabitation became much more frequent among all ethnic groups and it has been argued to have strongly influenced the decline in fertility.<ref>{{cite report |last=Speder |first=Zsolt |date=July 2001 |title=Turning Points of the Life Course |place=Budapest |publisher=Demographic Research Institute |url=http://demografia.hu/hu/letoltes/adatbazisok/eletunk-fordulopontjai/kutatasi_koncepcioEN.pdf |access-date=26 June 2023|url-status=live |archive-date=26 June 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230626041541/http://demografia.hu/hu/letoltes/adatbazisok/eletunk-fordulopontjai/kutatasi_koncepcioEN.pdf}}</ref> In 2015, 47.9% of births were to unmarried women.<ref name=tps00018/>

====Ireland====

[[File:Magdalen-asylum.jpg|upright=1.15|thumb|Irish [[Magdalene laundries|Magdalene Laundry]], {{circa|lk=no}} early 1900s. Women who had sexual relations outside marriage were often sent to Magdalene laundries until the mid-20th century.]]

Cohabitation in Ireland has increased in recent years, and 36.6% of births were to unmarried women in 2016.<ref name=tps00018/> Until a few decades ago, women who had children outside marriage were severely stigmatized and often detained in [[Magdalene laundries]]. The [[Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010]] gives some rights to unmarried cohabitants (under this act same-sex couples can enter into [[civil partnerships]], while long term unmarried couples – both heterosexual and same sex – who have not registered their relation have some limited rights and obligations).

====Italy====

In Italy, where [[Roman Catholicism]] had a historically strong presence, cohabitation is not as common as in other countries of Europe, yet it has increased in recent years. There are significant regional differences, with non-marital unions being more common in [[Northern Italy]] than in [[Southern Italy]]. A study published in 2006 found that long term cohabitation was still novel to Italy, though more common among young people.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Cohabitation in Italy: do parents matter?|journal = Genus|volume = 62|issue = 3/4|pages = 53–85|jstor = 29789325|last1 = Schröder|first1 = Christin|year = 2006}}</ref> As of 2015, the share of births outside marriage was 28.7%, but this varied by statistical regions as follows: [[Central Italy]] (33.8%), [[Northeast Italy]] (33.1%), [[Northwest Italy]] (31.3%), [[Insular Italy]] (24.2%), and [[South Italy]] (20.3%).<ref>{{Cite web |date=28 November 2016|title=NATALITÀ E FECONDITÀ DELLA POPOLAZIONE RESIDENTE |url=https://www.istat.it/it/files/2016/11/Statistica-report-Nati.pdf?title=Natalit%C3%A0+e+fecondit%C3%A0++-+28%2Fnov%2F2016+-+Testo+integrale+e+nota+metodologica.pdf |access-date=7 August 2022}}</ref>

====The Netherlands====

Dutch researchers have found that research participants see cohabitation as a risk-reduction strategy in a country with high relationship instability.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Risk-avoidance or utmost commitment? Dutch focus group research on cohabitation and marriage |author=Nicole Hiekel |author2=Renske Keizer |journal=Demographic Research |volume=32 |pages=311–340 |date=3 February 2015|doi=10.4054/DemRes.2015.32.10 |doi-access=free |url=http://www.demographic-research.org/volumes/vol32/10/32-10.pdf}}</ref> As of 2016, 50.4% births were to unmarried women.<ref name=tps00018/>

====Norway====

Cohabitation is a common type of partnership in Norway. Cohabitants have some rights if they have joint children, or if they have lived together for five years. Cohabitants can also regulate their relationship through a [[cohabitation agreement]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nyinorge.no/en/Familiegjenforening/New-in-Norway/Families-and-children-in-Norway-/Families-and-children-in-Norway/Cohabitation/|title=Cohabitation|access-date=22 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150722130026/http://www.nyinorge.no/en/Familiegjenforening/New-in-Norway/Families-and-children-in-Norway-/Families-and-children-in-Norway/Cohabitation/|archive-date=22 July 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> In Norway, in 2016, 56.2% of children were born outside marriage.<ref name=tps00018/>

====Poland====
In Poland, after the fall of Communism, the influence of religion has increased. Indeed, Poland has one of the most religious populations in Europe (see [[religion in Europe]]). Cohabitation in Poland has traditionally been associated with the lower social classes, but in recent years an increase has been seen among the more educated. Family structure in Poland remains traditional: Marriages are contracted at relatively young ages, and the incidence of divorce is relatively low (by European standards). The exact incidence of cohabitation is not well established, but it is quite low compared to other Western countries. However, Poland is not completely 'immune' to Western influence and, in 2016, 25% of children were born outside marriage.<ref name=tps00018/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Matysiak |first=Anna |date=18 August 2009|title=Is Poland really 'immune' to the spread of cohabitation? |url=http://www.demographic-research.org/volumes/vol21/8/21-8.pdf |access-date=7 August 2022|website=Demographic Research}}</ref>

====Slovakia====
Slovakia is more conservative and religious than neighboring Czech Republic. The principal form of partnership is marriage, but extramarital childbearing and cohabitation are slowly spreading, yet this trend is not without criticism; and some view these phenomena as a threat to traditional values.<ref name="demographic-research.org">{{cite journal |url=https://www.demographic-research.org/volumes/vol19/25/19-25.pdf |title=Slovakia: Fertility between tradition and modernity |year=2008 |publisher=Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research |doi=10.4054/DemRes.2008.19.25 |last1=Potancokova |first1=Michaela |last2=Vano |first2=Boris |last3=Pilinská |first3=Viera |last4=Jurcová |first4=Danuša |journal=Demographic Research |volume=19 |pages=973–1018 |article-number=25 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Michaela Potančoková |publisher=Demographic Research Centre |place=Bratislava, Slovakia |title=The Meaning of Cohabitation and Marriage in Slovakia: Comparing Generation |url=http://www.oeaw.ac.at/vid/download/col100319mp.pdf |access-date=17 July 2014|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140726132730/http://www.oeaw.ac.at/vid/download/col100319mp.pdf |archive-date=26 July 2014}}</ref> In 2016, 40.2% of births were to unmarried women.<ref name=tps00018/> Fertility in Slovakia has been described in a 2008 study as "between tradition and modernity".<ref name="demographic-research.org"/>

====Switzerland====
[[Switzerland]] has a tradition of strong conservatism; which can be seen in its legal and social history: in Europe, Switzerland was one of the last countries to establish gender equality in marriage: married women's rights were severely restricted until 1988, when legal reforms providing gender equality in marriage, abolishing the legal authority of the husband, come into force (these reforms had been approved in 1985 by voters in a [[Voting in Switzerland|referendum]], who narrowly voted in favor with 54.7% of voters approving).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/09/23/world/swiss-grant-women-equal-marriage-rights.html |title=Swiss Grant Women Equal Marriage Rights |newspaper=The New York Times|date=23 September 1985}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-17988450|title=Switzerland profile – Timeline|work=BBC News|date=28 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://history-switzerland.geschichte-schweiz.ch/chronology-womens-right-vote-switzerland.html|title=The Long Way to Women's Right to Vote in Switzerland: a Chronology|author=Markus G. Jud |website=history-switzerland.geschichte-schweiz.ch}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Women's movements of the world: an international directory and reference guide |author1=Sally Shreir |author2=F. John Harper |year=1988 |publisher=Longman |page=254 |isbn=9780897745086 |oclc=17353816}}</ref> [[Adultery]] was decriminalized in 1989.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hls-dhs-dss.ch/textes/f/F16108.php |title=Adultère|first=Anne-Lise|last=Head-König|website=HLS-DHS-DSS.CH}}</ref> Until the late 20th century, most [[Cantons of Switzerland|cantons]] had regulations banning unmarried cohabitation of couples; the last canton to end such prohibition was [[Valais]], in 1995.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.socialinfo.ch/cgi-bin/dicoposso/show.cfm?id=825|title=Dictionnaire Suisse de politique sociale : Union libre|website=www.socialinfo.ch|access-date=8 April 2016|archive-date=17 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160217012637/http://www.socialinfo.ch/cgi-bin/dicoposso/show.cfm?id=825|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Keller |first=Tomie |title=NATIONAL REPORT: SWITZERLAND |url=http://ceflonline.net/wp-content/uploads/Switzerland-IR.pdf |access-date=7 August 2022|website=ceflonline.net}}</ref> As of 2015, 22.5% of births were to unmarried women.<ref>{{cite web|title=Naissances et fécondité |trans-title=Births and fertility |website=Statistique suisse |url=http://www.bfs.admin.ch/bfs/portal/fr/index/themen/01/06/blank/key/02.html |access-date=17 June 2016|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160528231850/http://www.bfs.admin.ch/bfs/portal/fr/index/themen/01/06/blank/key/02.html |archive-date=28 May 2016|url-status=dead |language=fr}}</ref>
Births outside marriage are most common in the French speaking part (highest percentage in the cantons of [[Vaud]], [[Canton of Neuchâtel|Neuchâtel]], [[Canton of Geneva|Geneva]], [[Canton of Jura|Jura]]) and least common in the eastern German speaking cantons (lowest percentage in the cantons of [[Canton of St. Gallen|St. Gallen]], [[Canton of Zug|Zug]], [[Appenzell Innerrhoden]], [[Appenzell Ausserrhoden]]).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bfs.admin.ch/bfs/portal/fr/index/themen/01/06/blank/key/02/03.html |website=Statistique suisse |title=Proportion de naissances vivantes hors mariage |trans-title=Proportion of live births outside marriage |language=fr |access-date=8 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160411103759/http://www.bfs.admin.ch/bfs/portal/fr/index/themen/01/06/blank/key/02/03.html |archive-date=11 April 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

====Spain====

Spanish society has undergone major changes since the fall of the [[Francoist Spain|Franco regime]]. Important legal changes which have occurred throughout the 1970s and 1980s include legalization of divorce, decriminalization of [[adultery]], [[gender equality]] in [[family law]], and removing the ban on [[contraception]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://countrystudies.us/spain/ |chapter-url=http://countrystudies.us/spain/43.htm |editor1=Eric Solsten |editor2=Sandra W. Meditz |title=Spain: A Country Study |place=Washington, D.C. |publisher=GPO for the Library of Congress |year=1988 |chapter=SOCIAL VALUES AND ATTITUDES|access-date=22 August 2015}}</ref> The liberalization of the political climate has allowed for alternative family formation. In the mid-1990s, cohabitation in Spain was still described as a "marginal" phenomenon, but since the 1990s, cohabitation has increased dramatically in Spain.<ref name="Sweeney2015"/> In Spain, in 2016, 45.9% of births were outside marriage.<ref name=tps00018/> As in other countries, there are regional differences: in 2011, in [[Catalonia]] the figure was 42% – highest in mainland Spain in that year ([[Canary Islands]] 59% and [[Balearic Islands]] 43.5% were highest) while in [[Region of Murcia|Murcia]] it was only 30.7% (lowest).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.republica.com/2013/01/17/mas-de-un-tercio-de-los-nacimientos-en-espana-fuera-del-matrimonio/ |title=Más de un tercio de los nacimientos en España, fuera del matrimonio |work=Republica.com |date=16 January 2013|access-date=22 August 2015|archive-date=1 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210301053724/https://www.republica.com/2013/01/17/mas-de-un-tercio-de-los-nacimientos-en-espana-fuera-del-matrimonio/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

====Russia====

In Russia, many couples express a desire to cohabit before marriage, then register a civil marriage, and then at a later stage have a large church wedding.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Trust, responsibility, and freedom: Focus-group research on contemporary patterns of union formation in Russia |author=Olga Isupova |journal=Demographic Research |volume=32 |pages=341–368 |doi=10.4054/DemRes.2015.32.11 |date=3 February 2015|article-number=11 |doi-access=free |url=http://www.demographic-research.org/volumes/vol32/11/32-11.pdf}}</ref>

===Middle East===
The cohabitation rate in West Asian countries is much lower than in European countries. In some parts of the continent it is however becoming more common for young people.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}} As of 1994, the rate of premarital cohabitation in Israel was 25%.<ref>Kaplan, Amit. 2002. ''The roads of freedom: cohabitation patterns in Israel''. M. A. Thesis, Tel-Aviv University (in Hebrew)</ref>

Cohabitation is illegal according to [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] [[sharia]] law.<ref>See commentary on verses {{qref|23|1-6}}: Vol. 3, notes 7–1, p. 241; 2000, Islamic Publications.{{full citation needed|date=June 2023|reason=I believe this is a refernce to a book source, not the Quran. The qref template should not be used.}}</ref><ref>{{Qtaf|en:ibk|4|24}}</ref> Cohabitation, Bi'ah, is a legal status, "Yadua BetTzibbur", by the Jews [[Halakha]] (Halacha) religious Law.<ref>{{cite web |author=Maurice Lamm |title=Non-Jewish Wedding Ceremonies for Jews |url=https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/479943/jewish/Non-Jewish-Wedding-Ceremonies-for-Jews.htm |website=Chabad.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=C. G. Montefiore|author2=H. M. J. Loewe|title=A Rabbinic Anthology |date=12 July 2012|publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-04812-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nifOxU_RrCAC&pg=PR76 |pages=76–}}</ref>

==== Kuwait ====
Some legal recognition is extended to former common-law unions in Kuwait. Kuwaiti Family law applies the law of the father's, husband's or male partner's country in case of [[expatriate]] familial disputes. Hence, if the father's country of nationality recognises common-law marriages (like the United Kingdom), matters such as [[child support]] dues and [[Alimony|maintenance]] can be considered in a Kuwaiti court.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Expat divorce in Kuwait |website=Expatriate Law |url=https://expatriatelaw.com/where-to-divorce/divorce-where-you-live/expat-divorce-in-kuwait/|access-date=11 October 2020}}</ref> However, out-of-marriage sexual intercourse is an offence punishable in Kuwait with a prison sentence between 6 months and 6 years if caught in action by an official or an administrative [[deportation]] order. This meaning that common-law marriage recognition can only be practically seen in exceptional cases like where the illegitimate child was born aboard and/or former couples who have since expatriated to Kuwait.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ahmed|first=Fajer|date=28 August 2013|title=Kuwait Law: Sexual Crimes |website=248am.com |url=https://248am.com/fajer/kuwait/kuwait-law-sexual-crimes/|access-date=11 October 2020|url-status=dead |archive-date=29 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190629203323/https://248am.com/fajer/kuwait/kuwait-law-sexual-crimes/}}</ref> Single expat parents including expat mothers can legally sponsor their children for residency permits.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Yasmena Al Mulla |date=24 August 2020|title=Kuwait allows expat mothers to sponsor children |website=Gulf News |url=https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/kuwait/kuwait-allows-expat-mothers-to-sponsor-children-1.73390299|access-date=11 October 2020}}</ref> Couples where one or both parties are Kuwaiti are covered by local family law and hence do not have recourse to the limited recognition of common-law marriage.<ref name=":0"/>

==== United Arab Emirates ====
Children born out-of-wedlock are given partial recognition. Their single expat mother or single expat father can sponsor them for residency. However, sexual relations outside of marriage were illegal in the UAE until November 2020, when restrictions were eased.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sponsoring family residency visa by expatriates |url=https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/visa-and-emirates-id/residence-visa/sponsoring-family-residency-visa-by-expatriates |date=n.d. |orig-year=Updated on 3 February 2020 |access-date=11 October 2020|website=The United Arab Emirates' Government portal |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200517105801/https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/visa-and-emirates-id/residence-visa/sponsoring-family-residency-visa-by-expatriates |archive-date=17 May 2020|language=en}}</ref>

===Oceania===

====Australia====
In Australia, 22% of couples were cohabiting {{as of|2005|lc=y}}. 78% of couples who marry have lived together beforehand in 2008, rising from 16% in 1975.<ref>{{cite web
|title=Percentage of marriages preceded by cohabitation 1975–2008
|website=Family Facts & Figures
|url=http://www.aifs.gov.au/institute/info/charts/marriage/cohabit.html
|publisher=[[Australian Institute of Family Studies]]
|url-status=dead
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130723195654/http://www.aifs.gov.au/institute/info/charts/marriage/cohabit.html
|archive-date=23 July 2013
}}</ref> In 2013, 34% of all births were to unmarried women.<ref>{{cite web|title=3301.0 – Births, Australia, 2013 |date=23 October 2014|publisher=Australian Bureau of Statistics |url=https://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/Lookup/3301.0Main+Features12013?OpenDocument= |access-date=25 June 2023}}</ref> Australia recognizes [[Australian family law|de facto relationships]]. The proportion of births outside marriage varies by state/territory, being, in 2009, lowest in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] (at 28%), [[Australian Capital Territory]] (at 29%), and [[New South Wales]] (at 30%); and highest in [[Northern Territory]] (at 63%) and [[Tasmania]] (at 51%).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/0/960840A446DEDF4DCA2577CF000DF019?opendocument |title=3301.0 – Births, Australia, 2009 |date=3 November 2010|publisher=Australian Bureau of Statistics |access-date=22 August 2015}}</ref>

====New Zealand====
In New Zealand according to the 2001 census, 20.5% of couples were in ''de facto'' relationships.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Atkin |first=Bill |date=2003 |title=The Challenge of Unmarried Cohabitation—The New Zealand Response |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25740421 |journal=Family Law Quarterly |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=303–325 |jstor=25740421 |issn=0014-729X}}</ref> In New Zealand, 23.7% of couples were cohabiting as of 2006.{{citation needed|date=June 2023|reason=Previous ref used a Canadian govt. source with Canadian statistics.}} In 2010, 48% of births were outside marriage.<ref>{{cite report |title=New Zealand Families Today |date=July 2013 |publisher=Families Commission |isbn=978-0-478-36937-3 |url=http://www.superu.govt.nz/sites/default/files/downloads/New-Zealand-Families-Today.pdf |access-date=4 June 2015|url-status=dead |archive-date=15 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115023200/http://www.superu.govt.nz/sites/default/files/downloads/New-Zealand-Families-Today.pdf}}</ref> Like Australia, New Zealand recognizes ''de facto'' relationships.<ref>{{cite web |title=Property (Relationships) Act 1976 |work=New Zealand Legislation |publisher=New Zealand Government |url=http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1976/0166/latest/DLM441113.html |access-date=22 August 2015}}</ref>

=== Africa ===

==== South Africa ====
In South Africa, the 2011 census revealed that of South Africans aged 20 or older, 43.7% had never been married, 36.7% were married at the time of the census, [[Marriage in South Africa|11.0% were living together like married partners.]] Civil marriages fell by 22,5% between 2011 and 2019 and declined by a further 31,1% in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Is marriage an old-fashioned institution? |website=Statistics South Africa |date=24 March 2022|url=https://www.statssa.gov.za/?p=15247 |access-date=17 January 2023}}</ref>

== In popular culture ==
One example of how cohabitation is referenced in popular culture is in the 1978 novel [[Prudence (novel)|''Prudence'']] by British author [[Jilly Cooper]], where it is used as an example of where American language used to describe relationships - in this case "permanent commitment" - and is mocked in popular culture.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Probert |first=Rebecca |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPQgAwAAQBAJ&dq=prudence+jilly+cooper&pg=PA197 |title=The Changing Legal Regulation of Cohabitation: From Fornicators to Family, 1600–2010 |date=6 September 2012|publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-57690-1 |pages=197 |language=en}}</ref>

{{Counterculture 1960s movements}}
{{Progressivism sidebar}}
The '''counterculture of the 1960s''' was an [[anti-establishment]] cultural phenomenon and political movement that developed in the [[Western world]] from the mid-1960s to the early 1970s. It overlaps with [[cultural liberalism]] and with the various [[social change]]s of the decade, and its effects reverberate to the present day.<ref name="rebelsgone?">"[[iarchive:cubanc 000104|Where Have All the Rebels Gone?]]" Ep. 125 of ''Assignment America''. Buffalo, NY: [[WNET]]. 1975. ([https://americanarchive.org/catalog/cpb-aacip_75-39k3jf98 Transcript available] via [[American Archive of Public Broadcasting]].)</ref> The movement gained momentum along with the [[civil rights movement]] in the United States, which led to the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]] and the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965]]; it intensified along with the [[Vietnam War]], which drove some [[revolutionary]] sentiment.<ref>[[E. D. Hirsch|Hirsch, Eric D.]] 1993. ''The Dictionary of Cultural Literacy''. [[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|Houghton Mifflin]]. {{ISBN|978-0-395-65597-9}}. p. 419. "Members of a cultural protest that began in the U.S. in the 1960s and affected Europe before fading in the 1970s&nbsp;... fundamentally a cultural rather than a political protest."</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Anderson| first = Terry H.| title = The Movement and the Sixties| url = https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780195074093| url-access = registration| publisher = Oxford University Press| year = 1995| isbn = 978-0-19-510457-8 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Landis|editor1-first=Judson R.|title=Current Perspectives on Social Problems|date=1973|publisher=Wadsworth Publishing Co.|location=Belmont, California|isbn=978-0-534-00289-3|page=[https://archive.org/details/currentperspecti0000land/page/2 2]|edition=3rd|quote=Culture is the 'social heritage' of society. It includes the complex set of learned and shared beliefs, customs, skills, habits, traditions, and knowledge common to the members of society. Within a culture, there may be subcultures made up of specific groups that are somewhat separate from the rest of society because of distinct traits, beliefs, or interests.|url=https://archive.org/details/currentperspecti0000land/page/2}}</ref>

As the movement progressed, widespread [[social tension]]s also developed concerning other issues, and tended to flow along generational lines regarding [[Individualism|respect for the individual]], [[human sexuality]], [[Second-wave feminism|women's rights]], [[Traditional authority|traditional modes of authority]], rights of [[people of color]], end of [[racial segregation]], experimentation with [[psychoactive drug]]s, and differing interpretations of the [[American Dream]]. Many key movements related to these issues were born or advanced within the counterculture of the 1960s.<ref>"[https://resources.saylor.org/wwwresources/archived/site/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/POLSC301-9.1.3-Counterculture.pdf Counterculture]." ''POLSC301''. [[Saylor Academy]].</ref>

As the era unfolded, what emerged were new cultural forms and a dynamic [[subculture]] that celebrated experimentation, individuality,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-15 |title=The Counterculture Hippie Movement of the 1960s and 1970s |url=https://www.thecollector.com/hippie-counterculture-movement-1960s-1970s/ |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=TheCollector}}</ref> modern incarnations of [[Bohemianism]], and the rise of the [[hippie]] and other [[alternative lifestyle]]s. This embrace of experimentation is particularly notable in the works of popular musical acts such as [[the Beatles]], the [[Grateful Dead]], [[Jimi Hendrix]], [[the Doors]], [[Janis Joplin]] and [[Bob Dylan]], as well as of [[New Hollywood]], [[French New Wave]], and [[Japanese New Wave]] filmmakers, whose works became far less restricted by censorship. Within and across many disciplines, many other creative artists, authors, and thinkers helped define the counterculture movement.

Everyday [[1960s in fashion|fashion]] experienced a decline of the suit and especially of the wearing of hats; other changes included the normalisation of long hair worn down for women (as well as many men at the time),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yarwood |first=Doreen |url=http://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofwo0000yarw_i6a3 |title=The encyclopedia of world costume |date=1986 |publisher=New York : Bonanza Books : Distributed by Crown Publishers |via=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-517-61943-8}}</ref> the popularization of traditional African, Indian and Middle Eastern styles of dress (including the wearing of [[Natural hair movement|natural hair]] for those of [[African diaspora|African]] descent), the invention and popularization of the [[miniskirt]] which raised hemlines above the knees, as well as the development of distinguished, youth-led [[Subculture|fashion subcultures]]. Styles based around [[jeans]], for both men and women, became an important fashion movement that has continued up to the present day.

Several factors distinguished the counterculture of the 1960s from [[anti-authoritarian]] movements of previous eras. The [[mid-20th-century baby boom]]<ref name="CNN 2011-08-11">{{cite news |url=http://i2.cdn.turner.com/money/2011/08/11/pf/recession_birth_rate/chart-birth-rate-2.top.gif |format=GIF |title=Birth Rate Chart |work=CNN |date=August 11, 2011 |quote=Annotated Chart of 20th Century US Birth Rates }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.boomerslife.org/baby_boom_population_us_census_bureau_by_state.htm |title=Baby Boom population – U.S. Census Bureau – USA and by state |publisher=Boomerslife.org |access-date=June 9, 2009}}</ref> generated an unprecedented number of potentially disaffected youth as prospective participants in a rethinking of the direction of the United States and other [[democratic societies]].<ref name="Yale-New Haven Teachers Institute">{{cite journal |title=Student Protest in the 1960s |journal=Yale-New Haven Teachers Institute: Curriculum Unit 79.02.03 |year=1979 |last=Churney |first=Linda |url=http://www.yale.edu/ynhti/curriculum/units/1979/2/79.02.03.x.html |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=This unit focuses on student protest in the 60s |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160729084756/http://www.yale.edu/ynhti/curriculum/units/1979/2/79.02.03.x.html |archive-date=July 29, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Post–World War II economic expansion|Post-war affluence]] allowed much of the counterculture generation to [[Postmaterialism|move beyond the provision]] of the material necessities of life that had preoccupied their [[Great Depression|Depression-era]] parents.<ref name="KidnerBucur2007">{{cite book|author1=Frank Kidner |author2=Maria Bucur|author3=Ralph Mathisen|author4=Sally McKee |author5=Theodore Weeks|title=Making Europe: People, Politics, and Culture, Volume II: Since 1550|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yIMSNu5OFHoC&pg=PA831 |date=2007|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-0-618-00481-2|pages=831–}}</ref> The era was also notable in that a significant portion of the array of behaviors and "causes" within the larger movement were quickly assimilated within mainstream society, particularly in the United States, even though counterculture participants numbered in the clear minority within their respective national populations.<ref name="RubinCasper2013">{{cite book |author1=Joan Shelley Rubin |author2=Scott E. Casper|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_-lMAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA264|title=The Oxford Encyclopedia of American Cultural and Intellectual History|date=2013|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-976435-8|pages=264–}}</ref><ref name="Kimball2013">{{cite book|author=Roger Kimball|title=The Long March: How the Cultural Revolution of the 1960s Changed America|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DqXNlJxslm4C&pg=PT82|date=2013|publisher=Encounter Books|isbn=978-1-59403-393-3|pages=82–}}</ref>

==Historical background==
{{see also|Timeline of 1960s counterculture}}

===Post-war geopolitics===
[[File:Operation Crossroads Baker Edit.jpg|thumb|Underwater atomic test "[[Operation Crossroads|Baker]]", [[Bikini Atoll]], Pacific Ocean, 1946]]
The [[Cold War]] between [[communist state|communist]] and [[capitalist state]]s involved espionage and preparation for war between powerful nations,<ref name="BBC 2009-08-05">{{cite news |last=Corera |first=Gordon |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/8184338.stm |title=How vital were Cold War spies? |work=BBC |location=UK |date=August 5, 2009 |quote=The world of espionage lies at the heart of the mythology of the Cold War.}}</ref><ref name="Central Intelligence Agency (US)">{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/vol51no2/intelligence-in-recent-public-literature.html |title=Early Cold War Spies: The Espionage Trials That Shaped American Politics |date=June 8, 2007 |quote=This is a review of the book of same name by John Ehrman, a winner of Studies in Intelligence Annual awards. At pub date, Ehrman was an officer in the CIA's Directorate of Intelligence |access-date=October 29, 2013 |archive-date=May 1, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170501021750/https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/vol51no2/intelligence-in-recent-public-literature.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> along with political and military interference by powerful states in the internal affairs of less powerful nations. Poor outcomes from some of these activities set the stage for disillusionment with and distrust of post-war governments.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://coursesa.matrix.msu.edu/~hst306/documents/huron.html |title=Port Huron Statement of the Students for a Democratic Society, 1962 |publisher=Coursesa.matrix.msu.edu |access-date=July 11, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090705062937/http://coursesa.matrix.msu.edu/~hst306/documents/huron.html |archive-date=July 5, 2009 }}</ref> Examples included harsh responses from the [[Soviet Union]] (USSR) towards popular [[Anti-communism|anti-communist]] uprisings, such as the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956|1956 Hungarian Revolution]] and [[Czechoslovakia]]'s [[Prague Spring]] in 1968; and the botched US [[Bay of Pigs Invasion]] of [[Cuba]] in 1961.

In the US, President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]'s initial deception<ref>{{cite news|last1=Kessler|first1=Glenn |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/fact-checker/wp/2014/03/27/presidential-lies-and-consequences-video/ |title=Presidential deceptions – and their consequences (video) |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=May 2, 2014}}</ref> over the nature of the [[1960 U-2 incident]] resulted in the government being caught in a blatant lie at the highest levels, and contributed to a backdrop of growing distrust of authority among many who came of age during the period.<ref>[[David Frum|Frum, David]]. 2000. ''How We Got Here: The '70s''. New York: [[Basic Books]]. p. 27. {{ISBN|978-0-465-04195-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/u2.asp |title=Avalon Project – The U-2 Incident 1960 |publisher=Avalon.law.yale.edu |access-date=July 11, 2009}}</ref><ref name="US Department of State">{{cite web|title=Foreign Relations of the United States, 1958–1960, Volume X, Part 1, Eastern Europe Region, Soviet Union, Cyprus May–July 1960: The U-2 Airplane Incident|publisher=US Department of State |url=https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1958-60v10p1/ch11|website=history.state.gov|access-date=June 23, 2014}}</ref> The [[Partial Test Ban Treaty]] divided the establishment within the US along political and military lines.<ref name="Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty Organization">{{cite web |url=http://www.ctbto.org/the-treaty/history-1945-1993/1955-62-from-peace-movement-to-missile-crisis/ |title=1955–62: From peace movement to missile crisis |author=CTBTO |publisher=Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty Organization |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=The international Peace Movement played an essential role throughout the Cold War in keeping the public informed on issues of disarmament and pressuring governments to negotiate arms control treaties }}</ref><ref name="Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty Organization (Unknown)">{{cite web |url=http://www.ctbto.org/the-treaty/history-1945-1993/1963-77-limits-on-nuclear-testing/ |title=1963–77: Limits on nuclear testing |author=CTBTO |publisher=Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty Organization |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=1963–77: Limits on nuclear testing }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|date=August 30, 1963|title=Of Treaties & Togas|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,940699,00.html?promoid=googlep|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090818063132/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,940699,00.html?promoid=googlep|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 18, 2009|access-date=July 11, 2009}}</ref> Internal political disagreements concerning [[Treaty Obligations of the United States|treaty obligations]] in Southeast Asia ([[SEATO]]), especially in [[Vietnam]], and debate as to how other communist [[insurgencies]] should be challenged, also created a rift of dissent within the establishment.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://womenincongress.house.gov/educational/essay3.pdf |title=A Changing of the Guard |access-date=June 13, 2009 |website=womenincongress.house.gov |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090429220959/http://womenincongress.house.gov/educational/essay3.pdf |archive-date=April 29, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=1967 Executive Sessions of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee |publisher=Fas.org |url=https://fas.org/irp/congress/2007_hr/1967executive.html |access-date=July 11, 2009}}</ref><ref>[[George F. Kennan|Kennan, George F.]] 1951. ''[[American Diplomacy, 1900–1950]]'', (''Charles R. Walgreen Foundation Lectures''). New York: [[New American Library|Mentor Books]]. pp.&nbsp;82–89.</ref> In the UK, the [[Profumo affair]] also involved establishment leaders being caught in deception, leading to disillusionment and serving as a catalyst for liberal activism.<ref name="Fawcett2012">{{cite book |author=Bill Fawcett|title=Trust Me, I Know What I'm Doing: 100 More Mistakes That Lost Elections, Ended Empires, and Made the World What It Is Today |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e6tVsSHyLbAC&pg=PT294 |date= 2012|publisher=Penguin Group US|isbn=978-1-101-61352-8|pages=294–}}</ref>

The [[Cuban Missile Crisis]], which brought the world to the brink of nuclear war in October 1962, was largely fomented by duplicitous speech and actions on the part of the Soviet Union.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/vol46no1/article06.html |title=Soviet Deception in the Cuban Missile Crisis |last=Hansen |first=James |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=Learning from the past |archive-date=June 7, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100607061839/https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/kent-csi/vol46no1/pdf/v46i1a06p.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="New York Times (unknown)">{{cite news |last=Dobbs |first=Michael |url=https://www.nytimes.com/top/reference/timestopics/subjects/c/cuban_missile_crisis/index.html |title=Cuban Missile Crisis |department=Times Topics |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=(JFK's) first reaction on hearing the news from National Security Adviser McGeorge Bundy was to accuse the Soviet leader Nikita S. Khrushchev of a double-cross }}</ref> The [[Assassination of John F. Kennedy|assassination of US President John F. Kennedy]] in November 1963, and the attendant [[Kennedy assassination conspiracy theories|theories]] concerning the event, led to further diminished trust in government, including among younger people.<ref name="Pew Research Center for People & The Press 2013-10-18">{{cite press release |url=http://www.people-press.org/2013/10/18/trust-in-government-interactive/ |title= October 18, 2013 Public Trust in Government: 1958–2013 |publisher=Pew Charitable Trusts |agency=www.people-press.org |date=October 18, 2013 |quote=Sources: Pew Research Center, National Election Studies, Gallup, ABC/Washington Post, CBS/New York Times, and CNN Polls. From 1976 to 2010 the trend line represents a three-survey moving average. For party analysis, selected datasets obtained from searches of the iPOLL Databank provided by the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research, University of Connecticut }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/amex/oswald/program/pt.html |title=American Experience &#124; Oswald's Ghost |publisher=PBS |date=November 22, 1963 |access-date=July 11, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228015958/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/amex/oswald/program/pt.html |archive-date=December 28, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="National Archives (US)">{{cite web |url=https://www.archives.gov/research/jfk/warren-commission-report/ |title=Report of the President's Commission on the Assassination of President Kennedy |website=www.archives.gov |publisher=US Government |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=JFK Assassination Records }}</ref>

===Social issues and calls to action===
[[File:MarioSavio.JPG|upright|thumb|left|Free Speech activist [[Mario Savio]] on the steps of Sproul Hall, [[University of California, Berkeley]], 1966]]

Many social issues fueled the growth of the larger counterculture movement. One was a [[Nonviolent resistance|nonviolent movement]] in the United States seeking to resolve constitutional [[Civil and political rights|civil rights]] illegalities, especially regarding general [[racial segregation]], longstanding [[Disfranchisement after Reconstruction era|disfranchisement]] of Black people in the South by white-dominated [[State governments of the United States|state government]], and ongoing [[Racism in the United States|racial discrimination]] in jobs, housing, and access to public places in both the North and the South.

On college and university campuses, student activists fought for the right to exercise their basic constitutional rights, especially [[freedom of speech]] and [[freedom of assembly]].<ref>{{cite web |author=Elizabeth Stephens |url=http://bancroft.berkeley.edu/FSM/chron.html |title=Free Speech Movement Chronology |publisher=Bancroft.berkeley.edu |access-date=June 9, 2009 |archive-date=September 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927070543/http://bancroft.berkeley.edu/FSM/chron.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Many counterculture activists became aware of the plight of the poor, and [[community organizer]]s fought for the funding of [[poverty reduction|anti-poverty programs]], particularly in the South and within [[ghetto|inner city]] areas in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.trincoll.edu/depts/tcn/valocchi.htm |title=The Historical Development of Community Organizing |publisher=Trincoll.edu |access-date=July 11, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090821210336/http://www.trincoll.edu/depts/tcn/valocchi.htm |archive-date=August 21, 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Smith|first1=Lillian|title=Our Faces, Our Words|date=1964|publisher=Norton & Co.|location=New York|page=114|edition=1st (pbk)|quote=But there is something beyond rights, something not more important but more desperately urgent: bodily need. There are millions of Negroes in such desperate need in every town and country and city that talk of 'rights' leaves them dull and dazed. The young protesters who come, in large part, from middle-class families have stumbled on this: to their stunned amazement they have found a primitive misery which pushes the phrase 'civil rights' out of their vocabulary.}}</ref>

[[Environmentalism]] grew from a greater understanding of the ongoing damage caused by industrialization, resultant pollution, and the misguided use of chemicals such as [[pesticides]] in well-meaning efforts to improve the quality of life for the rapidly growing population.<ref name="US Census Bureau">{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov/population/international/data/idb/worldgrgraph.php |title=International Data Base World Population Growth Rates: 1950–2050 |publisher=US Department of Commerce |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=The world population growth rate rose from about 1.5 percent per year from 1950 to 1951, to a peak of over 2 percent in the early 1960s due to reductions in mortality. Growth rates thereafter started to decline due to rising age at marriage as well as increasing availability and use of effective contraceptive methods. Note that changes in population growth have not always been steady. A dip in the growth rate from 1959 to 1960, for instance, was due to the Great Leap Forward in China. During that time, both natural disasters and decreased agricultural output in the wake of massive social reorganization caused China's death rate to rise sharply and its fertility rate to fall by almost half |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140220064433/http://www.census.gov/population/international/data/idb/worldgrgraph.php |archive-date=February 20, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Authors such as [[Rachel Carson]] played key roles in developing a new awareness among the [[world population|global population]] of the [[Ecology|fragility of our planet]], despite resistance from elements of the establishment in many countries.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Muir|first1=Patricia|title=History of Pesticide Use|url=http://people.oregonstate.edu/~muirp/pesthist.htm|website=oregonstate.edu|publisher=Oregon State College|access-date=July 7, 2014|quote=Then, things began to temper the enthusiasm for pesticides. Notable among these was the publication of Rachel Carson's best selling book ''Silent Spring'', which was published in 1962. She (a scientist) issued grave warnings about pesticides, and predicted massive destruction of the planet's fragile ecosystems unless more was done to halt what she called the 'rain of chemicals.' In retrospect, this book really launched the environmental movement.}}</ref>

The need to address minority rights of women, gay people, the disabled, and many other neglected constituencies within the larger population came to the forefront as an increasing number of primarily younger people broke free from the constraints of 1950s orthodoxy and struggled to create a more inclusive and tolerant social landscape.<ref>Skrentny, John. 2002. ''The Minority Rights Revolution''. Cambridge: [[The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press]]. {{ISBN|978-0-674-00899-1}}.</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/12/11/opinion/in-praise-of-the-counterculture.html |title=In Praise of the Counterculture |date=December 11, 1994 |website=The New York Times |access-date=May 1, 2014}}</ref>

The availability of new and more effective forms of [[birth control]] was a key underpinning of the [[sexual revolution]]. The notion of "recreational sex" without the threat of unwanted pregnancy radically changed the social dynamic and permitted both women and men much greater freedom in the selection of sexual lifestyles outside the confines of traditional marriage.<ref>{{cite web |title=American Experience &#124; The Pill |publisher=Pbs.org |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/amex/pill/ |access-date=June 9, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170316080548/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/amex/pill/ |archive-date=March 16, 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref> With this change in attitude, by the 1990s the ratio of children born out of wedlock rose from 5% to 25% for Whites and from 25% to 66% for African-Americans.<ref>{{cite web |title=Determinants of Planned and Unplanned Childbearing among Unmarried Women in the United States |last1=Musick |first1=Kelly |date=April 1999 |website=wisconsin.edu |publisher=Center for Demography and Ecology, University of Wisconsin-Madison |url=http://www.ssc.wisc.edu/cde/cdewp/99-09.pdf |access-date=January 13, 2015}}</ref> However, the longtime popular belief that there was far less pre-marital sex in the decades prior to the 1960s would be disproven by 2005, with University of Florida history professor Alan Petigny noting how even U.S. Census Bureau statistics showed that out of wedlock pregnancies did in fact rise dramatically between 1940 and 1960, but were not as publicly disclosed;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.research.ufl.edu/publications/explore/v10n1/extract4.html|title="Silent" Sexual Revolution Began In 1940's and '50s|author=Explore Magazine, Vol 10, No. 1|publisher=University of Florida|date=Spring 2005|accessdate=August 9, 2026}}</ref> by 1958, [[fornication]] laws in the United States were also acknowledged to be rarely enforced.<ref name="jim_thompson">{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=Jim |title=The Role of Common Law Concepts in Modern Criminal Jurisprudence (A Symposium) III: Common Law Crimes against Public Morals |journal=[[Journal of Criminal Law & Criminology|The Journal of Criminal Law, Criminology, and Police Science]] |date=November–December 1958 |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=350–356 |jstor=1141593 |publisher=Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law|doi=10.2307/1141593 |url=https://scholarlycommons.law.northwestern.edu/jclc/vol49/iss4/12 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
{{clear}}

===Emergent media===
[[File:Martin Luther King - March on Washington.jpg|thumb|right|King's "[[I Have a Dream]]" speech, given in front of the [[Lincoln Memorial]] during the 1963 [[March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom|March on Washington]]]]

====Television====

For those born after [[World War II]], the emergence of television as a source of entertainment and information—as well as the associated massive expansion of [[consumerism]] afforded by post-war affluence and encouraged by TV advertising—were key components in creating disillusionment for some younger people and in the formulation of new social behaviours, even as [[ad agencies]] heavily courted the "hip" youth market.<ref name="Frank1998">{{cite book|author=Thomas Frank|title=The Conquest of Cool: Business Culture, Counterculture, and the Rise of Hip Consumerism|date=1998 |publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-26012-9 |url=https://archive.org/details/conquestofcoolbu00fran|url-access=registration|pages=[https://archive.org/details/conquestofcoolbu00fran/page/132 132]–}}</ref><ref name="AndersonHerr2007">{{cite book|author1=Gary L. Anderson |author2=Kathryn G. Herr|title=Encyclopedia of Activism and Social Justice|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fy11AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT1010|date=2007|publisher=Sage Publications|isbn=978-1-4522-6565-0|pages=1010–}}</ref> In the US, nearly [[Real-time communication|real-time]] [[TV news|TV news coverage]] of the [[civil rights movement]] era's 1963 [[Birmingham campaign]], the "[[Bloody Sunday (1965)|Bloody Sunday]]" event of the 1965 [[Selma to Montgomery marches]], and graphic news footage from Vietnam brought horrifying, moving images of the bloody reality of armed conflict into living rooms for the first time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Culbert|first=David|date=January 1988|title=Television's Vietnam and historical revisionism in the United States|journal=Historical Journal of Film, Radio and Television|volume=8|issue=3|pages=253–267 |doi=10.1080/01439688800260371|issn=0143-9685}}</ref>

====New cinema====
The breakdown of enforcement of the U.S. [[Hays Code]]<ref name="National Public Radio (US)">{{cite web |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=93301189 |title=Remembering Hollywood's Hays Code, 40 Years On |last=Mondello |first=Bob |publisher=npr.org |date=August 8, 2008 |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=It took just two years&nbsp;... for Midnight Cowboy to be re-rated from X to R, without a single frame being altered. Community standards had changed—as they invariably do }}</ref> concerning censorship in motion picture production, the use of new forms of artistic expression in European and Asian cinema, and the advent of modern production values heralded a new era of [[art-house]] and mainstream film production, distribution, and exhibition. The end of censorship resulted in a complete reformation of the Western film industry. With newfound artistic freedom, a generation of [[New Hollywood|New Wave]] film makers working across all genres brought depictions of previously prohibited or otherwise taboo subject matter to neighborhood theater screens for the first time, even as [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] film studios were still considered a part of the establishment by some elements of the counterculture. Successful 1960s new films of the New Hollywood were ''[[Bonnie and Clyde (film)|Bonnie and Clyde]]'', ''[[The Graduate]]'', ''[[The Wild Bunch]]'', and [[Dennis Hopper]]'s ''[[Easy Rider]]''.

Other examples of [[modernist film|hippie modernist cinema]] includes experimental short films made by figures like [[Jordan Belson]] and [[Bruce Conner]], the [[concert film]] ''[[Gimme Shelter (1970 film)|Gimme Shelter]]'', ''[[Medium Cool]]'', ''[[Zabriskie Point (film)|Zabriskie Point]]'' and ''[[Punishment Park]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bampfa.org/program/hippie-modernism-cinema-and-counterculture|title=Hippie Modernism: Cinema and Counterculture, 1964–1974|date=November 15, 2016|website=BAMPFA}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bampfa.org/event/theater-2-hippie-modernism-shorts|title=Theater 2 Hippie Modernism Shorts|date=February 2, 2017|website=BAMPFA}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://eastbayexpress.com/hippie-modernism-the-struggle-for-utopia-at-the-berkeley-art-museum-2-1/|title=Hippie Modernism: The Struggle for Utopia At The Berkeley Art Museum|date=February 7, 2017}}</ref>

====New radio====
[[File:Family watching television 1958.jpg|thumb|A family watches television, {{circa|1958}}]]
By the later 1960s, previously under-regarded [[FM broadcasting|FM radio]] replaced [[AM broadcasting|AM radio]] as the focal point for the ongoing explosion of [[rock and roll]] music, and became the nexus of youth-oriented news and advertising for the counterculture generation.<ref>Sterling, Christopher & Keith, Michael (2008). ''Sounds of Change: A History of FM Broadcasting in America''. UNC Press. {{ISBN|978-0-8078-3215-8}}</ref><ref name="Federal Communications Commission (US)">{{cite web |url=http://transition.fcc.gov/omd/history/radio/quality.html |title=The Quality that Made Radio Popular |publisher=US FCC |access-date=April 18, 2014 |quote=It was not until the 1960s&nbsp;... that the quality advantage of FM combined with stereo was enjoyed by most Americans }}</ref>

===Changing lifestyles===

[[Intentional community|Communes]], [[collective]]s, and [[intentional communities]] regained popularity during this era.<ref>{{cite web|title=Flower Power|url=http://www.ushistory.org/us/57h.asp|website=ushistory.org|publisher=ushistory.org/Independence Hall Association|access-date=July 28, 2014|date=2014|quote=Like the utopian societies of the 1840s, over 2000 rural communes formed during these turbulent times. Completely rejecting the capitalist system, many communes rotated duties, made their own laws, and elected their own leaders. Some were philosophically based, but others were influenced by new religions. Earth-centered religions, astrological beliefs, and Eastern faiths proliferated across American campuses. Some scholars labeled this trend as the Third Great Awakening.}}</ref> Early communities such as the [[Hog Farm]], [[Quarry Hill Creative Center|Quarry Hill]], and [[Drop City]] in the US were established as straightforward [[back to the land movement|agrarian]] attempts to return to the land and live free of interference from outside influences. As the era progressed, many people established and populated new communities in response to not only disillusionment with standard community forms, but also dissatisfaction with certain elements of the counterculture itself. Some of these self-sustaining communities have been credited with the birth and propagation of the international [[Green Politics|Green Movement]].

The emergence of an interest in expanded spiritual consciousness, [[yoga]], [[occult]] practices and increased [[Human Potential Movement|human potential]] helped to shift views on organized religion during the era. In 1957, 69% of US residents polled by [[The Gallup Organization|Gallup]] said religion was increasing in influence. By the late 1960s, polls indicated less than 20% still held that belief.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/103459/Questions-Answers-About-Americans-Religion.aspx# |title=Questions and Answers About Americans' Religion |date=December 24, 2007 |publisher=Gallup.com |access-date=August 31, 2013}}</ref>

The "[[generation gap]]", or the inevitable perceived divide in worldview between the old and young, was perhaps never greater than during the counterculture era.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.com/topics/1960s/videos/ask-steve-generation-gap#ask-steve-hippie-vs-yippie |title=Ask Steve: Generation Gap (Video)|website=history.com |publisher=History Channel/A&E|quote=Explore the existence of the generation gap that took place in the 1960s through this Ask Steve video. Steve Gillon explains there was even a larger gap between the Baby Boomers themselves than the Baby Boomers and the Greatest Generation. The massive Baby Boomers Generation was born between 1946 and 1964, consisting of nearly 78 million people. The Baby Boomers were coming of age in the 1960s, and held different cultural values than the Greatest Generation. The Greatest Generation lived in a time of self-denial, while the Baby Boomers were always seeking immediate gratification. However, the Baby Boomers were more divided amongst themselves. Not all of them were considered hippies and protesters. In fact, people under the age of 28 supported the Vietnam War in greater numbers than their parents. These divisions continue to play out today. |access-date=May 1, 2014}}</ref> A large measure of the generational chasm of the late 1960s and 1970s was born of rapidly evolving fashion and hairstyle trends that were readily adopted by the young, but often misunderstood and ridiculed by the old. These included the wearing of very long hair by men,<ref name="Macan1996">{{cite book|author=Edward Macan|title=Rocking the Classics: English Progressive Rock and the Counterculture|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b98dJ3cYAksC&pg=PT127|date=1996|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-988009-6|pages=127–}}</ref> the wearing of natural or "[[Afro]]" hairstyles by Black people, the donning of revealing clothing by women in public, and the mainstreaming of the psychedelic clothing and regalia of the short-lived hippie culture. Ultimately, practical and comfortable casual apparel, namely updated forms of [[T-shirts]] (often [[tie-dyed]], or emblazoned with political or advertising statements), and [[Levi Strauss & Co.|Levi Strauss]]–branded blue denim jeans<ref name="CunninghamLab1991">{{cite book|author1=Patricia Anne Cunningham|author2=Susan Voso Lab|title=Dress and Popular Culture|url=https://archive.org/details/dresspopularcult00essa|url-access=registration|year=1991|publisher=Popular Press|isbn=978-0-87972-507-5|pages=[https://archive.org/details/dresspopularcult00essa/page/31 31]–}}</ref> became the enduring uniform of the generation, as daily wearing of suits along with traditional [[Western dress codes]] declined in use. The fashion dominance of the counterculture declined with the rise of the [[disco]] and [[punk rock]] eras in the late 1970s and effectively died out by the early 1980s, even as the global popularity of T-shirts, denim jeans, and casual clothing in general have continued to grow.

====Emergent middle-class drug culture====
In the Western world, the ongoing criminal legal status of the recreational drug industry was instrumental in the formation of an anti-establishment social dynamic by some of those coming of age during the counterculture era. The explosion of [[marijuana]] use during the era, in large part by students on fast-expanding college campuses,<ref name="The Nation 1966-01-31">{{cite news |last1=Freedman |first1=Mervin B. |last2=Powelson |first2=Harvey |url=http://thenation.s3.amazonaws.com/pdf/drugsoncampus1966.pdf |title=Drugs on Campus: Turned On & Tuned Out |work=The Nation |location=New York |publisher=Nation Co. LP |date=January 31, 1966 |pages=125–127 |quote=Within the last five years the ingestion of various drugs has become widespread on the American campus.}}</ref> created an attendant need for increasing numbers of people to conduct their personal affairs in secret in the procurement and use of banned substances. The [[Legal history of cannabis in the United States|classification of marijuana as a narcotic]], and the attachment of severe criminal penalties for its use, drove the act of smoking marijuana, and experimentation with substances in general, deep underground. Many began to live largely clandestine lives because of their choice to use such drugs and substances, fearing retribution from their governments.<ref name="PBS Frontline">{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/drugs/buyers/socialhistory.html |title=A Social History of America's Most Popular Drugs |publisher=PBS.org [Frontline] |access-date=April 23, 2014 |quote=from 1951 to 1956 stricter sentencing laws set mandatory minimum sentences for drug-related offenses. In the 1950s the beatniks appropriated the use of marijuana from the black hepsters and the drug moved into middle-class white America in the 1960s.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/6331/Decades-Drug-Use-Data-From-60s-70s.aspx |title=Decades of Drug Use: Data From the '60s and '70s |date=July 2, 2002 |publisher=Gallup.com |access-date=August 31, 2013}}</ref>

===Law enforcement===
[[File:Vietnam War protestors at the March on the Pentagon.jpg|upright|thumb|Anti-war protesters]]
The confrontations between college students (and other activists) and law enforcement officials became one of the hallmarks of the era. Many younger people began to show deep distrust of police, and terms such as "[[List of police-related slang terms|fuzz]]" and "pig" as derogatory [[epithets]] for police reappeared, and became key words within the counterculture lexicon. The distrust of police was based not only on fear of [[police brutality]] during political protests, but also on generalized police corruption—especially police manufacture of false evidence, and outright entrapment, in drug cases. In the US, the social tension between elements of the counterculture and law enforcement reached the breaking point in many notable cases, including: the [[1968 Columbia University protests]] in New York City,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://exhibitions.cul.columbia.edu/exhibits/show/1968/timeline |title=1968: Columbia in Crisis |website=columbia.edu |publisher=Columbia University Libraries |access-date=May 20, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/28/nyregion/28columbia.html |title=Columbia's Radicals of 1968 Hold a Bittersweet Reunion |last1=Kifner |first1=John |date=April 28, 2008 |website=The New York Times |access-date=April 30, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.columbia1968.com/history/photos/ |title=Columbia 1968: History | website=columbia1968.com |access-date=May 20, 2014}}</ref> the [[1968 Democratic National Convention protests]] in Chicago,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Royko|first1=Mike|title=Boss: Richard J. Daley of Chicago|date=1971|publisher=New American Library/Signet|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/bossrichardjdale00royk/page/175 175–188]|title-link=Boss: Richard J.
