'''Cubans''' (Spanish: ''cubanos'') are the [[citizenship|citizens]] and [[Nationality|nationals]] of the [[Cuba|Republic of Cuba]], as well as members of the [[Cuban diaspora]] who identify culturally or ethnically as Cuban, irrespective of their current citizenship.

Cuba's resident population stood at approximately 9.7&nbsp;million at the end of 2024, according to preliminary figures released by the Oficina Nacional de Estadística e Información (ONEI).<ref name="efe2025">{{cite web |url=https://efe.com/mundo/2025-02-22/crisis-demografica-cuba/ |title=Cuba cerró 2024 con 300.000 habitantes menos que en 2023 y una población de 9,7 millones |website=EFE |date=22 February 2025 |language=es |access-date=19 May 2026}}</ref> According to the ONEI, the country's population has been undergoing a sustained decline driven by the combined effect of significant emigration and a negative rate of natural increase.<ref name="onei2024">{{cite web |url=https://www.onei.gob.cu |title=Oficina Nacional de Estadística e Información |publisher=Oficina Nacional de Estadística e Información (ONEI) |language=es |access-date=19 May 2026}}</ref> Independent demographic analyses suggest that the actual resident population may be lower than official figures indicate, owing in part to an underestimation of emigration to destinations other than the United States.<ref name="albizu">{{cite web |url=https://horizontecubano.law.columbia.edu/news/cuba-demographic-or-systemic-crisis |title=Cuba: Demographic or Systemic Crisis? |last=Albizu-Campos Espiñeira |first=Juan Carlos |website=Horizonte Cubano – Cuba Capacity Building Project |publisher=Columbia Law School |language=en |access-date=19 May 2026}}</ref>

Outside the island, the United States hosts by far the largest Cuban community, estimated at 2.9&nbsp;million people of Cuban origin in 2024, concentrated primarily in Florida—notably in the [[Miami metropolitan area]]—as well as in [[Texas]], California, [[New Jersey]], and New York City.<ref name="pew2026">{{cite web |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/05/07/10-facts-about-cubans-in-the-u-s/ |title=10 Facts about Cubans in the U.S. |last1=Passel |first1=Jeffrey S. |last2=Fahmy |first2=Dalia |website=Pew Research Center |date=7 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="mpi">{{cite web |url=https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/cuban-immigrants-united-states |title=Cuban Immigrants in the United States |website=Migration Policy Institute |date=September 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Spain constitutes the second-largest Cuban diaspora community, with smaller populations present in Brazil, Italy, and [[Uruguay]].<ref name="mpi" />

The population of Cuba descends primarily from three groups: Spanish settlers and immigrants – drawn largely from [[Andalusia]], Galicia, Asturias, and the [[Canary Islands]]<ref>{{cite book |last=Pérez Jr. |first=Louis A. |title=Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2006 |edition=3rd |isbn=978-0-19-517911-8}}</ref> — sub-Saharan Africans transported to the island through the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Klein |first=Herbert S. |title=The Atlantic Slave Trade |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2010 |edition=2nd |isbn=978-0-521-18250-8}}</ref> and the pre-Columbian indigenous peoples, chiefly the [[Taíno]] and [[Ciboney]].<ref name="mendizabal2008">{{cite journal |last1=Mendizabal |first1=Isabel |last2=Sandoval |first2=Karla |last3=Berniell-Lee |first3=Gemma |last4=Calafell |first4=Francesc |last5=Salas |first5=Antonio |last6=Martínez-Fuentes |first6=Antonio |last7=Comas |first7=David |title=Genetic origin, admixture, and asymmetry in maternal and paternal human lineages in Cuba |journal=BMC Evolutionary Biology |volume=8 |article-number=213 |year=2008 |issue=1 |doi=10.1186/1471-2148-8-213 |doi-access=free |pmc=2492877 |pmid=18644108 |bibcode=2008BMCEE...8..213M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lalueza-Fox |first1=Carles |last2=Gilbert |first2=M. Thomas P. |last3=Martínez-Fuentes |first3=Antonio J. |last4=Calafell |first4=Francesc |last5=Bertranpetit |first5=Jaume |title=Mitochondrial DNA from Pre-Columbian Ciboneys from Cuba and the Prehistoric Colonization of the Caribbean |journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology |volume=121 |issue=2 |pages=97–108 |year=2003 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.10236 |pmid=12740952 |bibcode=2003AJPA..121...97L }}</ref> A significant, though demographically contested, share of Cubans carries mixed ancestry from all three groups, not as a product of recent admixture but of centuries of intermarriage accumulated across many generations.<ref name="Sawyer 2006">{{cite book |last=Sawyer |first=Mark Q. |title=Racial Politics in Post-Revolutionary Cuba |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-521-61267-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Cuba |date=2 November 2023 |publisher=Minority Rights Group International |url=https://minorityrights.org/country/cuba/ |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> While [[Afro-Cubans]] and [[White Cubans|Cubans of Spanish descent]] have endured as distinct ethnocultural units, no equivalent indigenous-descended group survived the catastrophic demographic collapse of the sixteenth century;<ref>{{cite book |last=Cook |first=Noble David |title=Born to Die: Disease and New World Conquest, 1492–1650 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1998 |isbn=978-0-521-62730-6}}</ref> [[Taíno]] ancestry nonetheless persists in the Cuban population at the genetic level, as evidenced by mitochondrial DNA studies.<ref name="mendizabal2008"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bukhari |first1=A. |display-authors=etal |title=Taino and African maternal heritage in the Greater Antilles |journal=Gene |volume=637 |pages=33–40 |year=2017 |doi=10.1016/j.gene.2017.09.004 |pmid=28912065}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schroeder |first1=Hannes |display-authors=etal |title=Origins and genetic legacies of the Caribbean Taino |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=115 |issue=10 |pages=2341–2346 |year=2018 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1716839115 |doi-access=free |pmc=5877975 |pmid=29463742 |bibcode=2018PNAS..115.2341S }}</ref> [[Cuban Spanish]], a variety of Spanish, is the native language of virtually all Cubans on the island and remains widely spoken among a large proportion of the diaspora.

== History ==
{{Main|History of Cuba}}

The population of Cuba prior to European contact consisted primarily of the [[Taíno]] and [[Ciboney]] peoples, with smaller groups of [[Guanahatabey]] inhabiting the island's westernmost regions. Spanish colonization, initiated following [[Christopher Columbus]]'s arrival in 1492, resulted in the catastrophic decline of the indigenous population through epidemic disease, forced labor, and violence.<ref name="Perez2010_pp17-22">{{cite book |last=Pérez |first=Louis A. Jr. |title=Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution |edition=4th |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2010 |pages=17–22 |isbn=978-0-19-539296-8}}</ref>

To sustain the plantation economy that emerged in the eighteenth century—centered above all on sugar cultivation—the Spanish colonial administration oversaw the large-scale forced importation of enslaved Africans. By the mid-nineteenth century, Cuba had become one of the largest slave societies in the Western Hemisphere, with Africans and their descendants constituting a substantial portion of the island's population, drawn from numerous West and Central African societies, including Yoruba-, Fon-, and Kongo-speaking peoples.<ref>{{cite book |last=Knight |first=Franklin W. |title=Slave Society in Cuba during the Nineteenth Century |publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |year=1970 |pages=22–57 |isbn=978-0-299-05790-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Scott |first=Rebecca J. |title=Slave Emancipation in Cuba: The Transition to Free Labor, 1860–1899 |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=1985 |pages=3–19 |isbn=978-0-691-07667-6}}</ref>

Spanish settlers—both Iberian-born ''peninsulares'' and American-born ''criollos''—completed the colonial demographic triad. The prolonged and coerced cohabitation among these groups, along with the cultural exchange it engendered, gave rise to a syncretic society whose religious practices, music, and social customs reflected multiple origins. The Cuban ethnologist [[Fernando Ortiz Fernández|Fernando Ortiz]] described this process as ''[[transculturation]]''—a term he coined to denote the mutual transformation of cultures in sustained contact—and identified it as a defining characteristic of Cuban civilization.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ortiz |first=Fernando |title=Cuban Counterpoint: Tobacco and Sugar |others=Translated by Harriet de Onís |publisher=Duke University Press |year=1995 |orig-date=1940 |pages=97–103 |isbn=978-0-8223-1616-9}}</ref>

[[File:Cuba - The evening meal.jpg|thumb|A Cuban family at the evening meal, circa 1875.]]

By the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, a distinct creole consciousness—often articulated under the rubric of [[Cubanidad]]—had begun to emerge among the island's non-peninsular population. This developing identity was shaped by the plantation economy, by the growth of [[Havana]] as a cosmopolitan urban center, and by the proliferation of cultural forms that drew simultaneously on African, Spanish, and residual indigenous influences, including the [[danzón]], the [[décima]], the syncretic religious practices associated with [[Santería|Regla de Ocha]], and the mutual-aid and ritual societies of the [[Abakuá]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Pérez |first=Louis A. Jr. |title=On Becoming Cuban: Identity, Nationality, and Culture |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=1999 |pages=14–27 |isbn=978-0-8078-2487-0}}</ref> The emergence of a distinctly Cuban cultural identity developed alongside the political tensions of colonial society, including resentment of Spanish trade restrictions, the contradictions of a slaveholding creole elite seeking greater autonomy, and the gradual emergence of abolitionist sentiment.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pérez |first=Louis A. Jr. |title=Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution |edition=4th |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2010 |pages=78–104 |isbn=978-0-19-539296-8}}</ref>

The articulation of Cuban national identity as an explicit political project reached a decisive stage during the independence struggles of the second half of the nineteenth century. The [[Ten Years' War]] (1868–1878), initiated in part by creole planters such as [[Carlos Manuel de Céspedes]]—who freed his own slaves at the outset of the insurgency—placed questions of race and inclusion at the center of the emerging nationalist movement.<ref name="Ferrer1999_pp15">{{cite book |last=Ferrer |first=Ada |title=Insurgent Cuba: Race, Nation, and Revolution, 1868–1898 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=1999 |pages=15–42 |isbn=978-0-8078-4783-1}}</ref> The figure of [[José Martí]], the leading ideologue of Cuban independence, gave the movement its most influential theoretical expression. In essays including ''[[Nuestra América]]'' (1891) and ''Mi raza'' (1893), Martí argued that racial divisions were incompatible with the construction of a free republic and that Cuban identity itself constituted the basis of national unity.<ref name="Ferrer1999_pp112">{{cite book |last=Ferrer |first=Ada |title=Insurgent Cuba: Race, Nation, and Revolution, 1868–1898 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=1999 |pages=112–136 |isbn=978-0-8078-4783-1}}</ref> The [[Cuban War of Independence]] (1895–1898) gave material form to this vision: the ''[[mambí]]'' insurgent armies were notably multiracial in composition, and Afro-Cuban officers—most prominently [[Antonio Maceo]], known as the "Bronze Titan"—achieved prominence at the highest levels of command. The war's conclusion, however, brought not sovereignty but [[Spanish–American War|American military intervention]] and a prolonged period of U.S. occupation and political oversight, which significantly shaped the subsequent development of Cuban national identity.<ref name="Perez2003_pp147">{{cite book |last=Pérez |first=Louis A. Jr. |title=Cuba and the United States: Ties of Singular Intimacy |edition=3rd |publisher=University of Georgia Press |year=2003 |pages=147–178 |isbn=978-0-8203-2483-8}}</ref>

[[File:President Elect Gerardo Machado of Cuba, with daughter & 2 friends, (4-15-25) LCCN2016839603.jpg|thumb|[[Gerardo Machado]], president-elect of Cuba, photographed with his daughter and two companions on April 15, 1925. Machado was inaugurated on May 20, 1925, and governed Cuba until his forced resignation and exile in August 1933 amid the [[Revolution of 1933]].]]

The Cuban Republic established in 1902 inherited both the egalitarian ideals of the independence movement and the racial inequalities of the colonial period. The official republican ideology was grounded in Martí's concept of raceless nationalism, yet historians have argued that this universalist framework often discouraged autonomous Afro-Cuban political mobilization by portraying race-based advocacy as contrary to national unity.<ref name="deLaFuente2001_pp35">{{cite book |last=de la Fuente |first=Alejandro |title=A Nation for All: Race, Inequality, and Politics in Twentieth-Century Cuba |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2001 |pages=35–69 |isbn=978-0-8078-4922-4}}</ref> The [[Partido Independiente de Color]], founded in 1908 to advocate for Afro-Cuban political representation, was outlawed under the [[Morúa Amendment]] of 1910; its armed protest in 1912 was met with military suppression in which thousands of Afro-Cubans were killed.<ref>{{cite book |last=Helg |first=Aline |title=Our Rightful Share: The Afro-Cuban Struggle for Equality, 1886–1912 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=1995 |pages=193–226 |isbn=978-0-8078-4494-6}}</ref> Nonetheless, the [[Afrocubanismo]] cultural movement of the 1920s and 1930s—associated with figures including the poet [[Nicolás Guillén]], the novelist [[Alejo Carpentier]], and Ortiz himself—reasserted the African dimension of Cuban culture as fundamental to national identity.<ref name="deLaFuente2001_pp144">{{cite book |last=de la Fuente |first=Alejandro |title=A Nation for All: Race, Inequality, and Politics in Twentieth-Century Cuba |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2001 |pages=144–175 |isbn=978-0-8078-4922-4}}</ref> At the same time, the pervasive economic, political, and cultural influence of the United States contributed to the development of a reactive nationalism through which many Cubans increasingly defined their collective identity in opposition to American dominance.<ref name="Perez2003_pp147" />

[[File:Ecole primaire publique laïque à Cuba,.jpg|thumb|A public primary school classroom in Cuba. The Cuban state provides free, [[Education in Cuba|universal education]] from primary through university level, a system expanded after the [[Cuban Revolution]] and notable for achieving near-total [[Literacy in Cuba|literacy]] through the nationwide [[Cuban Literacy Campaign|1961 literacy campaign]].]]

The [[Cuban Revolution]] of 1959, led by [[Fidel Castro]] and the [[26th of July Movement]], represented both a political rupture and an attempt to reconstruct Cuban national identity on new ideological foundations. The revolutionary government declared the elimination of racial discrimination an immediate social objective and moved to dismantle many of the institutional structures it identified as mechanisms through which inequality had been reproduced.<ref name="deLaFuente2001_pp259">{{cite book |last=de la Fuente |first=Alejandro |title=A Nation for All: Race, Inequality, and Politics in Twentieth-Century Cuba |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2001 |pages=259–285 |isbn=978-0-8078-4922-4}}</ref> National identity was increasingly reframed in terms of revolutionary commitment and socialist internationalism. The ideal of the ''[[New Man (Marxism)|hombre nuevo]]'' (new man), theorized by [[Che Guevara]] in his 1965 essay ''El socialismo y el hombre en Cuba'', emphasized collective sacrifice, socialist construction, and anti-imperialism.<ref name="PerezStable1999_pp84">{{cite book |last=Pérez-Stable |first=Marifeli |title=The Cuban Revolution: Origins, Course, and Legacy |edition=2nd |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1999 |pages=84–112 |isbn=978-0-19-512749-2}}</ref> This anti-imperialist identity was projected internationally through Cuba's military and civilian interventions in Africa and Latin America, most notably in [[Angola]], where Cuban forces supported the [[MPLA]] government against [[UNITA]] and South African forces between 1975 and 1991, and in [[Ethiopia]], where Cuba intervened on behalf of the [[Derg]] during the [[Ogaden War]] of 1977–1978.<ref name="Gleijeses2002_pp246">{{cite book |last=Gleijeses |first=Piero |title=Conflicting Missions: Havana, Washington, and Africa, 1959–1976 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2002 |pages=246–280 |isbn=978-0-8078-2647-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Gleijeses |first=Piero |title=Visions of Freedom: Havana, Washington, Pretoria, and the Struggle for Southern Africa, 1976–1991 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2013 |pages=1–18 |isbn=978-1-4696-0968-3}}</ref> These interventions were presented by the Cuban government as expressions of [[Third Worldism|Third-Worldist]] solidarity and as continuations of anti-colonial struggle, drawing explicitly on Cuba's historical experiences of colonialism and slavery and on Martí's anti-imperialist legacy.<ref name="Gleijeses2002_pp13">{{cite book |last=Gleijeses |first=Piero |title=Conflicting Missions: Havana, Washington, and Africa, 1959–1976 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2002 |pages=13–40 |isbn=978-0-8078-2647-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Kapcia |first=Antoni |title=Cuba in Revolution: A History Since the Fifties |publisher=Reaktion Books |year=2008 |pages=118–145 |isbn=978-1-86189-402-1}}</ref> The revolution's emphasis on a unitary, state-centered national identity simultaneously marginalized political dissent and contributed to the formation of a substantial emigrant diaspora, particularly in the United States, whose members developed competing interpretations of [[Cuban Americans|Cuban identity]] rooted in exile and opposition to the revolutionary state.<ref name="PerezStable1999_pp155">{{cite book |last=Pérez-Stable |first=Marifeli |title=The Cuban Revolution: Origins, Course, and Legacy |edition=2nd |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1999 |pages=155–178 |isbn=978-0-19-512749-2}}</ref>

== Demographics of Cuba ==
{{Main|Demographics of Cuba}}

=== Census data ===

[[File:Enumerators, city of Habana.jpg|thumb|250px|Census enumerators in the city of Havana, 1899.]]

The [[Cuban Census of 2012]], conducted between 15 and 24 September of that year by the [[National Office of Statistics and Information]] (''Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información'', ONEI), remains, as of 2026, the most recent completed national population census on the island.<ref name="ONEI2012prel">{{cite web |author=Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información |title=Informe sobre Cifras Preliminares. Censo de Población y Viviendas 2012 |url=https://adsdatabase.ohchr.org/IssueLibrary/ONEI_Censo%20de%20Poblacion%20y%20Viviendas%202012.pdf |date=December 2012 |access-date=22 May 2026 |publisher=ONEI}}</ref> Cuba follows a decennial census cycle;<ref name="ONEI2012prel" /> a new Population and Housing Census had originally been scheduled for September 2022,<ref name="Granma2021">{{cite news |title=Los censos en Cuba |url=https://www.granma.cu/cuba/2021-10-12/los-censos-en-cuba-12-10-2021-00-10-23 |newspaper=[[Granma (newspaper)|Granma]] |date=12 October 2021 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> but has been postponed on multiple occasions – first to 2025, then to 2026 – owing to the country's severe [[Cuban economic crisis (2019–present)|economic crisis]] and the logistical constraints it has produced.<ref name="EFE2025">{{cite news |agency=[[EFE]] |title=Cuba prevé realizar el censo de población a finales de 2025 pero no descarta un retraso |url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/cuba-prev%C3%A9-realizar-el-censo-de-poblaci%C3%B3n-a-finales-de-2025-pero-no-descarta-un-retraso/89528268 |newspaper=[[SWI swissinfo.ch]] |date=17 June 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="Cubanet2024">{{cite news |title=Régimen confirma retraso del Censo de Población y Viviendas al menos hasta 2025 |url=https://www.cubanet.org/regimen-confirma-retraso-del-censo-de-poblacion-y-viviendas-al-menos-hasta-2025/ |newspaper=Cubanet |date=5 June 2024 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="MEP2026">{{cite web |author=Ministerio de Economía y Planificación |title=Realizarán en 2025 Censo de Población |url=https://www.mep.gob.cu/en/node/2660 |date=4 March 2026 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> ONEI conducted a census rehearsal in the municipality of [[Santa Cruz del Norte]], [[Mayabeque Province|Mayabeque]], in November 2025 in preparation for the 2026 census; the full results had not been published as of mid-year.<ref name="Granma2025">{{cite news |title=Cuba prepara censo de población y viviendas en 2026 |url=https://www.granma.cu/cuba/2025-10-20/cuba-prepara-censo-de-poblacion-y-viviendas-en-2026-20-10-2025-12-10-32 |newspaper=[[Granma (newspaper)|Granma]] |date=20 October 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="PL2025">{{cite web |title=Cuba prepara censo de población y viviendas en 2026 |url=https://www.prensa-latina.cu/2025/10/17/cuba-prepara-censo-de-poblacion-y-viviendas-en-2026/ |publisher=[[Prensa Latina]] |date=17 October 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> The demographic data presented in this section accordingly reflect conditions recorded in September 2012; subsequent changes are summarised in the subsection below.

According to the 2012 census, Cuba's resident population stood at 11,167,325 inhabitants, of whom 5,570,825 were male and 5,596,500 female, yielding a [[sex ratio]] of 995 males per 1,000 females.<ref name="ONEI2014">{{cite web |author=Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información |title=Informe Nacional. Resultados Definitivos de Indicadores Seleccionados en Cuba, Provincias y Municipios. Censo de Población y Viviendas 2012 |url=https://cubamemorias.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Cuba_INFORME_NACIONAL_CENSO_2012.pdf |year=2014 |access-date=22 May 2026 |publisher=ONEI}}</ref> This figure represented a slight decline from the 11,177,743 inhabitants recorded in the [[Cuban Census of 2002|2002 census]] — the first intercensal population decrease since the [[Cuban War of Independence|independence wars]] — attributable to a [[total fertility rate]] below [[replacement-level fertility|replacement level]] and a negative [[net migration rate|migration balance]].<ref name="ONEI2014" /><ref name="Cubanet2021">{{cite web |title=Censos de población en Cuba: apuntes históricos (II) |url=https://www.cubanet.org/censos-de-poblacion-en-cuba-apuntes-historicos-ii/ |publisher=Cubanet |date=24 September 2021 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> The most populous municipalities at the time of the census were [[Havana]] (2,106,146 inhabitants), [[Santiago de Cuba (municipality)|Santiago de Cuba]] (506,037), [[Holguín (municipality)|Holguín]] (346,195), [[Camagüey (municipality)|Camagüey]] (323,309), and [[Santa Clara, Cuba|Santa Clara]] (240,543).<ref name="ONEI2012prel" /><ref name="ONEI2014" />

=== Demographic changes since 2012 ===

Cuba's population has undergone accelerating decline since the [[Cuban Census of 2012|2012 census]], driven by three mutually reinforcing simultaneous processes: a [[total fertility rate]] that has remained persistently below [[replacement-level fertility|replacement level]], a negative [[natural population growth|natural increase]] — with deaths consistently exceeding births – and [[Cuban emigration|mass emigration]] of historically unprecedented scale.<ref name="ONEI2025conf">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]] |title=Éramos 9 millones 748 mil 007 habitantes al cierre de 2024 en Cuba |url=https://www.onei.gob.cu/node/2586 |date=23 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |publisher=ONEI}}</ref><ref name="Cubadebate2024ago">{{cite news |title=ONEI actualiza sobre indicadores de población efectiva en Cuba |url=http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2024/08/10/onei-actualiza-sobre-indicadores-de-poblacion-efectiva-en-cuba/ |newspaper=[[Cubadebate]] |date=10 August 2024 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref>

{{Chart|definition=Cuba Total Population.chart|data=Cuba Total Population.tab|width=700px|title=Cuban population residing in Cuba}}

=== Fertility rate and natural population change ===

Cuba has not reached [[replacement-level fertility]] since 1977 – though some official Cuban sources, such as the country's 2017 report to the UN Commission on Population and Development and the ''Statistical Health Yearbook 2022'', place the definitive fall below the threshold of 2.1 children per woman in 1978 —,<ref name="ENF2022">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]]–CEPDE |title=Encuesta Nacional de Fecundidad, Cuba, 2022 |url=https://www.infomed.scu.sld.cu/encuesta-nacional-de-fecundidad-cuba-2022/ |website=Infomed Santiago de Cuba |date=9 August 2023 |access-date=22 May 2026 |quote=Reproduces data from the primary report ONEI–CEPDE, ''Encuesta Nacional de Fecundidad ENF-2022'' (Havana, 2023).}}</ref> placing it among the earliest and most prolonged cases of sub-replacement fertility among [[developing country|developing economies]].<ref name="Farnosc2006">{{cite journal |last=Farnós Morejón |first=Alfonso |title=El descenso de la fecundidad en Cuba: de la Primera a la segunda transición demográfica |journal=Revista Cubana de Salud Pública |year=2006 |volume=32 |number=1 |url=http://scielo.sld.cu/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0864-34662006000100002 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="CEPAL2016">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]] |title=Informe de Cuba a la Tercera Reunión de la Conferencia Regional sobre Población y Desarrollo de América Latina y el Caribe |url=https://crpd.cepal.org/3/sites/crpd3/files/informe_cuba.pdf |publisher=CEPAL |year=2016 |access-date=22 May 2026 }}</ref>

The [[total fertility rate]] (TFR) fluctuated between 1.41 and 1.54 children per woman during the 2021–2023 triennium<ref name="SemMex2024" /> and fell to 1.29 in 2024 – the lowest value ever recorded in the country's history —,<ref name="ONEI2025conf_baja">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]] |title=Éramos 9 millones 748 mil 007 habitantes al cierre de 2024 en Cuba |url=https://www.onei.gob.cu/node/2586 |date=23 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |website=ONEI}}</ref><ref name="Javeriana2025">{{cite web |title=Cuba pierde población a un ritmo alarmante: entre la demografía y la crisis estructural |url=https://www.javerianacali.edu.co/noticias/cuba-pierde-poblacion-un-ritmo-alarmante-entre-la-demografia-y-la-crisis-estructural |website=[[Pontificia Universidad Javeriana]] Cali |date=28 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> well below the replacement threshold of 2.1. In 2024, registered live births totalled 71,358 – the lowest annual figure in 65 years —,<ref name="ONEI2025conf_baja" /><ref name="JTec2025">{{cite news |title=Población efectiva de Cuba decreció en 2024 |url=https://www.juventudtecnica.cu/articulos/poblacion-efectiva-de-cuba-decrecio-en-2024/ |newspaper=Juventud Técnica |date=24 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> with a [[crude birth rate]] of 7.2 per 1,000 inhabitants,<ref name="ONEI2025conf_baja" /> while registered deaths reached 128,098,<ref name="ONEI2025conf_baja" /><ref name="Cubadebate2025jun">{{cite news |title=Cuba en datos: la población cubana envejece, decrece y se urbaniza |url=http://www.cubadebate.cu/especiales/2025/06/12/cuba-en-datos-la-poblacion-cubana-envejece-decrece-y-se-urbaniza-video/ |newspaper=[[Cubadebate]] |date=12 June 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> producing a [[natural population growth|natural decrease]] of 56,740 persons<ref name="DiarioCuba2025dem">{{cite news |title=Solo un municipio de Cuba ganó población en 2024, el año de menos nacimientos desde 1960 |url=https://diariodecuba.com/cuba/1748019562_61256.html |newspaper=Diario de Cuba |date=23 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="JTec2025" /> and a deaths-to-births ratio of approximately 1.8:1. Deaths have continuously exceeded births since 2020.<ref name="ONEI2025conf_baja" /><ref name="Cubadebate2025jun" />

The combination of very low fertility with relatively high [[life expectancy]] reflects the social policies implemented following the [[Cuban Revolution]] of 1959 — [[universal health care|universal healthcare]], broad access to [[contraception|contraceptive methods]] and to abortion (institutionalised in 1965, making Cuba the first country in [[Latin America and the Caribbean]] to do so) —,<ref name="Granma2022aborto">{{cite news |title=El aborto en Cuba y el derecho a decidir |url=https://www.granma.cu/cuestion-de-leyes/2022-08-18/el-aborto-en-cuba-y-el-derecho-a-decidir-18-08-2022-00-08-00 |newspaper=[[Granma (newspaper)|Granma]] |date=18 August 2022 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> as well as high rates of female [[school enrolment]] and women's participation in the [[labour market]], which together produced a [[demographic transition]] characteristic of [[developed country|high-income societies]] without the corresponding level of [[economic development]].<ref name="GarciaQuinones2022">{{cite journal |title=La dinámica poblacional en el socialismo cubano |journal=Economía y Desarrollo |publisher=[[University of Havana]] |year=2022 |url=https://www.redalyc.org/journal/3238/323830084005/html/ |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="CEPAL2016" />

=== Median age ===

Cuba's [[median age]] stood at 39.5 years at the time of the [[Cuban Census of 2012|2012 census]],<ref name="ONEI2012mediana">{{cite news |title=Cuba en números: lo que el Censo nos dejó |url=http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2014/04/16/cuba-en-numeros-lo-que-el-censo-nos-dejo/ |newspaper=[[Cubadebate]] |date=16 April 2014 |access-date=22 May 2026 |quote=Data presented at a televised round table by ONEI officials: "the mean and median ages of Cuba's population rose to 38.8 and 39.5 years respectively".}}</ref> and had increased to approximately 42.5 years in the 2025–2026 period according to the 2024 revision of the [[World Population Prospects]] by the [[United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs|United Nations Population Division]].<ref name="WPP2024Cuba">{{cite web |author=[[United Nations Population Division]] |title=World Population Prospects 2024: Data Portal — Cuba Profiles |url=https://population.un.org/wpp/ |publisher=United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en |quote=Data corresponding to median age estimates and projections for 2025 and 2026 under the medium fertility variant.}}</ref> This figure contrasts markedly with the regional median age for [[Latin America and the Caribbean]], which stood at approximately 31 years in 2024 according to the [[Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean|ECLAC]].<ref name="CEPAL2024mediana">{{cite web |author=[[Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean]] |title=Population Growth in Latin America and the Caribbean Falls Below Expectations and Region's Total Population Reaches 663 Million in 2024 |url=https://www.cepal.org/en/pressreleases/population-growth-latin-america-and-caribbean-falls-below-expectations-and-regions |date=November 2024 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

Excluding [[Puerto Rico]] by virtue of its status as an [[Unincorporated territories of the United States|unincorporated territory]] — whose median age, at approximately 46.7 years, exceeds that of the island – Cuba is the sovereign country with the highest median age in the Americas, ahead of Canada (~40.6 years)<ref name="StatsCan2025">{{cite web |author=[[Statistics Canada]] |title=Canada's population estimates: Age and gender, July 1, 2025 |url=https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/250924/dq250924a-eng.htm |date=24 September 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> and the United States (~39.1 years).<ref name="Census2025med">{{cite web |author=[[United States Census Bureau]] |title=Older Adults Outnumber Children in 11 States and Nearly Half of U.S. Counties |url=https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/older-adults-outnumber-children.html |date=26 June 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Census2026med">{{cite web |author=[[United States Census Bureau]] |title=U.S. Population Aging as Nation Turns 250 |url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2026/04/age-and-sex.html |date=April 2026 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> This places Cuba in a demographic profile comparable to that of France (~42–43 years) and other Western European nations with [[developed country|advanced economies]].<ref name="CIAWFB2025comp">{{cite web |author=[[Central Intelligence Agency]] |title=Median Age — Country Comparison |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/field/median-age/country-comparison/ |publisher=The World Factbook 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In 2024, approximately 25.7% of Cuba's resident population was aged 60 or over, the highest proportion in Latin America and the Caribbean.<ref name="ONEI2025aging">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]] |title=Éramos 9 millones 748 mil 007 habitantes al cierre de 2024 en Cuba |url=https://www.onei.gob.cu/node/2586 |date=23 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |publisher=ONEI |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606174258/https://www.onei.gob.cu/node/2586 |archive-date=6 June 2025}}</ref><ref name="OnCuba2025aging">{{cite news |title=Cuba tras el 2024: un país más envejecido y cada vez con menos habitantes |url=https://oncubanews.com/cuba/sociedad-cuba/cuba-tras-el-2024-un-pais-mas-envejecido-y-cada-vez-con-menos-habitantes/ |newspaper=OnCuba News |date=24 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref>

This demographic profile – the product of historically low [[fertility rate]]s, relatively high [[life expectancy]], and the [[Cuban emigration|disproportionate emigration of young adults]] — is typically associated with high-income economies.<ref name="Farnosc2006"/><ref name="CEPAL2016Cuba">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]] |title=Informe de Cuba a la Tercera Reunión de la Conferencia Regional sobre Población y Desarrollo de América Latina y el Caribe |url=https://crpd.cepal.org/3/sites/crpd3/files/informe_cuba.pdf |publisher=[[Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean|CEPAL]] |year=2016 |access-date=22 May 2026 }}</ref> Cuba's advanced median age, coexisting with a comparatively low per capita income, constitutes a structurally anomalous demographic condition: among countries whose median age exceeds forty years, Cuba ranks among those with the lowest incomes, though figures for [[Economy of Cuba|Cuban GDP]] are not reported by the [[International Monetary Fund]] and available estimates vary considerably depending on the methodology employed.<ref name="IMFCubaAusencia">{{cite web |author=[[International Monetary Fund]] |title=World Economic Outlook Database, April 2025 |url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WEO/weo-database/2025/April |date=April 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en |quote=Cuba does not appear in the IMF database due to the absence of current verifiable economic data.}}</ref><ref name="WorldBankCubaGDP">{{cite web |author=[[World Bank]] |title=GDP per capita (current US$) — Cuba |url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.CD?locations=CU |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Sex distribution ===

According to the [[Cuban Census of 2012|2012 census]], the sex distribution of the Cuban population was nearly balanced, with 5,570,825 males and 5,596,500 females, corresponding to a [[sex ratio]] of 995 males per 1,000 females.<ref name="ONEI2012sexo">{{cite news |title=Cuba en números: lo que el Censo nos dejó |url=http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2014/04/16/cuba-en-numeros-lo-que-el-censo-nos-dejo/ |newspaper=[[Cubadebate]] |date=16 April 2014 |access-date=22 May 2026 |quote=ONEI data presented at a televised round table following the publication of the definitive results of the 2012 Census.}}</ref> At the close of 2024, ONEI recorded a ratio of 974 males per 1,000 females (4,808,909 males and 4,939,098 females), evidencing a measurable shift in the sex balance relative to the 2012 census.<ref name="ONEI2025node">{{cite web |author=[[National Office of Statistics and Information|Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información]] |title=Éramos 9 millones 748 mil 007 habitantes al cierre de 2024 en Cuba |url=https://www.onei.gob.cu/node/2586 |date=23 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026 |website=Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información}}</ref><ref name="Cubadebate2025sexo">{{cite news |title=La población cubana decreció en 307.961 habitantes en 2024 |url=http://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2025/05/23/la-poblacion-cubana-decrecio-en-307-961-habitantes-en-2024/ |newspaper=[[Cubadebate]] |date=23 May 2025 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref>

[[File:Cuba population pyramid 2026.png|thumb|right|alt=Population pyramid of Cuba for the year 2026.|Population pyramid of Cuba, 2026.]]

The migratory wave that began in 2021 has been characterised by a high proportion of women, accentuating a trend towards the [[feminisation of migration]] that, according to the academic literature, has been consolidating within [[Cuban emigration]] since the 1990s and reached unprecedented magnitude during the period 2021–2024.<ref name="AjaDiaz2017">{{cite journal |last=Aja Díaz |first=Antonio |title=La migración internacional de Cuba. Escenarios actuales |journal=Novedades en Población |publisher=Centro de Estudios Demográficos, [[University of Havana]] |year=2017 |volume=13 |number=26 |url=http://scielo.sld.cu/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1817-40782017000200004 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="Scielo2018ESP">{{cite journal |last1=Sosa |first1=Jorge Luis |last2=Pérez-Díaz |first2=Addiel |title=Las principales tendencias de la comunidad de emigrantes cubanos en España en los albores del siglo XXI |journal=Papeles de Población |publisher=[[Universidad Autónoma del Estado de México]] |year=2018 |volume=24 |issue=97 |pages=195–225 |doi=10.22185/24487147.2018.97.30 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="AlbizuCampos2024">{{cite journal |last=Albizu-Campos Espiñeira |first=Juan Carlos |title=Cuba. Una rápida mirada a la emigración y la población |website=Cuba Capacity Building Project |publisher=[[Columbia University]] |date=15 July 2024 |url=https://horizontecubano.law.columbia.edu/news/cuba-una-rapida-mirada-la-emigracion-y-la-poblacion |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> Approximately 56–57% of Cuban emigrants in the recent period were women – 56.6% according to the accumulated historical stock per UN data, and approximately 57% according to estimates of outgoing flows for 2022–2023 – as reported in the United Nations [[United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs|''International Migrant Stock'']]<ref name="UNIMS2024">{{cite web |author=[[United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs|United Nations, Population Division]] |title=International Migrant Stock 2024 |url=https://population.un.org/dataportal/home/ |year=2024 |access-date=22 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> and in analyses by economist and demographer Juan Carlos Albizu-Campos published through the Cuba Capacity Building Project at [[Columbia Law School]].<ref name="AlbizuColumbia2024">{{cite web |last=Albizu-Campos Espiñeira |first=Juan Carlos |title=Cuba: una rápida mirada a la emigración y la población |url=https://horizontecubano.law.columbia.edu/news/cuba-una-rapida-mirada-la-emigracion-y-la-poblacion |website=Horizonte Cubano, Cuba Capacity Building Project, Columbia Law School |date=July 2024 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="Estornudo2024">{{cite news |title=Menos cubanos en Cuba. ¿Cómo llegamos a esta crisis? |url=https://revistaelestornudo.com/crisis-demografica-cuba/ |newspaper=El Estornudo |date=July 2024 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> With regard to age structure, approximately 77% of the emigrant contingent was of working age, with estimates ranging between the 15–59 age bracket – used in Albizu-Campos's calculations,<ref name="AlbizuColumbia2024" /> in line with the Cuban definition of the [[working-age population|economically active population]] — and the 15–49 bracket, the standard demographic range for [[reproductive age]], employed by other sources.<ref name="UNAV2025sexo">{{cite web |title=Cuba se vacía: éxodo de un millón de personas que deja una población envejecida |url=https://www.unav.edu/web/global-affairs/cuba-se-vacia-exodo-de-un-millon-de-personas-que-deja-una-poblacion-envejecida |website=Global Affairs and Strategic Studies |publisher=[[University of Navarra]] |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> ONEI confirmed that by the close of 2023 the contingent of women of [[childbearing age]] (15–49 years) had decreased by 304,717 persons relative to the preceding reference calculation, with more than 70% of that loss concentrated in the 15–39 age group.<ref name="SemMex2024">{{cite news |title=Cuba: migraciones agravan brechas de género |url=https://semmexico.mx/cuba-migraciones-agravan-brechas-de-genero/ |newspaper=SemMéxico / SEMlac |date=23 September 2024 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="Cubadebate2024ago"/>

This dynamic has altered not only the size of the population but also the relative balance between the sexes – reflected in the decline of the masculinity ratio from 995 to 974 between 2012 and 2024 – and the age composition of the [[reproductive age|population of reproductive age]], with direct consequences for the [[fertility rate|total fertility rate]]<ref name="SemMex2024" /> and the structure of the labour market. The precise impact on the age and sex distribution cannot, however, be determined with census-level accuracy in the absence of an updated enumeration.<ref name="ONEI2025node" />

== Ethnography of Cuba ==
[[File:Young Boys in School Uniform - Pinar del Rio - Cuba.JPG|thumb|upright|Children in primary school uniforms in Pinar del Río.]]The ethnic and racial composition of Cuba is the product of a prolonged historical process of [[mestizaje|racial mixing]], forced displacement, and voluntary migration.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pérez |first=Louis A. Jr. |title=Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution |edition=4th |year=2010 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=New York |isbn=978-0-19-539296-8}}</ref>

The population classified as [[White Cubans|white]] descends primarily from [[Spaniards|Peninsular settlers and immigrants]], with a particularly notable presence of individuals from [[Andalusia]], the [[Canary Islands]], Asturias, and [[Galicia (Spain)|Galicia]] — regions whose imprint is still evident in the island's culture, speech, and toponymy.<ref>{{cite book |last=Naranjo Orovio |first=Consuelo |others=coord. |title=Historia de Cuba |series=Historia de las Antillas |volume=1 |year=2009 |publisher=CSIC / Doce Calles |location=Madrid |isbn=978-84-9744-077-6}}</ref>

The [[Afro-Cubans|black population]] derives primarily from the [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]ns introduced as enslaved people during the [[Atlantic slave trade]], which reached its greatest intensity between the late eighteenth century and the mid-nineteenth century, and in which individuals from the [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]], [[Fon people|Fon]], and [[Bantu peoples|Bantu]] peoples predominated, among other groups from West and Central Africa.<ref>{{cite book |last=Moreno Fraginals |first=Manuel |title=El Ingenio: Complejo económico social cubano del azúcar |year=1978 |publisher=Editorial de Ciencias Sociales |location=Havana}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Ortiz |first=Fernando |title=Los negros esclavos |year=1916 |publisher=Revista Bimestre Cubana |location=Havana}}</ref>

The indigenous peoples, principally of [[Taíno]] origin, largely disappeared during the first decades of colonisation as a result of violence, disease, and forced labour. Although no communities of unmixed Amerindian descent are recorded today, genetic studies point to the persistence of traces of that ancestral heritage in segments of the present population.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rouse |first=Irving |title=The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus |year=1992 |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |isbn=978-0-300-05696-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Marcheco-Teruel |first=Beatriz |author2=Parra, Esteban J. |author3=Fuentes-Smith, Evelyn |author4=Salas, Antonio |author5=Buttenschøn, Henriette N. |author6=Demontis, Ditte |author7=Torres-Español, María |author8=Marín-Padrón, Lilia C. |author9=Gómez-Cabezas, Enrique J. |author10=Álvarez-Iglesias, Vanesa |author11=Mosquera-Miguel, Ana |author12=Martínez-Fuentes, Antonio |author13=Carracedo, Ángel |author14=Børglum, Anders D. |author15=Mors, Ole |title=Cuba: Exploring the History of Admixture and the Genetic Basis of Pigmentation Using Autosomal and Uniparental Markers |journal=PLOS Genetics |year=2014 |volume=10 |number=7 |article-number=e1004488 |doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1004488 |doi-access=free |pmid=25058410 |pmc=4109857}}</ref>

To these principal streams are added, on a smaller scale, the descendants of Chinese workers who arrived under contract during the nineteenth century<ref>{{cite book |last=López |first=Kathleen M. |title=Chinese Cubans: A Transnational History |year=2013 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |location=Chapel Hill |isbn=978-1-4696-0712-2}}</ref> and those of immigrants from the Arab Levant, whose presence on the island consolidated between the late nineteenth century and the first half of the twentieth.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Klich |first1=Ignacio |last2=Lesser |first2=Jeffrey |title=Arab and Jewish Immigrants in Latin America: Images and Realities |year=1998 |publisher=Frank Cass |location=London |isbn=978-0-7146-4450-9}}</ref> A considerable proportion of Cubans carry mixed lineages combining, in varying proportions and across multiple generations, Spanish, African, and indigenous heritage.

=== Main ancestral and ethnic origins of the Cuban population ===

=== Pre-Columbian peoples ===
Cuba does not include an indigenous self-identification category in its official population surveys ([[Oficina Nacional de Estadística e Información]], ONEI), meaning that Amerindian ancestry can only be quantified through genetic studies.
At the arrival of [[Christopher Columbus]] in 1492, Cuba was inhabited by at least three distinct indigenous groups.

[[File:1919_The_Barrientos_family.jpg|thumb|right|250px|The Barrientos family, headed by an indigenous-descended woman from Baracoa, Cuba, and a Spanish ex-soldier, 1919.]]

==== Guanahatabey ====
The [[Guanahatabey]] were the earliest documented inhabitants, archaic [[hunter-gatherer]]s settled in the western tip of the island from approximately 4000 BC,<ref>{{cite book |last=Rouse |first=Irving |title=The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1992 |location=New Haven |isbn=0-300-05181-6 |pages=17–21}}</ref> whose language shows no demonstrable relationship to [[Taíno language|Taíno]] or any other documented language of the Arawakan family.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilson |first=Samuel M. |title=The Indigenous People of the Caribbean |publisher=University Press of Florida |year=1997 |location=Gainesville |isbn=978-0-8130-1531-6}}</ref>

==== Ciboney ====
The [[Ciboney]] (or Siboney), a Western Arawakan group, inhabited the central and western parts of the island. Although various sources describe them as the most geographically widespread group at the time of contact, their status as the most numerous is a matter of academic debate, given that the Taíno maintained higher-density settlements in the east.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rouse |first=Irving |title=The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1992 |location=New Haven |isbn=0-300-05181-6 |pages=20–24}}</ref>

==== Taíno ====
The [[Taíno people|Taíno]], an Arawakan people originating from the South American lowlands and possessing a more advanced level of technological development than the preceding groups, occupied primarily the eastern and central parts of Cuba and were the first group contacted by Columbus when he landed on the island's eastern shores on 28 October 1492.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rouse |first=Irving |title=The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1992 |location=New Haven |isbn=0-300-05181-6 |pages=5–10}}</ref> Estimates of the pre-contact indigenous population range from approximately 60,000 to 600,000, with the most recent academic estimates clustering toward the lower end of that range.<ref>{{cite book |last=Cook |first=Noble David |title=Born to Die: Disease and New World Conquest, 1492–1650 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1998 |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-521-62208-0 |pages=15–24}}</ref>
The Taíno were organised in villages under hereditary leaders called [[cacique]]s, practised the cultivation of maize and cassava, and developed a material culture whose imprint persists in contemporary Cuba: words such as ''tabaco'', ''hamaca'', and ''canoa'', as well as numerous [[toponymy|toponyms]] — among them [[Havana]], [[Camagüey]], and [[Baracoa]] — derive from the Taíno language.<ref>{{cite book |last=Keegan |first=William F. |title=Taino Indian Myth and Practice: The Arrival of the Stranger King |publisher=University Press of Florida |year=2007 |location=Gainesville |isbn=978-0-8130-3038-8}}</ref>

==== Spanish conquest and demographic collapse ====
The Spanish conquest of Cuba, initiated under [[Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar]] from 1511 onwards, brought about the near-total destruction of the indigenous population within a few decades.<ref>{{cite book |last=Thomas |first=Hugh |title=Cuba or the Pursuit of Freedom |publisher=Da Capo Press |year=1998 |orig-date=1971 |location=New York |isbn=978-0-306-80827-2 |pages=17–45}}</ref> The [[encomienda]] system – regulated by the [[Laws of Burgos]] of 1512 and their supplementary ordinances of 1513 – subjected Taíno and Ciboney communities to forced labour, principally in gold mining and agricultural production, under conditions that contemporaries such as [[Bartolomé de las Casas]] characterised as lethal.<ref>{{cite book |last=Las Casas |first=Bartolomé de |title=Historia de las Indias |volume=III |publisher=Fondo de Cultura Económica |year=1951 |orig-date=c. 1527–1561 |location=Mexico City |isbn=978-968-16-0996-2}}</ref> Las Casas documented the [[Massacre of Caonao]] (c. 1513), claiming in his account that several thousand indigenous people perished; this figure has been questioned by subsequent historiography, which notes the chronicler's tendency toward hyperbole in his numerical estimates.<ref>{{cite book |last=Las Casas |first=Bartolomé de |title=Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias |publisher=Cátedra |year=2005 |orig-date=1542 |location=Madrid |isbn=978-84-376-0341-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Thomas |first=Hugh |title=Cuba or the Pursuit of Freedom |publisher=Da Capo Press |year=1998 |orig-date=1971 |location=New York |isbn=978-0-306-80827-2 |pages=62–65}}</ref>
To the violence of conquest were added successive epidemics – including one that struck [[Hispaniola]] in 1493 prior to the permanent colonisation of Cuba, [[smallpox]] (1518–1519), and [[measles]] — which caused catastrophic mortality among populations with no prior [[herd immunity]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Cook |first=Noble David |title=Born to Die: Disease and New World Conquest, 1492–1650 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1998 |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-521-62208-0}}</ref> Survivors fled to mountain refuges or were confined to [[pueblo de indios|indigenous towns]], one of which, [[Guanabacoa]], is today a municipality of [[Havana]]. By the mid-sixteenth century, official Spanish records indicated that barely any identifiable indigenous communities survived, and the prevailing academic consensus for much of the twentieth century held that Cuba's Taíno had disappeared as a distinct population within one or two generations of contact.

==== Revision of the total extinction narrative ====
This thesis has been substantially revised by ethnographic and genetic research conducted since the 1980s. Nineteenth-century observers – among them the British abolitionist [[David Turnbull (abolitionist)|David Turnbull]] during his stay in Havana in 1838–1840<ref>{{cite book |last=Turnbull |first=David |title=Travels in the West: Cuba; with Notices of Porto Rico, and the Slave Trade |publisher=Longman, Orme, Brown, Green and Longmans |year=1840 |location=London}}</ref> and the Spanish naturalist [[Miguel Rodríguez Ferrer]], whose principal work on Cuba was published in 1876 on the basis of fieldwork conducted between 1840 and 1861<ref>{{cite book |last=Rodríguez Ferrer |first=Miguel |title=Naturaleza y civilización de la grandiosa isla de Cuba |publisher=Imprenta de J. Noguera |year=1876 |location=Madrid}}</ref> — described communities in [[Guanabacoa]], [[El Caney]], and the foothills of the [[Sierra Maestra]] displaying signs of indigenous ancestry, though such testimonies reflect the racial categories of their era and do not constitute genealogical or genetic verification.
The most rigorous work was initiated in 1989 by [[José Barreiro]], a Cuban-born scholar and then associate director of research at the [[National Museum of the American Indian]] of the [[Smithsonian Institution]], in collaboration with the historian of Baracoa [[Alejandro Hartmann Matos]]. Their ethnographic research estimated that at least 5,000 individuals with identifiable indigenous ancestry survived in Cuba, while hundreds of thousands might carry partial indigenous ancestry.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Barreiro |first=José |title=A Note on Taínos: Whither Progress? |journal=Northeast Indian Quarterly |year=1990 |volume=7 |number=3 |pages=66–77 |url=http://www.hartford-hwp.com/archives/41/013.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130118000000/http://www.hartford-hwp.com/archives/41/013.html |archive-date=18 January 2013 |access-date=18 January 2013}}</ref> The community of [[La Caridad de los Indios]], in the mountains southwest of Baracoa, is the most frequently cited in academic literature as the one that best preserves Taíno cultural continuity – including traditional agricultural practices, construction techniques, and oral tradition – within a predominantly mixed-race population. In 2018, the Smithsonian Institution returned to this community bone fragments of seven Taíno individuals removed nearly a century earlier by American archaeologist [[Mark R. Harrington]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Harrington |first=Mark R. |title=Cuba Before Columbus |volume=2 vols. |publisher=Museum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation |year=1921 |location=New York}}</ref>
It is essential to note that the evidence of indigenous survival in Cuba pertains almost exclusively to cultural practices and partial genetic ancestry, not to biologically "pure" populations by any genealogical criterion. All communities identified as Taíno descendants are predominantly [[mestizo|mixed-race]], with Spanish and African ancestry. Indigenous identity was moreover historically suppressed: Spanish colonial authorities actively persecuted it for the purpose of extinguishing indigenous land rights – the last land claim was rejected by courts in 1850 – and its stigmatisation led many families to conceal their ancestry for generations.<ref>{{cite book |last=Thomas |first=Hugh |title=Cuba or the Pursuit of Freedom |publisher=Da Capo Press |year=1998 |orig-date=1971 |location=New York |isbn=978-0-306-80827-2 |pages=45–52}}</ref>

==== Genetic evidence of Amerindian ancestry ====
Several genomic studies confirm the persistence of significant indigenous ancestry in the Cuban population, with a markedly asymmetric distribution with respect to sex and geography.
The largest-scale autosomal study, conducted by Marcheco-Teruel et al. (2014) and published in ''PLOS Genetics'' with a sample of 1,019 individuals from all Cuban provinces, estimated mean island-wide autosomal Amerindian ancestry at approximately 8% (compared to 72% European and 20% African), while the estimate based on [[mitochondrial DNA]] (mtDNA) rose to 34.5%.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marcheco-Teruel |first1=Beatriz |last2=Parra |first2=Esteban J. |last3=Fuentes-Smith |first3=Enrique |last4=Salas |first4=Antonio |title=Cuba: Exploring the History of Admixture and the Genetic Basis of Pigmentation Using Autosomal and Uniparental Markers |journal=PLOS Genetics |year=2014 |volume=10 |number=7 |article-number=e1004488 |doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1004488 |doi-access=free |pmid=25058410 |pmc=4109857 }}</ref> This marked asymmetry – indigenous ancestry traceable almost exclusively through the maternal line – is consistent with colonial-era dynamics, in which unions occurred between indigenous women and European and African men, while male indigenous lineages were effectively eliminated by the conquest and epidemics. The same study recorded a pronounced geographical variation: the eastern provinces of [[Granma Province|Granma]] (15%), [[Holguín Province|Holguín]] (12%), and [[Las Tunas Province|Las Tunas]] (12%) showed the highest rates of autosomal Amerindian ancestry, which coincides with the historical distribution of Taíno settlement.
Comparative studies of mtDNA in the Caribbean document high frequencies of Amerindian lineages in former Spanish colonies, while they are practically absent in territories of French and British colonisation, reflecting the differing colonial policies of each power and their different reliance on enslaved African labour.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martínez-Cruzado |first1=Juan Carlos |last2=Toro-Labrador |first2=Gladys |last3=Ho-Fung |first3=Vance |last4=Estévez-Montero |first4=M. A. |last5=Lobaina-Manzanet |first5=A. |last6=Padovani-Claudio |first6=D. A. |last7=Sánchez-Cruz |first7=H. |last8=Ortiz-Bermúdez |first8=P. |last9=Sánchez-Crespo |first9=A. |title=Mitochondrial DNA Analysis Reveals Substantial Native American Ancestry in Puerto Rico |journal=Human Biology |year=2001 |volume=73 |number=4 |pages=491–511 |doi=10.1353/hub.2001.0056 |pmid=11512677}}</ref> An analysis of [[ancient DNA]] from Ciboney individuals from Cuban archaeological sites confirmed the affinity of their mitochondrial lineages with Arawakan populations from South America.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lalueza-Fox |first1=Carles |last2=Gilbert |first2=M. Thomas P. |last3=Martínez-Fuentes |first3=Antonio J. |title=Mitochondrial DNA from pre-Columbian Ciboneys from Cuba and the prehistoric colonization of the Caribbean |journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology |year=2003 |volume=121 |number=2 |pages=97–108 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.10236 |pmid=12740952 |bibcode=2003AJPA..121...97L }}</ref>

==== Indigenous Florida refugees ====
The Amerindian demographic legacy of Cuba received a secondary contribution from indigenous refugees from northern Florida, displaced following the transfer of [[Spanish Florida]] to Britain under the [[Treaty of Paris (1763)|Treaty of Paris of 1763]]. During the colonial period, groups such as the [[Timucua people|Timucua]], [[Calusa]], [[Tequesta]], and [[Apalachee]] had maintained close ties with Cuba, particularly with [[Havana]]; the Calusa conducted regular canoe-borne trade with the city from around 1600.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hann |first=John H. |title=Missions to the Calusa |publisher=University Press of Florida |year=1991 |location=Gainesville |isbn=978-0-8130-1075-5}}</ref> These populations had already been drastically reduced by epidemics and raids by British-allied groups before 1763: by the 1720s, the once-numerous Timucua had been reduced to fewer than 40 individuals.<ref>{{cite book |last=Worth |first=John E. |title=The Timucuan Chiefdoms of Spanish Florida: Assimilation |volume=I |publisher=University Press of Florida |year=1998 |location=Gainesville |isbn=978-0-8130-1574-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Worth |first=John E. |title=The Timucuan Chiefdoms of Spanish Florida: Resistance and Destruction |volume=II |publisher=University Press of Florida |year=1998 |location=Gainesville |isbn=978-0-8130-1575-0}}</ref>
In 1763, a small number of indigenous refugees joined the Spanish exodus from [[St. Augustine, Florida|St. Augustine]], while a remnant population of Calusa descent – whose precise size is difficult to establish from available colonial sources, given the advanced state of tribal disintegration of that people by that date – was transported to Havana.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hann |first=John H. |title=Missions to the Calusa |publisher=University Press of Florida |year=1991 |location=Gainesville |isbn=978-0-8130-1075-5 |pages=349–367}}</ref> These communities, already broadly integrated into Spanish colonial society, were rapidly absorbed into the general Cuban population, and their specific genetic contribution cannot be quantified independently of the considerably more dominant Taíno component.

=== Cubans of predominantly European ancestry ("Whites") ===
{{Main|White Cubans|Spanish immigration to Cuba}}
{{See also|French immigration to Cuba|Italian Cubans}}
[[File:Nurse in Pinar del Rio - Cuba 01.JPG|thumb|right|upright=0.8|A Cuban nurse in [[Pinar del Río Province]], 2009.]]
In the [[2012 Cuba census|national census of 2012]], 64.1% of the population of [[Cuba]] identified as white.<ref name="ONEI2012">{{cite web |url=https://cubamemorias.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Cuba_INFORME_NACIONAL_CENSO_2012.pdf |title=Censo de Población y Viviendas 2012: Informe Nacional. Resultados Definitivos de Indicadores Seleccionados en Cuba, Provincias y Municipios |publisher=[[Oficina Nacional de Estadística e Información]] (ONEI) |via=cubamemorias.com |date=2014 |access-date=26 May 2026 }}</ref> In Cuban demographic and ethnoracial classification, the term ''blanco'' (white) designates persons of predominantly European ancestry and is not equivalent to the Anglophone category white, which carries distinct connotations – notably an association with Northern European ancestry – absent from Cuban usage.
Owing to the island's colonial history and patterns of immigration, the white Cuban population is overwhelmingly descended from Southern Europeans, principally Peninsular Spaniards and settlers from the [[Canary Islands]], whose migration to Cuba was substantial and sustained over several centuries.

==== Spanish settlers ====
[[File:El Ismaelillo.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.9|[[José Francisco Martí Zayas-Bazán]] (centre, seated), son of Cuban national hero [[José Martí]], surrounded by Cuban officials.]]
Spanish settlement in Cuba began in 1492 and continued, in successive and demographically distinct waves, for more than four centuries. The island served simultaneously as the administrative hub of the Spanish Caribbean and as a transit point for the broader colonial enterprise, making it a preferred destination for settlers from virtually every region of Spain. The character of each migratory wave – its regional origin, social composition, and economic motivation – varied substantially over time, producing a stratified European heritage that reflects both colonial policy and the economic rhythms of successive eras.

==== Early colonisation (1492–c. 1762) ====
The first Spanish settlers arrived with [[Columbus's first voyage]] in 1492, among them sailors and soldiers from [[Andalusia]] and the [[Canary Islands]]; the fleet had departed from the Andalusian port of [[Palos de la Frontera]], stopping at [[Gran Canaria]] en route.<ref name="Thomas1998">{{cite book |last=Thomas |first=Hugh |title=Cuba or the Pursuit of Freedom |year=1998 |publisher=Da Capo Press |location=New York |isbn=978-0-306-80827-2}}</ref> Formal colonisation of the island began in 1511 under [[Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar]], who founded seven towns between 1511 and 1515, including [[Santiago de Cuba]] and [[Havana]]. The earliest settlers were predominantly from [[Extremadura]] and Andalusia, consistent with the composition of the early Caribbean expeditions, which departed primarily from Seville – at the time the monopoly port for transatlantic trade under the [[Casa de Contratación]] system (1503–1790). Throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Cuba's population remained small and strategically oriented: Havana's natural harbour made it a mandatory stop for the [[Spanish treasure fleet]], and the island functioned more as a logistical base than as an agricultural colony. Settlement was concentrated in a handful of coastal towns and supplemented intermittently by royal decrees promoting emigration from the Canary Islands, whose chronic demographic surplus made the Canarians a convenient and economical source of agricultural colonists for the Spanish Caribbean.

==== Canarians (isleños) ====
Of all the Spanish regional groups, the Canarians – known in Cuba as [[isleños (Cuba)|isleños]] (islanders) — exercised the most profound and lasting influence on Cuban demography, agriculture, and linguistic culture. Canarian emigration to Cuba was a continuous process from the early sixteenth century, organised in part through population contracts by which the Spanish Crown encouraged Canarian families to settle in underpopulated areas of its Caribbean colonies. Unlike the predominantly male migrations from the Iberian Peninsula, Canarian emigration was familial in character – including women, children, and extended family groups – which gave Canarian communities a distinctive capacity for rural demographic consolidation. Canarians were the primary agents of tobacco cultivation in Cuba, becoming the archetypal [[veguero]]s (tobacco farmers), and were decisive in the development of the [[Vuelta Abajo]] region of [[Pinar del Río]], widely considered the world's foremost producer of premium cigar tobacco.<ref name="Thomas1998"/> Their role in town founding was equally significant: [[Santiago de las Vegas]], among others, was established by Canarian immigrants specialising in tobacco production. After the [[Cuban Revolution]], numerous cigar manufacturers of Canarian origin relocated to the Canary Islands, where they established a tobacco industry based on Cuban seeds and techniques.
The linguistic imprint of Canarian settlement on [[Cuban Spanish]] is substantial and well documented. Cuban Spanish belongs to the same [[Atlantic Spanish|Atlantic dialectal continuum]] as [[Canarian Spanish]], with which it shares [[seseo]], [[yeísmo]], the [[aspiration (linguistics)|aspiration]] and weakening of consonants in syllable-final position, and an [[Intonation (linguistics)|intonation]] that sets [[Caribbean Spanish]] apart from Peninsular varieties.<ref name="Lipski1994">{{cite book |last=Lipski |first=John M. |title=Latin American Spanish |year=1994 |publisher=Longman |location=London and New York |isbn=978-0-582-08760-6}}</ref> Numerous everyday words in Cuban Spanish derive directly from Canarian usage, the most frequently cited being [[guagua]] (bus), a term of Canarian origin now in universal use in Cuba and other Caribbean dialects. Of the seven Canary Islands, La Palma is the one whose accent most closely approximates Cuban Spanish, reflecting centuries of migration and cultural exchange.

==== Andalusians ====
[[Andalusia]] constituted the legal and commercial gateway to the Americas throughout the colonial period. Under the Casa de Contratación system (1503–1790), all transatlantic trade was monopolised through Seville, with the result that Andalusian merchants, officials, clergy, and artisans were overrepresented in the earliest waves of Caribbean settlement. Andalusians figure among the founders of Havana and other early towns, and their dialect – characterised by seseo, the aspiration of /s/ before consonants, and open vowels – reinforced the phonological features that would become hallmarks of Cuban Spanish, acting in parallel with the Canarian influences that intensified during the nineteenth century.<ref name="Lipski1994"/> The Andalusian community maintained a significant presence in Havana's cultural life throughout the colonial period. [[Bullfighting]], practised in Cuba from at least 1514 – the date of the first documented spectacle, recorded by [[Bartolomé de las Casas]] in his [[Historia de las Indias]]<ref group="note">The earliest mention of bullfighting in Cuba appears in Bartolomé de las Casas's [[Historia de las Indias]], where a contest involving "a bull or bulls" is recorded as having taken place on [[Feast of Corpus Christi|Corpus Christi]] 1514. The first formal bullfight is generally dated to 1538, in [[Santiago de Cuba]], on the occasion of the arrival of Governor [[Hernando de Soto]]. This work should not be confused with the [[Historia general y natural de las Indias]] of [[Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo]].</ref> — until its prohibition by American [[Military occupation of Cuba (1898–1902)|occupation forces]] in 1899,<ref name="Thomas1998"/> was sustained in large part by matadors and promoters from [[Cádiz]] and Seville.

==== Galicians ====
[[Galicia (Spain)|Galicia]] supplied one of the largest flows of Spanish emigrants to Cuba, to the point that the colloquial Cuban term for any Spaniard – regardless of regional origin – became ''gallego'', and remains so today. This linguistic conflation reflects a demographic reality: on the eve of the [[First World War]], [[Havana]] was home to the second-largest urban Galician community in the world, surpassed only by [[Buenos Aires]].<ref name="Thomas1998"/> Galician emigration to Cuba intensified steadily from the mid-nineteenth century, reached its peak in the first two decades of the twentieth century, and left a structural imprint on Cuban commerce, urban architecture, and vernacular language. In Havana, Galician immigrants founded and financed the [[Centro Gallego de La Habana]], which became one of the two most powerful mutual aid and cultural institutions on the island; its premises – a palatial building constructed on the western side of the [[Parque Central (Havana)|Parque Central]] facing the [[Centro Asturiano de La Habana|Centro Asturiano]] — were nationalised after 1961 and today house the [[Gran Teatro de La Habana]], the country's principal opera house. The [[Galician anthem]], [[Os Pinos]], received its world premiere in Havana on 20 December 1907, at the Teatro del Centro Gallego, reflecting the cultural weight of the diaspora community.<ref name="XuntaHimno">{{cite web |url=https://www.xunta.gal/es/o-himno-de-galicia |title=El himno de Galicia |author=[[Xunta de Galicia]] |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> Among the most prominent descendants of Galician immigrants is [[Fidel Castro]], whose father, [[Ángel Castro Argiz]], emigrated from the municipality of [[Láncara]], in the province of [[Lugo (province)|Lugo]].<ref name="CastroArgiz">{{cite web |url=https://www.elespanol.com/quincemil/cultura/20191117/origen-gallego-fidel-castro-cuna-revolucion-lancara/445206260_0.html |title=El origen gallego de Fidel Castro: la «cuna de la revolución» está en Láncara |website=El Español |date=17 November 2019 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> The Galician impact on Cuban vocabulary and speech was extensive; Galicians dominated broad sectors of the Havana commercial economy – running shops, cafés, and small businesses – and it was this everyday presence, rather than elite cultural influence, that transmitted linguistic elements into common usage.

==== Asturians ====
The Asturian community in Cuba stood alongside the Galician as one of the two numerically dominant Spanish regional groups of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Asturian immigrants settled primarily in Havana and the main provincial cities, concentrating in commerce, the food trade, and small-scale manufacturing. The [[Centro Asturiano de La Habana]] — erected directly opposite the Centro Gallego on the Parque Central – constituted the other great pillar of the Spanish mutual aid network in Cuba, offering its members healthcare, education, and social assistance. At its height, membership counted tens of thousands of affiliates. In 1900, when Cuba's total population stood at around 1.6&nbsp;million, the three largest groups of Spanish-born residents – Galicians, Asturians, and Canarians – jointly accounted for 68% of the island's total Spanish immigrant population.<ref name="Maluquer1992">{{cite book |last=Maluquer de Motes |first=Jordi |title=Nación e inmigración: los españoles en Cuba (siglos XIX y XX) |year=1992 |publisher=Ediciones Júcar |location=Gijón |isbn=978-84-7286-332-3}}</ref>

==== Catalans and other Peninsular groups ====
Catalans maintained a significant presence in Cuba from the eighteenth century, concentrated particularly in commerce and maritime trade. In [[Santiago de Cuba]], Catalan merchants established themselves as key intermediaries in the port economy. By 1900, some 6,400 Catalans resided in Cuba – a disproportionately high figure relative to [[Catalonia]]'s demographic weight within Spain as a whole, reflecting the region's mercantile traditions.<ref name="Maluquer1992"/> [[Basques]], [[Castilians]], [[Valencians]], and other Peninsular groups also contributed to the colonial and post-colonial population, though in absolute numbers they were smaller than the northwestern and southern Spanish groups.

==== Post-independence immigration (1898–c. 1931) ====
Paradoxically, the largest wave of Spanish emigration to Cuba did not occur during the colonial period but in the decades immediately following Cuban independence. Between 1902 and 1931, approximately 780,000 Spaniards constituted 60.8% of all immigrants arriving on the island during that period. The majority were young rural men from Galicia, Asturias, and the Canary Islands, drawn by wage labour in the rapidly expanding sugar industry.<ref name="Iglesias1988">{{cite book |last=Iglesias García |first=Fe |chapter=Características de la inmigración española en Cuba, 1904–1930 |editor-last=Sánchez-Albornoz |editor-first=Nicolás |title=Españoles hacia América: La emigración en masa, 1880–1930 |year=1988 |publisher=Alianza Editorial |location=Madrid |pages=270–295}}</ref> For four consecutive years between 1916 and 1920, Cuba was the leading destination for Spanish emigrants within Latin America, absorbing approximately 60% of total Spanish emigration to the region; between 1900 and 1930, it was surpassed only by Argentina.<ref name="NaranjoOrovio1992">{{cite journal |last=Naranjo Orovio |first=Consuelo |title=Trabajo libre e inmigración española en Cuba, 1880–1930 |journal=[[Revista de Indias]] |year=1992 |volume=52 |number=195–196 |pages=749–794 |doi=10.3989/revindias.1992.i195-196.1170|hdl=10261/267837 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Historians have described the half-century between 1880 and 1930 as the largest episode of Spanish migration to the Americas in Spain's entire history, greater in numerical terms than all the preceding centuries of conquest and colonisation combined; of the more than three million Spanish emigrants of that period, approximately one third settled in Cuba.<ref name="NaranjoOrovio1992"/> By 1920, Cuba's population had grown to nearly three million, of whom approximately 250,000 had been born in Spain.<ref name="Maluquer1992"/> This post-independence wave substantially reinforced the demographic and cultural substrate of the island's population, consolidating the patterns of regional origin – principally Galician, Asturian, and Canarian – already established during the colonial period.

==== Other European groups ====
==== French ====
French immigration to Cuba occurred in two distinct waves. The first, during the eighteenth century, consisted of merchants, officials, and settlers who established a modest presence in [[Havana]] and the eastern provinces. The second – considerably larger and of greater consequence – was precipitated by the [[Haitian Revolution]] (1791–1804), when tens of thousands of French colonists and the enslaved people they brought with them fled [[Saint-Domingue]] and took refuge primarily in eastern Cuba.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Debien |first=Gabriel |title=Les colons de Saint-Domingue réfugiés à Cuba (1793–1815) |journal=Revista de Indias |volume=XIII–XIV |number=53–54 |pages=559–605, 11–36 |year=1953–1954 |publisher=CSIC / Instituto Fernández de Oviedo}}</ref> Historical estimates place the total number of French refugees of all social classes arriving in eastern Cuba during the period 1800–1809 at more than 20,000,<ref>{{cite book |last=Cruz Ríos |first=Laura |title=Flujos inmigratorios franceses a Santiago de Cuba (1800–1868) |publisher=Editorial Oriente |location=Santiago de Cuba |year=2006 |isbn=978-959-11-0515-8}}</ref> with 1803 the year of greatest influx: according to contemporary sources cited in the historiography, some 27,000 French individuals arrived that year alone.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lux |first=William R. |title=French Colonization in Cuba, 1791–1809 |journal=The Americas |volume=29 |number=1 |pages=57–61 |year=1972 |doi=10.2307/980536 |publisher=Cambridge University Press / Academy of American Franciscan History |jstor=980536 }}</ref> The cumulative total for the entire period 1791–1810 may have been somewhat higher.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Yacou |first=Alain |title=L'expulsion des Français de Saint-Domingue réfugiés dans la région orientale de l'île de Cuba (1808–1810) |journal=Caravelle. Cahiers du monde hispanique et luso-brésilien |number=39 |pages=49–64 |year=1982}}</ref> They settled primarily in eastern Cuba – around Santiago de Cuba, [[Guantánamo]], and [[Baracoa]] — where they introduced coffee cultivation on a significant scale and transformed the regional economy within a decade. Their descendants, known locally as [[Franco-Haitian Cubans|Franco-haitianos]], maintained a distinct cultural identity in eastern Cuba for several generations.

==== Italians ====
Italian immigration to Cuba was modest compared to that recorded in [[Argentina]] or Brazil.<ref>{{cite web |last=Tamburini |first=Francesco |title=La colonia italiana di Cuba (1884–1902). Parte I |url=http://www.archivocubano.org/tamburini_01.html |website=Cuba.
