The [[1994 Cuban rafter crisis]] consisted of the exodus of more than 35,000 Cubans over a five-week period beginning 13 August 1994.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Pedraza |first=Silvia |title=Political Disaffection in Cuba's Revolution and Exodus |year=2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-521-68729-4 |pages=173–210}}</ref>

The Clinton administration ordered on 19 August that rafters be intercepted and transferred to camps at [[Naval Station Guantanamo Bay]] and in Panama rather than admitted to the continental United States, thereby abandoning the unconditional reception policy that had been in effect until then.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://scholar.library.miami.edu/digital/exhibits/show/guantanamo/crisis |title=Crisis & Response: Cuban Rafters at Guantánamo Bay, 1994–1996 |publisher=University of Miami Libraries |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> In September 1994 and May 1995, the two governments concluded agreements establishing a US commitment to grant a minimum of 20,000 annual visas to Cuban nationals, and the [[Wet feet, dry feet|wet foot/dry foot]] policy: Cubans intercepted at sea would be returned, while those who managed to reach US soil could apply for residency.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nackerud |first=Larry |last2=Springer |first2=Alyson |last3=Larrison |first3=Christopher |last4=Issac |first4=Alicia |title=The End of the Cuban Contradiction in U.S. Refugee Policy |journal=International Migration Review |volume=33 |issue=1 |year=1999 |pages=176–192 |doi=10.1177/019791839903300108}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Masud-Piloto |first=Félix Roberto |title=From Welcomed Exiles to Illegal Immigrants: Cuban Migration to the U.S., 1959–1995 |year=1996 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |location=Lanham |isbn=978-0-8476-8149-5 |pages=128–148}}</ref> This policy, in effect until January 2017, generated incentives for increasingly risky crossing methods at a human cost that no official statistics could precisely document.
[[File:Cuban_migrants_disembark_the_USS_VICKSBURG_(CG-69)_at_the_safe_haven_in_Guantanamo_Bay._These_are_the_first_Cubans_to_arrive_on_a_U.S._Naval_Vessel._The_U.S._Navy_has_taken_the_resp_-_DPLA_-_b95dac53c78031830a520186e5f390c3.jpeg|thumb|Cuban migrants disembarking from the {{USS|Vicksburg|CG-69|6}} at the U.S. Naval Base at Guantanamo Bay, 1994. They were among the first Cubans to arrive aboard a U.S. naval vessel during [[Operation Able Vigil]].]]

=== Diaspora in the 1990s and 2000s ===

The period following the balsero crisis was one of sustained but non-mass emigration, channeled in part through the 1994 visa framework and in part through irregular overland migration via Central America and Mexico. The Cuban-American community completed a political transformation begun in the 1970s: from an initial refugee community with limited electoral participation to one with structural electoral weight in Florida, overwhelmingly conservative in orientation. The Cuban-American community was a decisive factor in the outcome of the 2000 presidential election in that state.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Eckstein |first=Susan |title=The Immigrant Divide: How Cuban Americans Changed the US and Their Homeland |year=2009 |publisher=Routledge |location=New York |isbn=978-0-415-99923-6}}</ref>

Through the 2000s, the composition and attitudes of the diaspora began to shift. More recent arrivals came in larger proportions from working-class backgrounds, were more racially diverse, and had lived their entire lives under the post-1959 regime. Tensions between the "historic exile"—with its emphasis on property restitution, the embargo, and non-negotiation with the regime—and younger generations more inclined toward family contact and remittances began to erode the political unanimity that had long characterized Miami's exile community.

=== Sustained emigration in the 2000s and 2010s ===

Through the 2000s and 2010s, Cuban emigration remained quantitatively significant, with overland routes through Central America and Mexico gaining in importance. One contributing factor was that Ecuador did not require a Cuban visa until 2015, allowing Cubans to fly there and begin the overland journey northward.

[[File:Carnival_Liberty_Cuban_Refugees.JPG|thumb|right|alt=Cuban refugees aboard the Carnival Liberty cruise ship after being rescued at sea, August 2014|Cuban refugees rescued at sea by the cruise ship ''Carnival Liberty'' in August 2014. Improvised vessel crossings remained a common mode of escape decades after the 1980 [[Mariel boatlift]].]]

Between 2014 and 2016, thousands of Cubans were stranded in Costa Rica after Nicaragua closed its border in November 2015. Most were eventually authorized to transit toward the Mexican border through a regional agreement among the governments of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Belize, Mexico, and Panama, with logistical coordination by the [[International Organization for Migration]] (IOM).<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2015/12/29/cuban-migrants-stuck-in-costa-rica-allowed-us-passage |title=Cuban migrants stuck in Costa Rica allowed US passage |publisher=Al Jazeera |date=29 December 2015 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref>

President Obama's 17 December 2014, announcement of the normalization of diplomatic relations with Cuba<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/12/17/statement-president-cuba-policy-changes |title=Statement by the President on Cuba Policy Changes |publisher=The White House |date=17 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> had paradoxical effects on migration. In anticipation of the expected repeal of wet foot/dry foot—which occurred on 12 January 2017—flows accelerated sharply in 2015 and 2016. In fiscal year 2016, the United States recorded more than 56,000 Cuban arrivals, the highest figure since Mariel.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2017/01/13/cuban-immigration-to-u-s-surges-as-relations-warm/ |title=Surge in Cuban immigration to U.S. continued through 2016 |publisher=Pew Research Center |date=13 January 2017 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> The revocation of wet foot/dry foot in January 2017 meant that, for the first time since the 1960s, Cubans intercepted at sea or at the land border without documentation were processed under ordinary asylum law, without automatic access to permanent residency.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.cnn.com/2017/01/12/politics/us-to-end-wet-foot-dry-foot-policy-for-cubans |title=US ending 'wet foot, dry foot' policy for Cubans |publisher=CNN |date=12 January 2017 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.migrationpolicy.org/news/taking-action-reflect-current-reality-obama-administration-ends-wet-foot-dry-foot-policies |title=Taking Action to Reflect Current Reality: Obama Administration Ends "Wet Foot, Dry Foot" Policies on Cuban Migration |publisher=Migration Policy Institute |date=13 January 2017 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref>

=== The 2021–2026 migration crisis: the largest exodus in Cuban history ===

==== Background and triggering factors ====

The migration process that intensified from 2021 onward is unprecedented in the history of Cuban emigration for its volume, speed, and demographic impact on the island. Its origins lie in the convergence of structural and circumstantial factors.

Economically, the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] compounded an economy already deteriorating since the mid-2010s, itself a product of Venezuela's economic collapse—which had been the island's principal supplier of subsidized oil—the tightening of US sanctions under the Trump administration from 2017, and the structural inability of the state economic model to finance imports through its own exports.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://horizontecubano.law.columbia.edu/news/cuba-ten-consecutive-years-macroeconomic-deterioration |title=Cuba: Ten Consecutive Years of Macroeconomic Deterioration |last=Vidal Alejandro |first=Pavel |publisher=Centro de Derecho y Política Cubana, Columbia University |date=18 August 2025 |access-date=1 October 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://horizontecubano.law.columbia.edu/news/magnitude-economic-crisis-cuba |title=The Magnitude of the Economic Crisis in Cuba and the Causes of the Recent Protests |last=Mesa-Lago |first=Carmelo |publisher=Centro de Derecho y Política Cubana, Columbia University |date=10 September 2021 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> Tourism collapsed with the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://cri.fiu.edu/_assets/docs/cuba-economic-crisis.pdf |title=Cuba's Economy in Times of Crisis: 2020–2022 and Prospects for 2023 |last=Mesa-Lago |first=Carmelo |publisher=Cuban Research Institute, Florida International University |year=2023 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> Shortages of food, medicine, and fuel reached levels not seen since the 1990s; power outages extending up to sixteen to twenty hours daily in some provinces became recurrent. Cuba's healthcare system showed marked deterioration during the pandemic due to shortages of drugs, basic supplies, equipment, and personnel.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.paho.org/en/crisis-situation-cuba |title=Crisis Situation in Cuba |publisher=Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref>

Politically, the [[2021 Cuban protests|protests of July 11, 2021]]—known as ''11J''—marked an inflection point: the largest public demonstrations against the regime since the establishment of the one-party republic, with crowds taking to the streets across dozens of cities and towns under slogans including "[[Patria y Vida]]!", "¡Libertad!", and "¡Se acabó!".<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.hrw.org/report/2022/07/11/prison-or-exile/cubas-systematic-repression-july-2021-demonstrators |title=Prison or Exile: Cuba's Systematic Repression of July 2021 Demonstrators |publisher=Human Rights Watch |date=11 July 2022 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> The government's response included internet blackouts,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://freedomhouse.org/country/cuba/freedom-net/2022 |title=Cuba: Freedom on the Net 2022 |publisher=Freedom House |year=2022 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> mass detentions, prison sentences of up to thirty years imposed on protesters who had committed no acts of violence, and the deployment of paramilitary groups.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-60764403 |title=Cuba anti-government protesters jailed for up to 30 years |publisher=BBC News |date=9 March 2022 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/amr25/8266/2024/en/ |title=Cuba: Three Years After the Protests of 11–12 July 2021: Authorities Must Release Those Unjustly Imprisoned and Repeal Repressive Laws |publisher=Amnesty International |date=7 July 2024 |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> The repression of 11J, combined with continuing material deterioration, drove an emigration wave reaching segments of the population that had until then remained on the island.

==== Scale of the exodus and demographic impact ====

According to data from [[U.S. Customs and Border Protection]] (CBP) and the [[United States Department of Homeland Security]], between October 2021 and mid-2024 more than 860,000 Cubans arrived in the United States, the majority via the land border with Mexico.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/stats/southwest-land-border-encounters |title=Southwest Land Border Encounters |publisher=U.S. Customs and Border Protection |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> December 2022 saw the peak of the exodus, with 44,064 Cuban arrivals in a single month—a figure equivalent to the entire total for 2012. In calendar year 2022 alone, 313,488 Cubans arrived in the United States, representing approximately 3% of Cuba's population for that year; this single-year total surpassed the cumulative figures of the Golden Exile (354,963 between 1959 and 1962), the Freedom Flights (333,457 between 1965 and 1973), and every preceding Cuban migration episode. Total emigration toward all destinations in 2022 reached 369,393.

The demographic impact was confirmed by Cuban authorities. During the July 2024 session of the [[National Assembly of People's Power]], Juan Carlos Alfonso Fraga, deputy director of the [[Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas e Información|National Office of Statistics and Information]] (ONEI), reported that Cuba's effective population had fallen to 10,055,968 inhabitants at the close of 2023—a decline of 10.1% from 2020, returning the country to demographic levels last recorded in the mid-1980s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Actualizan cifras sobre la población efectiva en Cuba |url=https://www.juventudrebelde.cu/cuba/2024-07-19/actualizan-cifras-sobre-la-poblacion-efectiva-en-cuba |website=Juventud Rebelde |publisher=Agencia Cubana de Noticias |date=19 July 2024 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=La población de Cuba en 2024 cae a menos de 10 millones y «seguirá decreciendo» |url=https://efe.com/mundo/2024-07-19/cuba-cae-poblacion/ |work=EFE |date=19 July 2024 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> According to ONEI figures, Cuba's population fell from 11,181,595 on 31 December 2021, to 10,055,968 at the close of 2023—a reduction of more than one million persons in two years. The emigration of 1,011,269 persons was identified as the primary driver of this decline, followed by 405,512 deaths against only 284,892 births during the same period.<ref name="reuters2024"/> These estimates are based on the concept of "effective population", counting persons who accumulated at least 180 days of residence in Cuba during the preceding twelve months—a methodology adopted to more accurately reflect the impact of mass emigration since 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ONEI actualiza sobre indicadores de población efectiva en Cuba |url=https://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2024/08/07/onei-actualiza-sobre-indicadores-de-poblacion-efectiva-en-cuba/ |website=Cubadebate |date=7 August 2024 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref>

The official figures have been subject to methodological scrutiny by independent researchers. Demographer Juan Carlos Albizu-Campos estimated, drawing on migration data, vital records, and demographic statistics, that Cuba's effective resident population may have fallen to approximately 8.62&nbsp;million at the close of 2023—a reduction of close to 18% between 2022 and 2023.<ref>{{Cite news |title=La población de Cuba cayó un 18 % entre 2022 y 2023, según un estudio independiente |url=https://efe.com/mundo/2024-07-08/la-poblacion-de-cuba-cayo-un-18-entre-2022-y-2023/ |work=EFE |date=8 July 2024 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref name="reuters2024"/> In a subsequent update, Albizu-Campos estimated the effective resident population may have fallen to around eight million inhabitants at end-2024, representing a cumulative decline of approximately 24% from 2020.<ref>{{Cite news |title=La población de Cuba se reduce un 24 % en cuatro años |url=https://efe.com/mundo/un-estudio-estima-la-poblacion-de-cuba-en-ocho-millones-de-personas-tras-reducirse-un-24-en-cuatro-anos/ |work=EFE |date=25 March 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref name="lemonde2025">{{Cite news |title=Cuba faces population decline and aging amid mass migration exodus |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2025/04/30/cuba-faces-population-decline-and-aging-amid-mass-migration-exodus_6740756_4.html |work=Le Monde |date=30 April 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> ONEI reported an effective population of 9,748,007 as of 31 December 2024, a decline of 307,961 from the previous year at a rate of −30.6 per thousand inhabitants.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Cuba envejece: la isla reporta su tasa de natalidad más baja desde la Revolución |url=https://elpais.com/us/2025-03-02/cuba-es-un-pais-de-viejos-la-isla-reporta-su-tasa-de-natalidad-mas-baja-desde-la-revolucion.html |work=El País |date=2 March 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref name="lemonde2025" />

Of the more than one million persons who emigrated between 2022 and 2023, approximately 800,000 were aged 15 to 59—that is, of working age—compounding the impact on the island's economic structure and reducing the active labor force base. This pattern has been identified by ONEI and by independent demographic analyses as a key factor in the deterioration of Cuba's age structure.<ref name="reuters2024">{{Cite news |title=Cuba's 'migratory stampede' has no end in sight |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/cubas-migratory-stampede-has-no-end-sight-2024-09-11/ |work=Reuters |date=11 September 2024 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> The emigration of women of reproductive age further depresses birth rates in a context of persistently sub-replacement fertility, below replacement level since the late 1970s. Albizu-Campos has noted that the magnitude of Cuba's population decline since 2020 is structurally comparable, in demographic terms, to processes historically associated with armed conflict, given the combination of mass emigration, low fertility, and accelerated ageing.<ref name="reuters2024" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Cuba: Demographic or Systemic Crisis? |url=https://horizontecubano.law.columbia.edu/news/cuba-demographic-or-systemic-crisis |website=Cuba Capacity Building Project, Columbia University |author=Juan Carlos Albizu-Campos |date=2 September 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> Multiple independent demographic analyses concur that the combination of sustained emigration, low fertility, and rapid ageing constitutes a structural crisis with long-term effects on Cuba's economy and the sustainability of its social system.<ref name="lemonde2025" /><ref>{{Cite news |title=PHOTO ESSAY: Elderly Cubans cope with a deepening economic crisis |url=https://apnews.com/article/3a70faf96d41bee8bfbb4eea8cb53152 |work=Associated Press |date=13 October 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref>

==== The Central American route ====

The principal artery of the 2022–2023 exodus was the Central American route, made viable by Nicaragua's decision to waive the visa requirement for Cuban nationals on 22 November 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://oncubanews.com/cuba/nicaragua-suspende-el-libre-visado-para-cubanos-se-cierra-la-ruta-migratoria-de-los-volcanes/ |title=Nicaragua suspende el libre visado para cubanos |publisher=OnCuban News |date=9 February 2026 |access-date=15 February 2026}}</ref> This allowed Cubans to fly directly to Managua and from there undertake the overland journey through Honduras, Guatemala, Mexico, and ultimately the US border. Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, more than 514,000 Cubans crossed the [[Darién Gap]] jungle—the border passage between Colombia and Panama—and Mexican territory to reach the US southern border.

The CHNV (Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, Venezuela) humanitarian parole program, launched by the Biden administration in January 2023, permitted the legal entry of up to 30,000 persons per month from those four countries. By October 2024, more than 110,000 Cubans had used this channel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DHS Implements New Processes for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans and Eliminates Cap for Venezuelans |url=https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/alerts/dhs-implements-new-processes-for-cubans-haitians-and-nicaraguans-and-eliminates-cap-for-venezuelans |website=U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services |date=6 January 2023 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> The Trump administration, upon taking office in January 2025, suspended the program, cancelled previously granted paroles, and announced accelerated deportation policies, reducing flows toward the United States and redirecting them toward other destinations.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/03/25/2025-05128/termination-of-parole-processes-for-cubans-haitians-nicaraguans-and-venezuelans |title=Termination of Parole Processes for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans |publisher=Federal Register |date=25 March 2025 |access-date=1 May 2025}}</ref>

==== Diversification of migration destinations ====

A distinctive feature of the post-2021 exodus is the diversification of destinations. Where the United States had for decades been the primary destination of Cuban emigration, the contemporary crisis has redistributed the diaspora across a range of countries without precedent in Cuban migration history.

===== Spain =====
Spain has become the second most important destination, favored by cultural and linguistic proximity, an already established Cuban community, and the application of the [[Democratic Memory Law]] of 2022, which permitted descendants of emigrants from the Spanish Civil War and the Franco era to apply for Spanish nationality.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.exteriores.gob.es/Consulados/lahabana/es/ServiciosConsulares/Paginas/index.aspx?scca=Nacionalidad&scco=Cuba&scd=166&scs=Nacionalidad+espa%C3%B1ola+por+la+Ley+de+Memoria+Democr%C3%A1tica |title=Nacionalidad española por la Ley de Memoria Democrática |publisher=Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Consulate in Havana |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> Given that tens of thousands of Cuban families have direct Spanish ancestry, many Cubans were able to avail themselves of this legislation to obtain EU passports. According to the Spanish [[Instituto Nacional de Estadística (Spain)|National Statistics Institute]] (INE), as of 1 January 2023, 198,639 persons born in Cuba were residing in Spain.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ine.es/dyngs/INEbase/es/operacion.htm?c=Estadistica_C&cid=1254736177012&menu=ultiDatos&idp=1254734710990 |title=Estadística del Padrón Continuo |publisher=Instituto Nacional de Estadística (Spain) |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref> Cubans were the nationality that most benefited from the Democratic Memory Law: by end-2023 more than 226,000 applications had been submitted, with Havana as the leading consulate of origin. In 2023 at least 28,900 Cubans emigrated to Spain, and 33,900 in 2024, for an approximate two-year total of 62,800. The Cuban community resident in Spain exceeds 257,000 individuals by conservative estimates.

===== Brazil =====
{{main|Cuban immigration to Brazil}}
Brazil has become a significant destination for Cuban migration in South America, particularly within recent flows of international protection applications and immigration regularization. According to data from the Observatory of International Migration (OBMigra), linked to Brazil's National Migration Registry System, the number of Cuban nationals with migration registration in Brazil increased from 28,374 during 2011–2020 to 103,427 during 2021–2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Refúgio em Números e Publicações |url=https://www.gov.br/mj/pt-br/assuntos/seus-direitos/refugio/refugio-em-numeros-e-publicacoes |website=Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (Brasil) |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> Brazil recorded 68,159 asylum applications in 2024, of which 22,288 were from Cuban nationals, making them the second largest applicant group behind Venezuelans.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Brasil registra mais de 68 mil pedidos de refúgio em 2024 |url=https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/direitos-humanos/noticia/2025-06/brasil-registra-mais-de-68-mil-pedidos-de-refugio-em-2024 |work=Agência Brasil |date=13 June 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> UNHCR and media reports based on official data indicate that during certain months of 2025 Cubans led asylum application numbers in Brazil, surpassing Venezuelans, reflecting a shift in the composition of regional migratory flows.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brazil |url=https://www.unhcr.org/where-we-work/countries/brazil |website=UNHCR |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> Most Cuban migrants enter through the northern border in the state of Roraima, from where a significant proportion relocate to southern and southeastern regions, particularly São Paulo.<ref>{{Cite web |title=R4V Regional Refugee and Migrant Response Plan (RMRP) |url=https://rmrp.r4v.info/ |website=UNHCR / IOM R4V Platform |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref>

===== Uruguay, Costa Rica, and Mexico =====
Uruguay recorded 7,413 Cuban asylum applications in 2024 and a further 1,700 in the first quarter of 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |author=International Organization for Migration (IOM) |title=More Cubans Are Choosing to Stay in Latin America, New IOM Data Shows |date=23 March 2026 |website=ReliefWeb |url=https://reliefweb.int/report/cuba/more-cubans-are-choosing-stay-latin-america-new-iom-data-shows |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> The [[International Organization for Migration|IOM]] notes that Costa Rica has also become a significant settlement destination: a survey conducted among Cubans present in the country in January and February 2026 found that 94% intended to remain, citing institutional stability and access to international protection.<ref>{{Cite news |author=Rivera, Marcella |title=El 94% de los cubanos encuestados en Costa Rica expresa intención de permanecer en el país |work=[[Infobae]] |date=24 March 2026 |url=https://www.infobae.com/costa-rica/2026/03/24/el-94-de-los-cubanos-encuestados-en-costa-rica-expresa-intencion-de-permanecer-en-el-pais/ |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> Mexico remains statistically a transit country for most migrants, though a growing number have settled there; in 2024 it recorded 17,884 Cuban asylum applications.<ref>{{Cite news |author=Agencia EFE |title=Las peticiones de asilo en México caen casi a la mitad en 2024 pese al récord de migración |work=[[Swissinfo]] |date=11 January 2025 |url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/las-peticiones-de-asilo-en-m%C3%A9xico-caen-casi-a-la-mitad-en-2024-pese-al-r%C3%A9cord-de-migraci%C3%B3n/88707713 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref>

===== The Balkans =====
The "Balkan route" was used by Cuban migrants primarily between 2021 and 2023 as part of irregular flows toward the European Union. Investigations coordinated by Europol and Interpol documented people-smuggling networks that exploited the visa-free regime then in effect between Cuba and Serbia to transport migrants by air to Belgrade, from where they continued their irregular transit through the Western Balkans toward EU member states.<ref name="europol2023">{{Cite web |title=62 transcontinental migrant smugglers arrested |url=https://www.europol.europa.eu/media-press/newsroom/news/62-transcontinental-migrant-smugglers-arrested |work=Europol |date=24 July 2023 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Disruption of transnational migrant smuggling network leads to 62 arrests |url=https://www.interpol.int/News-and-Events/News/2023/Disruption-of-transnational-migrant-smuggling-network-leads-to-62-arrests |work=Interpol |date=24 July 2023 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> Criminal networks charged approximately €9,000 per person for the full journey, including transport, accommodation, and falsified documentation; an estimated 5,000 Cuban nationals were introduced irregularly into the EU through this corridor.<ref name="europol2023" /> Europol's analysis indicates that migrants flew from Cuba to Serbia and were subsequently transported by land through North Macedonia and Greece, with Spain as the primary final destination. In 2023, Serbia introduced visa restrictions for Cuban nationals as part of its progressive alignment with EU migration policy and in response to the use of its territory as a transit point toward the Schengen area.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Serbia tightens visa rules under EU pressure over migration route |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/serbia-tightens-visa-rules-migration-pressure-2023-10-26/ |work=Reuters |date=26 October 2023 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref>

== Culture ==
{{main|Culture of Cuba}}

Cuban culture is the result of a historical process of [[transculturation]]—a term coined by ethnologist and sociologist [[Fernando Ortiz Fernández|Fernando Ortiz]] in his work ''[[Cuban Counterpoint: Tobacco and Sugar]]'' (1940)—<ref name="ortiz1940">{{cite book |last=Ortiz |first=Fernando |title=Contrapunteo cubano del tabaco y el azúcar |year=1940 |publisher=Jesús Montero |location=Havana}}</ref> in which European traditions, primarily Spanish in origin, the traditions of various sub-Saharan African ethnic groups, and the indigenous traditions of the [[Taíno]] and [[Ciboney]] peoples converged over the course of five centuries. This process, which unfolded under conditions of colonialism, slavery, and successive waves of migration, gave rise to a distinct cultural identity of universal reach, whose most visible expressions are music, dance, literature, architecture, the visual arts, and cuisine. Cuba has exerted an influence on twentieth-century international popular culture that is notable and disproportionate to its size, above all through music and film.<ref>{{cite book |last=Carpentier |first=Alejo |title=La música en Cuba |year=1946 |publisher=Fondo de Cultura Económica |location=Mexico City}}</ref>

=== Historical roots and cultural composition ===

The indigenous presence in Cuba, primarily that of the [[Taíno]] and [[Ciboney]] peoples, underwent a near-total demographic collapse in the first decades of Spanish colonization in the sixteenth century.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rouse |first=Irving |title=The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus |year=1992 |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven |isbn=0-300-05181-6}}</ref> Their legacy, however, persists in the vocabulary—words such as ''tobacco'', ''[[hurricane]]'', ''maize'', ''[[yuca]]'', ''[[canoe]]'', and ''[[hammock]]'' are of [[Arawakan languages|Arawakan]] origin—<ref>{{cite book |last=Arrom |first=José Juan |title=Estudios de lexicología antillana |year=1980 |publisher=Casa de las Américas |location=Havana}}</ref> as well as in agriculture and cuisine. Spanish colonization, which began with the founding of [[Baracoa]] in 1511, laid the foundations of the Castilian language, ecclesiastical institutions, monumental architecture, and the literary forms that would shape the island's high culture for centuries.<ref>{{cite book |last=Torres Cuevas |first=Eduardo |last2=Loyola Vega |first2=Oscar |title=Historia de Cuba, 1492–1898: Formación y liberación de la nación |year=2002 |publisher=Editorial Pueblo y Educación |location=Havana |isbn=978-959-13-0746-0}}</ref>

The trade in enslaved Africans, which intensified from the seventeenth century onward and reached its height between the late eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries—when Cuba became the world's leading sugar producer—<ref>{{cite book |last=Moreno Fraginals |first=Manuel |title=El ingenio: Complejo económico social cubano del azúcar |year=1978 |volume=3 vols. |publisher=Editorial de Ciencias Sociales |location=Havana}}</ref> brought to the island populations from [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]] (known in Cuba as [[Lucumí people|Lucumí]]), [[Bantu peoples|Bantu]] (Kongo), [[Fon people|Fon]] ([[Arará]]), and [[Efik people|Efik]]–[[Ibibio people|Ibibio]] ([[Abakuá]]) ethnic groups,<ref>{{cite book |last=Ortiz |first=Fernando |title=Los negros brujos: Apuntes para un estudio de etnología criminal |year=1906 |publisher=Librería de Fernando Fe |location=Madrid}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Cabrera |first=Lydia |title=El monte: Igbo, finda, ewe orisha, vititi nfinda |year=1954 |publisher=Ediciones C.R. |location=Havana}}</ref> whose religious, musical, linguistic, and culinary systems merged with European ones to produce the cultural forms most characteristic of Cuban identity. Transculturation operated under the structural violence of slavery, yet gave rise to one of the most complex cultural syntheses in the Americas.<ref name="ortiz1940" /><ref>{{cite book |last=Palmié |first=Stephan |title=Wizards and Scientists: Explorations in Afro-Cuban Modernity and Tradition |year=2002 |publisher=Duke University Press |location=Durham |isbn=978-0-8223-2842-1}}</ref>

Subsequent waves of migration added further layers: [[Canary Islands|Canarian]] settlers, whose imprint on folk customs and rural tradition remains perceptible in rural areas;<ref name="naranjo2009">{{cite book |editor-last=Naranjo Orovio |editor-first=Consuelo |title=Historia de Cuba |year=2009 |publisher=Doce Calles / Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas |location=Madrid |isbn=978-84-9744-077-6}}</ref> Haitian and Jamaican immigrants who arrived in the [[Oriente Province|Oriente]] region from the late eighteenth century onward, bringing their own musical traditions;<ref>{{cite book |last=Casey |first=Matthew |title=Empire's Guestworkers: Haitian Migrants in Cuba during the Age of US Occupation |year=2017 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-1-107-12769-2}}</ref> Chinese contract workers who arrived between 1847 and 1874, leaving a lasting mark on cuisine;<ref>{{cite book |last=López |first=Kathleen M. |title=Chinese Cubans: A Transnational History |year=2013 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |location=Chapel Hill |isbn=978-1-4696-0713-9}}</ref> and Catalan, Asturian, Galician, and Basque communities established primarily within the urban commercial bourgeoisie.<ref name="naranjo2009" /> All these elements accumulated unevenly according to region, social class, and historical period, producing the internal heterogeneity that characterizes Cuban culture.

==== Tobacco culture ====

[[File:MRO_Cuba_Harvest_01.jpg|thumb|Harvesting tobacco leaves on a ''vega'' (tobacco plantation) in [[Vuelta Abajo]], [[Pinar del Río]].]]

Tobacco is one of the pillars of Cuban cultural identity and the agricultural product through which Cuba has acquired the greatest international renown.<ref name="Ortiz2002">{{cite book |last=Ortiz |first=Fernando |author-link=Fernando Ortiz |title=[[Contrapunteo cubano del tabaco y el azúcar]] |publisher=Cátedra |series=Letras Hispánicas, 528 |location=Madrid |year=2002 |orig-year=1940 |isbn=978-84-376-1987-3}}</ref> Cultivated and consumed by the [[Taíno people|Taíno]] before the arrival of Europeans, it was introduced to the European continent from Cuba by Spanish colonizers in the sixteenth century.<ref name="Ortiz2002" /> The [[Vuelta Abajo]] region, in the present-day [[Pinar del Río Province]], particularly the municipalities of [[San Juan y Martínez]], [[San Luis, Pinar del Río|San Luis]], and the [[Viñales Valley]], was identified as early as the seventeenth century as the area producing the finest [[Habano cigar|Havana cigars]] in the world, owing to the singular composition of its red soil (''tierra prieta'') and its specific climatic conditions.<ref name="Ortiz2002" /> The [[cultural landscape]] of the Viñales Valley was designated a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]] in 1999.<ref name="UNESCOVinales">{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/840/ |title=Viñales Valley |website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref>

The ''vega''—the tobacco plantation—and the figure of the [[veguero]] (tobacco grower) gave rise to a distinct peasant culture in western Cuba.<ref name="Ortiz2002" /> The hand-rolling of the [[Habano cigar|habano]]—the Cuban cigar—attained a singular level of artisanal refinement: the different components of the cigar (''capa'', ''capote'', and ''tripa'') require leaves with characteristics specific to each farm, and the craft of the [[torcedor]] (cigar roller) demands years of training and practice. Among the most prestigious historic brands are [[H. Upmann]] (founded 1844),<ref name="HUpmann">{{cite web |url=https://www.habanos.com/en/habanos/h-upmann/ |title=H. Upmann – Brand History |website=[[Habanos S.A.]] |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> [[Partagás]] (1845),<ref name="Partagas">{{cite web |url=https://www.habanos.com/en/habanos/partagas/ |title=Partagás – Brand History |website=Habanos S.A. |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> [[Romeo y Julieta (cigar)|Romeo y Julieta]] (1875),<ref name="RyJ">{{cite web |url=https://www.habanos.com/en/habanos/romeo-y-julieta/ |title=Romeo y Julieta – Brand History |website=Habanos S.A. |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> and [[Montecristo (cigar)|Montecristo]] (1935),<ref name="Montecristo">{{cite web |url=https://www.habanos.com/en/habanos/montecristo/ |title=Montecristo – Brand History |website=Habanos S.A. |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> all of which consolidated their reputations during the [[Republic of Cuba (1902–1959)|Republic]]. The [[Cohiba (cigar brand)|Cohiba]] brand was created in 1966 for use in Cuban state protocol.<ref name="Cohiba">{{cite web |url=https://www.habanos.com/en/habanos/cohiba/ |title=Cohiba – Brand History |website=Habanos S.A. |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref>

In the cigar factories—the large hand-rolling workshops—there operated from the mid-nineteenth century onward a cultural institution with no documented equivalent in any other industry in the world: the [[lector de tabaquería|factory reader]]. From 1865, when the practice was formalized with the support of labor leader [[Saturnino Martínez]] in [[Havana]],<ref name="Tinajero2007">{{cite book |last=Tinajero |first=Araceli |author-link=Araceli Tinajero |title=El lector de tabaquería: Historia de una tradición cubana |publisher=Verbum |location=Madrid |year=2007 |isbn=978-84-7962-392-0}}</ref> the tobacco workers themselves paid out of their own pockets for a reader who, seated on an elevated platform at the center of the workshop, read aloud while they worked: newspapers, novels, plays, philosophical essays, and works of political theory.<ref name="Tinajero2007" /> The practice contributed to the intellectual and political development of the tobacco-working class, to the spread of abolitionist and pro-independence ideas, and produced a working class of notably high cultural attainment.<ref name="Tinajero2007" /> Cuba has put forward to UNESCO the nomination of this tradition for possible inscription on the [[Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity]].<ref name="UNESCOlectores">{{cite news |title=Cuba Seeks World Heritage Designation for Cigar-Factory Readers |work=Arab News |date=26 November 2012 |url=https://www.arabnews.com/cuban-cigar-%E2%80%98readers%E2%80%99-touted-unesco-heritage-honor |language=en |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref>

==== Music ====
Music is one of the most internationally influential expressions of Cuban culture. It showcases the blend of European and African traditions that characterizes Cuban culture.<ref name="Carpentier1946">{{cite book|last=Carpentier|first=Alejo|title=La música en Cuba|publisher=Fondo de Cultura Económica|location=Mexico City|year=1946|language=Spanish}}</ref><ref name="Sublette2007">{{cite book|last=Sublette|first=Ned|title=Cuba and Its Music: From the First Drums to the Mambo|publisher=Chicago Review Press|location=Chicago|year=2007|isbn=978-1-55652-632-9}}</ref>

The oldest documented musical forms on the island include peasant songs of Spanish origin – romances, glossed décimas, tonadas – which coexisted with the ritual drumming and chants of African slaves. From this Spanish peasant substratum emerged the ''punto guajiro'', or ''punto cubano'', a vocal form of poetic improvisation in eight-syllable [[décima]]s, whose practice survives through ''[[repentismo]]'', the art of improvised, extemporaneous versification. The [[Décima|décima espinela]] is the quintessential stanzaic form of Cuban popular poetry.<ref name="Carpentier1946" />

The [[Contradanza|Cuban contradanza]], derived from the French [[Contra dance|Contredanse]] and the Spanish contradanza, became distinctly Cuban in the late eighteenth century through the incorporation of African syncopation and the rhythmic cell known as the [[Clave (rhythm)|clave]], thereby articulating the two principal axes of all subsequent Cuban music: melody of European origin and rhythm of African origin.<ref name="Sublette2007" /><ref name="Carpentier1946" /> The [[Habanera (music)|habanera]], a genre that achieved enormous international popularity in the nineteenth century, developed from the contradanza; the composer [[Sebastián Yradier]] used the habanera pattern in "[[La Paloma (song)|La paloma]]" (c. 1861),<ref name="Sublette2007" /> and [[Georges Bizet]] employed it in the celebrated aria from ''[[Carmen (opera)|Carmen]]'' (1875).

The [[Danzón]] evolved from the Cuban contradanza and was created by the Matanzas-born composer [[Miguel Faílde]], whose piece "Las alturas de Simpson" (1879) is regarded as the genre's first formally composed work.<ref name="Sublette2007" /><ref name="Manuel2006">{{cite book|last1=Manuel|first1=Peter|last2=Bilby|first2=Kenneth|last3=Largey|first3=Michael|title=Caribbean Currents: Caribbean Music from Rumba to Reggae|edition=2nd rev.|publisher=Temple University Press|location=Philadelphia|year=2006|isbn=978-1-59213-463-2}}</ref> The danzón was adopted as the national dance in the late nineteenth century and remained popular among the urban middle and working classes well into the twentieth century, being especially cultivated in the recreational societies of [[Matanzas]] and [[Havana]].

[[File:Bailarines de rumba cubana en la plaza de los trabajadores de Camagüey, Cuba.jpg|thumb|Dancers of Cuban rumba in the Plaza de los Trabajadores, Camagüey, Cuba.]]

[[Cuban rumba|Rumba]] emerged in the tenement courtyards (''solares'') and poor urban districts of Havana and Matanzas in the second half of the nineteenth century as a musical and choreographic expression of the working-class Afro-Cuban population. It should not be confused with Spanish [[flamenco]] rumba, nor with the ballroom dance styles bearing that name abroad. Cuban rumba comprises three modalities: [[Yambú]], slow in tempo and solemn in character; [[Columbia (dance)|columbia]], danced solo by men with great acrobatic virtuosity; and [[Guaguancó]], the most widespread form, narrative and expressive in character, danced by both men and women. Its principal instruments are the [[Conga (drum)|tumbadoras]] (congas), [[Clave (instrument)|claves]], and cajones (box drums).<ref name="Sublette2007" /><ref name="Manuel2006" /> [[UNESCO]] inscribed rumba on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016.<ref name="UNESCO2016">{{cite web|url=https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/rumba-in-cuba-a-festive-combination-of-music-and-dances-and-all-the-practices-associated-01185|title=Rumba in Cuba, a festive combination of music and dances and all the practices associated|work=Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity|publisher=UNESCO|year=2016|access-date=5 June 2026}}</ref>

[[Son cubano]], which would go on to exert a decisive influence on twentieth-century popular music of African descent throughout the Americas, developed in eastern Cuba – chiefly in what are now the provinces of [[Santiago de Cuba]] and [[Guantánamo Province|Guantánamo]] — in the late nineteenth century, out of the fusion of Spanish-derived ''trova'' singing with rhythmic percussion patterns of African origin, organized around the structure of the clave.<ref name="Sublette2007" /><ref name="Manuel2006" /> Its original instruments include the [[Tres (instrument)|tres]] — a three-course, six-string guitar with a distinctive timbre – along with [[maracas]], the [[bongo drum|bongó]], the [[güiro]], claves, and guitar; the trumpet was incorporated in later stages. Son moved from the eastern provinces to Havana in the early decades of the twentieth century and was widely disseminated by the [[Sexteto Habanero]] (founded in 1920) and the [[Septeto Nacional Ignacio Piñeiro]] (founded in 1927), which made the genre's first successful recordings.<ref name="Sublette2007" /> The tres player and singer [[Compay Segundo|Francisco Repilado, "Compay Segundo,"]] the composer [[Miguel Matamoros]], and the ''sonero'' [[Nico Saquito]] are towering figures of classic son. Several subforms derived from the genre: [[Son montuno]], guajiro-son, [[guaracha]] — festive and burlesque in character – and bolero-son.

[[File:Pacho Alonso, La Lupe & Benny Moré.jpg|thumb|right|300px|[[Pacho Alonso]], [[La Lupe]], and [[Beny Moré]], three emblematic figures of twentieth-century Cuban popular music.]]

Cuban [[bolero]], which emerged in Santiago de Cuba in the late nineteenth century as the sentimental branch of ''trova'', differs from Spanish bolero in tempo, harmonic structure, and expression. Its creation is credited to the Santiago-born ''trovador'' [[Pepe Sánchez (musician)|Pepe Sánchez]], author of "Tristezas" (c. 1885), considered the genre's first composition.<ref name="Sublette2007" /><ref name="Manuel2006" /> It was cultivated within the tradition of ''trova'' by figures such as [[Sindo Garay]], [[Alberto Villalón]], and [[Manuel Corona (musician)|Manuel Corona]], and in the twentieth century became the quintessential sentimental idiom of Spanish American popular music. [[Beny Moré]], [[Elena Burke]], [[Omara Portuondo]], and [[Ibrahim Ferrer]] represent its highest interpretive expressions.

[[Afro-Cuban jazz]] arose from the convergence of Cuban rhythms with American jazz beginning in the 1920s. The percussionist [[Chano Pozo]], who collaborated with [[Dizzy Gillespie]] in New York from 1947 onward, and the trumpeter and bandleader [[Mario Bauzá]], co-founder of the orchestra [[Machito|Machito and His Afro-Cubans]] in 1940, were decisive figures in the emergence of [[Latin jazz]], or ''cubop''.<ref name="Acosta2003">{{cite book|last=Acosta|first=Leonardo|title=Cubano Be, Cubano Bop: One Hundred Years of Jazz in Cuba|translator=Daniel S. Whitesell|publisher=Smithsonian Books|location=Washington, D.C.|year=2003|isbn=978-1-58834-147-1}}</ref> In Cuba, the [[Orquesta Casino de la Playa]], the Orquesta Riverside, and the pianist [[Bebo Valdés]] developed a jazz idiom of their own, later continued by [[Chucho Valdés]] and the ensemble [[Irakere]] (founded in 1973).<ref name="Acosta2003" />

[[Mambo (music)|Mambo]] emerged in the late 1930s and reached its height between the 1940s and 1950s, arising from the convergence of son with the [[big band]] format. The genre's paternity is disputed: the bassist [[Orestes López]] and his brother [[Cachao|Israel "Cachao" López]] are credited as the authors of the danzón "Mambo" (1938), considered its direct antecedent; [[Arsenio Rodríguez]] contributed fundamental rhythmic innovations; and the pianist and bandleader [[Dámaso Pérez Prado]], a Cuban born in Matanzas who settled in Mexico in 1948, propelled it to international fame with his recordings of the 1940s and 1950s.<ref name="Sublette2007" /><ref name="Manuel2006" /> The singer Beny Moré (1919–1963), regarded by much specialist criticism as the most accomplished Cuban musician of the twentieth century by virtue of his voice and exceptional stylistic versatility,<ref name="Sublette2007" /> was the foremost interpreter of mambo, son, and bolero in their most elaborate forms.

[[Cha-cha-chá (music)|Cha-cha-chá]] was created around 1953 by the Havana-born violinist and bandleader [[Enrique Jorrín]] as a rhythmic simplification of the danzón-mambo, intended to make the dance easier to follow.<ref name="Manuel2006" /><ref name="Sublette2007" /> Its name derives from the sound produced by dancers' feet performing the genre's characteristic offbeat step. It achieved immediate international popularity and became one of the most widely practiced [[ballroom dance]]s in the Western world during the second half of the twentieth century; the [[Orquesta Aragón]] — founded in [[Cienfuegos]] in 1939 – was its most representative ensemble.

[[File:Silvio Rodríguez en la presentación del libro "Por todo espacio, por este tiempo" en el CCK, 26 de mayo de 2015.jpg|thumb|[[Silvio Rodríguez]], singer-songwriter and co-founder of the ''nueva trova'' movement, one of the most influential voices in Spanish-language song-writing.]]

[[Nueva trova]] emerged in the late 1960s as a singer-songwriter movement linked to the revolutionary process, albeit with a complex relationship to state cultural institutions.<ref name="Moore2006">{{cite book|last=Moore|first=Robin D.|title=Music and Revolution: Cultural Change in Socialist Cuba|publisher=University of California Press|location=Berkeley|year=2006|isbn=0-520-24711-6}}</ref> Its principal figures, Silvio Rodríguez and [[Pablo Milanés]], developed a style that combined the Cuban ''trova'' tradition with American [[folk music]] and French [[chanson]], marked by texts of elaborate poetic construction. The [[Grupo de Experimentación Sonora del ICAIC]], active between 1969 and 1978, served as the laboratory in which many of the movement's ideas took shape.<ref name="Moore2006" /> [[Noel Nicola]], [[Sara González (singer)|Sara González]], and, in later generations, [[Carlos Varela (musician)|Carlos Varela]] represent other strands of the movement.

[[File:Image of Pedro Calvo.jpg|thumb|[[Pedrito Calvo]], lead vocalist of Los Van Van for nearly thirty years and one of the most representative voices of Cuban timba.]]

[[Timba]], developed in Havana from the late 1980s and consolidated during the 1990s, is the most influential contemporary expression of Cuban music. It combines son, rumba, jazz, funk, and the rhythmic patterns of the [[Batá drum|batá]] drums within structures of great rhythmic and harmonic complexity, performed by large ensembles.<ref name="Perna2005">{{cite book|last=Perna|first=Vincenzo|title=Timba: The Sound of the Cuban Crisis|publisher=Ashgate|location=Burlington|year=2005|isbn=978-0-7546-3941-1}}</ref><ref name="Moore2006" /> [[Los Van Van]] — founded by the bassist and composer [[Juan Formell]] in 1969 – and [[NG La Banda]] — founded by the flautist [[José Luis Cortés (musician)|José Luis Cortés]] in 1988 – are its most representative groups, along with [[Issac Delgado]], [[Bamboleo (band)|Bamboleo]], and [[Charanga Habanera]].<ref name="Perna2005" />

The [[Buena Vista Social Club]] project (recorded in 1996; released in 1997 by [[World Circuit Records|World Circuit]]/[[Nonesuch Records|Nonesuch]]), coordinated by the American guitarist [[Ry Cooder]] together with producer [[Nick Gold]], brought together a group of Cuban musicians from earlier generations – among them [[Compay Segundo]], Ibrahim Ferrer, [[Rubén González (musician)|Rubén González]], and Omara Portuondo – and produced an album of enormous international impact that renewed worldwide interest in classic Cuban son.<ref name="Manuel2006" /><ref name="Perna2005" /> The eponymous documentary directed by [[Wim Wenders]] (1999) further broadened its global reach.

==== Ballet ====

The antecedents of ballet in Cuba date to the 19th century, when the [[Gran Teatro de La Habana|Teatro Tacón]] in [[Havana]] — officially inaugurated on 15 April 1838, and reputed in its day to be the largest and most lavish theater in the Americas, and the third in the world in technical and acoustic terms, after [[La Scala]] in Milan and the [[Vienna State Opera]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://excelenciascuba.com/culturales/gran-teatro-de-la-habana-182-anos-de-virtud |title=Gran Teatro de La Habana: 182 años de virtud |trans-title=Gran Teatro de La Habana: 182 Years of Virtue |language=es |publisher=Excelencias Cuba |year=2020 |access-date=6 June 2026}}</ref> — regularly hosted touring European opera and ballet companies. The founding of the [[Sociedad Pro-Arte Musical]] on 2 December 1918, promoted by [[María Teresa García Montes de Giberga]],<ref name="pacheco">{{cite book |last=Pacheco Valera |first=Irina |title=La Sociedad Pro-Arte Musical: Testimonio de su tiempo |trans-title=The Sociedad Pro-Arte Musical: A Testimony of Its Time |language=es |publisher=Ediciones La Memoria, Centro Cultural Pablo de la Torriente Brau |location=Havana |isbn=978-959-7135-74-6}}</ref> created the institutional framework for the teaching and patronage of [[classical ballet]] on the island, attracting European-trained teachers and training the first generations of Cuban dancers.

[[File:Alicia Alonso by Annemarie Heinrich, 1958.jpg|thumb|[[Alicia Alonso]] (1920–2019), Cuban [[prima ballerina assoluta]] and founder and director of the [[National Ballet of Cuba]], in 1958.]]

The central figure of Cuban ballet is [[Alicia Alonso]] (1920–2019), a [[prima ballerina assoluta]], choreographer, and teacher of international standing. Trained first in Havana and subsequently at the [[School of American Ballet]] in New York City, she joined [[American Ballet Theatre]] in 1940,<ref name="singer">{{cite book |last=Singer |first=Toba |title=Fernando Alonso: The Father of Cuban Ballet |year=2013 |publisher=University Press of Florida |location=Gainesville, Florida |isbn=978-0-8130-4402-6}}</ref> where she danced the leading roles of the classical repertoire — [[Giselle]] in particular – despite progressively losing her sight from the late 1930s onward as a result of a bilateral retinal detachment.<ref name="obit">{{cite news |last1=Orsi |first1=Peter |last2=Rodríguez |first2=Andrea |title=Alicia Alonso, grande dame of Cuban ballet, dies at 98 |work=PBS NewsHour |agency=Associated Press |date=17 October 2019 |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/alicia-alonso-grande-dame-of-cuban-ballet-dies-at-98 |access-date=6 June 2026}}</ref> In October 1948 she founded, together with [[Fernando Alonso (dancer)|Fernando Alonso]] and [[Alberto Alonso]], the Ballet Alicia Alonso<ref name="singer"/> — renamed Ballet de Cuba in 1955 and, after the [[Cuban Revolution]], reorganized in 1959 under its definitive name, the [[National Ballet of Cuba]].<ref name="bnchist">{{cite web |url=https://www.ciudaddeladanza.com/bibliodanza/bibliodanza/ballet-clasico/historia-del-ballet-de-cuba.html |title=Historia del Ballet de Cuba |trans-title=History of the Ballet de Cuba |language=es |publisher=Ciudad de la Danza |access-date=6 June 2026}}</ref> The company developed a technique of its own, known as the [[Cuban school of ballet]], which combines the academic rigor of the Russian tradition with expressive elements particular to the Cuban dancer,<ref name="singer"/><ref>{{cite book |last=John |first=Suki |title=Contemporary Dance in Cuba: Técnica Cubana as Revolutionary Movement |year=2012 |publisher=McFarland |location=Jefferson, North Carolina |isbn=978-0-7864-4901-9}}</ref> and produced generations of internationally prominent artists. The National Ballet of Cuba received awards at festivals and competitions in Europe and the [[Soviet Union]] from the 1960s onward – taking part in the [[Varna International Ballet Competition]] for the first time in 1964 —<ref name="bnchist"/> and maintained a sustained international presence. Alonso continued to direct the company until her death on 17 October 2019, at the age of 98.<ref name="obit"/>

==== Literature ====
{{Main|Cuban literature}}

The oldest surviving text of literature produced in Cuba is the ''[[Espejo de paciencia]]'' (''Mirror of Patience'', 1608), an epic poem written in [[ottava rima]] by [[Silvestre de Balboa|Silvestre de Balboa Troya y Quesada]]—born in the [[Canary Islands]] but resident on the island—recounting the kidnapping of Bishop [[Juan de las Cabezas Altamirano]] by the French [[privateer]] Gilberto Girón and his subsequent rescue.<ref name="vitier">{{cite book |last=Vitier |first=Cintio |title=Lo cubano en la poesía |edition=2nd |publisher=Instituto del Libro |location=Havana |year=1970 |language=Spanish}}</ref><ref name="chllal1">{{cite book |last=González Echevarría |first=Roberto |last2=Pupo-Walker |first2=Enrique |title=The Cambridge History of Latin American Literature: Discovery to Modernism |volume=I |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-521-34069-4}}</ref> Rediscovered and published in 1838 by [[José Antonio Echeverría]], the poem has been claimed as the symbolic starting point of Cuban letters, although Cuban literature as a distinct body of expression really began to take shape in the late colonial period, when a series of individual voices started to articulate a [[Criollo peoples|Creole]] consciousness distinct from the Spanish metropole.

The first major name in Cuban letters is the [[Romanticism|Romantic]] poet [[José María Heredia (Cuban poet)|José María Heredia]] (1803–1839), whose odes "En el Teocali de Cholula" and "[[Oda al Niágara|Niágara]]" place him among the precursors of [[Romanticism in Hispanic America|Spanish-language Romanticism]] and among the first poets of continental renown.<ref name="chllal1" /> A contemporary of his, [[Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda]] (1814–1873), was born in [[Puerto Príncipe, Cuba|Puerto Príncipe]]—present-day [[Camagüey]]—and pursued most of her career in Spain, but her novel ''[[Sab (novel)|Sab]]'' (1841) stands as one of the earliest [[abolitionism|abolitionist]] texts written in Spanish, addressing [[slavery in Cuba]] from a critical standpoint unusual for its time.<ref>{{cite book |last=Luis |first=William |title=Literary Bondage: Slavery in Cuban Narrative |publisher=University of Texas Press |location=Austin |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-292-72463-1}}</ref> Havana's slaveholding society found its most precise and enduring portrait in ''[[Cecilia Valdés]]'' (definitive edition, 1882), by [[Cirilo Villaverde]] (1812–1894), a central work of nineteenth-century Cuban [[costumbrismo|costumbrist realism]] whose mixed-race protagonist became one of the most persistent symbols of national identity.<ref name="chllal1" />

No figure, however, carries the weight in Cuban culture of [[José Martí]] (1853–1895), whose importance transcends literature to encompass politics, ethical thought, and the very formation of the nation. As a writer, Martí renewed Spanish American prose and poetry with works such as ''[[Ismaelillo]]'' (1882) and ''[[Versos sencillos]]'' (1891), along with an extensive body of essays of extraordinary stylistic density, placing him among the founders of Spanish-language [[Modernismo]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Kirk |first=John M. |title=José Martí: Mentor of the Cuban Nation |publisher=University Press of Florida |location=Gainesville |year=1983 |isbn=978-0-8130-0736-6}}</ref><ref name="chllal1" /> His death in combat at [[Battle of Dos Ríos|Dos Ríos]] on 19 May 1895, during the [[Cuban War of Independence]], cemented his status as an irreplaceable founding figure.

In the early decades of the twentieth century, the poetic movement known as [[Negrismo]] reclaimed African heritage and popular [[Afro-Cuban]] culture as central components of national identity. Its foremost exponent was [[Nicolás Guillén]] (1902–1989), who in collections such as ''[[Motivos de son]]'' (1930), ''[[Sóngoro cosongo]]'' (1931), and ''[[West Indies, Ltd.]]'' (1934) incorporated the rhythms of [[son cubano|son]] and [[rumba]], popular Afro-Cuban speech, and a critical stance toward colonialism and racism, becoming a leading figure in twentieth-century Spanish American poetry and [[National Poet of Cuba]] after the [[Cuban Revolution]] of 1959.<ref>{{cite book |last=Williams |first=Lorna V. |title=Self and Society in the Poetry of Nicolás Guillén |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |location=Baltimore |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-8018-2666-5}}</ref> Those same years saw the emergence of [[Alejo Carpentier]] (1904–1980), a novelist, musicologist, and essayist born in [[Havana]] to a French father and a Russian mother, who would become the most influential Cuban novelist in twentieth-century world literature. In the preface to his novel ''[[The Kingdom of This World]]'' (1949), set during the [[Haitian Revolution]] led by [[Toussaint Louverture]], he formulated the concept of ''[[lo real maravilloso]]'' ("the marvelous real"), a direct precursor of the [[magic realism|magical realism]] that later flourished in Spanish America; his novels ''[[The Lost Steps]]'' (1953), ''[[Explosion in a Cathedral]]'' (1962), and ''[[Reasons of State]]'' (1974) combine historical and musicological erudition with an extraordinarily dense [[Neobaroque]] prose style.<ref>{{cite book |last=González Echevarría |first=Roberto |title=Alejo Carpentier: The Pilgrim at Home |publisher=Cornell University Press |location=Ithaca |year=1977 |isbn=978-0-8014-1029-1}}</ref>

[[File:Mariano_Rodriguez_-_Con_jóvenes_poetas.jpg|thumb|right|220px|[[José Lezama Lima]], [[Luis Rogelio Nogueras]], [[Antón Arrufat]], [[Pablo Armando Fernández]], [[Mariano Rodríguez (painter)|Mariano Rodríguez]], [[Heberto Padilla]], [[Sigifredo Álvarez Conesa]], [[Roberto Fernández Retamar]], and [[Víctor Casaus]], young poets and writers, Havana, c. 1950.]]

The mid-century cultural renewal found its most radical figure in [[José Lezama Lima]] (1910–1976). A Havana-born poet, essayist, and novelist, Lezama founded and edited the literary magazine ''[[Orígenes (magazine)|Orígenes]]'' (1944–1956), the principal hub of the Cuban cultural [[avant-garde]] of the period. His novel ''[[Paradiso (novel)|Paradiso]]'' (1966), with its labyrinthine structure and extremely dense neobaroque prose, ranks among the most ambitious and demanding works in Spanish-language literature.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pellón |first=Gustavo |title=José Lezama Lima's Joyful Vision: A Study of Paradiso and Other Prose Works |publisher=University of Texas Press |location=Austin |year=1989 |isbn=978-0-292-74020-4}}</ref> Close to him in sensibility but radically different in register, [[Virgilio Piñera]] (1912–1979)—primarily a playwright, though also a fiction writer and poet—represents the [[theatre of the absurd|absurdist]] and [[existentialism|existentialist]] strand of twentieth-century Cuban letters, producing a highly original body of work that endured periods of marginalization and official censorship during his lifetime.<ref name="chllal2">{{cite book |last=González Echevarría |first=Roberto |last2=Pupo-Walker |first2=Enrique |title=The Cambridge History of Latin American Literature: The Twentieth Century |volume=II |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-521-34070-0}}</ref>

The [[Cuban Revolution|Revolution of 1959]] produced a deep rupture in the Cuban literary field, dividing its principal voices between the island and exile. From London, where he settled permanently in 1966, [[Guillermo Cabrera Infante]] (1929–2005) published ''[[Three Trapped Tigers]]'' (''Tres tristes tigres'', 1967), a novel that reconstructs the nocturnal atmosphere of pre-revolutionary [[Havana]] through enormously inventive verbal play, indebted at once to [[James Joyce]] and to Havana colloquial speech.<ref name="chllal2" /> [[Reinaldo Arenas]] (1943–1990), persecuted by the state on account of his homosexuality and exiled from 1980, left behind a body of fiction of great intensity, the outstanding work being his autobiography ''[[Before Night Falls]]'' (''Antes que anochezca''), published posthumously in 1992 and adapted into a film in 2000.<ref>{{cite book |last=Soto |first=Francisco |title=Reinaldo Arenas: The Pentagonia |publisher=University Press of Florida |location=Gainesville |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-8130-1315-2}}</ref>

[[File:Leonardo_Padura_2015.jpg|thumb|right|Leonardo Padura in 2015.]]

Contemporary Cuban literature finds its figure of greatest international reach in [[Leonardo Padura]] (b. 1955). Still resident in Cuba, Padura built, through his series of [[crime fiction|noir crime novels]] featuring the detective [[Mario Conde (character)|Mario Conde]]—among them ''[[Havana Red]]'' (''Máscaras'', 1997) and ''[[Havana Fever]]'' (''La neblina del ayer'', 2005)—a literary chronicle of [[Havana]] and of post-revolutionary Cuban society marked by notable critical depth. His novel ''[[The Man Who Loved Dogs]]'' (''El hombre que amaba a los perros'', 2009), which reconstructs the final years of [[Leon Trotsky]] and the figure of his assassin [[Ramón Mercader]], won international acclaim. Padura received the [[National Prize for Literature (Cuba)|National Prize for Literature of Cuba]] in 2012<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cubadebate.cu/noticias/2012/12/20/leonardo-padura-recibe-el-premio-nacional-de-literatura/ |title=Leonardo Padura recibe el Premio Nacional de Literatura de Cuba |trans-title=Leonardo Padura receives the National Prize for Literature of Cuba |work=Cubadebate |date=20 December 2012 |access-date=9 June 2026 |language=Spanish}}</ref> and the [[Princess of Asturias Award for Literature]] in 2015.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fundacionprincesadeasturias.org/premiados/leonardo-padura-fuentes/ |title=Leonardo Padura Fuentes |work=Fundación Princesa de Asturias |access-date=9 June 2026 |language=Spanish}}</ref>

==== Visual arts ====

Cuban visual art has its roots in the academic painting of the colonial period, cultivated at the [[San Alejandro National Academy of Fine Arts]], founded in [[Havana]] on 12 January 1818, and generally regarded as the oldest continuously operating art school in Latin America.<ref group="note">The [[Academia de San Carlos]] in Mexico City, founded in 1781, is chronologically earlier; it was closed, however, between 1821 and 1824, interrupting its teaching. San Alejandro has undergone no comparable interruption since its foundation.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Cuba celebrates 205th anniversary of San Alejandro Fine Art Academy |url=https://www.plenglish.com/news/2023/01/12/cuba-celebrates-205th-anniversary-of-san-alejandro-fine-art-academy/ |work=Prensa Latina |date=12 January 2023 |access-date=7 June 2026}}</ref> Among the academic painters of the 19th and early 20th centuries who passed through its studios were [[Leopoldo Romañach]] and [[Armando Menocal|Armando García Menocal]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Sullivan |first=Edward J. |title=Latin American Art in the Twentieth Century |location=London |publisher=Phaidon Press |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-7148-3210-4 |pages=44–48}}</ref>

[[File:AmeliaJGS003.jpg|thumb|[[Amelia Peláez]] (1896–1968), a Cuban painter and a central figure of the island's artistic avant-garde.]]

The Cuban [[avant-garde]] emerged in the 1920s, when painters trained in Europe returned to the island with a renewed outlook. [[Amelia Peláez]] (1896–1968) developed an original pictorial idiom that fused [[Cubism]] and [[Fauvism]] with the decorative motifs of Havana's colonial architecture—leaded stained glass, wrought-iron grilles and polychrome [[azulejo]] tiles—in compositions of vivid color and pronounced geometric structure.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sullivan |first=Edward J. |title=Latin American Art in the Twentieth Century |location=London |publisher=Phaidon Press |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-7148-3210-4 |pages=48–52}}</ref> [[Eduardo Abela]] (1889–1965) is remembered for his paintings of rural subjects and for creating the satirical character "El Bobo", which was widely reproduced in the press of the day.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hartman |first=Joseph |title=Abela, Eduardo (1889–1965) |url=https://www.rem.routledge.com/articles/abela-eduardo-1889-1965 |work=Routledge Encyclopedia of Modernism |publisher=Taylor and Francis |date=5 September 2016 |access-date=7 June 2026}}</ref>

[[File:Wilfredo Lam.jpg|thumb|[[Wifredo Lam]] (1902–1982), whose work brought together European [[Surrealism]] and the iconography of Yoruba religion and Afro-Caribbean culture.]]

[[Wifredo Lam]] (1902–1982), born in [[Sagua la Grande]] to a father of Chinese descent and an [[Afro-Cuban]] mother, is the Cuban visual artist of greatest international standing of the 20th century. Trained in [[Madrid]] and formed within the Parisian [[Surrealism|Surrealist]] circle—with close ties to [[Pablo Picasso]] and [[André Breton]]—he developed a pictorial vocabulary that brought together European Surrealism and the iconography of [[Yoruba religion|Yoruba]] worship and Afro-Caribbean culture.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sims |first=Lowery Stokes |title=Wifredo Lam and the International Avant-Garde, 1923–1982 |location=Austin |publisher=University of Texas Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-292-77750-7}}</ref> His painting ''The Jungle'' (''La jungla'', 1942–1943) is part of the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wifredo Lam. ''La jungla (The Jungle)''. 1942–43 |url=https://www.moma.org/collection/works/34666 |work=The Collection |publisher=Museum of Modern Art |location=New York |access-date=7 June 2026}}</ref> [[René Portocarrero]] (1912–1985) explored the iconography of Afro-Cuban religion and of colonial architecture with an exuberant palette and an expressionist lyricism of considerable intensity.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sullivan |first=Edward J. |title=Latin American Art in the Twentieth Century |location=London |publisher=Phaidon Press |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-7148-3210-4 |pages=52–55}}</ref>

After the [[Cuban Revolution]] of 1959, the visual arts entered a period of ferment tied to the revolutionary cultural project, particularly evident in the political posters and graphic design of the [[Cuban Institute of Cinematographic Art and Industry|Cuban Institute of Cinematographic Art and Industry (ICAIC)]], which between the 1960s and the 1980s produced a school of poster design that won wide international recognition.<ref>{{cite book |last=Cushing |first=Lincoln |title=¡Revolución! Cuban Poster Art |location=San Francisco |publisher=Chronicle Books |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-8118-3582-4}}</ref> In January 1981 the group exhibition ''Volumen Uno'', held at the Centro de Arte Internacional in Havana,<ref group="note">The exhibition, which brought together eleven young artists, opened on 14 January 1981, at the newly established Centro de Arte Internacional on Calle San Rafael in Havana. The participants were [[Flavio Garciandía]], [[José Bedia Valdés|José Bedia]], [[Tomás Sánchez (painter)|Tomás Sánchez]], [[Juan Francisco Elso]], [[Gustavo Pérez Monzón]], [[Leandro Soto]], [[Rubén Torres Llorca]], [[Rogelio López Marín]], Ricardo Rodríguez Brey, [[Israel León]] and [[José Manuel Fors]].</ref> marked the emergence of a conceptually oriented generation of artists—among them [[José Bedia Valdés|José Bedia]], [[Flavio Garciandía]] and [[Juan Francisco Elso]]—who opened a dialogue with international currents in contemporary art.<ref>{{cite book |last=Camnitzer |first=Luis |title=New Art of Cuba |edition=revised |location=Austin |publisher=University of Texas Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-292-70517-3}}</ref><ref name="Weiss2011">{{cite book |last=Weiss |first=Rachel |title=To and from Utopia in the New Cuban Art |location=Minneapolis |publisher=University of Minnesota Press |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-8166-6515-0}}</ref> The collective [[Los Carpinteros]] (active from 1991; the name adopted in 1994)<ref group="note">The collective was founded in 1991 by Marco Antonio Castillo Valdés, Dagoberto Rodríguez Sánchez and Alexandre Arrechea while they were students at the [[Instituto Superior de Arte]] in Havana. In 1994 they took the name "Los Carpinteros" (The Carpenters) and formally renounced individual authorship in favor of a collective mode of production modeled on the craft guild. Arrechea left the group in 2003.</ref> gained international prominence in the 1990s with work combining humor, social criticism and the handcrafted fabrication of objects and imaginary architectures.<ref>{{cite web |title=Los Carpinteros |url=https://www.nga.gov/audio-video/audio/carpinteros-rodriguez.html |work=Exhibition audio guide |publisher=National Gallery of Art |location=Washington, D.C. |access-date=7 June 2026}}</ref> The painter [[Tomás Sánchez (painter)|Tomás Sánchez]] (born 1948) developed from the 1980s onward a [[Hyperrealism (visual arts)|hyperrealist]] idiom of marked spirituality in his renderings of the Cuban landscape.<ref name="Weiss2011" />

==== Cinema ====

The [[cinematograph]] arrived in Cuba on 24 January 1897, when the French technician [[Gabriel Veyre]], the [[Lumière brothers]]' representative in Latin America, gave the first public screening at a venue on Prado Street 126 in [[Havana]], barely thirteen months after the Lumières' first exhibition in Paris.<ref name="Chanan2004">{{cite book |last=Chanan |first=Michael |title=Cuban Cinema |year=2004 |publisher=[[University of Minnesota Press]] |location=Minneapolis |isbn=978-0-8166-3424-8 |pages=37–38}}</ref> Four European short films were shown at that inaugural session. On 7 February of the same year, Veyre filmed ''Simulacro de incendio'' (literally "Fire Drill")—a one-minute piece featuring Havana firefighters—regarded as the first film shot on Cuban soil, although the original print has been lost.<ref name="Chanan2004" /> The first Cuban to work in film projection and cinematography was José E. Casasús.{{citation needed|date=August 2026}}

During the early decades of the 20th century, Cuban film production was scarce and aimed at popular consumption, dominated by newsreel documentaries and homemade comedies. [[Cinema of the United States|American cinema]] and, from the 1930s onward, [[Cinema of Mexico|Mexican cinema]], dominated screens on the island. The domestic industry never developed a stable structure for production, distribution, or financing.<ref name="King2000">{{cite book |last=King |first=John |author-link=John King (academic) |title=Magical Reels: A History of Cinema in Latin America |edition=2nd |year=2000 |publisher=[[Verso Books|Verso]] |location=London |isbn=978-1-85984-233-1 |pages=144–152}}</ref>

The direct forerunner of modern Cuban cinema is ''[[El mégano]]'' (1955)—the title refers to a rural charcoal-burning encampment—a roughly twenty-five-minute documentary short co-directed by [[Julio García Espinosa]] and [[Tomás Gutiérrez Alea]], with the collaboration of [[Alfredo Guevara (filmmaker)|Alfredo Guevara]] and José Massip, shot in the style of [[Italian neorealism]] among the charcoal workers of the [[Zapata Swamp]], south of Havana.<ref name="Chanan2004_megano">{{cite book |last=Chanan |first=Michael |title=Cuban Cinema |year=2004 |publisher=[[University of Minnesota Press]] |location=Minneapolis |isbn=978-0-8166-3424-8 |pages=113–117}}</ref> The film exposed the living conditions of that working community under the government of [[Fulgencio Batista]]. Screened only twice—at the Varona Amphitheater of the [[University of Havana]] and at the Retiro Odontológico—it was immediately seized by the Cuban Military Intelligence Service (SIM), and García Espinosa was arrested. The print remained in SIM's archives until 1959. Both for its critical intent and for the profile of its makers, ''El mégano'' is regarded as the most important precursor of the Cuban New Cinema and one of the founding works of the [[New Latin American Cinema]] movement.<ref name="Chanan2004_megano" /><ref name="Paranagua2003">{{cite book |last=Paranaguá |first=Paulo Antonio |title=Cine documental en América Latina |trans-title=Documentary Cinema in Latin America |year=2003 |publisher=[[Ediciones Cátedra|Cátedra]] |location=Madrid |isbn=978-84-376-2060-2 |language=Spanish}}</ref>

The founding moment of modern Cuban cinema was the creation of the [[Cuban Institute of Cinematographic Art and Industry]] (ICAIC) on 24 March 1959, just weeks after the new government took power—reflecting the priority given to film as an instrument of cultural formation; the law establishing ICAIC was the first cultural measure enacted by the [[Cuban Revolution]].<ref name="Chanan2004_ICAIC">{{cite book |last=Chanan |first=Michael |title=Cuban Cinema |year=2004 |publisher=[[University of Minnesota Press]] |location=Minneapolis |isbn=978-0-8166-3424-8 |pages=139–145}}</ref> [[Alfredo Guevara (filmmaker)|Alfredo Guevara]] (1925–2013), a university classmate of [[Fidel Castro]] and one of the project's promoters, was appointed to head the institution, which he would lead, with one interruption, for roughly three decades.<ref name="Chanan2004_ICAIC" /> ICAIC's co-founders also included García Espinosa and Gutiérrez Alea, who had studied film direction at the [[Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia]] in Rome in the early 1950s. ICAIC concentrated within its structure a monopoly over film production, distribution, and exhibition in Cuba.{{citation needed|date=August 2026}}

A decisive episode in defining the limits of artistic autonomy in revolutionary Cuba was the banning of the short film ''[[PM (film)|PM]]'' (''Pasado Meridiano'', 1961), directed by [[Sabá Cabrera Infante]] and [[Orlando Jiménez Leal]]. The fourteen-minute film recorded, using the observational technique associated with the British [[Free Cinema]] movement, nightlife in the bars and taverns of the Havana waterfront. Although it had been broadcast on television without difficulty, ICAIC vetoed its release in theaters. The controversy sparked by the censorship led to a series of meetings between the revolutionary leadership and Cuban intellectuals, held in June 1961 at the [[José Martí National Library]]. Closing the meetings, Fidel Castro delivered the address known as "[[Words to the Intellectuals]]," which laid out the guiding principle of revolutionary cultural policy in the formula: "Within the Revolution, everything; outside the Revolution, nothing."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.presidencia.gob.cu/media/filer/public/2022/05/07/palabras_a_los_intelectuales_1961.pdf |title=Palabras a los intelectuales |trans-title=Words to the Intellectuals |last=Castro Ruz |first=Fidel |date=30 June 1961 |website=Presidencia de la República de Cuba |format=PDF |access-date=15 June 2026 |language=Spanish}}</ref><ref name="Chanan2004_PM">{{cite book |last=Chanan |first=Michael |title=Cuban Cinema |year=2004 |publisher=[[University of Minnesota Press]] |location=Minneapolis |isbn=978-0-8166-3424-8 |pages=145–155}}</ref> This episode marked out the boundaries within which cinema—and the arts as a whole—would operate for the following decades, delimiting a space of relative creative freedom that permitted internal criticism but excluded dissent.{{citation needed|date=August 2026}}

During the 1960s and 1970s, ICAIC produced films of notable artistic quality, recognized at European and Latin American festivals. [[Julio García Espinosa]] (1926–2016), one of ICAIC's founders and director of ''[[Las aventuras de Juan Quinquín]]'' (1967), contributed to international theoretical debate with the influential formulation of his manifesto ''[[Por un cine imperfecto]]'' ("For an Imperfect Cinema," written in 1969, published in the Peruvian journal ''Hablemos de cine'' in 1970).<ref>{{cite journal |last=García Espinosa |first=Julio |title=Por un cine imperfecto |trans-title=For an Imperfect Cinema |journal=Hablemos de cine |location=Lima |issue=40 |year=1969 |language=Spanish}}</ref> Against the technocratic aesthetic of [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] and of certain strands of European art cinema, García Espinosa called for an "engaged" cinema, made with whatever means were available, oriented toward the spectator's active participation and in the service of social transformation. The text became a fundamental reference point in Latin American film theory and within the broader context of what came to be called [[Third Cinema]].<ref name="King2000" />

[[Tomás Gutiérrez Alea]] (1928–1996), known as "Titón," is Cuban cinema's most acclaimed director.
