This variant and the theoretical contributions from Latin America have been later incorporated into English by diverse authors as "activists, journalists, and academics based in the United States and Canada have taken note of the work on femicide and feminicide by their Latin American counterparts and traveled some of these concepts back into the English language".<ref name=":19" /> For example, [[Judith Butler]] uses the term and talks about [[Ni una menos|Ni Una Menos]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Butler |first=Judith |title=The force of nonviolence: an ethico-political bind |date=2020 |publisher=Verso |isbn=978-1-78873-276-5 |location=London New York}}</ref> and [[Lauren Klein]] and [[Catherine D'Ignazio|D'Ignazio]] include it in their book [[Data Feminism]].<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Data Feminism |url=https://data-feminism.mitpress.mit.edu/ |journal=Data Feminism |language=en |archive-date=29 April 2025 |access-date=25 April 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250429140307/https://data-feminism.mitpress.mit.edu/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Causes ==
As defined by [[Diana E. H. Russell|Diana Russell]], femicide includes intimate partner femicide, lesbicide, racial femicide, serial femicide, mass femicide, [[honor killing]], [[dowry]]-related murder, and more. Any act of sexual terrorism that results in death is considered femicide. Covert femicide also takes form in the criminalization of [[abortion]] in cases where the mother's life is at risk, intentional spread of [[HIV/AIDS]],<ref name="Russell2" /> or death as a result of [[female genital mutilation]].

The most widespread form of femicide in the world is that committed by an intimate partner of a female. This accounts for approximately 38.6 percent of all murders of women globally, which may be an undercount.<ref name="WHO">{{cite journal |last1=Garcia-Vergara |first1=Esperanza |last2=Almeda |first2=Nerea |last3=Martín Ríos |first3=Blanca |last4=Becerra-Alonso |first4=David |last5=Fernández-Navarro |first5=Francisco |title=A Comprehensive Analysis of Factors Associated with Intimate Partner Femicide: A Systematic Review |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |date=15 June 2022 |volume=19 |issue=12 |page=7336 |doi=10.3390/ijerph19127336 |pmid=35742583 |pmc=9223751 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Different areas of the world experience femicide varyingly, i.e., the Middle East and South Asia have higher rates of [[honor killing]]: the murder of women by their family, due to an actual or assumed sexual or behavioral transgression, such as [[adultery]], sexual intercourse, or even having been raped.<ref name="WHO" />

Systemic [[criminal justice]] issues such [[error of impunity]]<ref>{{Citation |chapter=Errors of Impunity |date=2003 |title=Errors of Justice: Nature, Sources and Remedies |pages=22–30 |editor-last=Forst |editor-first=Brian |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/errors-of-justice/errors-of-impunity/69F1C9AC7957B9940BC49FAB5C567B8F |access-date=2026-02-14 |series=Cambridge Studies in Criminology |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511734953.004 |isbn=978-0-521-52882-5 |archive-date=7 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180907223432/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/errors-of-justice/errors-of-impunity/69F1C9AC7957B9940BC49FAB5C567B8F |url-status=live }}</ref> and low [[crime clearance rate]]s have been associated with femicide.<ref name="n854">{{cite journal | last1=Trejo | first1=Bricia Gonzalez | last2=Michael | first2=Yvonne L | last3=Diez Roux | first3=Ana V | last4=Sánchez | first4=Brisa N | last5=Sun | first5=Nina | last6=Stöckl | first6=Heidi | last7=Vidaña-Perez | first7=Dèsirée | last8=Correa-Salazar | first8=Catalina | last9=Ortigoza | first9=Ana | last10=de Lima Friche | first10=Amélia Augusta | last11=DiCecco | first11=Vanessa | last12=Mazariegos | first12=Mónica | last13=Bilal | first13=Usama | title=Characterising the killing of girls and women in urban settings in Latin America, 2000–2019: an analysis of variability and time trends using mortality data from vital registration systems | journal=BMJ Public Health | volume=2 | issue=1 | date=2024 | issn=2753-4294 | pmid=40018091 | pmc=11812913 | doi=10.1136/bmjph-2024-000985 | article-number=e000985 | url=https://bmjpublichealth.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/bmjph-2024-000985 | access-date=2026-02-22}}</ref>

=== Among intimate partners ===
'''Intimate partner femicide''', sometimes called '''intimate femicide''', or '''romantic femicide''', refers to the murdering of a woman by her intimate partner or her former intimate partner. Intimate partner femicide is often proceeded by intimate partner violence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ferguson |first1=Claire |last2=McLachlan |first2=Freya |date=December 2023 |title=Continuing Coercive Control After Intimate Partner Femicide: The Role of Detection Avoidance and Concealment |journal=Feminist Criminology |language=en |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=353–375 |doi=10.1177/15570851231189531 |issn=1557-0851|doi-access=free |hdl=10072/430101 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> In [[South Africa]], a [[female prostitute]] that is killed by her client is also classified as intimate femicide irrespective of the duration of their sexual relationship.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DOJCD Anti-Femicide Website l Forms of Femicide |url=https://www.justice.gov.za/vg/femicide/forms.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250701205803/https://www.justice.gov.za/vg/femicide/forms.html |archive-date=2025-07-01 |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=www.justice.gov.za}}</ref>

5–8% of all murders committed by male perpetrators are cases of intimate partner homicide.<ref name="Monckton">Monckton, Smith Jane. Murder, Gender and the Media: Narratives of Dangerous Love. New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2012. Print.</ref> For example, a 2020 examination from media and internet sources of every single murder of an elderly woman in Israel committed between 2006 and 2015 revealed that all the cases of female [[senicide|geronticide]] were intimate partner femicides, and perpetrated in the domestic arena.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Shalva |last1=Weil |last2=Keshet |first2=Noam N. |date=2020 |title=Female Geronticide: the Case of Israel |journal= Journal of Gender Studies |volume=29 |issue=5 |pages=39–51 |doi=10.1080/09589236.2020.1809361 |doi-access= |s2cid=225224843}}</ref>

Acts of [[incest]], [[sexual harassment]], [[rape]], [[battery (crime)|battering]], and other forms of violence are also found to escalate over time within a familial relationship, possibly resulting in femicide.<ref name="Russell2" /> The prevalence of intimate partner femicide is said to dispel the myth that women have the most to fear from strangers, and instead are most often murdered within the private sphere of the home.<ref name="Dawson">{{cite journal |last1=Dawson |first1=Myrna |last2=Gartner |first2=Rosemary |title=Differences in the Characteristics of Intimate Femicides |journal=Homicide Studies |date=24 July 2016 |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=378–399 |doi=10.1177/1088767998002004003|s2cid=145234420}}</ref> Argued by Jacquelyn Campbell, a common motive that causes men to murder their intimate partners is [[jealousy]], a result of male efforts to control and possess women to display ownership and reinforce [[patriarchy]].<ref name="Russell1" />

A "feminist reconceptualization" <ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Evelyn|first=Rose|date=November–December 2015|title=A feminist reconceptualisation of intimate partner violence against women: A crime against humanity and a state crime|journal=Women's Studies International Forum|volume= 53|pages= 31–42|doi=10.1016/j.wsif.2015.08.004}}</ref> claims a structural system is to blame for the murder of women rather than violent individuals. It is cross-cultural structure on a mass scale, and is suggested to be considered as a human rights violation by the [[Women's Studies International Forum]] and considered a "crime against humanity." While authors acknowledge "crimes are committed by individuals and not by abstract entities",<ref name=":5" /> the prevalence of domestic violence constitutes an epidemic. Contemporary feminists believe that re-framing intimate partner violence as a state crime and a [[Crimes against humanity|crime against humanity]] can help reduce violence against women committed by their significant others, as it is already recognized as a violation of the [[international human rights law]].

There is considerable debate over whether men or women are more likely to commit intimate violence with studies from the US and UK finding large variations across race, age, and income.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Understanding Domestic Abusers: Other Forms of Intimate Partner Violence - Responsive Violence - NYS OPDV |url=https://opdv.ny.gov/professionals/abusers/responsiveipv.html#note63 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210926144451/https://opdv.ny.gov/professionals/abusers/responsiveipv.html#note63 |archive-date=26 September 2021 |access-date=26 September 2021 |website=opdv ny Government}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Caetano |first1=R. |last2=Ramisetty-Mikler |first2=S. |last3=Field |first3=C.A. |date=August 2005|title=Unidirectional and Bidirectional Intimate Partner Violence among White, Black and Hispanic Couples in the United States |journal=Violence and Victims |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=393–406 |doi= 10.1891/0886-6708.20.4.393|pmid=16250407|s2cid=219209576}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Langhinrichsen-Rohling |first1=Jennifer |last2=Misra |first2=Tiffany A. |last3=Selwyn |first3=Candice |last4=Rohling |first4=Martin L. |s2cid=146475182 |date=2012 |title=Rates of Bidirectional Versus Unidirectional Intimate Partner Violence Across Samples, Sexual Orientations, and Race/Ethnicities: A Comprehensive Review |journal=Partner Abuse |volume=3 |issue=2 |page=199 |doi=10.1891/1946-6560.3.2.199}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hester |first1=Marianne |title=Who does what to whom? Gender and domestic violence perpetrators in English police records |journal=European Journal of Criminology |date=September 2013 |volume=10 |issue=5 |pages=623–637 |doi=10.1177/1477370813479078 |s2cid=31869458}}</ref>

Risk factors that increase the likelihood of intimate partner femicide include: when a male suffered physical abuse as a child, when a male has previously threatened to commit [[suicide]] or murder the woman if she cheats on him or leaves him, when there is elevated alcohol or drug abuse by either partner, or when a male attempts to control a woman's freedom. Two-fifths of intimate partner femicide is related to the use of [[intoxicants]].<ref name="Monckton" />

Other factors commonly associated with male perpetrators of femicide include [[gun ownership]], forcing sexual intercourse, and [[unemployment]]. Women's risk factors include: if they are [[pregnant]], have faced prior abuse from their partner, are estranged from their partner, or are attempting to leave a relationship, their likelihood of femicide increases.<ref name="WHO" /> The presence of [[Gun violence|firearms]] within a home is a large factor in intimate partner femicide, and worldwide, firearms are used in one-third of all femicides.<ref name=":14">{{cite web|title=Femicide: A Global Problem|url=http://www.smallarmssurvey.org/about-us/highlights/highlight-rn14.html|website=Small Arms Survey|date=28 February 2012|access-date=5 December 2017|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304195726/http://www.smallarmssurvey.org/about-us/highlights/highlight-rn14.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

As often reported in the public eye, male perpetrators are seen as "being driven" to commit femicide, due to a "breakdown in love attributed to the female".<ref name="Monckton" /> In defense trials, the defense of [[provocation (legal)|provocation]] is often used to reduce the time male murders serve in prison. Conversely, women are not often as successful with using this idea of provocation in their murder trials, and judges are statistically less likely to accept claims of [[self-defense]].<ref name="Russell1" />

Factors that decrease the risk of intimate partner femicide include a separate domicile for women and other societal factors, such as better [[police|policing]], as well as mandated arrest for violation of [[restraining order]]s related to [[intimate partner violence]]. Karen D. Stout found that, in the US, there is a correlation between the number of [[women's shelter]]s in a state, the number of [[rape crisis center]]s, and a lowered rate of femicide. One explanation of this correlation is that implementing these measures has positively affected lowering the femicide rate. Other effective legislation against femicide include legislation that defines civil injunction relief, defines physical abuse as a criminal offense', allows arrest without a warrant, requires data collection and reporting, and provides funds for women's shelters.<ref name="Russell1" />

==== Gun violence ====
In the US, about 67% of the women murdered by their partners are murdered with a gun.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Jacquelyn C. |author-link1=Jacquelyn Campbell |last2=Webster |first2=Daniel |last3=Koziol-McLain |author-link3=Jane Koziol-McLain |first3=Jane |last4=Block |first4=Carolyn |last5=Campbell |first5=Doris |last6=Curry |first6=Mary Ann |last7=Gary |first7=Faye |last8=Glass |first8=Nancy |last9=McFarlane |first9=Judith |last10=Sachs |first10=Carolyn |last11=Sharps |first11=Phyllis |date=1 July 2003 |title=Risk Factors for Femicide in Abusive Relationships: Results From a Multisite Case Control Study |journal=American Journal of Public Health |volume=93 |issue=7 |pages=1089–1097 |doi=10.2105/AJPH.93.7.1089 |pmc=1447915 |pmid=12835191}}</ref> Access to guns therefore plays an important role in this. On average, 70 American women are "shot and killed" by their intimate partner every month.<ref>{{cite report |title=CDC Releases First National Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS) Data: (557252006-001) |date=2005 |publisher=American Psychological Association |doi=10.1037/e557252006-001 }}</ref><ref name="ReferenceA" /> Nechama Brodie, in her book ''Femicide in South Africa'', indicates that more than 80% of femicide victims attacked by their partner were 'killed by a firearm injury, mostly from a single gunshot to the head or face ... In three-quarters of these cases, the perpetrator is a legal firearm owner using a licensed weapon.'<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fewer guns will save women's lives in South Africa |url=https://issafrica.org/iss-today/fewer-guns-will-save-womens-lives-in-south-africa |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=ISS Africa |language=en |archive-date=21 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260421003732/https://issafrica.org/iss-today/fewer-guns-will-save-womens-lives-in-south-africa |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Racially motivated femicide ===
The Hope Movement defines '''racist femicide''' as the racially motivated murdering of women by men who are members of a different [[Race (human categorization)|race]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hopemovement.com/open-ur-eyes/16-femicide.html |title=Femicide |website=Hope Movement |access-date=1 April 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130426143512/http://www.hopemovement.com/open-ur-eyes/16-femicide.html |archive-date=26 April 2013}}</ref> According to Diana Russell and fellow writer Jill Radford, "[[Racism]] interacts with [[violence against women]], and shapes both femicide itself, and the ways it is addressed by the local community, the police, the media, and the legal system."<ref name="Russell1" />
Russell and Radford assert that when looking at femicide within the United States specifically, one must consider the politics of [[Intersectionality|both]] sexism and racism in the murders of black women and the little justice that is often served.<ref name="Russell1" />

Media coverage can especially exhibit bias when covering the murders of Black versus white women. Jaime Grant writes on the murder of 12 young women in [[Boston|Boston, Massachusetts]], and exposes the "racism in media coverage, which virtually ignored these killings initially, and later depicted the victims in racist and sexist stereotypes, such as runaways, drug addicts, or prostitutes."<ref name="Russell1" /> In addition, police response and investigation can often differ based on the victim's race.<ref name="Russell1" />

Engaging in work with [[Black feminism|Black Feminist Studies]], author Manshel claims that the narrative which is formed around [[domestic violence]] is traditionally associated with a white, middle class, female victim, leaves victims of different races and social classes to receive unequal care,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Manshel|first=Hannah|date=October 2018|title=The Desire for Fact: Anti-Racist Ethics in Discourses of Sexual Violence|journal=Criticism|volume= 60 |issue=4|pages= 511–531|doi=10.13110/criticism.60.4.0511|s2cid=192530094}}</ref> and it can also lead to more victimization of the woman who is murdered/abused due to not aligning with the vulnerability which is typically expected of female victims. Manshel also traces the history of assaults of Black women, and she makes the distinction that "the circumstances" of white victims were "wholly different" from those of "enslaved women" in the 19–20th century, and she proposes that [[Anti-racism|anti-racist]] frameworks about sexual violence should be put into writing.

=== Sexually motivated (lesbophobic) femicide ===
According to Diana Russell and Jill Radford, '''lesbicide''', also known as '''homophobic femicide''',<ref name="Russell1" /> the murder of [[lesbian]]s, has a long history as a legalized act. In [[Roman civilization]], a married woman convicted of engaging in any sexual activity with another woman could be murdered by her husband as a "just penalty for her crime".<ref name="Russell1" /> In [[medieval Europe]], secular and religious doctrines mandated death for lesbianism. "The famous 1260 Code of Orleans{{Dubious|date=December 2025}} in France secularized the prohibition of lesbianism, mandating that for the first two offenses, a woman would 'lose her member'; for the third offense she would be [[execution by burning|burned]]."<ref name="Russell1" /> This doctrine persisted into the [[Witch trials in the early modern period|witch hunt]]s of the 15th century, among whose perpetrators [[witchcraft]] was linked with [[heresy]] and homosexuality. The phrase ''femina cum feminus'' (woman with woman) was often an accusation in witch trials.<ref name="Russell1" />

In the 21st century, lesbianism is no longer a capital crime, but it remains criminalized by many governments, and is condemned by most religions.<ref name="Russell1" /> [[Torture]] and murder of lesbians occur in every part of the world.<ref name="Hawthorne" /> According to [[Susan Hawthorne]] of [[Victoria University, Melbourne|Victoria University]], "domination is exemplified in the punishment of lesbians as outsiders in patriarchal culture".<ref name="Hawthorne" /> Hawthorne goes on to elaborate that lesbians are often killed, tortured, or generally denied rights due to their invisibility in terms of political power and social representation: "When it comes to campaigns on violence against women, lesbians are either left out or included only in a footnote".<ref name="Hawthorne" />

A case study<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |doi=10.1177/1097184X14551204 |title=Accomplishing Masculinity through Anti-Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Homicide |journal=Men and Masculinities |volume=18 |pages=3–29 |year=2015 |last1=Kelley |first1=Kristin |last2=Gruenewald |first2=Jeff |s2cid=145171441}}</ref> conducted in 2014 analyzing multiple [[Violence against LGBT people|anti-LGBT cases of violence]] suggests that crimes like lesbicide can, in part, be explained by existing hyper-masculinity theories that observe the "[[Doing Gender|accomplishment of gender]]" and that "constructing masculinity is relevant to bias crime offending".<ref name=":6" /> One common occurrence that [[Sociology|sociological]] researchers have found is the escalation of violence towards LGBT members when they were met with "unwanted heterosexual advances".{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

==== Corrective rape ====

There are documented cases of [[corrective rape]] in South Africa,<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Middleton |first=Lee |date=8 March 2011 |url=http://content.time.com/time/world/article/0,8599,2057744,00.html |title='Corrective Rape': Fighting a South African Scourge |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-date=20 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231120011057/https://content.time.com/time/world/article/0,8599,2057744,00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Zimbabwe,<ref>{{cite web |last=Shaw |first=A |date=7 April 2010 |url=https://www.salon.com/2010/04/07/af_zimbabwe_gay_rights_1/ |title=US Reports Harassment and Rape of Gays in Zimbabwe |work=Salon |access-date=18 April 2012 |archive-date=17 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190417112724/https://www.salon.com/2010/04/07/af_zimbabwe_gay_rights_1/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Ecuador,<ref>{{citation |author=Caselli, Irene |date=10 February 2012 |title='Corrective Rape,' Torture among Methods Used to 'cure' Homosexuality in Ecuador |work=[[Alaska Dispatch]]}}</ref> and Thailand.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.poz.com/pdfs/gmhc_treatmentissues_2009_12.pdf |author=Mieses, Alexa |title=Gender Inequality and Corrective Rape of Women Who Have Sex with Women |work=GMHC Treatment Issues |year=2009 |access-date=16 November 2024 |archive-date=26 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240626200055/https://www.poz.com/pdfs/gmhc_treatmentissues_2009_12.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Corrective rape has led to death in some cases.<ref name="Hawthorne" />

Corrective rape is defined by Hawthorne as a hate crime that constitutes forced sexual activity with a person who is either a woman, [[Gender variance|gender non-conforming]], or identifies as something other than heterosexual e.g lesbian or asexual, whose goal is to "correct" the victim's sexual orientation and make them heterosexual or behave in a more gender-conforming manner.<ref name="Hawthorne">{{cite journal |last=Hawthorne |first=Susan |author-link=Susan Hawthorne |date=2005 |title=Ancient Hatred and Its Contemporary Manifestation: The Torture of Lesbians |journal=Journal of Hate Studies |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=33–58 |doi=10.33972/jhs.32 |doi-access=free }}{{void|Fabrickator|direct link using doi: https://jhs.press.gonzaga.edu/articles/32/files/submission/proof/32-1-154-1-10-20190227.pdf}}</ref>

[[Eudy Simelane]] was a famous soccer player who played for the [[South Africa women's national football team]] and an LGBTQ+ rights activist; her murder in 2008 was a highly publicized instance of simultaneous corrective rape and lesbicide in [[South Africa]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=BBC Audio {{!}} Witness History {{!}} The South African football star murdered for being a lesbian |url=https://www.bbc.com/audio/play/w3ct1x3z |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB |archive-date=27 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260427151752/https://www.bbc.com/audio/play/w3ct1x3z |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Transfemicide ===

{{Further|Transfemicide|Transgender genocide|Vicky Hernández (murder victim)}}

'''Transfemicide''' or '''transfeminicide''' is defined as the killing of a [[trans woman]] motivated by [[Transphobia|transphobic]], [[misogynistic]] and [[transmisogynistic]] hatred that has its origins in [[cissexist]] cultural and political norms.<ref>{{Citation|edition=1|chapter=Continuities and Discontinuities Between the Concepts of Feminicide and Transfeminicide in Mexico|chapter-url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/9781003202332/chapters/10.4324/9781003202332-40|publisher=Routledge|title=The Routledge International Handbook of Femicide and Feminicide|date=2023-04-20|access-date=2025-11-30|place=London|isbn=978-1-003-20233-2|pages=380–389|doi=10.4324/9781003202332-40|language=en|first1=Sayak|last1=Valencia|first2=Liliana|last2=Falcón|first3=Alan|last3=Mendoza}}</ref> Journalists and academics alike believe the prevalence of transfemicide to be vastly underreported.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Transfemicide becomes a crime in a 'watershed' moment for Mexico City|url=https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/article/2024/jul/24/mexico-city-transfemicide-law|work=The Guardian|date=2024-07-24|access-date=2025-11-30|issn=0261-3077|language=en-GB|first=Thomas|last=Graham}}</ref> Journalists Emma Landeros and Joel Aguirre argue that, as hate crimes, transfemicides constitute a 'silent epidemic' in Mexico, with many deaths receiving little or no media coverage.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Journalists investigate 'silent epidemic' of transfemicide in Mexico|url=https://latamjournalismreview.org/articles/journalists-investigate-silent-epidemic-of-transfemicide-in-mexico/|website=LatAm Journalism Review by the Knight Center|date=2025-07-17|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en|first=César López|last=Linares|archive-date=14 December 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251214102809/https://latamjournalismreview.org/articles/journalists-investigate-silent-epidemic-of-transfemicide-in-mexico/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Under [[Transgender Europe]], or TGEU, the Trans Murder Monitoring project reported 281 trans and gender-diverse people murdered in 2025 alone, with 90% of those killed being trans women. Notably, [[sex worker]]s comprised 34% of these deaths, with most of the overall deaths occurring in Latin America.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trans Murder Monitoring 2025 reveals new trend in anti-trans violence: Systematic targeting of activists and movement leaders - TGEU - Trans Europe and Central AsiaTGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia|url=https://tgeu.org/trans-murder-monitoring-2025-reveals-new-trend-in-anti-trans-violence-systematic-targeting-of-activists-and-movement-leaders/|date=2025-11-12|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en-US|archive-date=26 February 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260226060139/https://tgeu.org/trans-murder-monitoring-2025-reveals-new-trend-in-anti-trans-violence-systematic-targeting-of-activists-and-movement-leaders/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The [[Human Rights Watch]], in their report on violence against LGBT people in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, note that Central American governments have long excluded transgender women from preexisting legal structures meant to prosecute femicides. Guatemalan officials have justified this by stating that transgender women are not "biological women" in their eyes and therefore their murders are not covered by such laws.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The Normative Dilemmas of the Feminist Struggles Against (Trans-)Feminicide in Mexico|url=https://elibrary.utb.de/doi/abs/10.3224/feminapolitica.v31i2.03|journal=Femina Politica|date=2022-12-07|pages=29–41|volume=31|issue=2|doi=10.3224/feminapolitica.v31i2.03|first=Ana Maria Miranda|last=Mora}}</ref>

In the case of ''Vicky Hernández v Honduras,'' tried before [[Inter-American Court of Human Rights]] (IACHR), the [[Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights]] organization and Red Lésbica Cattrachas successfully argued that the government of Honduras held responsibility for the death of trans activist and sex worker [[Vicky Hernández (murder victim)|Vicky Hernández]]. The result of the case was seen as a landmark ruling establishing a powerful precedent for the defense of transgender women and LGBT Latin Americans broadly.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Fighting transfemicide in the Americas|url=https://www.ibanet.org/Fighting-transfemicide-in-the-Americas|website=www.ibanet.org|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en|archive-date=16 February 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260216095357/https://www.ibanet.org/Fighting-transfemicide-in-the-Americas|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=International Court Rules in Favor of Trans Rights in Honduras (Published 2021)|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/28/world/americas/honduras-trans-rights-ruling.html|date=2021-06-29|access-date=2025-12-01|language=en|archive-date=8 February 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260208230337/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/28/world/americas/honduras-trans-rights-ruling.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Tendency in serial killings ===
{{See also|Recidivism}}
'''Serial femicide''' is defined as "the sexually [[Sexual sadism disorder|sadistic]] killing of women", also called "sexual terrorism". Over 90% of serial killers are male.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://crimecasefiles.com/forum/diagnosis-of-categories-and-symptoms/50-characteristics-of-serial-killers.html |publisher=Internal Association of Forensic Science |author=Robert K. Ressler |author-link=Robert K. Ressler |title=The Serial Killer |via=Harold Schechter |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708055554/http://www.crimecasefiles.com/forum/diagnosis-of-categories-and-symptoms/50-characteristics-of-serial-killers.html |archive-date=8 July 2009}}</ref>

Male serial murderers tend to use more brutal methods of killing, such as suffocation and beatings. In contrast, women use poison or less violent measures. In addition, while a large percentage of male serial killers focus on women as their targets, female serial killers are less likely to focus exclusively on males. Some male serial killers focus on males as targets, such as [[Jeffrey Dahmer]] and [[Wayne Williams]].<ref name="Taylor">{{cite journal|last1=Taylor|first1=Rae|date=February 2009|title=Slain and Slandered|journal=Homicide Studies|volume=13|issue=1|pages=21–49|doi=10.1177/1088767908326679|s2cid=145783630}}</ref> The ways serial murderers are portrayed in the media reflect the views on femicide and gender in society. Often, murders of prostitutes, low-income women, and women of color by serial killers receive less attention in the media than [[Missing white woman syndrome|the killings of younger, prettier, more affluent women]], usually married, engaged, or in relationships with much handsome, affluent, younger men their age.<ref name="Taylor" />

According to the FBI's Supplementary Homicide Report, local police reported that about 33,000 homicides of women remain unsolved.
<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.gosanangelo.com/news/2010/nov/27/most-serial-killing-victims-are-women-fbi/ |title=Most serial killing victims are women, FBI reports |date=27 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101205150030/http://www.gosanangelo.com/news/2010/nov/27/most-serial-killing-victims-are-women-fbi/ |archive-date=5 December 2010}}</ref>

Feminists such as Diana Russell and {{interlanguage link|Jane Caputi|es}} believe in a link between the rise of serial murders and the advent of [[pornography]]. Specifically, the advent of films that eroticize violence and murder of women has been correlated to the desires of serial killers. Numerous serial murderers filmed their victims as they violently killed them.<ref name="Russell1" /> However, the link between pornography and serial murders is not proven.<ref name="Taylor" />

=== Female infanticide and geronticide ===
[[Female infanticide]] is the killing of female infants.<ref name="Campbell2003">{{cite thesis |last1=Campbell |first1=Sarah Ann Sparks |title=Female infanticide in China and India: a comparative study |date=2003 |doi=10.5353/th_b29520253 |doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 |hdl=10722/31024}}</ref> It is found all over the world regardless of a country's sophistication. A common misconception is that it is only related to abortions, but it also includes "girl-child murders".<ref name="Campbell2003"/> Female infanticide plays an important role in the imbalance of gender populations. In countries where female infanticide is practiced, the male populations is higher than the female population.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BBC - Ethics - Abortion: Female infanticide |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/ethics/abortion/medical/infanticide_1.shtml#:~:text=Female%20infanticide%20is%20the%20deliberate,selective%20killing%20or%20%22gendercide%22. |access-date=15 March 2022 |publisher=BBC |language=en-GB |archive-date=21 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121144257/http://www.bbc.co.uk/ethics/abortion/medical/infanticide_1.shtml#:~:text=Female%20infanticide%20is%20the%20deliberate,selective%20killing%20or%20%22gendercide%22. |url-status=live }}</ref>

Similarly, female [[geronticide]] refers to the killing of elderly females, and "this may be because they are elderly or because they are women, or for both reasons."<ref>Shalva Weil & Noam S. Keshet (2021) "Female geronticide: the case of Israel", ''Journal of Gender Studies'', 30:1, 39–51, p. 3 DOI: 10.1080/09589236.2020.180936</ref> One challenge of characterizing female geronticide is defining age; in other words, who can be considered an elder. This changes according to culture which itself is a critical factor within research.<ref>For example, see the case of Ethiopia noted in Weil, 2004.</ref>

== Worldwide ==
Every year around the world, one woman or girl is killed on behalf of her gender by an intimate partner or someone in her family approximately every 10 minutes, equivalent to 6 women per hour with over 50,000 of such cases annually and nearly 140 daily.<ref>{{cite web | title=One woman or girl is killed every 10 minutes by their intimate partner or family member &#124; UN Women – Headquarters | work=UN Women – Headquarters | url=https://www.unwomen.org/en/news-stories/press-release/2024/11/one-woman-or-girl-is-killed-every-10-minutes-by-their-intimate-partner-or-family-member | access-date=11 December 2024 | archive-date=10 December 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241210095355/https://www.unwomen.org/en/news-stories/press-release/2024/11/one-woman-or-girl-is-killed-every-10-minutes-by-their-intimate-partner-or-family-member | url-status=live }}</ref> In 2022, the number of women and girls murdered globally was nearly 89,000.<ref>{{Cite web |date=23 November 2022 |title=Gender-related killings of women and girls (femicide/feminicide): Global estimates of female intimate partner/family-related homicides in 2022 |url=https://www.unwomen.org/en/digital-library/publications/2023/11/gender-related-killings-of-women-and-girls-femicide-feminicide-global-estimates-2022 |access-date=1 February 2024 |website=UN Women – Headquarters |language=en |archive-date=1 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240201224747/https://www.unwomen.org/en/digital-library/publications/2023/11/gender-related-killings-of-women-and-girls-femicide-feminicide-global-estimates-2022 |url-status=live }}</ref> According to a 2000 report by the [[United Nations Population Fund|U.N. Population Fund]] (UNFPA), approximately 5,000 women are murdered each year in [[honor killings]], with one intentional murder every 1 hour and 45 minutes.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/swp2000_eng.pdf |title= The State of World Population 2000 |author= Sadik, Nafis |date= 2000 |publisher= [[United Nations Population Fund]] |access-date= 17 November 2019 |author-link= Nafis Sadik |archive-date= 22 May 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200522174746/https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/swp2000_eng.pdf |url-status= live }}</ref> and a girl dies to [[female genital mutilation]] yearly every 12 minutes <ref>{{cite web | title=A Girl Dies Every 12 Minutes as a Result of Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting | date=6 February 2025 | url=https://globalgoals.org/news/a-girl-dies-every-12-minutes-as-a-result-of-female-genital-mutilation-cutting | access-date=4 December 2025 | archive-date=19 December 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251219044436/https://globalgoals.org/news/a-girl-dies-every-12-minutes-as-a-result-of-female-genital-mutilation-cutting | url-status=live }}</ref> The rates of femicide differ depending on the specific country, but of the countries with the top 25 highest femicide rates, 50% are in Latin America, with number one being [[El Salvador]]. Also included in the top 25 are seven European countries, three Asian countries, and one African country, [[South Africa]]. Social beliefs and acceptability about gender based violence varies from country to country<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Perrin |first1=Nancy |last2=Marsh |first2=Mendy |last3=Clough |first3=Amber |last4=Desgroppes |first4=Amelie |last5=Yope Phanuel |first5=Clement |last6=Abdi |first6=Ali |last7=Kaburu |first7=Francesco |last8=Heitmann |first8=Silje |last9=Yamashina |first9=Masumi |last10=Ross |first10=Brendan |last11=Read-Hamilton |first11=Sophie |last12=Turner |first12=Rachael |last13=Heise |first13=Lori |last14=Glass |first14=Nancy |date=8 March 2019 |title=Social norms and beliefs about gender based violence scale: a measure for use with gender based violence prevention programs in low-resource and humanitarian settings |journal=Conflict and Health |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=6 |doi=10.1186/s13031-019-0189-x |doi-access=free |issn=1752-1505 |pmc=6408811 |pmid=30899324}}</ref>

Data on femicide worldwide is poor, and often countries do not report gender differences in murder statistics.<ref name="Geneva">{{cite web |url=http://www.genevadeclaration.org/fileadmin/docs/GBAV2/GBAV2011_CH4.pdf |title=When the Victim Is a Woman - In Geneva Declaration Secretariat |pages=113–144 |author=Alvazzi del Frate, Anna |year=2011 |access-date=1 November 2013 |archive-date=9 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009095646/http://www.genevadeclaration.org/fileadmin/docs/GBAV2/GBAV2011_CH4.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Many communities do not have access to resources or accurate data.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Reis |first1=Chen |last2=Meyer |first2=Sarah R. |date=18 January 2024 |title=Understudied and underaddressed: Femicide, an extreme form of violence against women and girls |journal=PLOS Medicine |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |article-number=e1004336 |doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1004336 |doi-access=free |issn=1549-1676 |pmc=10795990 |pmid=38236843}}</ref> In addition, reporting data on migrants is particularly scarce.<ref name="Failed Femicides among Migrant Survivors">{{cite journal |last=Weil |first=S. |year=2016 |title=Failed femicides among migrant survivors |journal=Qualitative Sociology Review |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=6–21 |doi=10.18778/1733-8077.12.4.01 |s2cid=245031321 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/309768478|doi-access=free}}</ref> High-income countries have seen more decreases in femicide than low-income countries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Whittington |first1=Richard |last2=Haines-Delmont |first2=Alina |last3=Bjø‌rngaard |first3=Johan Hå‌kon |date=2 January 2023 |title=Femicide trends at the start of the 21st. century: Prevalence, risk factors and national public health actions |journal=Global Public Health |volume=18 |issue=1 |article-number=2225576 |doi=10.1080/17441692.2023.2225576 |pmid=37401752 |issn=1744-1692|hdl=11250/3104973 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

=== Africa ===
[[File:Cape Town anti-femicide demonstration 04.jpg|thumb|Demonstration against femicide in [[Cape Town]], South Africa following the [[murder of Uyinene Mrwetyana]], 2019]]
The continent varies in the manifestations of femicide depending on the country or region.<ref>{{cite web |title=Global study on homicide. Gender-related killing of women and girls |url=https://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/gsh/Booklet_5.pdf |access-date=2 February 2023 |work=unodc. |archive-date=17 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230317142647/https://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/gsh/Booklet_5.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2023, Africa recorded 21,000 cases<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |last=Dahir |first=Abdi Latif |date=10 December 2024 |title=Rage Grows Over a Spate of Brutal Murders of Women in Kenya |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/10/world/africa/kenya-femicide-protests.html |website=New York Times |access-date=11 December 2024 |archive-date=11 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241211144317/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/10/world/africa/kenya-femicide-protests.html |url-status=live }}</ref> which led to the highest rates and absolute numbers of intimate partner and family-related femicide, the rate is followed by the Americas, and then by Oceania. Asia recorded the second highest absolute numbers.<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 November 2024 |title=One woman or girl is killed every 10 minutes by their intimate partner or family member |url=https://www.unwomen.org/en/news-stories/press-release/2024/11/one-woman-or-girl-is-killed-every-10-minutes-by-their-intimate-partner-or-family-member |website=UN Women |access-date=11 December 2024 |archive-date=10 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241210095355/https://www.unwomen.org/en/news-stories/press-release/2024/11/one-woman-or-girl-is-killed-every-10-minutes-by-their-intimate-partner-or-family-member |url-status=live }}</ref>

Between 1990 and 2021, the number of female homicides in Africa rose from 12,570 to 19,769, though the age-standardized death rate decreased from 4.58 to 3.34 per 100,000 women, remaining nearly double the global average of 1.76 per 100,000 in 2021.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Van Der Walt |first1=G. |last2=Bantjes |first2=J. |last3=Walker |first3=A. |last4=Naghavi |first4=M. |last5=Stein |first5=D. J. |title=Homicidal Violence Against Women in Africa: Country-Level Trends From 1990 to 2021 |journal=Journal of Interpersonal Violence |article-number=08862605251353497 |year=2025 |volume=0 |doi=10.1177/08862605251353497 |pmid=40662497 }}</ref>

==== Burundi ====
As of 2023, it has been noted there is a growing problem of femicide.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Manishatse |first=Lorraine Josiane |date=4 April 2023 |title=Burundi's growing femicide problem |url=https://africanarguments.org/2023/04/burundis-growing-femicide-problem/ |access-date=12 December 2023 |website=African Arguments |language=en-GB |archive-date=4 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231004224912/https://africanarguments.org/2023/04/burundis-growing-femicide-problem/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Kenya ====
Although [[Kenya]] has had an increase in femicide reports, there is a lack of proper data management systems.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Okech |first=Awino |author-link=Awino Okech |date=29 January 2025 |title=Femicide in Kenya: William Ruto has set up a task force – feminist scholar explains its flaws |url=http://theconversation.com/femicide-in-kenya-william-ruto-has-set-up-a-task-force-feminist-scholar-explains-its-flaws-248313 |access-date=2 September 2025 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US |archive-date=18 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250818201143/https://theconversation.com/femicide-in-kenya-william-ruto-has-set-up-a-task-force-feminist-scholar-explains-its-flaws-248313 |url-status=live }}</ref> There is a lack of media representation in many counties, underreported murder cases and omission of details under the murder circumstances.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web |title=Femicide Kenya |url=https://www.africadatahub.org/femicide-kenya |access-date=2 September 2025 |website=www.africadatahub.org |archive-date=25 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250825131723/https://www.africadatahub.org/femicide-kenya |url-status=live }}</ref> As a result, [[Nairobi]], [[Nakuru]] and [[Kiambu County|Kiambu]] have been reported as the leading counties with femicide victims.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |title=Look at the Visuals |url=https://femicidecount.org/visuals/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119053107/https://femicidecount.org/visuals/ |archive-date=19 January 2025 |access-date=11 December 2024 |website=Femicide Count Kenya}}</ref>

Africa Data Hub analyzed 930 female murders between 2016 and 2017 in Kenya, with 628 of them meeting the [[United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime]] (UNODC)'s definition of femicide, with the highest femicide specific cases occurring in 2024, totaling to 127 from 82 in 2023.<ref name=":21" /> According to the Inspector General (DIG) of Police Eliud Lagat, law enforcement recorded 97 cases between September and November 2024, which translated to approximately one woman killed everyday.<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 November 2024 |title=4,000 cases monthly: The hidden face of Kenya's GBV tragedy |url=https://nation.africa/kenya/news/gender/4-000-cases-monthly-the-hidden-face-of-kenya-s-gbv-tragedy-4816576 |access-date=2 September 2025 |website=Daily Nation |language=en |archive-date=17 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250917181501/https://nation.africa/kenya/news/gender/4-000-cases-monthly-the-hidden-face-of-kenya-s-gbv-tragedy-4816576 |url-status=live }}</ref> Femicide Count reported that there were 160 cases of femicide in 2024 with the highest month being January.<ref name=":22" />

Intimate partners and family members have been found to be the biggest perpetrators. An analysis from Africa Data Hub showed that 77% of reported cases were from people that the victims knew; friend, relative, intimate partner. Husbands then boyfriends have been found to be the biggest perpetrators. Approximately 72% of cases take place within the confines of their home.<ref name=":21" />

Once a perpetrator is arrested and brought to court, it takes an average of 1900 days for a case to be concluded and the suspect sentenced, not encompassing appeals that might lengthen the process even further.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Silencing Women |url=https://femicide.africauncensored.online/ |website=Africa Data Hub |access-date=11 December 2024 |archive-date=11 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241211211330/https://femicide.africauncensored.online/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 10 December 2024, thousands of people, mostly women, marched in the capital city, Nairobi, in protest against a wave of femicides. Some smaller groups also marched in other towns. The main demand was for the government to take action. Despite the protest being peaceful, the police used tear gas to disperse the group in Nairobi.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mwangi |first=Monicah |date=10 December 2024 |title=Kenyan police fire teargas at protesters marching against femicide |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/kenyan-police-fire-teargas-protesters-marching-against-femicide-2024-12-10/ |website=Reuters |access-date=11 December 2024 |archive-date=23 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250323111907/https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/kenyan-police-fire-teargas-protesters-marching-against-femicide-2024-12-10/ |url-status=live}}</ref> At least 3 activist protesters were detained.<ref name=":17" />

In the year 2025, at least 220 femicide cases were documented with 129 cases occurring in the first three months, indicating an average of one woman killed every day.<ref name=":24">{{Cite web |title=She Did Not Die by Accident: Mapping Femicide in Kenya (2025). {{!}} Heinrich Böll Stiftung {{!}} Nairobi Office Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania |url=https://ke.boell.org/en/2026/01/27/she-did-not-die-accident-mapping-femicide-kenya-2025 |access-date=2026-08-11 |website=ke.boell.org |language=en}}</ref> After March 2025, the Government stopped publicly releasing consolidated data on femicide thus creating a gap in accountability and transparency.<ref name=":24" />

==== South Africa ====
{{See also|Women For Change}}
South Africa has one of the world's highest femicide rates. The [[United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime]] (UNODC) recorded the global female homicide rate at roughly 2.2 per 100,000 in 2021. In 2022, South Africa's femicide rate was 12.2 per 100,000 – about six times higher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How does South Africa's femicide rate compare? |url=https://africacheck.org/infofinder/explore-facts/how-does-south-africas-femicide-rate-compare |access-date=9 February 2026 |website=Africa Check |language=en |archive-date=25 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240225043518/https://africacheck.org/infofinder/explore-facts/how-does-south-africas-femicide-rate-compare |url-status=live }}</ref> According to [[UN Women]], South Africa has five times higher than the global average of femicide rates. [[Women For Change|Women for Change]] (WFC), an [[Non-governmental organization|NGO]] dedicated to combating [[Gender-related violence|gender-based violence]] (GBV) and femicide (GBVF), noted that 5,578 women were killed between April 2023 and March 2024, with femicide rising 33.8% year on year. "The sad reality within [[South Africa]] when it comes to GBVF is that we have a conviction rate of 12%," WFC's national spokesperson, Cameron Kasambala said, claiming that at least 86% of the time nothing was done when victims of GBVF reported cases to the police.<ref>{{Cite news |first=Nontokozo |last=Mchunu |date=4 December 2025 |title=South Africa's gender violence disaster: What's next |url=https://www.dw.com/en/south-africas-gender-violence-disaster-whats-next/a-74999037 |access-date=9 February 2026 |work=[[Deutsche Welle]] |language=en}}</ref> In 2019, President [[Cyril Ramaphosa]] described South Africa as one of "the most unsafe places in world to be a woman".<ref>{{Cite news |date=18 September 2019 |title=South Africa: Violence against women like a war - Ramaphosa |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-49739977 |access-date=9 February 2026 |work=[[BBC News]] |language=en-GB}}</ref> GBVF had been declared a national crisis in 2019.<ref name=":23">{{Cite news |first1=Khanyisile |last1=Ngcobo |first2=Nomsa |last2=Maseko |first3=Danai Nesta |last3=Kupemba |date=21 November 2025 |title=South Africa declares gender violence a national disaster after protests |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn979g302l9o |access-date=9 February 2026 |work=[[BBC News]] |language=en-GB |archive-date=9 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260109232604/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn979g302l9o |url-status=live }}</ref> In November 2025 during the G20 Summit, The National Disaster Management Centre (NDMC) upgraded GBVF to a [[national disaster]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Baker |first=Abigail |date=4 December 2025 |title=GBV DECLARED A NATIONAL DISASTER: WHAT HAPPENS NOW? |url=https://fwdeklerk.org/gbv-declared-a-national-disaster-what-happens-now/ |access-date=9 February 2026 |website=FW de Klerk Foundation |language=en-US |archive-date=7 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260107200115/https://fwdeklerk.org/gbv-declared-a-national-disaster-what-happens-now/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":23" />

=== Asia ===
==== China ====
{{See also|Female infanticide in China}}
In present-day China, despite official condemnation and outrage, female infanticide continues. In late 1982, the Chinese press was the first to indicate that female infanticide was being practiced as the final option to circumvent the [[one-child policy]].<ref name="UCLA Pacific Basin Law Journal" /> An expert from the [[City University of New York]], however, disagrees with the tendency to characterize female infanticide as "the unfortunate consequence of Chinese population control and modernization policies".<ref name="Columbia Human Rights Law Review">{{cite book |title=Columbia Human Rights Law Review |edition=Summer 1992}}</ref> She defines female infanticide as "part of a crime of gender", which she refers to as "social femicide", and relates it to the broader problem of [[Gender inequality in China|gender inequality in Chinese society]].<ref name="Columbia Human Rights Law Review" />

Female infanticide was common in traditional [[China]], where natural hardships such as famines reinforced cultural norms favoring sons, and encouraged hard-pressed families to abandon or kill their infant daughters.<ref name="UCLA Pacific Basin Law Journal">{{cite book |title=UCLA Pacific Basin Law Journal |edition=Spring 1990}}</ref> Furthermore, daughters became liabilities, as gender was also crucial to the system of ancestor worship, in which only sons were allowed to carry out ritual sacrifices. Thus, "if a couple failed to produce a son, its crucial links to the past and future were broken".<ref name="UCLA Pacific Basin Law Journal" />

==== India ====
{{See also|Female infanticide in India}}
[[Rita Banerji]], feminist author and founder of {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110212051454/http://www.50millionmissing.info/ The 50 Million Missing Campaign]}} to end female [[gendercide]] in India, has said that there are also millions of girls and women killed through various forms of femicides that extend across various age groups. In a U.N. Symposium on Femicide in Vienna on 26 November 2012, she talked about the six most widespread forms of femicide in India.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 November 2012 |title=Video: Six Wide-spread forms of Femicide. Gender Equal: A blog on India's Gendercide |url=https://www.worldpulse.org/story/video%3a-6-forms-of-femicide-in-india-from-the-symposium-on-femicide-in-vienna-2727 |access-date=4 December 2012 |work=authorstream |archive-date=12 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250812064227/https://www.worldpulse.org/story/video%3a-6-forms-of-femicide-in-india-from-the-symposium-on-femicide-in-vienna-2727 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>[http://acuns.org/femicide-the-killing-of-a-woman-because-she-is-a-woman/ Symposium on Femicide] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121211142909/http://acuns.org/femicide-the-killing-of-a-woman-because-she-is-a-woman/ |date=11 December 2012}}</ref> These included [[female infanticide]], the killing of girls under six years through starvation and violence, the killing of women due to [[forced abortion]]s, so-called [[honor killing]]s, [[Dowry death|dowry murders]], and [[Witch-hunt]]s.

{{blockquote|In colonial India, certain forms of girl femicide were associated with ancient Hinduism. The most infamous was sati, the Hindu practice of self immolation after the death of a husband. Coerced sati was tantamount to femicide, according to modern definitions, but it is important to point out that in practice most satis were child widows, and de facto they were girl femicides.<ref name=SWNM/>}}

Many of the femicides in [[Violence against women in India|India]] are perpetrated against girls.<ref name="Femicide of girls in India">{{cite report |chapter=Femicide of Girls in India |url=http://acuns.org/femicide-volume-vi-violence-against-girls-in-flight/ |last1=Weil |first1=Shalva |last2=Mitra |first2=Nishi |date=2016 |title=Femicide Volume VI: Violence Against Girls in Flight |publisher=ACUNS |access-date=4 December 2016 |archive-date=9 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509063112/https://acuns.org/femicide-volume-vi-violence-against-girls-in-flight/ |url-status=dead}}</ref>
Despite progressive legal reforms in many parts of the country, strong patriarchal values are maintained, and help perpetuate the subordination of women.<ref name="HRC2">{{citation |author-link=Rashida Manjoo |author=Manjoo, Rashida |title=Report of the Special Rapporteur on violence against women, its causes and consequences |date=18 March 2013}}</ref> According to the [[United Nations special rapporteur|Special Rapporteur]] on violence against women for the [[United Nations Human Rights Council|Human Rights Council]], key factors behind gender-motivated killings of women in Asia are the high level of importance placed on women's [[chastity]] and their subordination in the greater society.<ref name="HRC2" /> For example, while the [[Indian Penal Code|Penal Code of India]] now specifically prohibits dowry, the reported number of dowry-related deaths of women has almost doubled from 4,836 to 8,383 over the past twenty years (1990–2009).<ref name="HRC2" /> The code is also criticized for having a low impact on the criminalization of perpetrators, noted in the low conviction rate of ten percent.<ref name="HRC2" />

The country has attempted to manage femicide through some policy enactment. India has primarily focused on creating legislation related to [[Population control in India|population control]], resulting in pressures to have a son. Some regions in India have incentivized parents to birth daughters by offering money to families with girls, in order to offset the expenses associated with having a daughter.<ref name=":9">{{Citation |chapter=Figuring out Son Preference |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Academic]] |isbn=978-1-84520-467-9 |doi=10.5040/9781474215534.ch-003 |title=Son Preference: Sex Selection, Gender and Culture in South Asia |year=2010}}</ref> However, there have been research studies analysing femicide policy, specifically in relation to India, that have found "the criminalization of sex selection has not been successful".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eklund |first1=Lisa |last2=Purewal |first2=Navtej |date=2017 |title=The bio-politics of population control and sex-selective abortion in China and India |journal=[[Feminism & Psychology]] |language=en |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=34–55 |doi=10.1177/0959353516682262|s2cid=152171783 |url=https://eprints.soas.ac.uk/23079/1/Bio-Politics-Population-Control-Sex-Selective-Abortion-China-India.pdf |archive-date=31 July 2020 |access-date=29 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731065129/https://eprints.soas.ac.uk/23079/1/Bio-Politics-Population-Control-Sex-Selective-Abortion-China-India.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Iran====
{{Main|Femicide in Iran}}

During 2021–2024, around 180 women reportedly were murdered by their husbands mostly honor killings. The bill against violence on women was passed in 2023 after a decade in government.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kayhanlife.com/authors/domestic-violence-in-iran-leads-to-alarming-number-of-deaths-report-says/ |title=Domestic Violence in Iran Leads to Alarming Number of Deaths, Report Says |website=kayhanlife.com |date=10 July 2023 |access-date=26 July 2024 |archive-date=26 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726035743/https://kayhanlife.com/authors/domestic-violence-in-iran-leads-to-alarming-number-of-deaths-report-says/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kayhanlife.com/news/iran/femicide-surges-in-iran-which-still-ranks-near-bottom-of-global-gender-gap-index/ |title=Femicide Surges in Iran, Which Still Ranks Near Bottom of Global Gender Gap Index |website=kayhanlife.com |date=24 July 2024 |access-date=26 July 2024 |archive-date=26 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726035743/https://kayhanlife.com/news/iran/femicide-surges-in-iran-which-still-ranks-near-bottom-of-global-gender-gap-index/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.irna.ir/news/85078393/%D8%AA%D8%B5%D9%88%DB%8C%D8%A8-%D9%84%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AD%D9%87-%D8%AD%D9%85%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D8%B2-%D8%B2%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AF%D8%B1-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%B1-%D8%AE%D8%B4%D9%88%D9%86%D8%AA-%D9%BE%D8%B3-%D8%A7%D8%B2-%DB%8C%DA%A9-%D8%AF%D9%87%D9%87-%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA%DA%A9%D9%84%DB%8C%D9%81%DB%8C |script-title=fa:تصویب لایحه حمایت از زنان در برابر خشونت پس از یک دهه بلاتکلیفی |website=www.irna.ir |date=10 April 2023 |access-date=26 July 2024 |archive-date=26 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726035743/https://www.irna.ir/news/85078393/%D8%AA%D8%B5%D9%88%DB%8C%D8%A8-%D9%84%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AD%D9%87-%D8%AD%D9%85%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D8%B2-%D8%B2%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AF%D8%B1-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%B1-%D8%AE%D8%B4%D9%88%D9%86%D8%AA-%D9%BE%D8%B3-%D8%A7%D8%B2-%DB%8C%DA%A9-%D8%AF%D9%87%D9%87-%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA%DA%A9%D9%84%DB%8C%D9%81%DB%8C |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Nepal====
Suicide is the leading cause of death for [[Suicide in Nepal|Nepalese women]] in the reproductive age group, with causes ranging from domestic abuse, forced marriage, casting out of widows, and lack of property rights.<ref name="HRC2" /> In this context, there is minimal acceptance and respect of young girls and women, and often an absence of family support. This results in a variety of context-specific versions of femicide and gender-based violence in the region: honor killings, [[acid attack]]s, witch-hunting, [[foeticide]], and gender-based violence during [[caste]] and communal conflict.<ref name="HRC2" />

==== South Korea ====
{{See also|2016 Seocho-dong public-toilet murder case}}
In South Korea, violence towards women has been increasing. In 2012, a man named Oh Won-choon killed a woman while attempting to [[Sexual assault|sexually assault]] her while going home. In 2014, while waiting for a bus, a woman was stabbed to death by a drunk man. Then in 2016, a 34-year-old whose surname is Kim randomly murdered a woman in her twenties in a Gangnam Station bathroom. Regarding motives, Kim clearly stated that he murdered her out of hatred for women saying: "women have always ignored me."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gangnam murderer says he killed "because women have always ignored me" |url=https://english.hani.co.kr/arti/english_edition/e_national/744756.html |access-date=17 December 2022 |website=english.hani south Korea |archive-date=17 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221217223427/https://english.hani.co.kr/arti/english_edition/e_national/744756.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

The rise in [[Violence against women|violence towards women]] has made women fearful. In 2019, The South Korean government released the 2019 Domestic Violence Survey Study that found that only 27.6 percent of women over the age of 13 feel society is safe for them. The study also found that women accounted for 98 percent of victims in intimate partner femicide (domestic violence) cases. In 2019 32,000 sex crimes against women were reported; that is 12,000 more cases than in 2010. All the while domestic violence cases have reached 50,000 in 2019 compared to 6,800 cases in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |script-title=ko:여성가족부가 평등사회를 만들어 가겠습니다 |url=http://www.mogef.go.kr/kor/skin/doc.html. |access-date=17 December 2022 |publisher=Ministry of Gender Equality and Family 여성가족부 |language=ko |archive-date=21 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221221182711/http://www.mogef.go.kr/kor/skin/doc.html. |url-status=live }}</ref>

While these numbers may not be completely accurate; it is estimated that there are more femicide, and intimate partner femicide cases not being reported due to Confucianist influences on South Korean society. Confucianism believes women should be subordinate to men and assumes women's status as inferior from men. These values also hold that women have only three roles: Daughter, wife, and mother and that women must obey the head of the family, that is to say her father before marriage and her husband after marriage. South Korea's traditional patriarchal culture and values assign strict roles to female members, as well as their strong belief that a woman's place should be with her family no matter what, cause women to be wary of reporting violence towards them due to fear of bringing shame to the family or affecting the family' social status.

In a study focusing on the experiences of 14 female victims of intimate partner femicide in getting help with [[domestic violence]] found that victims didn't talk to their family or sought them out for support. Only one participant escaped their abusive relationship because their parents saw the bruises and called the police. Victims were scared to talk to their families. They were scared that their parents would get angry and be saddened by seeing their daughters get abused. Additionally, it is also taboo for women to talk about their romantic relationships with their parents.<ref name="Park 320–338">{{cite journal |last1=Park |first1=Sihyun |last2=Ko |first2=Yejung |title=Victims of Intimate Partner Violence in South Korea: Experiences in Seeking Help Based on Support Selection |journal=Violence Against Women |date=March 2021 |volume=27 |issue=3–4 |pages=320–338 |doi=10.1177/1077801220905638 |pmid=32089083 |s2cid=211262910}}</ref>

In the study, four victims chose the police as a support to escape their abuser. They decided to call the police when the relationship became a risk for their health. Two out of the four victims shared their negative experiences with the police. The police refused to get involved because they thought that what they were experiencing were normal relationship conflicts. These victims saw that current laws in South Korea are inadequate for protecting them from domestic femicide victims. They were deeply frustrated about it and they felt anxious and scared since they felt no one could protect them.<ref name="Park 320–338" />

The legal system does not favor women suffering from femicide and intimate partner femicide. Victims find it hard to report an aggressive male behavior, domestic partner violence, and violence towards women due to the idea that sexual assault and domestic violence is a matter that should be handled "privately". In South Korea two legislations that protected women were enacted for the first time in 1997. "Special Action Punishment of Domestic Violence Crimes" legislation was established to punish the perpetrators. This law states if someone is found to be guilty of psychological, mental and physical violence the perpetrator will be fined or face jail time. The "Act on Prevention of Domestic Violence and Protection of Victims" legislation is used to protect the victims by reporting systems, provision of protection facilities and support services for victims.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Han |first1=Young Ran |last2=Jeong |first2=Geum Hee |last3=Kim |first3=Shin-Jeong |title=Factors influencing beliefs about intimate partner violence among adults in South Korea |journal=Public Health Nursing |date=September 2017 |volume=34 |issue=5 |pages=412–421 |doi=10.1111/phn.12326 |pmid=28419632 |s2cid=22929638}}</ref> Even though this law protects victims it is limited since it only protects married couples and does not address couples who are not married and face intimate partner violence.

Olivia Shieber, a senior program manager of foreign and defense policy studies, describes Korean courts as lenient with sex crime punishments. In 2013, the Korean Supreme court upheld the country's first [[spousal rape]] conviction which is something in which South Korea was lagging behind when compared to other first world countries. It wasn't until the year 2020 when the age of consent was raised from 13 to 16, with a stipulation that the perpetrator must be 19 or older to be prosecuted for sex crimes against victims between the age of 13 and 16.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://law.go.kr/%EB%B2%95%EB%A0%B9/%ED%98%95%EB%B2%95/%EC%A0%9C305%EC%A1%B0 |title=형법 |website=law.go.kr |access-date=1 October 2023 |archive-date=9 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231109193631/https://law.go.kr/%EB%B2%95%EB%A0%B9/%ED%98%95%EB%B2%95/%EC%A0%9C305%EC%A1%B0 |url-status=live }}</ref> Additionally, the fact that just 30% of judges and less than 4% of police personnel are women clearly affects how crimes of this sort are handled by the Korean judicial system.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schieber |first=Olivia |title=South Korea Needs to Contend With Sexual Violence |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2020/08/10/south-korea-needs-to-contend-with-sexual-violence/ |access-date=17 December 2022 |website=Foreign Policy |date=10 August 2020 |language=en-US |archive-date=17 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221217223425/https://foreignpolicy.com/2020/08/10/south-korea-needs-to-contend-with-sexual-violence/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Even in cases where prosecutors successfully prosecute a defendant for a sex offense, the offenders are usually given a suspended sentence. Additionally, due to the country's strict legal definitions, it is still challenging to prove rape and other sex crimes in South Korea and some defendants have even exploited South Korea's tough defamation laws to sue their alleged victims for defamation making victims scared to come forward. Ultimately, women that face intimate partner violence or femicide in Korea are left feeling isolated and disenfranchised, neglected by the legal system and socially outcast while having to increasingly worry about femicide rates rising.

==== Turkey ====
{{main|Femicide in Turkey}}

[[File:Rode schoenen op de Dam in Amsterdam.jpg|thumb|Red shoes as a symbolic protest for femicide]]
A gender-based discriminatory notion of honor is sometimes the cause of serious cases of health deterioration or mutilation among women in Turkey. According to the ''Report on Custom and Honor Killings'' by the country's [[General Directorate of Security (Turkey)|General Directorate of Security]], 1,028 custom and [[honor killings]] were committed between the years of 2003 and 2007.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gursoy |first1=Elif |last2=McCool |first2=William F. |last3=Sahinoglu |first3=Serap |last4=Yavuz Genc |first4=Yasemin |s2cid=42606938 |title=Views of Women's Sexuality and Violence Against Women in Turkey |journal=[[Journal of Transcultural Nursing]] |date=15 September 2014 |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=189–198 |doi=10.1177/1043659614550485|pmid=25225236}}</ref> However, according to the World Data Bank, femicide rates in Turkey were 0.9 women murdered due to violence against women per 100k women. Which ranks it about the same femicide rate as Istanbul-convention [[Ratification|ratifiers]] such as Germany & Austria,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Intentional homicides, female (per 100,000 female) {{!}} Data |url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/VC.IHR.PSRC.FE.P5?end=2018&name_desc=false&start=2018&view=map |access-date=18 July 2021 |publisher=The World Bank |archive-date=18 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210718022533/https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/VC.IHR.PSRC.FE.P5?end=2018&name_desc=false&start=2018&view=map |url-status=live }}</ref> but still significantly higher than most of the other ratifiers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Intentional homicides, female (per 100,000 female) - Germany, Turkiye, Austria, Poland, Norway, Switzerland, France, Italy, Spain, United Kingdom, Ireland, Denmark, Netherlands, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Greece, Luxembourg, Malta, Moldova, Monaco, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia {{!}} Data |url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/VC.IHR.PSRC.FE.P5?end=2020&locations=DE-TR-AT-PL-NO-CH-FR-IT-ES-GB-IE-DK-NL-AL-BA-HR-CY-EE-GR-LU-MT-MD-MC-ME-MK-RO-RS-SI&most_recent_value_desc=true&start=2010 |access-date=10 August 2022 |publisher=The World Bank |archive-date=10 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220810185829/https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/VC.IHR.PSRC.FE.P5?end=2020&locations=DE-TR-AT-PL-NO-CH-FR-IT-ES-GB-IE-DK-NL-AL-BA-HR-CY-EE-GR-LU-MT-MD-MC-ME-MK-RO-RS-SI&most_recent_value_desc=true&start=2010 |url-status=live }}</ref> Since 2019, Turkeys femicide rate have seen a significant drop of 44.9%.<ref>{{Cite web|title=2020 Report of We Will End Femicide Platform|url=http://kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net/veriler/2949/2020-report-of-we-will-end-femicide-platform|access-date=18 July 2021|website=kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net|archive-date=16 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416120635/http://kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net/veriler/2949/2020-report-of-we-will-end-femicide-platform|url-status=live}}</ref>

According to the data of the [[General Directorate of Security (Turkey)|General Directorate of Security]] covering killings in Turkey until 2007, honor killings happen predominantly in the Southeastern part of the country. The rates of murderers born in Eastern and Southeastern [[Anatolia]] are much higher than murderers born in other regions. With 24% of the murderers born in Southeastern Anatolia and 21% in Eastern Anatolia, they share the top spot. While in comparison, only 8% of the murderers are born in the [[Marmara region]]. Even though that region has the highest rate of honor killings, which means that the killings are primarily committed by people born outside that region.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Cesur-Kılıçaslan, Seher |date=2013 |title=Honor Killings in Turkey |journal=The International Journal of Interdisciplinary Cultural Studies |volume=7 |issue=3 |page=28 |doi=10.18848/2327-008X/CGP/v07i03/53168}}</ref> The reason behind this is the fact that honor killings are still receiving support in Eastern and Southeastern Anatolia. According to a survey in [[Diyarbakir]], a city in Southeastern Anatolia, 40% of the respondents supported honor killing.<ref>{{cite news |last=Rainsford |first=Sarah |author-link=Sarah Rainsford |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/4357158.stm |title='Honour' crime defiance in Turkey |work=BBC News |date=19 October 2005 |access-date=23 December 2013 |archive-date=30 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430204622/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/4357158.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> In some court cases this has led the court to decide to send the entire family to prison. For example, in 2009, an entire Kurdish family was sent to prison for life, because they were involved in the honor killing of their daughter, who got pregnant after being raped.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.canada.com/story.html?id%3De6256f9e-e8e4-4f58-af6f-46c19bcc6423 |title=Shift in 'honour' killings |website=www.canada.com |access-date=23 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160407194238/http://www.canada.com/story.html?id=e6256f9e-e8e4-4f58-af6f-46c19bcc6423 |archive-date= 7 April 2016}}</ref>

In 2020, 300 women died as a result of femicide in Turkey, which is 174 (36%) less than the year before<ref>{{cite news |title=Challenge accepted: Turkish feminists spell out real meaning of hashtag |url=http://kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net/veriler/2949/2020-report-of-we-will-end-femicide-platform |access-date=4 August 2020 |work=The Guardian |date=31 July 2020 |archive-date=27 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127100526/http://kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net/veriler/2949/2020-report-of-we-will-end-femicide-platform |url-status=live }}</ref> The source started differentiating between confirmed femicides and suspicious deaths in 2020, so the more representative numbers to compare are: 474 in 2019 and 471 in 2020, a decrease of about 0,5%. According to the same source, suspicious deaths have been rising for the past years. Totaling the numbers from confirmed and suspicious deaths in 2021 497 have been killed, in 2020 471 have been killed and in 2019 474 have been killed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2021 Annual Report of We Will Stop Femicides Platform |url=https://kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net/veriler/3005/2021-annual-report-of-we-will-stop-femicides-platform |access-date=10 August 2022 |website=kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz. |archive-date=10 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220810185831/https://kadincinayetlerinidurduracagiz.net/veriler/3005/2021-annual-report-of-we-will-stop-femicides-platform |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2021, via presidential decree, the Turkish government made the decision to leave the Istanbul convention, making it the first and only country in the Council of Europe to have withdrawn from any international human rights convention.<ref>{{Cite web |date=30 June 2021 |title=Turkey's withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention rallies the fight for women's rights across the world |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2021/07/turkeys-withdrawal-from-the-istanbul-convention-rallies-the-fight-for-womens-rights-across-the-world-2/ |access-date=10 August 2022 |publisher=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref> This has sparked outrage in the population, as according to polls, only 26% of the population voted in favor of leaving.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 April 2021 |title=Turkey: poll, 52% reject withdrawal from Istanbul Convention - General news |url=http://www.ansamed.info/ansamed/en/news/sections/generalnews/2021/04/01/turkey-poll-52-reject-withdrawal-from-istanbul-convention_771821fc-37e1-42c6-a84b-9e38dc339d14.html |access-date=10 August 2022 |website=ANSAMed |language=en |archive-date=23 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221123210815/https://www.ansamed.info/ansamed/en/news/sections/generalnews/2021/04/01/turkey-poll-52-reject-withdrawal-from-istanbul-convention_771821fc-37e1-42c6-a84b-9e38dc339d14.html }}</ref> In the past the president has stated, that the women's rights movement is diverting women from their original roles as mothers and wives, while also normalizing tolerance to homosexuality. National women's rights organizations, who had been criticizing lack of implementation of the convention for years, now have concerns about rising femicide rates in Turkey.

Seven women were killed by current or former partners in one day in 2024.<ref name="tr2024">{{Cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/feb/27/seven-women-across-turkey-savagely-killed-by-current-or-ex-spouses-in-a-single-day |title=Seven women in Turkey 'savagely killed' by current or ex-spouses in single day |department=Europe |agency=[[Agence France-Presse]] |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=1756-3224 |oclc=60623878 |date=27 February 2024 |access-date=27 February 2024}}</ref>

=== Australia ===
In 2019, a recent statistic<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://aic.gov.au/publications/rip/rip38 |author1=Tracy Cussen |author2=Willow Bryant |title=Domestic/family homicide in Australia |quote=see Table 3: Overview of victim characteristics by homicide type, 2002–03 to 2011–12 |date=5 May 2015 |website=aic.gov.au |access-date=29 September 2019 |archive-date=29 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190929204838/https://aic.gov.au/publications/rip/rip38 |url-status=live }}</ref> from the [[Australian Institute of Criminology]] indicated that on average, one woman a week is murdered in an act of femicide in [[Women in Australia|Australia]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-australia-48591402 |title=I've mapped child murders since my stepfather killed two girls |author=Gary Nunn |date=24 September 2019 |work=BBC |access-date=25 September 2019 |quote=On average, one woman a week is murdered by her current or former partner in Australia, according to the most recent Australian Institute of Criminology statistics. |archive-date=24 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190924223225/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-australia-48591402 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Europe ===
[[File:Femicide rates in Europe (2017).svg|thumb|upright=2|Victims of femicide per 100.000 women (2017)<ref>{{cite news |author1=European Data Journalism Network |title=Femminicidio in Europa, due anni dopo |url=https://www.balcanicaucaso.org/aree/Europa/Femminicidio-in-Europa-due-anni-dopo |access-date=26 November 2019 |publisher=[[Osservatorio Balcani e Caucaso Transeuropa]] |date=26 November 2019 |language=it |archive-date=28 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191128181121/https://www.balcanicaucaso.org/aree/Europa/Femminicidio-in-Europa-due-anni-dopo |url-status=live }}</ref><br />
{{legend|#a6ce39|Femicide by family and relatives}}
{{legend|#6f2c91|Femicide by intimate partners}}]]
In Europe, agencies have funded initiatives on gender and violence but not specifically on femicide. Research is in its infancy and uncoordinated.
