A COST Action IS1206<ref name=":13" /> has established the first pan-European coalition on femicide with researchers who are already studying the phenomenon nationally to advance research clarity, agree on definitions, improve the efficacy of policies for femicide prevention, and publish guidelines for the use of national policy-makers.<ref name="Femicide across Europe" /> EU reports show that additional support has been needed during the period of pandemic lockdown in many countries <ref>{{Cite web |title=COVID-19 wave of violence against women shows EU countries still lack proper safeguards {{!}} EIGE {{!}} Femicide Watch |url=http://femicide-watch.org/products/covid-19-wave-violence-against-women-shows-eu-countries-still-lack-proper-safeguards-eige |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928054309/http://femicide-watch.org/products/covid-19-wave-violence-against-women-shows-eu-countries-still-lack-proper-safeguards-eige |archive-date=28 September 2021 |access-date=14 March 2021 |website=femicide-watch.}}</ref>

Available data are limited: [[Eurostat]] covers only 20 countries<ref>Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, France, Italy, Slovenia, Czech Republic, Germany, Latvia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Netherlands, Spain, Finland, Hungary, Lithuania, Slovakia, Switzerland, and United Kingdom.</ref> and there are discrepancies in the way in which the data is collected. According to available data in [[Western Europe]], the average annual rate is 0.4 victims of femicide for every 100,000 women. The worst situations are found in [[Montenegro]], [[Lithuania]], and [[Latvia]]. In most countries, the partner is the most common perpetrator. However, there are exceptions: in Lithuania and [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], most femicides are committed by family members. Also, while male victims of homicide have been in a sharp decline in recent years, the number of women murdered in Europe, not necessarily at the hands of a partner or family member, remains constant, with a slight increase from 2013 to 2015.<ref name=edjnet>{{cite news |last1=Bona |first1=Marzia |last2=Burba |first2=Alberto |title=Femicide in Europe is a widespread issue |url=https://www.europeandatajournalism.eu/index.php/eng/News/Data-news/Femicide-in-Europe-is-a-widespread-issue |access-date=7 September 2018 |work=OBC Transeuropa/EDJNet |date=28 November 2017 |archive-date=7 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180907101253/https://www.europeandatajournalism.eu/index.php/eng/News/Data-news/Femicide-in-Europe-is-a-widespread-issue |url-status=live }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016050101/https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ |date=16 October 2017 }}.</ref> From 2013 to 2017, 30 European countries joined a COST ([[European Cooperation in Science and Technology|Cooperation on Science and Technology]]) project called "femicide across Europe.<ref name="Femicide across Europe" />

The [[European Union]] first enacted COST (Cooperation on Science and Technology), a program known as COST Action. COST Action led to four different femicide research groups: definitions, data collection, cultural issues, and advocacy and prevention. Thirty countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding with COST that promoted international efforts to address femicide and the Action program.<ref name=":12">{{cite book |doi=10.1332/9781447347163 |hdl=20.500.12657/28243 |oclc=1014458042 |title=Femicide across Europe |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-4473-4716-3 |s2cid=239929694 |url=https://www.doabooks.org/doab?func=search&query=rid:31422 |editor-last1=Weil |editor-last2=Corradi |editor-last3=Naudi |editor-first1=Shalva |editor-first2=Consuelo |editor-first3=Marceline |archive-date=19 January 2025 |access-date=19 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119053254/https://www.doabooks.org/doab?func=search&query=rid:31422 |url-status=live }}{{page needed|date=July 2023}}</ref> [[Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence|The Istanbul Convention]] was a gathering of multiple independent states who had a common goal of acknowledging and addressing femicide. However, the convention "is not a treaty, and not legally binding for all states", and thus is not an official policy.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9781315652436-2 |chapter=Domestic violence as a human rights issue |title=The Istanbul Convention, Domestic Violence and Human Rights |year=2017 |pages=10–36 |isbn=978-1-315-65243-6}}</ref>

==== France ====
Depending on the sources, between 122 and 149 women were murdered in [[France]] in 2019 by their partners or ex-partners.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kheniche |first=Ouafia |date=31 December 2019 |title=2019: l'année où le féminicide s'est imposé dans la société française |url=https://www.franceinter.fr/societe/2019-l-annee-ou-le-feminicide-s-est-impose-dans-la-societe-francaise |access-date=11 March 2020 |website=franceinter France |language=fr |archive-date=26 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200226003848/https://www.franceinter.fr/societe/2019-l-annee-ou-le-feminicide-s-est-impose-dans-la-societe-francaise |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/11/21/europe/france-femicide-intl/index.html |title=137 women have been killed by their partners in France this year. Critics blame a 'deeply sexist society' |first1=Saskya |last1=Vandoorne |others=Video by Edward Kiernan, Rosie Tomkins and Mark Esplin |publisher=CNN |date=22 November 2019 |access-date=11 March 2020 |archive-date=14 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200414051714/https://www.cnn.com/2019/11/21/europe/france-femicide-intl/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Germany ====
[[Women in Germany|Germany]] has one of the highest absolute femicide numbers in Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cazenave |first=Fabien |date=4 September 2019 |title=France and Germany have high femicide rates compared to rest of EU |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/justice-home-affairs/news/france-and-germany-have-high-femicide-rates-compared-to-rest-of-eu/ |access-date=11 March 2020 |website=euractiv |language=en-GB |archive-date=4 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200304030121/https://www.euractiv.com/section/justice-home-affairs/news/france-and-germany-have-high-femicide-rates-compared-to-rest-of-eu/ |url-status=live }}</ref><!-- Germany has more inhabitants than all other european countries. Only counting numbers is senseless -->

====Italy====
{{Main|Femicide in Italy}}

Statistics of femicide in [[Women in Italy|Italy]] are reported by year (1995–2019) by the independent Women NGO.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://femicidiocasadonne.wordpress.com// |title=Femicidio Casadonne |website=femicidiocasadonne.wordpress.com |access-date=24 February 2019 |archive-date=28 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928054306/https://femicidiocasadonne.wordpress.com/ }}</ref>

On 25 November 2025, the Italian parliament passed a bill explicitly classifying femicide as a distinct crime. It was introduced into the country's criminal code with the penalty of life imprisonment.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-26 |title=Italy now recognizes the crime of femicide and punishes it with life in prison |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/25/europe/italy-femicide-law-intl-hnk |access-date=2026-01-21 |website=CNN |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260210160821/https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/25/europe/italy-femicide-law-intl-hnk |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-26 |title=Italy officially makes femicide a crime – punishable with life imprisonment |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/italy-femicide-murder-prison-women-b2872700.html |access-date=2026-01-21 |website=The Independent |language=en |archive-date=26 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260126160730/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/italy-femicide-murder-prison-women-b2872700.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Italian parliament unanimously votes to make femicide a crime | date=26 November 2025 | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1dzp050yn2o.amp | access-date=27 November 2025 | archive-date=26 November 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251126054016/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1dzp050yn2o.amp | url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Ireland ====

====Spain====
Statistics and structure of femicide in [[Women in Spain|Spain]] are reported by year (2010–2019).<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://feminicidio.net/ |title=Listado de feminicidios y otros asesinatos de mujeres cometidos por hombres en España en 2019 |website=feminicidio.net |access-date=9 September 2019 |archive-date=17 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190917064927/https://feminicidio.net/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Switzerland====
The research project ''Stop Femicide'' reports that in [[Switzerland]], one woman is killed every two weeks by a man she knows – typically a husband, partner, ex-partner, or male relative. At least one more woman each week survives an attempted femicide.<ref name="stopfemizid.ch">{{Cite web |title=Stop Femizid * Rechercheprojekt Femizide in der Schweiz |url=https://www.stopfemizid.ch/deutsch |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=Stop Femizid |language=fr-CH |archive-date=28 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251128115546/https://www.stopfemizid.ch/deutsch |url-status=live }}</ref>

There is no official government body that systematically records femicides or maintains its own statistics on gender-based killings.<ref name="stopfemizid.ch"/> This lack of data is criticized by researchers, politicians, and civil society groups, as it makes it more difficult to analyze, prevent, and strategically combat violence against women.<ref>{{Cite web |last=n.a. |date=2022-10-12 |title=«Femizid»: ein blinder Fleck in der Statistik |url=https://www.unilu.ch/news/femizid-ein-blinder-fleck-in-der-statistik-7118/ |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=Universität Luzern |language=de-CH}}</ref>

==== United Kingdom ====

<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is femicide?|url=https://www.womensaid.org.uk/what-we-do/campaigning-and-influencing/femicide-census__trashed/what-is-femicide/|access-date=14 March 2021|publisher=Women's killed by partners and ex-lovers,<ref>{{Cite web |date=20 February 2020 |title=Femicide Census reveals half of UK women killed by men die at hands of partner or ex |website=ons government United Kingdom |archive-date=11 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210311153739/https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/articles/homicideinenglandandwales/yearendingmarch2018#how-are-victims-and-suspects-related |url-status=live }}</ref> or those killed during lockdown.<ref>{{Cite web|date=15 April 2020|title=Domestic abuse killings appear to double during UK's lockdown|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/coronavirus-domestic-abuse-uk-killings-women-girls-a9467131.html|access-date=14 March 2021|website=The Independent|language=en|archive-date=16 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210316183204/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/coronavirus-domestic-abuse-uk-killings-women-girls-a9467131.html|url-status=live}}</ref> On average, in the UK, a woman is killed by a man every three days, or by a current or former partner, every four days. The data is not gathered in Scotland. Data published in 2022 shows that in year ending March 2021, 177 women were murdered in England and Wales (for comparison, 416 men were killed in this period). Where there was a known suspect, 92% of the women were killed by men.<ref>{{Cite news |date=30 June 2022 |title=How many violent attacks and sexual assaults on women are there? |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/explainers-56365412 |access-date=17 July 2022 |archive-date=17 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220717130559/https://www.bbc.com/news/explainers-56365412 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2023, Labour MP for domestic abuse, [[Jess Phillips]], received significant criticism from gender critical activists for naming the trans-girl, [[Murder of Brianna Ghey|Brianna Ghey]] as a victim of femicide, stating that this inclusion was "an insult to the memory of the women and children tragically killed this year".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://transsafety.network/posts/gc-hate-femicide-brianna/|title=GC hatred pours out over Jess Phillips naming murdered trans girl as femicide|first=Jess|last=O'Thomson|publisher=Trans Safety Network|date=10 March 2023|access-date=6 November 2025|archive-date=15 November 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251115113625/https://transsafety.network/posts/gc-hate-femicide-brianna/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://metro.co.uk/2023/03/15/the-reaction-to-brianna-ghey-tributes-shows-how-far-the-uk-is-from-accepting-trans-people-18445400/|title=The reaction to Brianna Ghey tributes shows how far the UK is from accepting trans people|first=Ugla Stefanía|last=Kristjönudóttir Jónsdóttir|work=Metro|date=15 March 2023|access-date=6 November 2025|archive-date=28 May 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240528235824/https://metro.co.uk/2023/03/15/the-reaction-to-brianna-ghey-tributes-shows-how-far-the-uk-is-from-accepting-trans-people-18445400/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2024, there were growing concerns of black femicides within the UK as [[Black people|black]] women and girls in recent statistics were more likely than those of other races to be killed by their partners, family members or non-intimate people in [[Greater London]]; they faced not only higher rates but also formed the majority of victims. 2022 data from the [[Metropolitan Police]] showed that Black women made up 43% of femicide victims despite just 14% of the London population being Black. This was a significant increase from 2021, when just 12% of femicide victims were Black. The figures of black femicide rose to 62% in 2023. [[Southall Black Sisters]] and the Femicide Census had been critical of the Metropolitan Police and mayor, [[Sadiq Khan]], for undermining such killings targeting exclusively black women.<ref>{{cite web | title=Black women in London facing 'crisis' as higher femicide rates revealed | date=28 May 2024 | url=https://www.standard.co.uk/news/crime/black-women-killings-femicide-london-crime-met-police-b1160466.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Black women in London facing 'crisis' as higher femicide rates revealed | date=28 May 2024 | url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/national/24348643.black-women-london-facing-crisis-higher-femicide-rates-revealed/ | access-date=12 November 2025 | archive-date=14 November 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251114073316/https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/national/24348643.black-women-london-facing-crisis-higher-femicide-rates-revealed/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2025, recent studies from the Femicide Census indicated that there had been more mothers [[parricide|killed]] by their sons than women by strangers. These types of femicides are hidden and the census said that there is still insufficient help available for women and girls facing violence from their families, including mothers by their sons. Out of 121 women killed by men in 2022, 12% were by sons whilst 11% were by someone unknown.<ref>{{cite web | title=Femicide Census says more mums killed by sons than by strangers | date=2 September 2025 | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/czxw1yrlx5go | access-date=14 October 2025 | archive-date=14 November 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251114141512/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/czxw1yrlx5go | url-status=live }}</ref>

====Lithuania====

Lithuania is among the few countries in Europe in which family-related femicides (such as fathers, mothers, brothers, or uncles) outnumber intimate partners.<ref>/[https://www.balcanicaucaso.org/eng/Areas/Europe/Femicide-the-numbers-in-Europe-184329#:~:text=In%20most%20countries%2C%20the%20partner%20is%20the,of%20femicides%20are%20committed%20by%20family%20members.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250907215950/https://www.balcanicaucaso.org/eng/Areas/Europe/Femicide-the-numbers-in-Europe-184329#:~:text=In%20most%20countries%2C%20the%20partner%20is%20the,of%20femicides%20are%20committed%20by%20family%20members. |date=7 September 2025 }}</ref>

=== Latin America ===
{{main|Femicide in Latin America}}

[[File:No femicidio.jpg|thumb|A candle memorial to women killed by femicide (femicidio), [[Chile]], 2007.]]
[[Feminism in Latin America|Feminists in Latin America]] have been among the first to adopt the term ''femicide'', referring to the [[Femicides in Ciudad Juárez|female homicides]] in [[Ciudad Juárez]], [[Mexico]]. This term inspired feminists in Latin America to organize anti-feminicide groups to challenge this social injustice towards women.<ref name="Russell 3" /> The use of the term femicide, and the creation of anti-femicide feminist organizations, spread from Mexico, to many other Latin American countries, like [[Guatemala]].<ref name="Guatemala" /> In Latin America, femicide is an issue that occurs in many countries, but most predominantly in Central America, in countries such as [[Gender inequality in El Salvador|El Salvador]] and [[Gender inequality in Honduras|Honduras]], and other places, such as [[Women's rights in Brazil|Brazil]] and Mexico. The Latin American region includes 5 of the 12 countries with the highest rate of femicide in the world.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Boira |first1=Santiago |last2=Nudelman |first2=Anita |title=Professionals' support role for survivors of femicide and relatives of victims: The case of Ecuador |journal=Journal of Comparative Social Work |date=25 July 2018 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=81–102 |doi=10.31265/jcsw.v13i1.160 |s2cid=81660207 |doi-access=free}}</ref> According to Julia Estela Monárrez-Fragoso of the Colegio de la Frontera Norte based in Ciudad Juárez, victims are often blamed for being out late at night, or for hanging around "questionable" areas, such as discotecas or nightclubs.<ref name="Monarrez">Monárrez Fragoso, Julia Estela. 2010. "The Victims of Ciudad Juárez Feminicide: Sexually Fetishised Commodities". In ''Terrorising Women: Feminicide in the Americas''. Durham: Duke University Press. 59–69.</ref> Between 2000 and 2010, more than five thousand Guatemalan women and girls were murdered. Guatemala's historical record reveals a long history of acceptance of gendered violence, and the [[Armed Forces of Guatemala|military]], [[Politics of Guatemala|government]], and judiciary's role in normalizing misogyny.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last1=Carey |first1=D Jr |last2=Torres |first2=MG |title=Precursors to femicide: Guatemalan women in a vortex of violence |journal=Latin American Research Review |date=2010 |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=142–64 |doi=10.1017/S0023879100011146 |pmid=21188891|s2cid=43479251 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In a Report on the Violations of Women's Rights in Guatemala by a [[United Nations Human Rights Committee]], the state's failure to enforce laws protecting women from femicide is seen as highly problematic. The report argues that enforcing laws against the murder of women is a low priority of state governments, due to patriarchal beliefs, and assumptions about the role of women in society.<ref name="Guatemala">{{cite report |last1=Davis |first1=Lisa |last2=Parker |first2=Bradley |publisher=United Nations. United Nations Human Rights Committee |title=Report on the Violations of Women's Human Rights in Guatemala in response to the Third Periodic Report of Guatemala |place=New York |date=2012 |url=https://www.madre.org/sites/default/files/PDFs/1329260402_Guatemala%20Shadow%20Report-%20ENG.pdf |access-date=18 December 2022 |archive-date=21 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221221182725/https://www.madre.org/sites/default/files/PDFs/1329260402_Guatemala%20Shadow%20Report-%20ENG.pdf }}</ref>

Various activists and scholars, such as Monárrez, have argued that connections exist between the femicides and neoliberal policies, namely [[North American Free Trade Agreement]] (NAFTA). They believe that the treaty has served to open trade borders, and to increase foreign investment targeted at manufacturing low-cost garments in [[maquiladora]]s.<ref name="Monarrez" />

Intimate partner femicide is the most common form of femicide,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Joseph|first=Janice|date=2017|title=Victims of femicide in Latin America: Legal and criminal justice responses|journal=Temida|volume=20|issue=1|pages=3–21|doi=10.2298/tem1701003j|doi-access=free}}</ref> and high violence and crime rates in these countries also contribute to this issue. There is a lack of an organized system to record information and statistical data to support this issue. [[Machismo]], a history of civil wars, and other cultural influences can also contribute to this issue, specifically in Latin America. Torture, mutilation, defacement, sexual assault, and the dumping of bodies is a common trend with femicide.

It has been observed that many of the women killed in Ciudad Juárez are young mothers who migrate to this region seeking employment in maquiladoras.<ref name="Monarrez" /> They then become easy targets, due to the fact that they are separated from their family, and are typically alone when traveling home. Policy solutions in Central America have tried making transportation safer (see below for policy solutions). Other scholars, such as Itallurde, point to the culpability of corporations "based on the concepts and doctrines of tortuous negligence, failure to protect, and aiding and abetting".<ref name="Itullurde">Iturralde, Christina. 2010. "Searching for Accountability on the Border: Justice for the Women of Ciudad Juárez". In ''Terrorising Women: Feminicide in the Americas''. 251.</ref> Other scholars, such as historians Steven Volk and Marian Schlotterbeck, hypothesize that there may be a "macho backlash" behind these killings: "Certainly male egos, of fathers and would-be boyfriends, must suffer some deflation from this dramatic change in the economic influence of these young women."<ref name="VolkSchlotterbeck">{{cite journal |last1=Volk |first1=Steven S. |last2=Schlotterbeck |first2=Marian E. |title=Gender, Order, and Femicide: Reading the Popular Culture of Murder in Ciudad Juárez |journal=[[Aztlán: A Journal of Chicano Studies]] |date=1 January 2007 |volume=32 |issue=1 |page=62 |doi=10.1525/azt.2007.32.1.53 |s2cid=141331183}}</ref>
[[File:8M en Paraná - Entre Ríos - Paula Kindsvater 8.jpg|thumb|Protest against femicide in Argentina, 2020]]
In 2015, [[Supreme Court of Mexico|Mexican Supreme Court]] required the police to reopen and investigate a murder case from a femicide "perspective".<ref>{{cite book |last=Camp |first=Roderick Ai |year=2017 |title=Mexico: What Everyone Needs to Know |page=189 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-049417-9 |edition= 2nd}}</ref> The case of Mariana Lima Buenida, was reopened almost thirteen years later. She was found dead in her home on 28 June 2010, at the time her husband, a police officer, insisted she committed suicide. [[Irinea Buendia]], Mariana's mother, fought and advocated for her daughter's case. The reopening of the case would lead to justice after more than a decade, a monumental moment in Mexico's judicial history that acknowledges the first case of femicide within the Mexican Supreme Court.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.scjn.gob.mx/derechos-humanos/sites/default/files/sentencias-emblematicas/sentencia/2020-12/AR%20554-2013.pdf | title=AR 554-2013 | access-date=19 September 2025 | archive-date=15 November 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251115035823/https://www.scjn.gob.mx/derechos-humanos/sites/default/files/sentencias-emblematicas/sentencia/2020-12/AR%20554-2013.pdf | url-status=live }}</ref>

However, there have been some actions taken to address this issue. The criminalization of femicide and various laws passed in specific countries have aimed to stop this problem. In addition, the United Nations has taken a role in stopping this with a commission that calls for action to be taken. There is a growing social awareness around this issue with #NiUnaMenos (Not One Woman Less) or #NiUnaMas (Not One More Woman). Lastly, female friendly urban zones have been created as a concrete solution. These zones include [[Women-only passenger car|female-only transportation]], and government centers offering services specifically for women.

Central American policymakers have experimented with creating "female-friendly urban zones".<ref name="McAnarney">{{cite news |last=McAnarney |first=Alex |url=https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/opensecurity/femicide-in-central-america-is-creating-female-friendly-urban-zones-real/ |title=Femicide in Central America: is creating Female-Friendly Urban Zones really the solution? |work=Open Democracy |date=15 November 2012 |access-date=18 March 2013 |archive-date=7 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190907215417/https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/opensecurity/femicide-in-central-america-is-creating-female-friendly-urban-zones-real/ |url-status=live }}</ref> "Pink" public transportation networks have been established in Mexico, Brazil, El Salvador, and Guatemala to provide women-only forms of public transportation to stem [[sexual harassment]], and to provide safety for women. These efforts have received substantial praise and criticism.<ref name="McAnarney" />

Criticism from feminists and others often point to the efficacy of [[Sex segregation|gender segregation]] in changing gender norms of oppression - specifically the Latin American cultural conventions of "machismo" and "[[marianismo]]", which are potent social regulators throughout the region.<ref name="McAnarney" />

Feminist philosopher and gender studies scholar [[Judith Butler]] spoke on ''feminicido'' in an interview for their 2024 book "[[Who's Afraid of Gender?]]".<ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last1=Butler |first1=Judith |last2=Halberstam |first2=Jack |date=2025 |title=Who's Afraid of Gender? Solidarity, Radical Democracy, and the Global Politics of the Anti–Gender Ideology Movement: A Conversation with Judith Butler and Jack Halberstam |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/950768 |journal=GLQ: A Journal of Lesbian and Gay Studies |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=137–158 |doi=10.1215/10642684-11573873 |issn=1527-9375 |archive-date=29 August 2025 |access-date=22 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250829170055/https://muse.jhu.edu/article/950768 |url-status=live }}</ref> They note how some feminist movements in Latin America lie in opposition to feminicide, particularly in their failure to acknowledge how this same violence impacts groups beyond cis-women; including trans women, gender non-conforming, and the queer community.<ref name=":20" /> Butler firmly poses this as a "brutal failure of [[coalition]]al politics",<ref name=":20" /> and emphasizes the need to look at freedom in terms of not only individual liberty, but as a collective.<ref name=":20" />

====Brazil====
Through the Law No. 13,104 in 2015, the femicide is a crime provided for in the [[Penal Code of Brazil|Brazilian Penal Code]], item VI, paragraph 2, of art. 121, when committed "against a woman on grounds of female condition".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brazilian Penal Code |url=http://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/decreto-lei/Del2848compilado.htm |access-date=16 December 2019 |website=planalto government Brazil |archive-date=13 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313000246/http://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/decreto-lei/Del2848compilado.htm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Lei do Feminicídio faz cinco anos - Notícias |url=https://www.camara.leg.br/noticias/643729-lei-do-feminicidio-faz-cinco-anos/ |access-date=16 January 2024 |website=Portal da Câmara dos Deputados |language=pt-br |archive-date=16 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240116164155/https://www.camara.leg.br/noticias/643729-lei-do-feminicidio-faz-cinco-anos/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The Paragraph 2-A, of art. 121, complements the section, by stating that there are reasons of female condition when the crime involves domestic and family violence or contempt or discrimination against women. The penalty for this crime is 12 to 30 years in prison.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://professorlfg.jusbrasil.com.br/artigos/173139525/feminicidio-entenda-as-questoes-controvertidas-da-lei-13104-2015|title=Feminicídio: entenda as questões controvertidas da Lei 13.104/2015|website=Jusbrasil|language=pt-br|access-date=16 December 2019|archive-date=14 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160914080822/http://professorlfg.jusbrasil.com.br/artigos/173139525/feminicidio-entenda-as-questoes-controvertidas-da-lei-13104-2015|url-status=live}}</ref>

On the other hand, despite the increased rigor of criminal law, in a survey carried out by the newspaper Folha de S. Paulo, in 2019, there were 1,310 murders resulting from domestic violence or motivated by gender, characteristics of femicide. It was an increase of 7.2% compared to 2018.<ref name=":8" /> In 2023, during the first half of the year, the country had already recorded 722 cases of femicide, 2.6% more than crimes of the same nature recorded in the same period of 2022, according to data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum (FBSP).<ref>{{Cite web |date=13 November 2023 |title=Brasil registra 722 feminicídios no 1º semestre de 2023 |url=https://www.cartacapital.com.br/sociedade/brasil-registra-722-feminicidios-no-1o-semestre-de-2023/ |access-date=16 January 2024 |website=CartaCapital |language=pt-BR |archive-date=16 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240116164621/https://www.cartacapital.com.br/sociedade/brasil-registra-722-feminicidios-no-1o-semestre-de-2023/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Colombia ====
[[Women in Colombia|Colombia]] has followed 16 other Latin American countries by passing a law defining and punishing femicide for being a specific crime.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Colombia confronts femicide, the 'most extreme form of violence against women' |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-colombia-women-murder-idUSKCN0QP0CM20150820 |publisher=Reuters |date=20 August 2015 |access-date=3 December 2015 |archive-date=9 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151209000643/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-colombia-women-murder-idUSKCN0QP0CM20150820 |url-status=live }}</ref> On 6 July 2015, the government of Colombia passed a law that legally defines femicide as a crime with 20 to 50 years of jail time.<ref name=":3">{{cite web |title=Colombia approves femicide law to tackle violence against women |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/r-colombia-approves-femicide-law-to-tackle-violence-against-women-2015-6 |website=Business Insider |access-date=3 December 2015 |archive-date=8 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208150813/http://www.businessinsider.com/r-colombia-approves-femicide-law-to-tackle-violence-against-women-2015-6 |url-status=live }}</ref> This new law is named after Rosa Elvira Cely, a Colombian woman who was raped and murdered in 2012.<ref name=":3" /> Cely's death sparked national outrage, and caused thousands to march down the streets of [[Bogotá]]. Her murderer was found guilty, and was sentenced to 48 years in prison. The challenge now becomes implementing the law. Miguel Emilio La Rota, head of public policy and planning at Colombia's attorney general's office, said that the prosecutor's office must change how it investigates femicide.<ref>{{cite web |title=Colombia's new 'femicide' law targets violence against women |url=https://nypost.com/2015/08/20/colombias-new-femicide-law-targets-violence-against-women/ |website=New York Post |date=20 August 2015 |access-date=3 December 2015 |archive-date=8 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208111306/http://nypost.com/2015/08/20/colombias-new-femicide-law-targets-violence-against-women/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Colombia prosecuted a [[transgender]] woman's murder as a femicide for the first time in 2018, sentencing Davinson Stiven Erazo Sánchez to twenty years in a psychiatric center for "aggravated femicide" a year after he killed Anyela Ramos Claros, a transgender woman.<ref>{{cite web |date=19 December 2018 |title=For the first time, Colombia prosecutes a transgender woman's murder as a femicide |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/first-time-colombia-prosecutes-transgender-woman-s-murder-femicide-n950021 |access-date=23 December 2018 |publisher=NBC News |archive-date=4 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200304134004/https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/first-time-colombia-prosecutes-transgender-woman-s-murder-femicide-n950021 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== El Salvador ====
In El Salvador, an endeavor has been made to create multiple government centers that house many gender-specific services in one place, to cut down on commute time, and to increase the physical safety of women as they seek services such as counseling, child care, and reproductive health.<ref name="McAnarney" /> "The first center hopes to provide access to an estimated 162,000 women from the neighboring departments of [[La Libertad Department (El Salvador)|La Libertad]] and [[Sonsonate, El Salvador|Sonsonate]]. Supported by former Chilean president and head of [[UN Women]] [[Michelle Bachelet]], the initiative cost $3.2 million, with an additional $20 million loan from the Inter-American Development Bank earmarked for the construction of new sites."<ref name="McAnarney" />

Critics of this action point to the contradictory [[Abortion in El Salvador|abortion laws in El Salvador]] that are some of the harshest in the world: abortion is completely illegal, even to save the life of the mother, or to help a survivor of [[incest]] or rape. "Coupled with the judicial system's weaknesses, violence is abetted by the same government that aims to protect and defend. High levels of impunity leave many crimes unresolved or unreported."<ref name="McAnarney" /> Following legal reforms in the country, 2026 saw the first life sentenced handed out by the country's court over femicide.<ref>{{Cite web |title=El Salvador court hands down 1st life sentence for femicide |url=https://www.dw.com/en/el-salvador-court-hands-down-first-life-sentence-for-femicide/a-79268746 |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=dw.com |language=en}}</ref> 

==== Guatemala ====
[[Guatemala]] has championed the use of femicide as a concept by incorporating the term in its constitution: Decree 22. Lawmakers in this country passed Decree 22 in 2008 that defined Laws Against Femicide and Other Forms of Violence Against Women. These laws include 28 articles about prosecutable types of [[violence against women]]. They also created the Office of the Presidential Commission Against Femicide, enforcing the concept in the government and an anti-femicide unit of the National Police. Some results of the laws have proved encouraging, allowing many women to now report violence perpetrated against them. In the first month of 2010, a total of 27,000 women reported violence against them to the state, a large increase in the number of reported crimes. The laws also have helped several people jail their assailants, and have increased the severity of punishments for perpetrators. However, the actual enforcement of the new laws has been varied.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/healthcare-network/2018/mar/07/health-workers-stop-thousand-women-killed-guatemala-femicide |title=Can health workers stop thousands of women being killed in Guatemala? |website=[[The Guardian]] |date=7 March 2018}}</ref> Few offenders are ever actually convicted for the specific crime of femicide, and there are only three public prosecution offices in the entire country able to deal with the issue of femicide.<ref name=Shulman>{{Cite magazine |url=https://newrepublic.com/femicide-guatemala-decree-22?page=0,0 |author=Shulman, Aaron |title=The Rise of Femicide |magazine=[[The New Republic]] |date=29 December 2010 |access-date=1 April 2013 |archive-date=23 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211223034141/https://newrepublic.com/article/80556/femicide-guatemala-decree-22 |url-status=live }}</ref> In fact, only 127 convictions in 2010 occurred for female violence even though 46,000 cases overall were registered. Also, from 2000 to 2008, 98 percent of all femicide cases have remained in [[impunity]]. Some feminists argue that the culture in Guatemala is to blame. They cite that many male judges and other male government officials are sympathetic to the view that men's actions are justified, because they remain within the private sphere of the home. Attorney Romeo Silverio Gonzalez argued for this viewpoint when he stated that the new laws of Decree 22 were unconstitutional. He said that the laws were in contradiction to the private affairs of marriage. Attorney General Claudia Paz countered his viewpoint, ultimately defending the laws by justifying their existence because they protect women's rights. Overall, the legislation of these new laws has helped Guatemala improve the awareness of femicide and reporting of the crime, but enforcement and justice for femicide still have not been achieved.<ref name=Andrade>{{Cite web |url=http://www.americasquarterly.org/node/2963 |author=Andrade, Kara |title=Protecting the Rights of Guatemalan Women |work=[[Americas Quarterly]], Americas Society and the Council of the Americas |date=13 October 2011 |access-date=1 April 2013 |archive-date=9 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509063104/https://www.americasquarterly.org/node/2963 }}</ref> Femicide as the socially tolerated murder of women in Guatemala relies on the presence of systematic impunity, historically rooted gender inequalities, and the pervasive normalization of violence as a social relation.<ref name=":4" />

====Mexico====
{{Main|Femicide in Mexico}}

{{See also|Femicides in Ciudad Juárez}}
[[File:A memorial against femicide in Mexico-2.jpg|thumb|right|210px|The ''[[Antimonumenta (Mexico City)|Antimonumenta]]'', an [[Anti-monuments in Mexico|anti-monument]] against [[Femicides in Mexico|femicides]] in Mexico, in front of the [[Palacio de Bellas Artes]] in Mexico City]]
[[Amnesty International]] estimates that there have been around 34,000 female homicides in Mexico between 1986 and 2009.<ref name=":9" /> According to the National Citizen Observatory on Femicide, only 49 percent of the 800 cases of women killed in Mexico between June and July 2017 were investigated as femicide.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/stories/2017/11/feature-prosecuting-femicide-in-mexico |title=The long road to justice, prosecuting femicide in Mexico |website=www.unwomen.org |date=29 November 2017 |access-date=13 May 2021 |archive-date=16 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210516035813/https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/stories/2017/11/feature-prosecuting-femicide-in-mexico |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2018, "93 percent of crimes were either not reported or not investigated."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sandin |first1=Linnea |date=19 March 2020 |title=Femicides in Mexico: Impunity and Protests |url=https://www.csis.org/analysis/femicides-mexico-impunity-and-protests |language=en |access-date=15 April 2022 |website=CSIS |archive-date=21 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220321060950/https://www.csis.org/analysis/femicides-mexico-impunity-and-protests |url-status=live }}</ref> One activist, Natalia Reyes, reported that only 8 percent of femicides in Mexico are punished.<ref name=":15">{{cite web |url=http://sites.sandiego.edu/tbi-femicide/files/2017/12/2016-2017-Femicide-Report-Final.pdf |author=Lettieri, Michael |title=Violence Against Women in Mexico |work=Trans-Border Institute |year=2017 |access-date=19 February 2020 |archive-date=11 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711214508/https://sites.sandiego.edu/tbi-femicide/files/2017/12/2016-2017-Femicide-Report-Final.pdf }}</ref> Almost 35,000 people were murdered in 2019,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.csis.org/analysis/femicides-mexico-impunity-and-protests |title=Femicides in Mexico: Impunity and Protests |website=www.csis.org |date=19 March 2020 |last1=Sandin |first1=Linnea |access-date=17 May 2020 |archive-date=21 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200521220742/https://www.csis.org/analysis/femicides-mexico-impunity-and-protests |url-status=live }}</ref> Mexico's most violent year on record. Additionally, in 2012, Mexico was ranked as the 16th country in the world with the highest rates of femicides.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/cedaw/docs/ngos/CDDandCMDPDH_forthesession_Mexico_CEDAW52.pdf |title=Femicide and Impunity in Mexico: A context of structural and generalized violence |date=17 July 2012 |publisher=Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights |access-date=5 June 2018 |archive-date=24 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424140151/https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/cedaw/docs/ngos/CDDandCMDPDH_forthesession_Mexico_CEDAW52.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In August 2021, a total of 108 femicides occurred in Mexico, the highest since 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Statista - The Statistics Portal |url=https://www.statista.com/ |access-date=14 April 2022 |website=Statista |language=en |archive-date=9 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220409065239/https://www.statista.com/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2016, Mexico had a rate of female homicides of 4.6 femicides per 100,000, and there were a total of 2,746 female deaths with the presumption of homicide, but that has more than doubled in the past 5 years. On average, about 10 women are killed everyday.<ref>{{Cite web |date=9 March 2020 |title=Outraged By Femicides, Mexican Women Demand Change During Nationwide Walkout |url=https://www.kut.org/texas/2020-03-09/outraged-by-femicides-mexican-women-demand-change-during-nationwide-walkout |access-date=14 April 2022 |publisher=KUT Radio, Austin's NPR Station |language=en |archive-date=13 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220313044232/https://www.kut.org/texas/2020-03-09/outraged-by-femicides-mexican-women-demand-change-during-nationwide-walkout |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=La Violencia Femenicida En Mexico, Aproximaciones y Tendencias 1985-2016 |website=www.gob.mx |date=December 2017 |url=http://www.gob.mx/cms/uploads/attachment/file/293666/violenciaFeminicidaMx_07dic_web.pdf |access-date=16 November 2024 |archive-date=25 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210325164207/https://www.gob.mx/cms/uploads/attachment/file/293666/violenciaFeminicidaMx_07dic_web.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In this year, the top three states with the highest rates of female deaths with the presumption of homicide were [[Colima]] (with 16.3 deaths per 100,000 women), [[Guerrero]] (13.1 per 100,000), and [[Zacatecas]] (9.7 per 100,000).<ref name=":10" /> The top three municipalities in 2016 were [[Acapulco de Juárez Municipality|Acapulco de Juárez]] (24.22 per 100,000), [[Tijuana Municipality|Tijuana]] (10.84 per 100,000), and [[Juárez Municipality, Chihuahua|Juárez]] (10.36 per 100,000). During the years 2002–2010, the state of [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]] had the highest rate of female homicides in the world: 58.4 per 100,000.<ref name=":9" /> The rates of femicide in the municipality of Juárez have decreased significantly in just five years; in 2011, the rate of female deaths with the presumption of homicides was 31.49 per 100,000, and by 2016 it had decreased to 10.36 per 100,000.<ref name=":10" />

There has been large demonstrations in Mexico against femicides; however, most took place after 11 February 2020. This was the day seven-year old Fatima Cecilia was kidnapped from school. She was found dead in a plastic bag a couple of days later. A movement called "Un Dia Sin Mujeres" (a day without women) spread all over the country right after Fatima's murder.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Panuco-Mercado |first1=Gabriel |title=Melodrama and Italicized Language in an Era of #MeToo: A 2020 Review of Jeanine Cummins's American Dirt |journal=Georgetown Journal of International Affairs |date=2020 |volume=21 |pages=216–219 |id={{Project MUSE|766375}} |doi=10.1353/gia.2020.0007 |s2cid=225095790 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== North America ===
==== United States ====
{{update section|date=February 2024}}
Femicide in the [[Violence against women in the United States|United States]] accounts for the deaths of more than five women daily, and 70% of the total deaths of women among high-income countries.<ref>{{cite web |title=When Men Murder Women: An Analysis of 2018 Homicide Data |url=https://vpc.org/studies/wmmw2020.pdf |website=When Men Murder Women |publisher=Violence Policy Center |access-date=9 May 2021 |archive-date=11 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210811220907/https://vpc.org/studies/wmmw2020.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hememway |first1=David |last2=Shinoda-Tagawa |first2=Tomoko |last3=Miller |first3=Matthew |date=2002 |title=Firearm availability and female homicide victimization rates among 25 populous high-income countries |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11379728 |via=Research Gate |journal=Journal of the American Medical Women's Association |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=100–104 |pmid=11991417 |s2cid=26869606 |access-date=9 May 2021}}</ref> One of the largest predictors of femicide in the United States is the appearance of physical abuse, which was found in 79% of all femicide cases in [[North Carolina]].<ref name="Moracco">{{cite journal |last1=Moracco |first1=Kathryn E. |last2=Runyan |first2=Carol W. |last3=Butts |first3=John D. |title=Femicide in North Carolina, 1991-1993 |journal=Homicide Studies |date=24 July 2016 |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=422–446 |doi=10.1177/1088767998002004005|s2cid=144780101}}</ref> [[Gun politics in the United States|Gun availability in the United States]] has also had a substantial effect on femicide, correlating to 67.9% of deaths in a study by Karen D. Stout.<ref name="Russell2" /> Living in neighborhoods with increased [[poverty]], ethnic heterogeneity, and decreased collective efficacy (social cohesion among neighbors) are all found to be linked to increased femicide rates in that area.<ref name="Frye">{{cite journal |last1=Frye |first1=Victoria |last2=Galea |first2=Sandro |last3=Tracy |first3=Melissa |last4=Bucciarelli |first4=Angela |last5=Putnam |first5=Sara |last6=Wilt |first6=Susan |title=The Role of Neighborhood Environment and Risk of Intimate Partner Femicide in a Large Urban Area |journal=American Journal of Public Health |date=August 2008 |volume=98 |issue=8 |pages=1473–1479 |doi=10.2105/AJPH.2007.112813|pmid=18556618 |pmc=2446466}}</ref> Also, reporting of female victims of femicide in the US is stymied, due to the assumption that female victims are not an anomaly, but are driven by their perceived vulnerability and passivity.<ref name="Russell2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=De Lia |first=Andrea |date=2 September 2025 |title="Men who hate women": il femminicidio negli Stati Uniti d'America. Spunti di riflessione in ottica comparata |url=https://www.quotidianolegale.it/men-who-hate-women-il-femminicidio-negli-stati-uniti-damerica-spunti-di-riflessione-in-ottica-comparata-di-andrea-de-lia/ |journal=Quotidiano Legale |volume=2025 |issue=3 |pages=1–34 |archive-date=11 September 2025 |access-date=20 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250911062206/https://www.quotidianolegale.it/men-who-hate-women-il-femminicidio-negli-stati-uniti-damerica-spunti-di-riflessione-in-ottica-comparata-di-andrea-de-lia/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Canada ====
Proper statistics of femicide in [[Violence against women in Canada|Canada]] can be difficult to come across, since possible acts of femicide are regularly labelled as the killing of a spouse.<ref name=":32">{{cite journal |id={{ProQuest|194880968}} |last1=Gartner |first1=Rosemary |last2=Dawson |first2=Myrna |last3=Crawford |first3=Maria |title=Woman killing: intimate femicide in Ontario, 1974–1994 |journal=Resources for Feminist Research |volume=26 |issue=3/4 |date=1998 |pages=151–173}}</ref> However, femicide is a widespread violent act that takes place in countries all over the world, and Canada is no exception.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shalhoub-Kevorkian |first1=Nadera |author-link1=Nadera Shalhoub-Kevorkian |title=Reexamining Femicide: Breaking the Silence and Crossing 'Scientific' Borders |journal=Signs: Journal of Women in Culture and Society |date=January 2003 |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=581–608 |doi=10.1086/342590 |s2cid=146450193}}</ref> In 2019, there was a total of 678 homicides Canada-wide, of these cases 144 of the victims were female.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Government of Canada|first=Statistics Canada|date=29 October 2020|title=Homicide in Canada, 2019|url=https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-627-m/11-627-m2020055-eng.htm|access-date=2 February 2021|website=www150.statcan.gc.ca|archive-date=11 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111134910/https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-627-m/11-627-m2020055-eng.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Additionally, the rate at which female victims were killed by a spouse or intimate partner, was over eight times greater than the number of males killed by a spouse or intimate partner.<ref name=":0" />

Historically speaking, less data exists regarding femicide in Canada; however, what is available shows a disproportionate amount of violence and femicide towards Indigenous women. Reports of the last few decades indicate over [[Missing and murdered Indigenous women|600 murders of Indigenous women and girls in Canada]].<ref name=":1" /> Unfortunately, in many cases, homicidal acts towards Indigenous females often aren't characterized as femicides,<ref name=":1" /> indicating that not all victims of femicide are treated in the same framework.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Dawson |first1=Myrna |title=Punishing femicide: Criminal justice responses to the killing of women over four decades |journal=Current Sociology |date=November 2016 |volume=64 |issue=7 |pages=996–1016 |doi=10.1177/0011392115611192 |s2cid=147295649}}</ref> Yet the research indicates that certain ethnic groups are at a greater risk for femicide compared to the rest of the population.<ref name=":32" /> To understand these statistics in Canada, an intersectional approach must be considered, to recognize the historical and ongoing effects of [[colonialism]] that disproportionately target [[Indigenous peoples in Canada|Indigenous peoples]] within the country. Canada's continued negligence as a state to examine the effects of colonialism on Indigenous peoples has related to the high risk of femicide, and violence for Indigenous women and girls.<ref name=":2" /> Failure to acknowledge the deaths of Indigenous women ignores the decades of inequality and injustice that have, and continue to be, perpetuated by colonialism. &nbsp;

Colonialism produces a sense of dominant authoritative power that allows for the disregard of Indigenous individuals, and in this case, a disregard for the murders of Indigenous females. Indigenous women are reported to be five times more likely to experience violence and death compared with other groups in Canada.<ref name=":1" /> These murders are acts of [[Ethnic violence|racialized violence]], in addition to the gendered violence of femicide. However, more often than not, these murders are regarded as a spousal homicide,<ref name=":32" /> rather than femicide, disregarding the violence and oppression Indigenous women face. In the mid-twentieth century, Indigenous women and girls were [[Compulsory sterilization|forced and coerced into undergoing sterilization]] procedures as an act of femicide, as well as [[Genocide of indigenous peoples|genocide]], at fourteen different [[Indian hospital|Indian Hospitals]] across the state that were federally operated.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Amy |first1=Jean-Jacques |last2=Rowlands |first2=Sam |title=Legalised non-consensual sterilisation – eugenics put into practice before 1945, and the aftermath. Part 1: USA, Japan, Canada and Mexico |journal=The European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care |date=4 March 2018 |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=121–129 |doi=10.1080/13625187.2018.1450973 |pmid=29624082 |s2cid=4603052 |url=http://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/30553/3/Forced%20sterilisation-Part%201%20Final.pdf |archive-date=1 September 2023 |access-date=29 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901152601/http://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/30553/3/Forced%20sterilisation-Part%201%20Final.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Sterilization policies were implemented as a way to reduce the size and influence of Indigenous communities, resulting in there being about 1,200 cases of forced or coerced sterilization, that directly targeted the reproductive rights and properties of Indigenous women and girls.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collier |first1=Roger |title=Reports of coerced sterilization of Indigenous women in Canada mirrors shameful past |journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal |date=21 August 2017 |volume=189 |issue=33 |pages=E1080–E1081 |doi=10.1503/cmaj.1095471 |pmid=28827444 |pmc=5566614}}</ref> Exclusionary politics and legal discrimination throughout the history of Canada, means that the violence faced by Indigenous women and girls has gone unacknowledged, serving to further state-controlled colonial power over Indigenous peoples.<ref name=":1" /> The scattered reports of femicide in Canada indicate a lack of understanding of how various acts of gender, race, class, and sexuality all intersect to create the environment of violence Indigenous women are subjected to.<ref name=":1" /> While femicide in Canada affects all women, it disproportionately targets the lives of Indigenous women and girls due to historical and ongoing actions of colonialism within the state. &nbsp;

One prominent instance of femicide occurring in Canada is the [[École Polytechnique massacre|1989 École Polytechnique massacre]], which was an [[Antifeminism|antifeminist]] mass shooting, which killed fourteen women, and injured ten women and four men.

Another example of a femicide attack in Canada is the [[Toronto van attack|2018 Toronto van attack]], a [[vehicle-ramming attack]] which saw eleven casualties, and fifteen injured.<ref>{{Cite news |date=27 April 2018 |title=Toronto van attack: How you can help and what we know so far |language=en-CA |work=The Globe and Mail |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/toronto/article-toronto-van-attack-what-we-know-so-far/ |access-date=16 May 2022 |archive-date=26 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180426015802/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/toronto/article-toronto-van-attack-what-we-know-so-far/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The perpetrator is a self-described "[[incel]]", whose goal was to exact revenge on women, after self-perceived [[social rejection]].

=== United Nations ===
In 2013, the [[United Nations General Assembly]] updated their policy by recognizing that "gender-related killing of women and girls was criminalized in some countries as 'femicide' or 'feminicide', and has been incorporated as such into national legislation in those countries." Currently, Dr. [[Dubravka Šimonović]] is the special rapporteur to the UN. She has been an advocate of anti-femicide policy implementation. She has presented the UN with reports such as "Modalities for the establishment of femicides/gender-related killings". Dr. Šimonović has also proposed a "femicide watch" program to monitor femicide practices across the globe. The goal of Simonovic's academic program is to analyze data on femicide cases, to identify risk factors and any issues in public policy.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Femicide Volume VII establishing a femicide watch in every country|last=Hemblade, Helen|date=2017|publisher=Academic Council on the United Nations System (ACUNS)|isbn=978-3-200-03012-1|oclc=1029877523}}</ref>

== Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic ==
The [[COVID-19 pandemic]] led not only to heightened rates of domestic violence against and suicide by girls and young women, but also to increased rates of femicide.<ref>Katerina Standish & Shalva Weil (2021) Gendered pandemics: ''suicide, femicide and COVID-19,'' Journal of Gender Studies, 30:7, 807–818 (see p. 815), DOI: 10.1080/09589236.2021.1880883</ref> Around 50,000 women were being murdered every year. This was due to the stay-at-home measures that increased the levels of isolation for women and girls. This became a life-or-death situation if they were locked in with violent partners or relatives. "The increasing economic instability and unemployment rates worldwide" led to "heightened violence" for women.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Impact Of Covid-19 On The "Shadow Pandemic" Of Femicide And Gender-Based Violence |url=https://www.humanrightspulse.com/mastercontentblog/the-impact-of-covid-19-on-the-shadow-pandemic-of-femicide-and-gender-based-violence |access-date=14 April 2022 |website=Human Rights Pulse |date=16 February 2021 |language=en-US |archive-date=13 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213122258/https://www.humanrightspulse.com/mastercontentblog/the-impact-of-covid-19-on-the-shadow-pandemic-of-femicide-and-gender-based-violence |url-status=live }}</ref> Additionally, there was an increase in calls to domestic violence hotlines in various countries after the lockdown began.{{citation needed |date=November 2024}}

Most countries also "diverted" resources and efforts "from violence against women response to immediate COVID-19 relief".<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Shadow Pandemic: Violence against women during COVID-19 |work=UN Women – Headquarters |url=https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/in-focus-gender-equality-in-covid-19-response/violence-against-women-during-covid-19 |access-date=14 April 2022 |language=en |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413223926/https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/in-focus-gender-equality-in-covid-19-response/violence-against-women-during-covid-19 |url-status=live }}</ref>

UK policeman [[Wayne Couzens]] used the Covid restrictions to detain and arrest [[Sarah Everard]]. He then murdered her and a few days later he was arrested.<ref name="Dodd 2021 0608">{{cite news |last1=Dodd |first1=Vikram |date=8 June 2021 |title=PC Wayne Couzens pleads guilty to kidnap and rape of Sarah Everard |url=http://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2021/jun/08/pc-wayne-couzens-pleads-guilty-to-kidnap-and-of-sarah-everard |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

== Prevention ==
Attempting to prevent femicide could include implementing laws that would specifically work to improve the safety of women and address the risk factors mentioned. For example, harsher punishments for those that murder a woman solely based on their gender.<ref name="Femicide and the Law">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203701850-6 |chapter=Preventing femicide |title=Femicide and the Law |year=2018 |last1=Dayan |first1=Hava |pages=111–143 |isbn=978-0-203-70185-0 |s2cid=242101722}}</ref>

Fatality reviews could aid in addressing what contributes to femicide. This practice helps identify risk factors and encourages prevention.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Baldry |first1=Anna Costanza |chapter=Prevention of femicide |date=26 September 2018 |title=Femicide across Europe |pages=71–92 |publisher=Bristol University Press |isbn=978-1-4473-4716-3 |last2=Magalhães |first2=Maria José|doi=10.2307/j.ctv8xnfq2.10}}</ref> In general, more research on femicide would contribute to the creation of potential solutions.<ref name=":16" />

=== Raising awareness ===
Raising awareness amongst the public about how femicide differs from other murders and crimes could also help with prevention by encouraging support for change in policy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Guns and Violence Against Women: America's Uniquely Lethal Intimate Partner Violence Problem |url=https://everytownresearch.org/report/guns-and-violence-against-women-americas-uniquely-lethal-intimate-partner-violence-problem/ |access-date=7 April 2022 |publisher=Everytown Research & Policy |language=en-us |archive-date=20 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230420201217/https://everytownresearch.org/report/guns-and-violence-against-women-americas-uniquely-lethal-intimate-partner-violence-problem/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Advocacy groups raise awareness, especially if there is an absence of governmental action. These groups include women's advocacy groups as well as nongovernmental or non-profit organizations<ref name=":12" />

=== Training officials ===
All officials involved in a gender-based crime should be adequately trained in order to offer support. Service workers, police officers, and legal professionals are some of the groups that should receive extensive training on signs of violence in different social groups, including minorities and migrants. Training is the first step to creating policies to prevent femicide.<ref name="Femicide and the Law" />

== Legal solutions ==
Legal solutions to femicide include making laws and policies to prevent violence against women, as well as to prevent domestic and family violence. It has been suggested by some that countries should consider improving the status of women in terms of gender equality and create laws that support it.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Laurent |first1=Claire |last2=Platzer |first2=Michael |last3=Idomir |first3=Maria |title=Femicide: A Global Issue that Demands Action |date=2013 |publisher=Academic Council on the United Nations System |isbn=978-3-200-03012-1 |pages=6–7}}</ref>

In Latin America there have been many new laws to label the murders of women as femicide or feminicide using the definition of a woman targeted by a man based on misogyny. At the same time, feminicide goes beyond this definition and implicates the state's complicity in maintaining violence against women. These changes have been made due to global human rights norms, like the 1994 Inter-American Convention on the Prevention and the Eradication of Violence against Women, which expresses that gender violence is the state's responsibility. Nevertheless, these international norms are not regulated. They do not implement how a state should exercise new laws and policies to enforce violence against women.<ref name="LandSR"/>

Some countries have passed laws regarding femicide or crimes labeled as feminicides. In Mexico and Nicaragua, female activists became involved in legal activism so these states would have increased responsibility for female violence. In Nicaragua, the codification of Femicide came about from the country's response to feminist demands during a small political opportunity under the rule of a strict regime.<ref name="LandSR"/> In Mexico, prosecuting feminicides became successful because of good campaigning by local feminists connected to national arenas and through the intervention of feminist federal legislators. A known Mexican female activist, Marcela Lagarde, saw the rise of women being murdered in Mexico and demanded that the state take responsibility for the murders. She brought in the concept of femicide (the murder of females), which quickly spread across Latin America, and as of 2017, femicide and feminicide became crimes in 18 countries.<ref name="LandSR">{{cite journal |last1=García-Del Moral |first1=Paulina |last2=Neumann |first2=Pamela |title=The Making and Unmaking of Feminicidio/Femicidio Laws in Mexico and Nicaragua |journal=Law & Society Review |date=June 2019 |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=452–486 |doi=10.1111/lasr.12380 |s2cid=150238783}}</ref>
